articles.title: Licences d'occasion : la justice inflige un camouflet (de plus) à Microsoft
articles.text:
La justice britannique vient de refuser à Microsoft l’autorisation de porter son litige avec ValueLicensing devant la Cour suprême. Un nouveau revers pour l’éditeur, déjà contraint de s’expliquer sur un document interne vieux de treize ans.
Microsoft peine décidément à faire entendre ses arguments dans l’affaire des licences logicielles d’occasion. Le 13 octobre, la Cour d’appel britannique a rejeté sa demande d’autorisation de recours devant la Cour suprême sans même détailler les motifs de sa décision. L’éditeur espérait pourtant faire annuler un jugement favorable à ValueLicensing, une entreprise spécialisée dans la revente de licences Windows et Office.
Cette décision conforte les précédents jugements reconnaissant, sous certaines conditions, le droit de revendre des licences perpétuelles déjà utilisées. Mais elle ne clôt pas le contentieux opposant les deux entreprises.
Microsoft dispose encore d’une dernière possibilité de recours
L’entreprise américaine peut en effet toujours saisir directement la Cour suprême britannique. Elle dispose pour cela de 28 jours (à compter du refus du 13 octobre) et devra convaincre les juges que son dossier mérite un nouvel examen.
Le conflit remonte à 2021, lorsque ValueLicensing a réclamé 270 millions de livres sterling à Microsoft. Le revendeur accuse le groupe d’avoir organisé la raréfaction des licences Office d'occasion, notamment en accordant des remises aux entreprises acceptant de conserver ou d’abandonner leurs anciennes licences lors de leur passage à Microsoft 365.
Microsoft conteste ces accusations et a tenté de défendre sa position sur le terrain du droit d’auteur. Sans succès jusqu’ici. En novembre 2025, le tribunal britannique de la concurrence avait reconnu la possibilité de revendre certaines licences perpétuelles, y compris lorsqu’elles provenaient de contrats achetés en volume. La Cour d’appel avait confirmé cette décision en juillet dernier.
La légalité de cette revente a donc été reconnue dans le cadre du litige, mais la justice doit encore déterminer si les pratiques commerciales reprochées à Microsoft étaient anticoncurrentielles.
Un document interne de 2013 pourrait compliquer les affaires de Microsoft
Les ennuis judiciaires de l’éditeur ne se limitent pas à ses recours. Une ordonnance du 14 septembre 2026 impose à Microsoft de nouvelles recherches documentaires auprès de plusieurs dirigeants actuels et anciens. Elle réclame également des explications sur la communication tardive d’une présentation interne de 2013 consacrée aux logiciels d’occasion.
Baptisé Second-Hand Software Presentation, ce fichier est qualifié dans la procédure de Known Adverse Document, une catégorie qui désigne des éléments potentiellement défavorables à la partie qui les détient.
Son contenu n’a pas été rendu public, mais une question embarrassante se pose déjà. Pourquoi Microsoft a-t-il attendu décembre 2025 pour communiquer ce document, alors que la procédure avait commencé quatre ans auparavant ? L’entreprise doit fournir des explications d’ici au 31 octobre.
Une autre action pourrait coûter plusieurs milliards à l’éditeur
Le dossier intéresse également Alexander Wolfson, qui porte un projet d’action collective distincte au nom de millions de clients britanniques. Cette procédure réclame entre 1,3 et 3,5 milliards de livres sterling de dédommagements pour les pratiques présumées de Microsoft sur le marché des licences d'occasion.
La bataille judiciaire pourrait donc prendre une ampleur financière considérable. Avant cela, Microsoft devra encore expliquer quand ses responsables ont eu connaissance du document de 2013 et poursuivre la communication des pièces réclamées par le tribunal. Winter is coming.
Source : The Register

articles.title: Fake Web3 Accelerator Uses npm Packages to Spread Malware and Hijack AI Agent Traffic
articles.text:
A fake Web3 accelerator has been observed pushing information stealers and backdoors to Windows and macOS systems using malicious npm packages under the pretext of offering free artificial intelligence (AI) credits for Anthropic Claude and Google Gemini, coding tools, and security audits.
"The tools delivered information-stealing malware and backdoors for macOS and Windows machines," Elastic Security Labs researchers Jia Yu Chan and Daniel Stepanic said. "The operation also repackaged a legitimate coding agent to send model requests through attacker-controlled services, while its audit tools generated fabricated security findings."
The scheme poses as a Web3 venture capital accelerator named Apex Accelerator to target cryptocurrency startups and founders. It's being tracked under the moniker REF8801. The names of the npm packages, each of which targets both Windows and macOS machines, are listed below -
- @apexacc/cli (Apex Copilot CLI — AI advisor for Web3 founders) -
- @apexacc/audit (Web3 Security Scanner — 18 tools for DYOR and smart contract auditing)
While both the packages and their associated GitHub repositories are no longer accessible, "@apexacc/cli" was advertised as an "AI advisor for Web3 founders" that's powered by Claude Fable 5 and Gemini 2.5 Flash.
"@apexacc/audit," on the other hand, claimed to be a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposing 18 security tools for scanning tokens, wallets, and smart contracts. Both packages were published by an npm user named "apexaccelerator" and linked to a GitHub account called "apexaccs" and an entity referred to as the Apex Foundation.
It's unclear who is behind the operation, but Elastic Security Labs said it spotted Russian-language comments in the source code commit history. However, these clues alone are not sufficient to definitively establish their identity or origins.
Interestingly, the campaign itself is not new. In late July 2026, SafeDep detailed three other npm packages linked to the same operation that were found distributing a macOS stealer belonging to the Atomic Stealer (aka AMOS) family -
- @apexfdn/apex
- @copilot-mcp/apex, which features the same package description as "@apexacc/cli"
- @apexfdn/copilot-mcp, which claims to be an Apex Copilot and MCP server for "portfolio diligence and operator tools"
Artifacts captured by Socket show that the Apex Foundation has been linked to at least two distinct domains since April 2026
- apexaccs[.]org
- apexfdn[.]xyz
According to Internet Archive snapshots dating back to March 19, 2026, the foundation states: "The Apex Foundation offers $235,000 investments, grants, and partnerships, and connects projects with VCs, angels, and private equity if they don't meet our criteria."
Posts shared on X show the accelerator approaching developers of cryptocurrency wallets and market intelligence tools for traders with offers of direct investment and instructions to run their due diligence tool ("@apexacc/cli"). In the case of the latter, the npm package has been found to drop an encrypted malware loader disguised as an Apple app ("com.apple.system.loader").
"The group also sought to build credibility through its presence at TOKEN2049 in Singapore and other in-person events it has hosted in the past," Elastic said. "The group attempts to manufacture legitimacy by appearing at widely attended conferences, indirectly lending credibility to the project."
Once installed, neither of the npm packages provides the promised functionality. The 18 security tools part of the @apexacc/audit package generate fabricated findings, while @apexacc/cli's scoring test returns an unsupported assessment of a fictitious project.
Instead, their primary responsibility is to propagate a macOS backdoor called CloudSyncD and a custom Windows information stealer that exfiltrates data through Telegram. The platform-specific executables are retrieved from the projects' GitHub releases.
Both packages implement a distinct verification path for Windows and macOS by sending an HTTP POST request to "win32" or "darwin" to "vrf.apexaccs[.]org/api/v1/vrf" to initiate the appropriate next stage. The Windows and macOS infection chains are as follows -
Windows -
- The malware retrieves a Base64-encoded PowerShell command, which reaches out to another endpoint ("0auth-chromium[.]com/APIService") to fetch a second PowerShell script ("drop.ps1") that downloads an executable ("bludness.exe") from "ehegisnightmare[.]icu" and launches it in a hidden window.
- The PyInstaller executable is a Python loader that checks if it already has administrator privileges and, if so, downloads the next stage from "ehegisnightmare[.]icu," saves it as "%TEMP%\exegis.exe," and launches it. If not, it attempts to bypass User Account Control (UAC) using UACME's ucmDebugObjectMethod().
- The "exegis.exe" binary is another PyInstaller executable that collects system metadata, running processes, and performs anti-virtual-machine (anti-VM) checks before decrypting and launching a bundled loader as "%TEMP%\updater_loader.exe."
- The Golang executable patches Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) and Event Tracing for Windows (ETW), unhooks "ntdll.dll" to blind endpoint security tools, and loads the next-stage shellcode into its own memory.
- The shellcode is a native information stealer that examines for signs of a prior infection and then harvests system information, clipboard text, process listings, Wi-Fi profile names, screenshots, and data from wallets, browser extensions, messengers, remote-access and file transfer protocol (FTP) applications, virtual private network (VPN) clients, browsers (Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and Yandex), and game clients. The stealer can also bypass Chrome's app-bound encryption (ABE) protections to extract saved passwords, session cookies, browsing history, download records, and profile metadata. The collected data is exfiltrated through Telegram.
macOS -
- The malware downloads a remotely hosted bash script and executes it on the machine.
- The shell script downloads a GZIP-compressed archive from "verify.apexfdn[.]xyz/unix/," saves it as "package.tar.gz" in a temporary directory, and extracts its contents.
- The archive contains a dropper for CloudSyncD, which first phishes the victim's system login password using a fake authorization prompt and then uses it to launch an embedded payload with sudo privileges. The payload performs host discovery, collects hardware and operating-system details, and then contacts an external server ("ccmihr[.]com") to transmit the data and receive further tasks that allow the malware to download and run additional payloads.
It's worth noting that CloudSyncD was first documented by Jamf Threat Labs late last month, detailing its propagation via a fake Zoom installer. The malware was detected in the wild in mid-September 2026.
"Its behaviors illustrate how macOS malware continues to move toward native implementations, string protection, and execution paths that attempt to avoid writing payloads to disk, while still depending on the oldest technique available: asking the user for their password," Jamf said.
Besides deploying a stealer and backdoor depending upon the infected operating system, the packages are capable of intercepting and redirecting OpenRouter large language model (LLM) traffic, as well as registering an MCP server under their control in the victim's agent configuration.
"These changes allow the attacker-controlled API to receive the prompts, conversation history, code snippets, and tool outputs included in the agent's LLM requests," Elastic researchers explained.
"The attacker's MCP server can also supply instructions that are added to the agent's prompt, along with tool names, descriptions, and accepted inputs that help the model decide which tools to invoke and how to use them. Together, these mechanisms give the attacker visibility into the submitted data and a way to influence the agent's subsequent actions."

articles.title: La pareja de Elizabeth Holmes recaudó USD 20 millones para una startup que evoca a Theranos
articles.text:
Billy Evans, pareja de la fundadora de Theranos Elizabeth Holmes, recaudó hasta USD 20 millones para una startup de diagnóstico médico llamada Haemanthus, según documentos revisados por The New York Times y citados por Wired. La empresa busca testear sangre, orina y saliva con un aparato de mesa.
El propio Evans se resiste al apodo que la prensa y hasta él mismo mencionan: “Theranos 2.0”. En un comunicado público, Haemanthus afirmó que “no es Theranos 2.0” y que su enfoque es “un paradigma diferente”, no una mejora de la tecnología que llevó a Holmes a prisión.
Sin embargo, en el documental You Can See Everything, dirigido por Nathan Fielder y Lance Oppenheim, Evans acepta esa comparación frente a cámara mientras discute con Holmes ideas de producto para la compañía, según reconstruyó Wired. “Podría pensar que esto fue lo más estúpido que hice”, dijo el heredero hotelero sobre su participación en el filme, en declaraciones al podcast All-In conducido por David Friedberg.
Una tecnología distinta a la de Theranos
Si bien Haemanthus fue fundada formalmente en 2024, Evans comenzó a trabajarla de manera oculta a finales de 2022. Apenas tiene presencia pública: no publicó productos y su perfil en LinkedIn es mínimo, indicó Wired. La compañía obtuvo una patente el 21 de enero de 2025 para un sistema basado en espectroscopía Raman, una técnica que analiza cómo la luz rebota en una muestra biológica para detectar patrones moleculares.
A diferencia de Theranos, que intentó miniaturizar análisis de laboratorio existentes a partir de una gota de sangre, la nueva startup plantea usar luz láser para leer información molecular que las pruebas actuales no detectan, de acuerdo con el comunicado de la empresa citado por Wired.
Eric Potma, profesor de química de la Universidad de California en Irvine y consultor de la compañía, explicó a la recista que “los ingenieros de Haemanthus son legítimos y están llevando la detección por Raman hacia direcciones interesantes”. Aclaró que su vínculo como asesor le impide profundizar más en los detalles técnicos.
El dinero y la falta de supervisión
Según The New York Times, Haemanthus había recibido el año pasado una inversión de USD 3,5 millones de “amigos y familia”. Wired reporta que esa cifra creció hasta unos USD 20 millones. La empresa les dijo a sus inversores que perfeccionar el sistema láser y llevarlo a un dispositivo portátil del tamaño de una estampilla demandaría tres años y USD 70 millones adicionales.
Materiales de presentación revisados por The New York Times sugirieron a inversores que la compañía no enfrentaría “ninguna supervisión regulatoria”, en parte porque el aparato se probaría primero en enfermedades veterinarias. El diario confirmó con el Departamento de Agricultura de Estados Unidos que esa agencia sí regula los diagnósticos veterinarios.
Evans manifestó a Times que la empresa está “en modo sigiloso” y que seguirá así: “No van a encontrar nada asociado con el nombre Haemanthus”. Las direcciones vinculadas a la empresa corresponden en su mayoría a viviendas particulares en un barrio de Austin, Texas, y empleados contactados por Wired se negaron a confirmar su rol.
Quién es el hombre detrás de la empresa
Evans se graduó en economía en el MIT y trabajó en LinkedIn y en Luminar Technologies, una empresa de sensores para autos autónomos, antes de fundar Haemanthus. Conoció a Holmes en 2017, durante un evento benéfico en la bahía de San Francisco, y la describió en una carta al juez como alguien que lo “cautivó” con su “asombro infantil”.
Esa carta fue una de varias que familiares y amigos enviaron antes de la sentencia de Holmes en 2022, cuando un tribunal la condenó a 11 años y tres meses de prisión por fraude contra inversores de Theranos. Una corte de apelaciones confirmó esa condena.
Según una persona cercana al negocio citada por The Wall Street Journal, Holmes no tiene ningún rol formal en Haemanthus. Wired también consignó que, en la documentación de constitución de la empresa, el nombre de Holmes no figura en ningún lado. Pese a eso, NPR había informado en 2025 que Holmes asesoraba a Evans sobre la startup desde la prisión federal donde cumple condena en Bryan, Texas, aunque la naturaleza exacta de ese asesoramiento nunca quedó clara.
Wired señaló que, de acuerdo con reportes periodísticos, Holmes podría trasladarse a una casa de transición el año próximo. Mientras tanto, Haemanthus sigue sin mostrar un producto terminado ni abrir su sitio web al público. El contraste entre el hermetismo de la empresa y la decisión de Evans de participar en un documental de varios años de filmación llamó la atención de Wired, que describió esa combinación como poco habitual para una compañía que se define a sí misma como secreta.

articles.title: Nabta Health advances $3 million pre-Series A with backing from PVP
articles.text: UAE-based healthtech startup Nabta Health has secured a fresh investment from Phoenix Venture Partners (PVP), which led the second close of the company's ongoing $3 million pre-Series A round. PVP's investment includes both primary and secondary capital, while the amount raised in this closing was not disclosed. Founded in 2017 by Sophie Smith, Nabta Health develops AI-powered preventive healthcare solutions, with a focus on women's health, combining early disease detection, digital health services and clinical care. The company offers Aya, an AI-supported care navigation tool, alongside preventive screening and personalised care pathways, connecting patients, employers, insurers and healthcare providers to facilitate earlier intervention and coordinated care. The funding will support Nabta Health's commercial expansion, customer acquisition and strategic partnerships, particularly with employers, insurance companies and healthcare providers. In November 2025, Nabta Health raised $2 million pre-Series A , bringing its total funding to $4.5 million. Press release: Phoenix Venture Partners Limited (“PVP”), a venture capital fund manager domiciled in the Abu Dhabi Global Market (“ADGM”) and regulated by the Financial Services Regulatory Authority (“FSRA”), today announced that it has led the second close of Nabta Health's (“NABTA”) ongoing $3 million Pre-Series A financing. PVP’s investment comprises a blend of primary and secondary capital, further institutionalising a longstanding relationship with NABTA as the company enters its next stage of growth. The Pre-Series A has attracted participation from institutional investors, venture capital firms, family offices and high-net-worth investors. Founded in 2017 by Sophie Smith, NABTA has evolved significantly from its origins as a direct-to-consumer women’s health platform. Following years of investment in technology, clinical infrastructure and R&D, the company is entering a new phase focused on building AI-powered preventive healthcare infrastructure for employers, insurers and healthcare providers. NABTA combines early disease detection, AI-supported care navigation through Aya, and hybrid digital and clinical care, positioning the business as a connecting layer across patients, payors and providers. The company’s model is increasingly focused on enabling earlier intervention, more coordinated care and improved health outcomes, while helping employers and insurers address long-term healthcare costs through prevention and better population health management. NABTA’s clinics and expertise in women’s health remain important enablers of this broader platform. The investment marks the next chapter in PVP's longstanding relationship with NABTA. Dr. Mussaad Al-Razouki, Co-Founder and Non-Executive Director of PVP, who has supported NABTA since its early days as a founding investor and former Executive Chairman, will transition from his position on NABTA's Board, with Steve Khayat joining the Board as PVP's representative. The transition comes as NABTA moves from an extended period of product development and R&D into a phase increasingly focused on commercialisation and scale. Steve Khayat, Founder and CEO of Phoenix Venture Partners, said: “NABTA has done the hard work of building its technology, clinical infrastructure and model, and is already demonstrating strong commercial traction. We believe the company is now at an inflection point where the focus can shift decisively toward go-to-market and sales acceleration. Our role at PVP will be to work alongside Sophie and the team to deepen strategic partnerships, accelerate customer acquisition and help translate that traction into scalable growth.” Sophie Smith, Founder and CEO of Nabta Health, added: “We are delighted to welcome PVP as a shareholder and Steve to our Board at an important stage in NABTA’s journey. PVP brings not only capital, but also the regional relationships and hands-on support that can help us accelerate our next phase of commercial growth and deepen our partnerships with employers, insurers and healthcare providers.” The funding will support NABTA as it accelerates its go-to-market strategy, expands its enterprise proposition and develops new commercial relationships across the employer, insurance and healthcare ecosystems. PVP will work alongside NABTA’s leadership team to support this next stage of growth, leveraging its regional network and value-creation capabilities to help accelerate commercial partnerships and position the company for its next phase of institutional growth.

articles.title: Coupez Internet, gardez l'essentiel : ce logiciel gratuit fait presque tout sans connexion
articles.text:
Une encyclopédie, un assistant IA, des cartes et des outils personnels réunis sur un ordinateur, sans connexion permanente ni compte utilisateur. Avec sa nouvelle version 2.0, Offlined défend une autre manière d'utiliser l'informatique, loin de la dépendance aux services cloud.
Difficile aujourd'hui de se passer d'Internet, tant les services en ligne occupent une place centrale dans nos usages numériques. Même les assistants IA, devenus des outils du quotidien pour certains, reposent le plus souvent sur des serveurs distants. Avec Offlined, deux développeurs, Álvaro Cuadrado Chulvi et Eric Uguet, proposent de prendre le problème à l'envers : pourquoi ne pas conserver nos connaissances, nos outils et nos données directement sur notre ordinateur ?
Disponible sur Windows 10 et 11, leur logiciel vient de franchir une nouvelle étape avec sa version 2.0, lancée mi-octobre et déjà suivie de plusieurs correctifs, dont la version 2.0.2 du 18 octobre. Son ambition est de constituer un environnement numérique autonome, utilisable sans aucune connexion à Internet. 
Wikipédia, des cartes et une IA pour apprendre sans connexion
Le cœur d'Offlined repose sur une bibliothèque de connaissances consultable localement. Wikipédia, mais aussi Wiktionary, Wikivoyage, Wikiquote et WikiMed peuvent être téléchargés dans différentes langues, dont le français. Le logiciel s'appuie sur les archives ZIM, dont Kiwix se sert aussi pour rendre ces contenus accessibles sans connexion.
Offlined intègre un assistant IA reposant sur llama.cpp, capable de répondre à des questions en s'appuyant sur les ressources téléchargées et de citer les articles utilisés. Autre nouveauté de la version 2.0.1 : la possibilité de connecter un serveur IA local déjà installé, notamment avec Ollama, LM Studio ou LocalAI. Le modèle peut ainsi fonctionner sur une autre machine du réseau domestique, par exemple un PC plus puissant, tout en conservant les échanges en local.
Le logiciel propose aussi Michael Encartha, un assistant pédagogique dont le nom rappelle celui de l'ancienne encyclopédie Encarta. Il peut expliquer un article, générer des quiz ou interroger l'utilisateur pour vérifier ses connaissances. Une approche intéressante pour transformer une simple consultation documentaire en véritable séance d'apprentissage, même si la pertinence des explications produites par l'IA reste à vérifier.
L'environnement comprend enfin des cartes géographiques, une carte du ciel et plusieurs outils éducatifs. Autant de ressources que l'utilisateur peut préparer à l'avance pour les consulter ensuite sans réseau.
Un espace personnel portable, mais pas sans contraintes
Au-delà de la recherche documentaire, Offlined entend devenir un véritable espace personnel. Il rassemble un calendrier, des contacts, des outils de prise de notes, une bibliothèque multimédia et un coffre chiffré pour conserver des informations sensibles. Il permet aussi de récupérer des données provenant d'autres services, notamment des courriels au format MBOX ou PST, des contacts VCF et des calendriers ICS. Depuis la version 2.0.1, plusieurs membres d'un foyer peuvent utiliser des profils distincts pour conserver leurs propres informations et conversations avec l'IA.
L'un de ses principaux atouts est son fonctionnement portable. Le programme peut être lancé depuis un SSD externe ou une clé USB, sans installation Windows traditionnelle. Il faut toutefois prévoir de la place : les développeurs évoquent environ 12 Go pour le modèle IA gpt-oss proposé, tandis qu'une édition de Wikipédia avec images peut peser de 20 à 80 Go selon la langue. Les cartes du monde entier représentent, à elles seules, environ 120 Go. Heureusement, chacun reste libre de télécharger uniquement les ressources qui l'intéressent.
Côté matériel, Offlined demande au minimum 8 Go de RAM, mais 16 Go sont recommandés pour profiter plus confortablement de l'IA locale. Les performances dépendent naturellement du processeur et du modèle choisi ; une carte graphique dédiée n'est cependant pas obligatoire.
Quelques réserves méritent enfin d'être soulignées. Offlined est gratuit pour un usage personnel ou éducatif, mais n'est pas un logiciel open source au sens strict : son code est consultable sur GitHub, tandis que sa licence soumet notamment les modifications et les utilisations commerciales à l'autorisation des auteurs. Le programme Windows n'est pas non plus signé numériquement, ce qui peut déclencher une alerte Microsoft SmartScreen. Pour une première découverte, mieux vaut privilégier une machine virtuelle ou Windows Sandbox, sans y importer immédiatement de données personnelles, plutôt que désactiver les protections du système.
Offlined reste un projet jeune, dont la fiabilité et les performances demandent encore à être éprouvées. Mais son approche mérite l'attention. À l'heure où nos logiciels, nos documents et nos assistants IA dépendent toujours davantage de services distants, il rappelle qu'une partie de notre vie numérique peut encore tenir dans un ordinateur, voire sur un simple disque externe.
Pour découvrir Offlined et télécharger sa dernière version, rendez-vous sur son site officiel ou sa page sur GitHub.

articles.title: Whopper of a data breach sees Burger King Japan expose over 11 million customer records
articles.text:
Whopper of a data breach sees Burger King Japan expose over 11 million customer records
First Russia, now Japan
- Burger King Japan discloses breach affecting 11.18 million customer records from its mobile app platform
- Exposed data included personal details and order histories, though payment information was not compromised
- Company reported no confirmed misuse and notified regulators while investigating the intrusion
The Japanese subsidiary of Burger King has confirmed suffering a data breach and apologized for losing sensitive data on millions of customers.
In a breach notification letter, Burger King Japan confirmed the exact date of the breach, as well as the nature of the data that was stolen.
"We identified a potential unauthorized third-party access to the system that manages member information for our official app and conducted an investigation," the company said in the letter. "As a result, it was determined on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, that unauthorized access occurred between Friday, October 2, 2026, and Wednesday, October 7, 2026, resulting in a leak of member information. Upon becoming aware of the unauthorized access, we immediately blocked access from the source in question."
Echoes of Russia
The investigation determined that 11.18 million customer records were nabbed, which was mostly data on people using the company’s official smartphone app.
It includes people’s names, dates of birth, genders, email addresses, phone numbers, and order histories. While credit card and other payment data was not exposed, personally identifiable information (PII) is still more than enough to launch convincing phishing emails and escalate to business email compromise (BEC), malware, or even ransomware attacks.
Burger King Japan stressed that there is no evidence of data misuse yet and added that the breach was reported to the country’s Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC).
"We sincerely apologize for the great inconvenience and concern this situation has caused to our customers and all others involved," it added. "At this time, no secondary damage, such as fraudulent use, resulting from this incident has been confirmed."
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Burger King’s food isn’t the only tasty thing about the company, it seems. Cybercriminals also love breaking in and stealing data. Back in 2024, for example, the Russian arm of Burger King suffered a data breach at the hands of unknown threat actors and in late September this year, that data leaked online.
In October 2024, Burger King told local media about an attack on Mindbox, a domestic marketing automation platform the company had been using. Through Mindbox, the threat actors managed to obtain sensitive company data, including information belonging to the customers.
"Among the victims of the attack may also be the data of customers of the Burger King restaurant chain," the company said at the time. “Burger King confirms that among the personal data, the accuracy of which is being clarified, there is no information about payment details: open information about transactions is not transmitted or stored by third parties.”
Just like in the Japan incident, the Russia one did not discuss the details of the attack, or how it was pulled off. Third-party supply chain attacks are common and often rather disruptive, affecting numerous companies using the same tools. For Mindbox, however, there have been no reports of additional victims.
Supply chain attacks
In its 2024 results announcement, Mindbox said the attack was its “first serious information security incident”, which was quickly detected and contained “thanks to threat detection tools.”
In the aftermath of the breach, Mindbox said it “found and eliminated points where employees without access rights to sensitive data could indirectly obtain them,” hinting that the attack was, in fact, an identity-based attack rather than a zero-day exploit.
The company also “changed development processes to find such points before they get into the product,” and reformed Mindbox's internal role system to make permissions stricter and more granular. It also limited project access scenarios, introduced a mechanism for confirming access by another employee, and introduced mandatory two-factor authentication, among other things.
Have I Been Pwned?, a website that aggregates information stolen in various hacks and helps people learn if their email addresses and other information had been compromised in the past, has Burger King Russia on its list, but not Burger King Japan.

articles.title: Unpatched Broadcom Wi-Fi Flaw Lets Attackers in Range Run Code as Root on Routers
articles.text:
A flaw in Broadcom's Wi-Fi setup software lets an attacker within radio range run code as root on Broadcom-based routers, without the network password or any pairing step, security researcher Quentin Kaiser disclosed on October 16.
He showed the attack working against home gateways supplied by three Belgian internet providers, in one case reading the Wi-Fi password off the device and in another opening a remote shell over the air. No CVE has been assigned to the flaw, and no fix has been deployed to the affected routers, Kaiser says.
The flaw is in Broadcom's version of Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS), the feature that lets a device join a Wi-Fi network without the password being typed in. Broadcom's code mishandles the reassembly of fragmented WPS setup messages, so an attacker in range can send crafted messages that corrupt the router's memory. From there, Kaiser built two things: a way to read memory back off the device, and a way to run his own code on it.
Against an Orange Belgium gateway, the Askey TCG3000 read the Wi-Fi password (the PSK) from the router's stored settings, sent it back over the air, and then joined the network with it.
Against a Proximus gateway, the Sagemcom-built BBOX3V+, the exploit opened a reverse shell, a remote command line, carried over Wi-Fi frames, so no outside server was needed.
Both ran without any login, and the attack works at a distance, not only up close, Kaiser says. He reports no real-world attacks using the flaw. The working exploits are his own.
What's Affected
Broadcom's WPS code is embedded in routers and access points from dozens of vendors, and Kaiser estimates that millions of devices worldwide are affected.
The vulnerable chips fall into two families: older eCos-based models (the BCM3380, BCM3383 and BCM33834), where he found no usable fix and calls the bug a permanent "forever day," meaning a flaw that will never be patched on those devices, and newer Linux-based models (the BCM3390, BCM65xx and BCM68xx), which could be fixed if their makers switch Wi-Fi software.
In Belgium, Kaiser found the flaw present and exploitable on gateways from three of the four big providers: Proximus, Orange Belgium and VOO. A fourth, Telenet, may be affected too, but he could not test one.
A wider list he published, ranging from Cisco small-business access points to Huawei and ARRIS routers, mixes confirmed and unconfirmed entries, and some rest on an automated check that only flags a device as "likely vulnerable."
The Belgian per-provider counts, he says, run into the hundreds of thousands of gateways, but are rough estimates.
Why There's No Patch, and No CVE
The flaw is old. Kaiser traces the code back to at least 2010 and says Broadcom shipped an incomplete fix in 2018, then told customers to switch to a different Wi-Fi software package, called hostapd, rather than relying on the fix. On the older eCos chips, he says, no working fix was ever shipped, which is why he calls it a forever day.
No CVE, the tracking identifier that lets defenders and vendors follow a flaw, has been assigned to it. Kaiser says Broadcom told him it has known about the bug since 2018 and had heard about it from others, but would not register a CVE or say anything publicly, which he believes is why so many device makers never patched.
When he took the case to the CERT Coordination Center, it was closed the same day, because Broadcom itself holds the authority to assign CVEs for its products and would not do so. The Hacker News found no CVE for the flaw as of October 19.
What Defenders Can Do
There is no patch to install, and no setting Kaiser points to that blocks the attack over the air. What he provides instead is a way to find affected gear: YARA rules that spot the vulnerable code in extracted firmware, and a script that listens to a live access point and reports whether it looks vulnerable.
Both are triage aids, he notes: a patched device can still match the rules, so a hit is a reason to check further, not a confirmed finding. For gear that will never be fixed, replacement is the practical option.
Kaiser frames the bug as well suited to attackers who reach a target over nearby Wi-Fi rather than the internet, a technique Russian state hackers have used to breach networks from across the street.

articles.title: Trust in AI: What adoption really looks like for Gulf SMEs
articles.text: An article by Ahmed Sameh, Chief Marketing Officer at Fortis Every AI story coming out of the UAE this year seems to feature the same cast: sovereign AI strategies, enterprise transformation programmes and government ministries preparing to deploy agentic AI across 50% of federal services and operations within two years . It’s an impressive story, but it is also the wrong one if you want to understand how AI is changing the way most Gulf businesses operate. Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) account for 94% of businesses in the UAE, according to the Ministry of Economy , yet relatively little of the AI conversation focuses on them. We see the gap between these two stories every day. What we hear from merchants rarely matches the enterprise AI narrative. Their concerns are more practical, their resources more constrained, and their adoption story arguably more interesting. The readiness gap A 2025 study of 315 respondents from UAE hospitality SMEs found that top management support was among the strongest predictors of intention to adopt AI, alongside competitive pressure and government regulation. These factors carried more weight than the technology’s perceived usefulness. The problem is not simply whether the technology works. It is whether someone inside the business trusts it enough to champion it and has the time to put it to use. This helps explain why so much enterprise-grade AI tooling falls flat with SME merchants. A restaurant owner running three venues with a skeleton back-office team does not need a sprawling analytics suite that requires a dedicated administrator to configure. During our field research with food and beverage (F&B) merchants, operators often described software decisions in terms of risk rather than features. They wanted fast checkout, an easy way to set up menus, minimal staff training, reliable support and clear pricing. Our main conclusion was straightforward: "POS systems are chosen to minimise risk, not to maximise features." That distinction matters. Enterprise software is often designed around the breadth of its capabilities, while SME merchants are primarily concerned with whether it will make their day-to-day operations easier or more complicated. AI adapted from enterprise software can demand exactly what smaller businesses lack: dedicated IT staff, lengthy onboarding and patience for features built around problems they do not have. Where AI adoption is taking hold On the customer-facing side, AI is already changing how merchants sell. And much of that change is happening on customers’ terms, not merchants’. Consumers in the region are increasingly using AI to inform their purchasing decisions. Tabby’s 2026 shopping survey , covering more than 20,000 respondents in the UAE and Saudi Arabia, found that 43% use AI to help decide what to buy. Among 18- to 29-year-olds, 51.8% have used AI somewhere in their shopping journey. But adoption does not automatically mean trust. The same survey found that only 30% fully trust AI recommendations. For merchants, the opportunity is clear, but so is the challenge. AI-powered ordering, personalised loyalty offers and customer messaging may help businesses respond to changing shopping habits, but only if customers see value in the experience. We are observing a similar pattern from our end, although at an earlier stage. In our research into merchants’ use of AI, the tools they had adopted independently — ChatGPT, Gemini and DeepSeek — clustered around a fairly consistent set of tasks. Most of these were marketing-related: writing social media captions, generating campaign ideas and coming up with product names. Merchants were also using AI to explore pricing decisions, such as what to charge for a new item or how to structure a bundle or discount. A smaller number were experimenting with AI-generated product images. What they had not explored, at least among the merchants we researched, was AI-powered sales analytics or forecasting. That gap is not necessarily about hesitation. It is also about the limitations of the tools they are using. A standalone AI assistant has no visibility into a merchant’s actual business performance unless it is connected to the relevant sales and operational data. And without that visibility, its usefulness has limits. Operations present a different but equally pressing challenge. For UAE retailers and hospitality businesses, staffing and inventory planning can be complicated by employment costs, visa requirements and seasonal fluctuations in demand. AI could help with forecasting, reordering and shift planning without requiring particularly sophisticated systems. But that is not what the merchants we speak to are asking for right now. They want faster answers. Not another dashboard, but a simple way to ask: What were today's sales? What changed from yesterday? What's selling best? Is anything unusual? Are we on track? Who sold the most? Which customers came back? Across our research, one request came up more frequently than any other: "Tell me what's happening in my business right now." That is a much more immediate starting point than predictive analytics. Before merchants can trust AI to tell them what might happen next week, they need to trust it to tell them what is happening today. Why the gap will get harder to close The difference between experimenting with AI and using it to improve business performance is already becoming clear. McKinsey’s 2025 State of AI report found that organisations it classified as AI high performers, representing about 6% of respondents, were three times more likely than their peers to report strong senior leadership ownership and commitment to AI initiatives. They were also more likely to have moved beyond experimentation and started scaling AI across their businesses. These findings concern organisations of different sizes, not Gulf SMEs specifically. But the underlying lesson is relevant: adopting AI tools and extracting measurable value from them are two different things. For smaller merchants, the implications could be significant. A restaurant that can anticipate a slow Tuesday and adjust staffing accordingly, or a retailer that can identify and re-engage customers who have stopped returning, may be able to operate more efficiently than a competitor relying entirely on manual decisions. Over time, those advantages can compound, particularly in retail and hospitality, where margins leave little room for error. But getting there requires tools designed around how SMEs actually operate: thin teams, tight margins and no time for a six-month rollout. It does not require SMEs to become AI companies. Nor should they have to make do with a stripped-down version of a platform designed for a 500-person enterprise. The starting point is simpler: it gives merchants access to their own business information in a way that is immediate, understandable and useful. Build trust through reliable answers before asking them to rely on more complex predictions or automated decisions. For Gulf SMEs, the next stage of AI adoption may have less to do with how sophisticated the technology becomes and more to do with how well it fits the businesses expected to use it. The merchants who find tools that fit will be better placed to pull ahead.

articles.title: Logitech's $70 MX Anywhere 3S wireless mouse is 'a traveler's dream'
articles.text:
Logitech's MX Anywhere 3S wireless mouse works on almost any surface, combines quiet clicks, precise tracking, and lightning-fast scrolling
It has a compact design and customizable buttons
A cheap wireless mouse might get the job done, but there's a noticeable difference when you move to something designed for precision and comfort. The Logitech MX Anywhere 3S, currently $70 (was $90) at Amazon, packs several useful features into a compact design.
One of the biggest attractions of the Logitech MX Anywhere 3S mouse is that you don't need a mat to use it. Its 8,000 DPI Darkfield sensor can track on a wide range of surfaces, including glass that's at least 4mm thick.
• Best for: Laptop owners, mobile professionals, and anyone who regularly works across multiple computers.
• Why it matters: You get premium features such as MagSpeed scrolling, an 8,000 DPI sensor, quiet clicks, and multi-device connectivity without paying over the top. Weighing just 99g and measuring around 100mm long, it won't take up much space in your laptop bag either.
Today's best Logitech wireless mouse deal
This compact wireless mouse features 8000 DPI tracking, MagSpeed scrolling, quiet clicks, six buttons, three-device Bluetooth connectivity, customizable shortcuts, USB-C charging, glass-surface tracking, and up to 70 days of battery life.
Why we recommend it
In his 4-star review of an earlier version, our expert Nick said: "Despite its small size, the Logitech MX Anywhere 3 packs plenty of features seen in some of Logitech’s more advanced models. Scrolling through documents or websites is ridiculously satisfactory, and its ability to work across multiple surfaces is a traveler’s dream."
With the MX Anywhere 3S, the 3's successor, Logitech has made the clicks quieter than before, which will be welcome when working in shared spaces.
The MagSpeed wheel can scroll through up to 1,000 lines per second, allowing it navigate large files much quicker. Horizontal scrolling can be activated by holding a side button while turning the wheel.
The six-button design includes customizable controls, and Options+ software lets you assign shortcuts and create application-specific settings in Windows and macOS. You can pair the mouse with three Bluetooth devices and quickly switch between them.
Price context & historical value
The Logitech MX Anywhere 3S normally costs $89.99, but it's currently available for $69.99. That saves you $20. That's a great reduction, although we have seen it as low as $60 in the past, and it could get cheaper around Black Friday.
Should you buy it?
✅ Buy the Logitech MX Anywhere 3S if...
You regularly use a laptop away from your usual desk and want a reliable mouse that can track on almost any surface. It's also a good choice if you use it with several different computers.
❌ Skip the Logitech MX Anywhere 3S if...
You mainly use your computer for occasional web browsing and don't need advanced features. A basic wireless mouse will cost considerably less.
Also consider
This ergonomic wireless mouse features 8000 DPI tracking, quiet clicks, MagSpeed scrolling, programmable buttons, customizable app profiles, Bluetooth connectivity, thumb controls, and cross-computer file transfers between Windows and macOS devices.

articles.title: Preventa del iPhone Duo se agota en minutos y extiende entregas hasta 2027: qué solución hay para no esperar
articles.text:
La preventa del iPhone Duo, el primer teléfono plegable de Apple, agotó en pocos minutos las unidades previstas para el día de lanzamiento y extendió parte de las entregas hasta enero de 2027. El dispositivo que parte de 1.999 dólares salió a la venta anticipada el viernes 16 de octubre de 2026.
Quienes completaron el pedido durante los primeros minutos recibieron como fecha estimada el viernes 23 de octubre. Para el resto, los plazos pasaron con rapidez a noviembre y diciembre, mientras que algunas configuraciones ya muestran entregas para enero.
Ante ese escenario, muchos usuarios buscan una forma de acelerar el envío, aunque las alternativas disponibles son limitadas.
¿Existe una forma de adelantar la entrega del iPhone Duo?
La respuesta es no. Una vez que Apple asigna una fecha estimada a la reserva, el comprador no cuenta con un mecanismo para adelantarla. Los plazos dependen de la producción, la configuración elegida, el color, la capacidad de almacenamiento y el inventario destinado a cada región.
La compañía sugirió preparar con anticipación el color y la capacidad para agilizar el pedido. Aun así, algunos compradores comentaron en redes sociales que tuvieron problemas para finalizar la compra en la tienda en línea. Esa preparación podía reducir pasos durante la preventa, pero no garantiza una unidad ni modifica una fecha ya asignada.
Por qué no conviene comprar el teléfono en mercados de reventa
Comprar un iPhone Duo en mercados de reventa puede implicar riesgos. La alta demanda inicial suele derivar en precios por encima del valor oficial, publicaciones sin unidades disponibles y operaciones en las que no es sencillo verificar el origen del dispositivo o las condiciones reales de entrega.
Además, existen riesgos si el vendedor ofrece una reserva en lugar de un dispositivo en su poder. El comprador podría pagar por adelantado y depender de que el revendedor reciba el teléfono en la fecha prometida.
Antes de realizar una operación, conviene comprobar la identidad del vendedor, la existencia física del producto, el número de serie y las condiciones de devolución.
Qué alternativa hay para quien necesita un teléfono plegable ahora
La única alternativa para evitar la espera consiste en elegir un teléfono plegable de otra marca que tenga disponibilidad inmediata. Esa decisión supone renunciar al modelo de Apple, pero permite acceder antes a un dispositivo con formato plegable sin depender de la lista de pedidos del Duo.
El iPhone Duo llega a una categoría donde otros fabricantes ya tienen presencia, aunque Apple busca diferenciarse mediante su integración con el sistema operativo y su diseño. El modelo cuenta con una pantalla externa de 5,4 pulgadas y un panel interior de 7,6 pulgadas cuando está abierto, con una superficie 80% mayor que la del iPhone 18 Pro.
Cómo es el primer plegable de Apple
El teléfono tiene formato tipo pasaporte, bordes de titanio, dos cámaras traseras y un mecanismo diseñado para que la marca central del pliegue resulte poco visible. Cerrado puede utilizarse con una mano; abierto, permite ejecutar dos aplicaciones lado a lado y ofrece una interfaz orientada a tareas de productividad.
El modelo plegable usa una versión adaptada de iOS 27, incorpora un dock vertical en el borde derecho y habilita modos específicos cuando queda semiplegado. Su batería promete hasta 24 horas de autonomía con el dispositivo cerrado, mientras que la carga rápida recupera el 50% en 20 minutos.
Asimismo, la cámara principal es de 48 megapíxeles, graba video en 4K y ofrece zoom de dos aumentos. El sistema trasero suma una cámara ultra gran angular, sin teleobjetivo dedicado. Apple reemplazó Face ID por Touch ID e integró un chip desarrollado para este dispositivo.
Analistas de Bloomberg estimaron que las ventas del Duo podrían superar los 14 millones de unidades y generar USD 28.000 millones de ingresos durante el año fiscal 2027.

articles.title: OpenCode Console Breach May Have Exposed OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google API Keys
articles.text:
An intruder reached a legacy system at OpenCode on the night of October 16 and may have exposed the third-party AI provider keys that users had saved in OpenCode Console, the company said.
Console is OpenCode's optional hosted service: a workspace saves its own OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google key there, and Console uses that key to call the provider so team members can use the models without ever seeing the key.
The affected group is 1.4% of Console users, all of whom have an outside provider linked, and OpenCode has told them via email to revoke those keys with each provider and replace them.
The email went out on the morning of October 17 under the subject line "Action Required: Potential provider key breach." Anyone who did not get one was not affected, OpenCode said in a post on X later that day.
The keys at risk are the ones pasted into Console. The OpenCode command-line and desktop apps keep provider keys added on the machine in a SQLite database there. The breach involves "the OpenCode Console, not OpenCode itself," co-founder Dax Raad wrote in a reply on X, and those keys "never come to us."
A provider key is a bearer credential: whoever holds a copy can run billable requests against the owner's account until the provider revokes it. Deleting the key from Console does not revoke it, and a Console budget cannot cap that use either, because Console only sees requests that pass through its own gateway.
For a key that was saved in a Console workspace, OpenCode's email and the providers' own guidance give these steps:
- Revoke the key in the provider's own dashboard and create a new one, following the instructions from OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google.
- Update every application and script that used the old key.
- Review usage and billing at the provider for requests you did not make, going back at least to October 16. OpenCode has not said when the unauthorized access began.
- Set a spend limit or alert at the provider and give each tool its own key, so a copied key does less damage and its use is easier to trace.
Some users say they have already paid for usage they did not run. Dealroom reported that Colin Parsons wrote on X that his OpenAI key had been used for $281 and his Anthropic key for $168, and that Preston Zeller put his losses at $1,700.
Notebookcheck reported a Reddit user's claim of $400 of unauthorized usage on an Anthropic account, and another's of about €200 of Google usage, with the project then suspended.
Those are the users' own accounts. OpenCode's own wording is that the keys "may have been exposed," and it has not said that any key was copied or used.
OpenCode's October 17 post also called the incident ongoing, said the company was working with Anthropic, OpenAI and Google to fix it, and described the breach as "related to a large-scale distillation attack." The company has not named anyone or said how the two connect, what the legacy system was, how it was reached, how many keys it held, or how many users 1.4% represents.
Distillation is the term AI model providers use for campaigns that pull a model's answers in huge numbers to train a rival model. Anthropic said in September that the labs behind such campaigns reach its models through networks of fake accounts created with stolen credit cards, login credentials and harvested API keys. A stolen key has other uses too: criminal markets resell AI tokens and keys and use them to run up bills.
Attackers were still trying to get into OpenCode's systems on October 18, Raad wrote on X: they had been "non stop trying to attack our systems for the past 48 hours," and "a side effect is everything is getting hardened."

articles.title: Windows 11 is getting a free performance boost for apps which looks like it'll make a big difference to launch speeds
articles.text:
Windows 11 is getting another free speed boost for apps — I just wonder why all this performance tuning didn't happen before now
Want faster app launch times in Windows 11? Microsoft is making this happen
- Windows 11 has a new preview build with a change to boost performance
- It's just for Edge to begin with, and it means that if the browser is already running, new instances of the app will launch faster
- Microsoft's plan is to introduce this to a wider range of Windows 11 apps
Microsoft is making another move to tune up Windows 11 so it launches some apps more swiftly, although this is just in testing for now.
Windows Latest noticed that the latest build in the Release Preview channel (the final stage of testing) applies a change to bring in "accelerated app launches" for Microsoft Edge in a certain scenario. Namely that when Edge is already running, further instances of the web browser being opened will appear at a faster speed.
Microsoft tells us that: "When you select a link or open Edge from the taskbar or Start menu while Edge is already running in the background, Windows now routes your request directly to the running instance instead of first starting an extra, temporary process."
This shortened launch path for when Edge is 'warm' (already running) means a considerably faster launch time, as Windows Latest verified.
The tech site also points out that only the first 'cold' start of the browser will be slower (with the longer launch process), as even if you open Edge, then close it, if you run the app again, it's still 'warm' as the relevant processes have spun up in the background.
Analysis: broader benefits, but why did all this take so long?
If you don't use Edge (and that's doubtless most of you), then you might be thinking: what's the big deal anyway? Well, this is a first step in testing towards a grander goal, namely a "broader Windows capability that any app can adopt to speed up its own launches" as Microsoft explains in the preview build's release notes.
Eventually, we could see multiple apps benefiting from what's an apparently considerable performance boost when launching, assuming that they're already running (and warmed up). It could be some time before Microsoft opens this up to third-party developers, mind, and then they have to get around to implementing the functionality.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
At any rate, it's a useful new feature, and one that comes on top of Microsoft's existing work in enabling preloading for certain Windows 11 apps, notably Edge itself and File Explorer. We've also witnessed the introduction of the Low Latency Profile feature, which represents a nice CPU speed boost for Windows 11's menus and also apps.
The main question is: why did it take Microsoft so long to get around to these performance improvements? File Explorer being slow was a complaint from the start with Windows 11, and yet we've had to suffer this – and various other instances of sluggishness – for years before they've been fixed. It was only this year, when Microsoft properly turned its attention to fixing Windows 11, that we've seen solutions flooding forth.
And don't get me wrong, that's great, but it also shows that Microsoft didn't take these performance problems seriously until the Windows 11 userbase was more or less in open rebellion over AI features being pushed while all these issues continued to frustrate people. It's clear enough that the optimization of Windows 11 could have been done in the past, if Microsoft was willing to graft at the task, it was just that the company didn't see it as enough of a priority – bafflingly.
I concede that even when Microsoft is doing a good thing here, I'm moaning, and that in this respect the company can't win. Fair enough, and all's well that ends well as they say, but what I'm really hoping is that Microsoft can learn from this in the future and act earlier to troubleshoot its desktop OS when it clearly has problems.
Whatever next-gen Windows turns out to be, it needs to take this new attitude and go forward with it, until Microsoft has an operating system which is running smoothly for daily operations in every important respect, from performance to usability – not to mention reliability and stable updates which is still a big issue that's left to resolve.
