articles.title: Estados Unidos quiere regular los robotaxis: Waymo, Tesla y más deberán tener monitoreos humanos y límites
articles.text:
Ciudades y estados de Estados Unidos avanzan con leyes propias para frenar o condicionar la circulación de robotaxis, los autos sin conductor que operan empresas como Waymo, Zoox y Tesla, ante la falta de una regulación federal que ordene al sector.
Un freno que llega desde lo local
El Congreso de Estados Unidos no logró aprobar una ley nacional que fije reglas de seguridad para los vehículos autónomos, según describió el medio especializado The Verge. Esa parálisis dejó en manos de concejos municipales y legislaturas estatales la tarea de definir qué pueden y qué no pueden hacer estos autos en sus calles.
El resultado es un mosaico de normas distintas según la ciudad, algo que la propia industria de los vehículos autónomos buscaba evitar. Las municipalidades no tienen autoridad sobre los estándares de fabricación de los autos, pero sí sobre el uso de sus calles, y ahí concentraron su respuesta.
En Minneapolis, el Concejo Municipal avanza con una ordenanza que exigiría un monitor humano pago dentro de cada vehículo autónomo, una medida que en los hechos equivaldría a prohibir la operación sin conductor.
La concejala Robin Wonsley, autora del proyecto, dijo que la ciudad “no va a desplegar la alfombra roja para que las grandes tecnológicas saqueen nuestra economía y desplacen a nuestros trabajadores”, según publicó el medio Minnesota Reformer.
Bomberos, aeropuertos y pujas políticas
En San Diego, el Concejo Municipal aprobó una resolución que busca prohibir que Waymo opere en el aeropuerto internacional de la ciudad y que le otorga a las agencias locales control directo sobre los vehículos autónomos en situaciones de emergencia.
El concejal Sean Elo-Rivera, impulsor de la medida, sostuvo que “los conductores locales y los pequeños comercios cumplen regla tras regla para ganarse la vida acá”, según reportó la cadena NBC San Diego.
En Austin, los bomberos expresaron preocupación por los Cybercab de Tesla, que no tienen volante ni pedales. El cuerpo de bomberos pide que los fabricantes de vehículos autónomos establezcan protocolos de remolque de respuesta rápida y canales directos de comunicación con operadores humanos para emergencias, de acuerdo con lo relevado por The Verge.
La disputa también llegó a Washington D.C., donde el concejal Charles Allen impulsa un proyecto que limitaría a doscientos vehículos la flota de cada operador y postergaría hasta 2028 el inicio del servicio comercial, además de cobrar una tarifa por milla recorrida para financiar al subterráneo local y compensar a choferes de aplicaciones de transporte.
La futura alcaldesa Janeese Lewis George se opuso públicamente: “Washington enfrenta una crisis de empleo. Apurar la legalización de los vehículos autónomos es irresponsable”, escribió en la red social X, según citó Axios. Allen respondió que “seguimos negociando” y que espera una votación en su comisión antes de fin de noviembre.
Una grieta que no sigue el mapa político tradicional
El fenómeno desarma la lógica política habitual: durante años se asumió que los republicanos eran más receptivos a los autos autónomos y los demócratas más escépticos, pero ciudades gobernadas por demócratas como Nueva York, Chicago y Washington todavía no legalizaron la circulación de autos sin conductor, según el relevamiento de The Verge.
Nevada fue el primer estado en permitir la circulación de autos autónomos en la vía pública, en junio de 2011, varios años antes de que esa tecnología estuviera realmente disponible.
15 años después, varias de esas mismas jurisdicciones que recibieron a los autos autónomos con entusiasmo vuelven a sentarse a redactar leyes para contenerlos.
Waymo, que opera más de 500.000 viajes semanales en 15 ciudades de Estados Unidos sin exigir monitores humanos, calificó a la propuesta de Minneapolis como “una prohíbición de hecho” a los vehículos autónomos, según declaró a Axios Adam Lane, gerente de políticas estatales y locales de la empresa.
El próximo hito concreto llegará en Washington D.C., donde Allen espera cerrar la votación en su comisión antes de Acción de Gracias, lo que habilitaría un voto del pleno del Concejo en diciembre.
.

articles.title: J’ai testé le Tineco Floor One S9 Master : sa meilleure surprise arrive après le ménage
articles.text:
Avec le Floor One S9 Master, Tineco promet un lavage plus efficace et moins de traces, grâce à l’eau chaude et à une nouvelle raclette. Après plusieurs jours d’utilisation, c’est aussi le nettoyage de sa propre brosse qui m’a convaincu.
- Excellentes performances d’aspiration et de lavage
- Peu de traces après séchage
- Très bonne maniabilité grâce aux roues motorisées
- Auto-nettoyage et séchage du rouleau particulièrement efficaces
- Éclairage frontal vert vraiment utile
- Station encombrante, obligeant à soulever l’appareil
- Mode Heat peu différenciant durant nos essais
- Détection de saleté parfois incohérente
- Accès limité sous les meubles les plus bas
- Cycle rapide d’entretien assez bruyant
Tineco continue d’enrichir sa famille d’aspirateurs laveurs, au point qu’il faut parfois s’accrocher pour distinguer les différentes références. Après un S9 Artist particulièrement convaincant et un S9 Scientist dont le jet d’eau m’avait laissé un peu sur ma faim, voici le Floor One S9 Master.
Au programme : une aspiration annoncée à 25 000 Pa, un lavage à l’eau chaude, une raclette StreakFree pour limiter les traces et une station capable de nettoyer puis sécher le rouleau en quelques minutes. De belles promesses pour un appareil dont la boutique française affiche un prix de référence de 699 euros, avant remise.
J’ai utilisé ce S9 Master sur tous les sols de ma maison, pour le ménage quotidien. De quoi vérifier si ce nouveau maître du lavage mérite son nom.
Test réalisé sur un exemplaire prêté par le constructeur.
Design et ergonomie : il se laisse pousser, un peu moins ranger
Le Floor One S9 Master joue la sobriété, avec une finition noire brillante et des lignes assez classiques. Il fait moins son intéressant que le S9 Artist, dont j’avais apprécié le soin apporté au design. Les plastiques paraissent également un peu moins flatteurs au toucher, mais l’assemblage reste sérieux.
Tineco annonce un poids de 5,1 kg. Sur le sol, les roues motorisées compensent efficacement cette masse : l’appareil accompagne les mouvements, les changements de direction sont naturels et les longues sessions ne se transforment pas en séance de musculation. La position parking permet aussi de le laisser debout le temps de déplacer un obstacle.
C’est un point appréciable après le S9 Scientist, dont le poids proche de 6 kg m’avait davantage gêné. Le Master est agréable à manœuvrer, même si son assistance ne change évidemment rien lorsqu’il faut le porter d’un étage à l’autre.
L’appareil peut se coucher pour nettoyer sous les meubles, avec une épaisseur annoncée de 9,9 cm. Cela ne lui ouvre toutefois pas toutes les portes : dans mon usage, la tête reste trop épaisse pour atteindre les espaces les plus bas. Avant de lui confier le dessous du canapé, mieux vaut regarder la place disponible.
La station oblige à soulever entièrement l’aspirateur pour le repositionner sur son socle. Ce n’est pas très gênant la première fois. Quand le geste revient après chaque nettoyage, on finit par trouver la manipulation un peu pénible.
L’écran couleur rectangulaire est bien lisible et présente les informations utiles : batterie restante, mode sélectionné et alertes d’entretien. Les boutons sont accessibles et permettent également de régler les annonces vocales, de changer leur langue ou de couper le son. Tout se passe directement sur l’appareil, sans application mobile à installer.
Aspiration : le mode Auto fait le gros du travail
Avec une aspiration maximale annoncée à 25 000 Pa, le S9 Master ne manque pas d’arguments sur sa fiche technique. Les résultats suivent : les poussières sont correctement ramassées, les poils aussi, et les liquides sont récupérés efficacement.
Le mode Auto suffit largement à l’entretien courant. Je n’ai pas eu besoin de passer systématiquement en puissance maximale pour obtenir un sol propre. On met l’appareil en marche et l’on avance, sans devoir jouer avec les réglages dans chaque pièce.
Quatre modes sont proposés : Auto, Quiet, Heat et Max. Quiet réduit sensiblement le bruit et conserve une bonne efficacité sur les petites saletés. Max permet de solliciter toute la puissance disponible lorsque le nettoyage le demande.
Je suis moins convaincu par la détection automatique de saleté. Le système iLoop doit ajuster l’aspiration et l’apport d’eau selon ce qu’il repère. Certaines réactions paraissent pertinentes, d’autres sont plus difficiles à comprendre. Le résultat du nettoyage reste bon, mais je ne me fierais pas uniquement à son indicateur pour décider qu’une zone est impeccable.
L’éclairage vert à l’avant est, en revanche, très utile. Il fait ressortir les poussières que l’on distingue mal à l’œil nu et permet de voir immédiatement où repasser. Une petite lumière qui rend davantage service qu’un grand discours sur l’intelligence de l’appareil.
Lavage des sols : une raclette convaincante, une eau chaude moins décisive
Le lavage est l’un des grands points forts de ce S9 Master. La sauce fraîche est rapidement retirée et les taches séchées de café ou de sauce disparaissent également après quelques passages insistants. Le nettoyage est homogène et les traces résiduelles sont peu nombreuses.
Tineco met en avant sa raclette StreakFree pour limiter les résidus d’eau. Difficile d’isoler son rôle de celui du rouleau et de l’aspiration, mais l’ensemble fonctionne très bien : le sol conserve un aspect uniforme après séchage. Devoir ressortir la serpillière pour corriger son passage aurait un intérêt assez limité.
Le mode Heat me laisse davantage sur ma faim. Il chauffe l’eau utilisée pour laver les sols, mais je n’ai pas constaté de différence assez nette avec Auto pour en faire un passage obligé. Sur les taches testées, le lavage classique était déjà très efficace.
La pulvérisation ThermoBlast se commande séparément, en maintenant un bouton dédié. Elle projette de l’eau chaude sous pression devant la tête, avec une durée maximale de dix secondes par pulvérisation.
Lors des premiers essais, je trouvais l’ajout assez anecdotique : sur une tache isolée, le jet n’a pas transformé le résultat. Son intérêt est apparu pendant certains nettoyages prolongés, lorsque le rouleau avait tendance à perdre en humidité. Un apport supplémentaire permet alors de remouiller la zone et de poursuivre dans de meilleures conditions.
Le bouton rend donc service, mais il compense aussi une limite rencontrée durant l’utilisation. J’aurais préféré que l’alimentation automatique maintienne une humidification suffisante sans intervention. Le mode Auto nettoie très bien dans l’ensemble ; il ne m’a pas totalement dispensé de reprendre la main sur ce point.
La solution de nettoyage fournie s’est montrée efficace et permet de démarrer immédiatement, sans achat supplémentaire.
Autonomie et réservoirs : une marge confortable pour mon ménage
Tineco annonce jusqu’à 65 minutes d’autonomie. Durant mes essais, le nettoyage d’un étage consommait un peu moins de la moitié de la batterie. J’avais donc une réserve confortable pour poursuivre, sans surveiller constamment le pourcentage restant.
Ce résultat ne permet pas de valider les 65 minutes annoncées ni d’établir une surface maximale. À l’échelle de mes sessions, la batterie ne m’a toutefois pas posé de problème.
Les réservoirs accueillent 850 ml d’eau propre et jusqu’à 700 ml d’eau sale. Cette dernière limite descend à 500 ml lorsque l’appareil est utilisé à plat, ce qui mérite d’être gardé en tête avant de passer sous les meubles.
En pratique, je n’ai pas eu l’impression de devoir interrompre constamment le nettoyage pour remplir l’un ou vider l’autre. Leur transparence permet aussi de surveiller facilement les niveaux, en complément des alertes de l’appareil.
La notice annonce quatre à cinq heures pour une recharge complète. L’appareil se recharge donc surtout entre deux sessions ; une batterie vide ne se remplira pas le temps de déplacer les chaises.
Entretien : le rouleau ressort propre, et ça change tout
Une fois le sol lavé, il reste généralement une tâche dont on se passerait bien : nettoyer ce qui vient de nettoyer la maison. Sur ce point, le S9 Master est particulièrement convaincant.
Durant mes essais, le cycle rapide complet, nettoyage et séchage compris, prenait environ cinq minutes. Le rouleau en ressort propre, sec et prêt à repartir. Le résultat est impressionnant et constitue l’un des meilleurs arguments de cet appareil.
La rapidité se paie avec un niveau sonore assez élevé. Le programme plus discret demande environ quarante minutes, avec un résultat tout aussi convaincant. Le choix est donc simple : quelques minutes bien audibles ou davantage de patience. Pendant le lavage des sols, le bruit reste modéré et ne m’a pas paru particulièrement agressif.
Comme sur le S9 Artist, l’entretien automatisé reste un vrai point fort. Le bénéfice est appréciable après chaque utilisation.
La station ne dispense pas de vider et de rincer le réservoir d’eau sale. Heureusement, la séparation entre les liquides, les déchets et les poils est très réussie. Elle facilite la vidange et évite de récupérer un mélange dans lequel il faudrait aller pêcher les saletés.
Le filtre et les éléments amovibles demandent également leur entretien habituel, comme le rappelle la notice du S9 Master. La station allège surtout le travail sur le rouleau, et elle le fait suffisamment bien pour que l’on apprécie de lui laisser cette corvée.
Tineco Floor One S9 Master : l’avis de Clubic
Le Floor One S9 Master est un excellent aspirateur laveur. Il récupère efficacement les déchets, vient à bout des taches testées et laisse peu de traces après séchage. Les roues motorisées rendent les déplacements agréables, l’éclairage frontal aide à repérer les poussières et la station assure un nettoyage du rouleau particulièrement convaincant.
Les fonctions supplémentaires ne sont pas toutes aussi décisives. Le mode Heat ne m’a pas apporté de gain notable et la détection de saleté manque parfois de cohérence. ThermoBlast est utile, mais il m’a surtout servi à compenser une humidification parfois insuffisante lors de longues sessions. Ajoutez la nécessité de soulever l’appareil pour le replacer sur sa station, et vous comprenez pourquoi je ne parle pas de sans-faute.
Au quotidien, le Floor One S9 Master reste néanmoins un appareil très convaincant. Parmi les modèles Tineco que j’ai testés, c’est l’un de ceux qui m’ont demandé le moins d’efforts tout en offrant un nettoyage efficace. Il ne cherche pas à tout révolutionner, mais il simplifie réellement la corvée : le sol est propre, la brosse reste prête à servir et son nettoyage automatique allège vraiment l’entretien. C’est finalement ce qui le rend si agréable à utiliser.
- Excellentes performances d’aspiration et de lavage
- Peu de traces après séchage
- Très bonne maniabilité grâce aux roues motorisées
- Auto-nettoyage et séchage du rouleau particulièrement efficaces
- Éclairage frontal vert vraiment utile
- Station encombrante, obligeant à soulever l’appareil
- Mode Heat peu différenciant durant nos essais
- Détection de saleté parfois incohérente
- Accès limité sous les meubles les plus bas
- Cycle rapide d’entretien assez bruyant

articles.title: Fabriqué par Stellantis en Espagne, ce SUV électrique chinois à moins de 30 000 € pourrait coûter encore moins cher en France
articles.text:
Fabriqué par Stellantis en Espagne, ce SUV électrique chinois à moins de 30 000 € pourrait coûter encore moins cher en France
Le Leapmotor B10 est maintenant assemblé par Stellantis en Espagne. Une production européenne qui devrait clairement réduire la facture du SUV électrique en France, et ce, pour deux raisons bien précises.
Confrontées aux taxes douanières sur les importations de voitures électriques, les marques chinoises produisent de plus en plus en Europe. Le Leapmotor B10 commence d’ailleurs à sortir des chaînes de production espagnoles de Stellantis. Un choix qui devrait rendre le SUV électrique beaucoup plus concurrentiel dans les semaines à venir. La prime CEE en France pourrait aussi alléger son tarif, mais à une condition bien précise.
Leapmotor B10 : l'assemblage européen par Stellantis fait chuter son prix
Stellantis vient d’accueillir Leapmotor au sein de son usine espagnole de Figueruelas. Assemblant déjà les Peugeot 208, Opel Corsa et Lancia Ypsilon, elle est maintenant mise à profit pour le B10, un SUV électrique vendu aujourd’hui juste en dessous de 30 000 €. Cette opération permet au géant automobile de rentabiliser son outil industriel, tout en aidant son partenaire chinois à accélérer son implantation en Europe avec ses modèles à bas prix.
Cette stratégie permet en effet à ce véhicule d’échapper aux 30,7 % de droits de douane imposés par l’Union européenne sur les importations d’électriques chinoises. En prime, cette relocalisation le rapproche des critères d’éligibilité à la prime CEE renforcée en France, comprise entre 3600 et 6100 €. Pour décrocher ce coup de pouce gouvernemental, le SUV devra toutefois intégrer des cellules de batterie produites localement et valider son éco-score auprès des autorités françaises.
Pour rappel, le Leapmotor B10 est un SUV familial de 4,52 m de long équipé d’un moteur de 218 ch et d’une autonomie de 361 ou 434 km WLTP en fonction de la batterie choisie. Affiché à partir de 29 900 € pour le moment sur le site officiel de la marque, ce modèle pourrait facilement passer sous la barre des 26 000 € (voire 24 000 € selon les revenus) s’il obtient bien le précieux sésame.
Ce partenariat industriel ne fonctionne cependant pas à sens unique. Dès 2028, un nouveau SUV électrique badgé Opel devrait être assemblé à Saragosse en reprenant les composants de l’écosystème Leapmotor afin d’abaisser ses coûts de revient. Un second modèle chinois rejoindrait au passage l’usine Stellantis de Madrid pour entretenir cette alliance. Un échange de bons procédés qui permet à Leapmotor de contourner les barrières douanières européennes, pendant que Stellantis profite d’une technologie électrique abordable pour ses propres marques.

articles.title: Zaragoza celebraba Pilares así que un jabalí terminó de madrugada en un bar de fiesta del casco histórico
articles.text:
Si has estado en Zaragoza durante estas fiestas del Pilar habrás visto calles anegadas de gente, colas para entrar a casi cualquier local y estado festivo general. La SEO y otras plazas se atestaron de chavales (se han alcanzado los 3 millones de visitas y se estima un total de 6) pero lo que no se esperaba ver era un animal salvaje infiltrado en este hábitat. Salvaje de verdad: en la madrugada del sábado 17 al domingo 18 de octubre, un jabalí se cruzó casi todo el centro de Zaragoza. Heraldo recoge el testimonio del animal corriendo al galope entre niños. Y El Periódico de Aragón también cuenta cómo atravesó las calles en plenas fiestas.
Qué ha pasado. El primer aviso llegó a las 0:40 a la Unidad Central Operativa de la Policía Local: un jabalí corría por las calles Asalto y Jorge Cocci, junto al río Huerva y las vías del tranvía, según HOY Aragón. Hacia la una ya se movía entre la gente por zonas muy concurridas. La Policía de Zaragoza avisó a los viandantes de que tuvieran cuidado. Se movilizaron Policía Local, Policía Nacional, Bomberos y la unidad de rescate y recuperación animal para cercarlo y reconducirlo fuera de la ciudad.
La ruta. Según las fuentes policiales, el animal pasó por Aznar Molina, el Camino de las Torres, Cesáreo Alierta, la plaza de los Sitios, la calle Sanclemente, el paseo de la Independencia y la calle Coso, con parada en la plaza San Felipe, hasta llegar a la zona de bares del Casco.
Y acabó en el Jardín del Temple, un bar al que se accede por una vía bastante angosta. La hipótesis es que pudo entrar desde Las Fuentes, aunque Aragón Digital recuerda que también podría proceder de huertas, de la ribera o de pinares de la periferia.
Dentro del local. El jabalí no llegó a salir de la ciudad. En su huida entró en un local de ocio nocturno de la calle Temple, en el Casco Viejo, donde embistió a una mujer y le causó lesiones leves. Alberto Samperio, que estaba dentro, cuenta a HOY Aragón que primero creyó que era una persona caída y luego un perro, hasta que vio que era un jabalí y que la gente se apartaba asustada. El balance, dice, fue “muy heavy”.
¿Una alucinación? No todos lo vieron igual. El animal pasó frente al Höhle Club, donde esa noche pinchaba el mítico DJ Rush (una figura clave de la escena techno de Chicago). Durante un buen rato, algunos visitantes pensaron que era una alucinación.
Por suerte, y según fuentes policiales, el responsable del local ayudado por algunos clientes lograron neutralizar al animal. Después lo sacrificaron “para evitar un peligro mayor”, antes de que llegaran los agentes. El servicio de FCC retiró el cuerpo con un vehículo específico. No ha trascendido cómo se produjo la muerte ni si habrá actuaciones al respecto.
Por qué aparecen. El caso de Zaragoza no es aislado. Según El Español, que cita el censo del Gobierno de 2024, en España había 1,2 millones de jabalíes, y se preveía que la cifra se duplicara en 2025. Sus causas: el abandono del medio rural, el aumento de cultivos de regadío y las temperaturas más altas, que favorecen la reproducción.
En Barcelona, la Generalitat planeó sacrificar a 12.000 ejemplares para frenar la peste porcina africana. Los expertos consultados por Maldita explican que, cuando un jabalí identifica un recurso disponible en la ciudad, incorpora calles y carreteras a sus desplazamientos habituales.
Si te cruzas con uno. Lo mejor es no hacer nada: los jabalíes no suelen ser agresivos, salvo que estén heridos o se sientan acorralados. Conviene no hostigarlos, no intentar capturar una cría y atar o sujetar al perro si estás paseándolo. Al volante, la situación cambia, porque son la principal causa de accidentes con fauna en España. El 49%, nada menos: el año pasado se registraron casi 5.300 accidentes de tráfico con animales en 2025, un 4,5% más que en 2024, y una tercera parte eran jabalís.
Falta por saber por dónde entró realmente el jabalí y por qué no pudo reconducirse fuera de la ciudad. En cuanto a la mujer herida, se sabe que sus lesiones fueron leves. El único que acabó entrando en la fiesta y saliendo de ella con las patas por delante fue el pobre animal.

articles.title: 100 frases que no deberías mandar por WhatsApp en el Día de la Madre
articles.text:
El Día de la Madre suele llenar WhatsApp de mensajes breves, emotivos y repetidos, pero algunas frases pueden sonar impersonales, incómodas o poco cuidadas. Antes de pulsar el botón de enviar, conviene revisar el tono, evitar comparaciones y elegir palabras que expresen cercanía sin convertir el saludo en una obligación.
La fecha también impulsa mensajes enviados a toda prisa, textos copiados de cadenas o comentarios que trasladan asuntos familiares sensibles a una conversación que debería centrarse en el reconocimiento. Un saludo sencillo, personal y respetuoso puede ser más adecuado que una frase automática o una broma fuera de lugar.
Frases que pueden sonar frías, interesadas o poco personales
- “Feliz día, mamá”.
- “Que tengas un buen día”.
- “Luego hablamos”.
- “Te escribo porque toca”.
- “No sabía qué regalarte”.
- “Espero que estés bien”.
- “Te mando este mensaje rápido”.
- “Feliz Día de la Madre a todas”.
- “Copié este texto para ti”.
- “No tenía tiempo para llamarte”.
- “Gracias por todo, supongo”.
- “Eres una buena madre”.
- “Hoy es tu día, disfrútalo”.
- “Te mando un abrazo virtual”.
- “Perdón por escribir tarde”.
- “Mañana te felicito mejor”.
- “No encontré otra imagen”.
- “Este mensaje sirve para todas”.
- “Te debía este saludo”.
- “Cumplo con felicitarte”.
- “Qué suerte tener madre”.
- “Felicidades por ser mamá”.
- “Espero que recibas regalos”.
- “Te mando flores por aquí”.
- “No te enfades, se me olvidó”.
Mensajes que convierten la fecha en un reclamo
- “¿Ya viste lo que publiqué?”.
- “¿Por qué no respondes?”.
- “Espero que me llames primero”.
- “Hoy deberías estar disponible”.
- “Mereces que te visite más”.
- “No te quejes, es tu día”.
- “Aprovecha porque hoy te toca”.
- “No esperaba menos de ti”.
- “Te felicito, aunque discutimos”.
- “Luego hablamos de lo pendiente”.
- “No olvides transferirme dinero”.
- “¿Qué vas a preparar hoy?”.
- “Espero que hayas cocinado”.
- “Hoy no quiero discutir”.
- “No menciones ese tema”.
- “No pongas mensajes tristes”.
- “No hagas drama hoy”.
- “No te pongas sensible”.
- “Tampoco es para tanto”.
- “No esperes demasiado de mí”.
- “Es solo una fecha comercial”.
- “No tengo presupuesto para regalos”.
- “Ya sabes que te quiero”.
- “No hace falta celebrarlo”.
- “Después compenso el olvido”.
Comentarios sobre apariencia, edad o vida personal
- “Te ves cansada últimamente”.
- “Ya estás mayor para eso”.
- “Deberías descansar más”.
- “Tienes que cuidarte mejor”.
- “No subas tantas fotos”.
- “No publiques esa imagen”.
- “Te falta actualizarte”.
- “Aprende a usar WhatsApp”.
- “No entiendes estas cosas”.
- “Sigues siendo muy intensa”.
- “Siempre exageras todo”.
- “Eres igual que antes”.
- “No cambies nunca, por favor”.
- “No te preocupes por envejecer”.
- “Te queda bien ser abuela”.
- “Ya deberías viajar más”.
- “Necesitas salir de casa”.
- “No te pongas esa ropa”.

articles.title: Motive Technologies revs up new AI Agents to automate fleet management - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Motive Technologies revs up new AI Agents to automate fleet management
Motive Technologies Inc. is pushing the needle for fleet management automation with the launch of a new artificial intelligence offering called Agents today.
As the name strongly hints at, Motive’s Agents are autonomous AI agents designed to take a more proactive approach to fleet operations by anticipating problems before they occur and taking action to prevent them, without constant human supervision.
San Francisco-based Motive is the developer of a comprehensive fleet management software platform for trucking companies. Its platform comes with multiple sensors that can be installed into individual vehicles, so the system can track their location, fuel levels and other data, such as the temperature of refrigerated loads – basically anything that might be useful to monitor. Those sensors send all that data back to the company’s cloud-based platform, providing tons of useful information for managers trying to keep their fleets organized.
Motive has long excelled at tracking and monitoring fleets, and says now is the time to move beyond just passive monitoring and start taking action where possible. It’s turning to AI to do that.
Fleet operations teams have unparalleled visibility into their fleets thanks to Motive’s platform, but many struggle to take action on the insights it provides quickly enough. That’s because, while data can provide those teams with warnings, it’s still up to humans to do everything else, such as chasing down and investigating alerts, calling drivers individually and verifying any fixes manually.
This problem was made clear in Motive’s recently published 2026 ROI Report, which found that 42% of its customers cite operational inefficiencies relating to administrative work as a major problem. The lag in response time can be very expensive, with Motive estimating that fleet operators lose about $46 billion annually due to issues that could, and should be prevented, such as unplanned vehicle downtime, unproductive engine idling and compliance violations.
That’s why Motive believes its new Agents can save customers an awful lot of money. The Agents are designed to do more than just flag specific problems and notify a human manager to solve them. According to Motive Chief Product Officer Hemant Banavar, they can actually predict problems will happen before they arise, and take action autonomously to ensure they don’t.
“Our customers don’t need another alert,” Banavar explained. “They need action. The data that prevents collisions and breakdowns already lives in Motive. Agents put that data to work the moment it matters, so teams can grow without adding headcount.”
Agents take action
Banavar said Motive’s existing customers will be able to deploy Agents in minutes by following a guided workflow and ready-to-use templates it has created. Once they’re set up, they’ll be able to resolve issues regarding compliance, maintenance and safety without any human involvement.
For example, if one of the Agents detects early signs of driver fatigue, it will alert Atlas, the company’s in-vehicle assistant. It will then speak to the driver and tell them it’s time to take a break, and even direct them to the nearest place where they can safely park the vehicle and rest.
That’s not all the Agents can do. They can also warn drivers of severe weather conditions before they occur. With regard to maintenance, they actively monitor each vehicle and when they spot signs of wear and tear, they can automatically create a work order and mark the vehicle as being out of service while it’s being repaired. In every case, customers will be able to specify the exact conditions that would trigger a maintenance order.
Motive’s Agents can also help fleets to save on money that’s wasted to engine idling, which burns through fuel and wears down engines over time. The company will flag excessive idling when it occurs and prompt the driver through AI Dashcam Plus to shut the engine down. It takes into account ambient temperature conditions too, so drivers who are purposely idling the engine to keep the air conditioner or heater running won’t be penalized for doing so.
Existing customers can access and deploy the Agents starting from today, and this is just the start, Banavar said. The company is planning to bring much greater autonomy to fleet operators in future. Early next year, it will enhance Agents with a new feature that allows teams to create their own Agents simply by describing the task they need them to do.
Ultimately, Motive wants to take automation to such an extreme that a fleet operator can simply tell it what their specific business objectives are, Banavar said. When customers set a simple goal, such as “more on-time deliveries” or “fewer collisions,” the Agents will determine the best way to achieve that objective and issue the necessary instructions to get it done.

articles.title: Hands on: The Ugreen HomeAgent HA100 delivers local AI in a new and curious form
articles.text:
Early Verdict
Part of me wonders why they didn’t just add voice and vision to an existing NASync model, but adding PoE ports and a modular accelerator lets this hardware go beyond that. How useful this is to you depends on how far down the AI rabbit hole you’ve already gone and how rapidly this platform evolves.
Reasons to buy
- + Made for AI
- + Four PoE LAN ports
- + Inbuilt microphone
- + Can run Qwen 3.5 out of the box
Reasons to avoid
- - Only RAID 0 and 1
- - No upgrade paths
- - PoE is only 10/100
- - Local AI is underwhelming so far
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Rather than a review, this is a ‘hands-on’ since the HomeAgent hardware isn't in retail channels yet.
So much has happened since it's difficult to comprehend that Ugreen only sold its first NAS in 2021 exclusively in China, but its global retail products only arrived in 2024.
Since the initial five NASync models, we’ve seen the incredible iDX6011, HD products, GT series updates for the DXP machines, Pro series additions, and a new DXP8800 Ultra that I covered recently.
Now, alongside those thirteen NAS devices, Ugreen has taken another branch and created the HomeAgent series. It combines some of the development path of the UGOS Pro, a basic NAS hardware platform, with a device that’s made to create a bubble of AI away from the internet to handle a variety of agentic tasks.
Initially available only via pre-order and Kickstarter, with a retail release in early 2027, there are three models: HomeAgent HA100 reviewed here, the HA100 Pro for those who want more AI performance, and the MasterAgent MA100 that pushes local AI power to the max.
Alongside the HomeAgent devices, Ugreen has also created a collection of peripheral devices, including three AI-connected cameras, a smart speaker, and a connected colour E-Paper picture frame.
While the launch ecosystem may seem modest, Ugreen will likely expand this collection in the near future.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
These systems are designed to address issues that smart home (or business) users face when technology is so fragmented. Typically, people have components from different brands, Google and Amazon, alongside peripherals made by others, and they try to bring it together using a platform like Home Assistant run on a NAS or dedicated PC.
The Ugreen HomeAgent takes all that technology and control, adds AI components that will still work even if the internet isn’t functional and distils it into an attractive white plastic box.
Instead of needing regular attention, the AI in the HomeAgent is meant to run the NAS and connected peripherals without intervention, and it can tell you if a problem is beyond its ability to address.
Asus Ascent GX10: Price and availability
- How much does it cost? From $799
- When is it out? Available for pre-order, shipping in February 2027
- Where can you get it? Via Kickstarter
Ugreen has offered some amazing deals when launching NAS on Kickstarter, and this hardware is no exception.
The HA100 costs only $799 at the pre-launch early-bird price, down from a $1,599 MSRP. Conversely, the HA100 Pro is $2,699 on a $5,399 MSRP, and the MA100 is $9,999 on a $19,999 MSRP.
The Kickstarter initiates on November 17th, but Ugreen is taking reserve deposits before then, where you get a 50% discount on the HA100, HA100 Pro and MA100.
After the Kickstarter is launched, early bird pricing will be 40% off, and presumably full MSRP will be the norm after February 2027, when the Kickstarter ends.
To get those prices, you need a $50 reserve deposit for the HA100 and HA100 Pro, and a $200 deposit for the MA100. As an additional sweetener, Ugreen is bundling the SynCare ID500 Pro camera with the HA100 and HA100 Pro (MSRP $149) and four 8TB NAS drives with the MA100, which must easily be worth another $1200.
The HA100 pricing is for a NAS with only three HDD bays and 16GB of RAM. That said, it includes an AI accelerator, which makes it hard to compare to Ugreen’s DXP and iDCX series machines.
Therefore, if you are primarily looking for a NAS, then this might not be the product range for you; if you are more interested in AI, it might be.
I should also mention the high-end MA100, which I believe has four drive bays and is built around an NVIDIA accelerator. Considering it was possible a few months ago to get an NVIDIA DGX Spark system for around $3000, that does seem pricey, but it should offer similar performance.
However, the ASUS Ascent GX10 I was referring to now costs twice as much, and that’s for a machine with 128GB of RAM, whereas the MA100 has 256GB. So, at the Kickstarter price, the MA100 might be a bargain.
What I can say with some certainty is that no other NAS brand is making anything remotely like this right now, although there is some overlap with the DXG Spark platforms.
Ugreen HomeAgent HA100: Specs
| Item | Spec | 
| HomeAgent Model: | HA100 | 
| CPU: | Rockchip RK3588 (8 Cores, 4x Cortex-A76 + 4x Cortex-A55 | 
| GPU: | ARM Mali-G610 MP4 | 
| NPU: | Rockchip RK1828 (6 TOPS) Ugreen AI Accelerator T20, RK1228, 5GB (20TOPS) | 
| RAM: | 16GB LPDDR5 (not expandable) | 
| Internal Storage: | 64GB eMMC for UGOS Pro | 
| SATA Storage: | 3x 3.5/2.5-inch SATA III (2x NAS, 1x Surveilance Drive) | 
| M.2 Storage: | 1x M.2 NVMe PCIe Gen 3 x1 | 
| Ports: | 1x USB-C 3.2 Gen 1 (5Gbps) | 
|  | 2x USB-A 3.2 Gen 1 (5Gbps) | 
|  | 1x HDMI 2.0b | 
|  | 1x SD 3.0 slot (front) | 
| Networking: | 1x 2.5GbE RJ45 4x PoE 10/100Mbps (Max power 65W) | 
| Wireless: | Thread 1.4 ZigBee 3.0 Bluetooth 6.0 Bluetooth 5.3 | 
| OS: | UGOS Pro | 
| File Systems: | EXT4, Btrfs | 
| Maximum Capacity: | 68TB (2x 30TB SATA) + 1x 8TB M.2) | 
| RAID Modes: | JBOD/Basic/RAID 0/RAID 1 | 
| Microphone: | Omnidirectional 4-microphone array | 
| Speakers: | 2x 5W | 
| PSU: | 20V 9A 180W external | 
| Power Consumption: | 42.36 W (drive access), 18.12 W(drive hibernation) | 
| Dimensions: | 192 x 218 x 251mm (LxWxH) | 
| Weight: | 520g (including PSU and drives) | 
| Warranty: | 2 Years | 
Ugreen HomeAgent HA100: Design
- Large enclosure
- PoE switch inside
- Three HDD bays, dual-function storage
The first thing that strikes you about the HA100 is how much bigger it is than a typical four-bay NAS, like the DXP4800 Pro or Plus.
Standing about 218mm high and 251mm deep, this is a large, shiny white box that feels substantial when you pull it from its packaging.
On the top front is a wide OLED panel, which I think is the same one that I saw on the iDX6011 Pro, but on its side. This acts as both a touch-sensitive menu and can also display various useful information.
Just above this on the left is a volume rocker, and to the right is a microphone mute, which hints that you can talk to this device, or rather the AI running on it.
The front face also has a single USB-C port and an SD card slot; the USB-C is 3.2 Gen 1 (5Gbps), and the SD card reader is SD 3.0 spec. And just below them is an LED that projects different colours to indicate whether there is a problem or all is well.
On the back, there are two USB-A ports, both 5Gbps, a single 2.5GbE RJ45 LAN port and a four-port PoE 10/100Mbps (Max power 65W) switch. That last feature matters for the unit's surveillance function, since you can directly connect and power PoE cameras.
Finally, we come to drive bays, and the HA100 isn’t quite like anything else Ugreen has made so far, though it has minor similarities to the DH4300 in that it’s a top loader.
The top of the HA100 is magnetically attached, making it easily removed to reveal four bays, with three for hard drives and one for an AI accelerator. These are all lockable and colour-coded. The drives have plastic tool-less cradles if you use 3.5-inch media, and screws if you insist on 2.5-inch HDDs.
But what genuinely surprised me is that two of the HDD bays are allocated to NAS storage, and one, coloured purple, is meant to hold a surveillance-tailored drive. I’ve never seen that predefined on a NAS before, but it does reveal one way that Ugreen envision the HA100 being used.
On the underside of the unit, there is also a removable panel that provides access to an M.2 NVMe PCIe Gen 3 x1 slot, which can be used for caching or a high-performance drive for AI models. You are recommended to use it for the latter.
I won’t be tempted to say the HA100 breaks the NAS mould, but it certainly strays off the beaten NAS path, and in some truly interesting ways.
Ugreen HomeAgent HA100: Features
- ARM SoC
- T20 accelerator
- M.2 and PCIe slots
- No upgrade path in series
Given how many newer Ugreen NAS designs use mobile Intel platforms, it seems odd that none of the HomeAgent hardware uses them.
Even more curiously, the three machines (HA100, HA100 Pro, and MA100) all use different ARM SoCs, completely eliminating any consistency.
Of these, the Rockchip RK3588 in the HA100 is the most recognisable, since it's an Armv8.2-A platform with four each of Cortex-A76 plus and Cortex-A55 cores, much like is often found in phones or tablets.
The HA100 Pro is rocking more cores with an Armv9.2-A platform, the 12-core CIX P1 CP8180. SoC diversity is completed with the MA100 that uses a fourteen-core NVIDIA Jetson Thor T5000.
Similarly, GPU power scales by level, starting with the Arm Mali-G610 MC4 on the HA100, moving to the Arm Immortalis-G720 MC10 on the HA100 Pro, and ending with the 2,560-core NVIDIA Blackwell GPU with 5th-generation Tensor Cores on the MA100. This helps explain why MA100 hardware costs so much, but it's hardly a smooth power ramp.
When the CPU, GPU, and NPU all work on an AI task, the HA100 has an advertised total AI performance of 26 TOPS (6 TOPS platform, 20 TOPS T20 accelerator).
That’s actually not enough to run CoPilot locally on a PC, but it can still run some LLM models adequately. But the total performance of the Pro model with an as-yet-unnamed accelerator is a much more sprightly 205 TOPS, and the MA100, as you might expect, has up to 2,070 FP4 sparse TFLOPS.
So, in summary, for AI, it scales 10x and then 1000x, approximately. Those are not exactly incremental jumps.
It also makes the HA100 look decidedly underpowered, although the Kickstarter entry-level pricing does make it attractive to someone who wants to explore local AI.
What confuses me is that HA100 or HA100 Pro owners have no upgrade path, since the systems aren’t interchangeable in any way. As I assume you can’t put the accelerator from the HA100 Pro in the HA100, what was the point of having the accelerators removable? And why make the MA100 the only one with four bays?
Surely, if all the cases were the same, Ugreen could redirect production more easily than it does now?
I understand that part of the purpose of using Kickstarter in this instance isn’t about funding; it's about getting indicators of demand for each model. But if you’ve already made too many black four-bay MA100 cases for demand, it's too late to repurpose them for the HA100 Pro. But then Ugreen already undermined that flexibility with the three-bay designs.
And, here’s the real rub. If you get a low-profile RTX 460 video card and mount it in one of the DXP or iDX machines, then that can generate 242 TOPS of AI processing, making that NAS more powerful than the HA100 Pro. How well that would work in reality is debatable, and I’ve never tried it, but the issue is obvious if you look at the costs.
In a similar vein, the MA100 is up against DXG Spark systems. But all of those I’ve seen come with dual 10GbE LAN ports, not one and four 1GbE PoE ports. But critically, the DXG systems also have the Nvidia ConnectX-7 SmartNIC on them, which is a 200GbE network connection designed to fuse two DXG systems into a single platform.
The MA100 doesn’t have this port, I assume, and therefore, unless Ugreen releases an accelerator upgrade, moving from Blackwell to Vera Rubin when it arrives, then there isn’t an upgrade path here either.
Coming back to the HA100, the basis for my experience so far, the T20 accelerator on this machine is modest, yet it took up most of the free PCIe lanes, leaving only a single lane for the M.2 slot, once all the other ports were covered.
Given the price, I think it should have shared an architecture with the DXP4800 Pro, or better, and maybe had either dual M.2 slots, Gen 3 x4 or a single Gen4 x4 slot. Because Gen3 x1 is only 1000MB/s, and external devices on this machine can go that quickly.
I guess, based on the number of pledges they get, Ugreen will know whether the performance ramp from the HA100 to the HA100 Pro and the MA100 was right or wrong.
My feeling, and it’s a gut reaction, is that all the systems should have shared the same enclosure, the HA100 should have been more powerful, and there should have been more consideration given to a potential upgrade path, at least from the HA100 to the HA100 Pro.
Ugreen HomeAgent HA100: Software
- UGOS Pro
- Local Gwen 3.5
- Smart Home
The hardware in this series is effectively done, and I’d be massively surprised if anything changes between the machines reviewers received and what ultimately arrives for those on Kickstarter and in later retail.
That leaves the software side of the equation, and it isn’t at the same stage of production, even if it is underpinned by the same UGOS Pro platform as all the DH, DXP, and iDX NAS Ugreen has already launched.
However, at the time of writing, my DXP8800 Plus workhorse is running UGOS Pro 1.20.0.0142 and the HomeAgent HA100 is on 1.20.0.0127 Beta.
That might not seem hugely different, but there are significant differences between the two, so much that the HomeAgent machine needs a special version of the mobile application to even be accessible.
It seems reasonable to assume that closer to retail release, all the extra functionality needed for HomeAgent will be settled into the latest general-purpose UGOS Pro release, rather than it spawning a whole new separate OS.
The biggest difference anyone who has used UGOS Pro will notice is that you can’t access this version from a web interface, although Ugreen has promised that in a future update.
Using it from the mobile app doesn’t limit what you can control, but it's nice to use the web interface when it's available.
It’s a generalisation, but the NAS side of the HomeAgent is practically identical to that in prior Ugreen NAS, where you can install apps, manage the drives and data. Obviously, in this configuration with only two data drives, you can’t configure a RAID 5 pack, but you can configure RAID 0 or 1, and you can create backups to another NAS.
The app selection is mostly the same as that on the standard NAS, with a couple of special function apps that bind the T20 accelerator into the system and an IoT Gateway that are loaded by default. What’s genuinely interesting is how some of the apps we’ve seen before on UGOS Pro now have added significance in this context.
The one that stands out most is Model Manager, since the whole AI function of this system is built around a locally run AI on this app using Docker as a subsystem. By default, the system loads the LLM Qwen 3.5 4B.
This 4B model is a sensible fit for this hardware, as being quantised, it occupies only a few gigabytes, which leaves plenty of the 16GB for the operating system and camera analysis running alongside it. Anything much larger would start to squeeze this box.
To try and make things as efficient as possible, the model has modules that you can either install or not depending on if you want it to recognise people, pets or even the appearance of a parcel. As these features infer, it works closely with Surveillance Centre and the new camera peripherals.
It can also link to Smart Home functionality, enabling it to turn things on and off, like lights and also read temperature and security sensors.
The HomeAgent box and some of the peripherals, such as the SynCare cameras and the Smart Speaker, allow you to verbally interact with an AI assistant, Uliya.
And frankly, this is where things need some considerable work. While the hardware in the HA100 can process 40 or more tokens a second, I’d hardly describe it as conversational.
It can alert you when someone is approaching the house, has left a package, or where a known person is in the home, but ask it anything more complicated, and it often says it can’t do that yet.
While I’ve not tried the HA100 Pro or the MA100, I’d assume they can run much more sophisticated LLMs with greater capabilities, but the AI component of the basic system is more agentic-focused than something like ChatGPT.
That said, you can plug a Cloud-based AI in alongside Qwen 3.5. The current options are OpenAI (ChatGPT), Qwen, MiniMax, DeepSeek, GLM and Kimi, and you will need an API key to plug those in.
However, Ugreen made it clear that the purpose of the HomeAgent was to provide a local AI that wasn’t dependent on the internet, so using a Cloud model undermines that assertion.
Obviously, the engineers can do plenty with the local Qwen 3.5 4B model to make it more interactive and able to handle a wider range of scenarios, but at this point in development, it is rather underwhelming.
The other part of this solution that needs considerable effort is the Smart Home app, since currently it only connects to the associated Ugreen peripherals or Matter-compliant devices.
Since all my home automation hardware is older and doesn’t use Matter, that’s a problem.
I did consider using the Matter Hub on my Home Assistant installation to make non-Matter hardware visible, but the way this is handled on the HA100 requires either a Matter QR code or pairing number. At a minimum, this needs to be expanded to include older Google and Amazon equipment, as well as popular brands like Tapo, SmartLife, and Hue.
I’m sure these things will be added, but unless you have Matter hardware or Ugreen peripherals, it's a bit of a technological desert right now. Once these items become part of this ecosystem, you can easily build automations and interact with Uliya to control them, or that’s the promise.
For my assessment, Ugreen provided two peripherals: the SynCare ID500 Pro and the SynCare OD600 Pro. If you didn’t connect the dots, ID is for indoors and OD is for outdoors.
The ID500 Pro, which you can get for only $89 as part of the Kickstarter offering, comes for free with the HA100 and HA100 Pro. This device gets power via USB and comes with a phone-style power source and a long USB cable.
Equipped with a 4K camera on a smooth pan-tilt tracking system that enables it to follow movement automatically across a room or even outdoors. Working with AI, it can identify people, vehicles, pets, and packages, and record those events on the HomeAgent for later review.
The only issue I ran into was that I put it in a window to cover anyone approaching, and it did that well, but at night, when it turned on its IR lights for night vision, it blinded itself with the IR reflection off the glass.
Undoubtedly, a superior option for tracking outside activity is the OD600 Pro, which is designed to be mounted outside, ideally on the eaves of a property. It has dual cameras and takes its power from a PoE LAN connection, allowing it to be directly connected with a single LAN cable to the HomeAgent PoE switch. A more advanced version, the OD800 Pro, includes a solar panel and battery to power the camera and can use Wi-Fi, so it can be installed without cabling.
I'm slightly disappointed the PoE ports are only 10/100 and not gigabit or even 2.5GbE, but that's a choice Ugreen made.
As part of the launch, the OD600 Pro can be had for $159 (MSRP $269) and the OD800 Pro for $199 (MSRP $339), which, given their specifications and build quality, seems a good deal. Hopefully, the devices will also work with an ordinary Ugreen NAS at some point, because they don’t currently.
Having been part of the original DXP NAS launch, HomeAgent has a strong element of things repeating themselves. However, since UGOS Pro has had two or more years of development, the underlying platform is more mature.
Updates for the extra HomeAgent part of this package are arriving often, and things are improving, but with the Kickstarter about to officially begin, and its end a few months away, this solution needs to become much more sophisticated quickly.
Today, it’s another Ugreen work in progress, but UGOS Pro was one not so long ago.
Ugreen HomeAgent HA100: Early verdict
First, I think it's far too early in the HA100's gestation to fully appreciate what this device might accomplish, since much of the software side of this equation isn’t nearly complete.
That said, when Ugreen first launched the NASync DXP series globally, UGOS Pro looked decidedly primitive, and two and a half years later it is much more sophisticated.
It wouldn’t be unrealistic to expect it to be much more functional by the time this hardware hits retail, and to continue rapid development from there.
Where I’m less on board is the three different platforms, each based on a unique platform and with a different accelerator.
The HA100 is built on a Rockchip RK3588, the HA100 Pro uses the CIX-CP8180(P1), which previously appeared in the Minisforum MS-R1 ARM workstation, and the MA100 is powered by the NVIDIA Jetson Thor T5000.
The problem with this range is that even if the accelerator modules are removable, there isn’t an upgrade path that can take you between these options. Had the HA100 and HA100 Pro had a common platform, that would have made sense, with the differences being in the accelerator module.
But since the accelerator on the HA100 uses a PCIe 3.0 slot, and the one on the HA100 Pro uses a PCIe 4.0 slot, then that was never going to work.
Unfortunately, upgrading forces you to buy an entirely new machine if you want more AI power.
I also have some negative feelings about having a NAS for home use with the potential of a $20,000 price tag. But that version's future depends on a company now utterly dependent on the AI bubble not bursting, which seems, at best, unrealistic.
I’ve been a big supporter of what Ugreen has done with its NAS products; since before they arrived on the scene, things seemed disturbingly cosy between the various NAS brands.
The HomeAgent is their most ambitious leap yet, since it glues two elements together in a way few users are considering until now. People who like NAS understand what it offers and how it's used, whereas AI has unresolved PR issues, a less defined use case, and users who are either negative or, at best, agnostic about AI.
The HA100 is a product Ugreen created to elevate NAS with AI, but it could just as easily drag it down. Only time will tell, but for those who want to ride, the tickets start at $50 for a reservation.
To crystallise my thoughts, there are two ways to think about HomeAgent hardware, and I’m not inclined to favour either. One is that these represent a new hybrid type of appliance where AI and local information come together, creating new efficiencies and fewer dependencies on external services. Or, from this point onwards, all NAS will have a shell of AI logic around them, and the era of dumb NAS will soon be behind us.
Either way, the NAS market needs to buckle up, because this ride could get bumpy.

Mark is an expert on 3D printers, drones and phones. He also covers storage, including SSDs, NAS drives and portable hard drives. He started writing in 1986 and has contributed to MicroMart, PC Format, 3D World, among others.
What is a hands on review?
Hands on reviews' are a journalist's first impressions of a piece of kit based on spending some time with it. It may be just a few moments, or a few hours. The important thing is we have been able to play with it ourselves and can give you some sense of what it's like to use, even if it's only an embryonic view. Points forts
- Format qui gagne (encore) en finesse.
- Affichage lumineux.
- De la puissance sans surchauffe.
- Charge (enfin) rapide.
Points faibles
- Téléobjectif un peu faiblard la nuit.
- Certification IP48 seulement.
- Pas de compatibilité S Pen.
Plus fin, plus puissant mais également plus cher, le Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra profite de deux écrans très lumineux, d’une pliure discrète, d’un volet photo polyvalent, de performances remarquables et d’un multitâche maîtrisé. Son autonomie solide, sa charge améliorée et son suivi logiciel longue durée renforcent encore l’ensemble. Quelques limites subsistent, notamment l’absence de S Pen, une étanchéité perfectible et quelques logiciels préinstallés. Une évolution très aboutie, davantage fondée sur le perfectionnement que sur la révolution, réservée au nouveau format de son petit frère.

articles.title: Derrière les concerts de Céline Dion, une IA française réalise une prouesse que le public ne soupçonne pas
articles.text:
Pendant les concerts de Céline Dion à Paris, une intelligence artificielle française travaille discrètement à rendre sa voix plus claire. Développée par L-Acoustics, cette technologie promet de transformer le son des spectacles, sans remplacer les ingénieurs qui travaillent dans les coulisses.
Lorsque Céline Dion entonne My Heart Will Go On devant 35 000 spectateurs, difficile d’imaginer la débauche de technologie nécessaire pour faire entendre sa voix jusqu’au dernier rang. Entre les instruments, les cris du public et les réverbérations d’une salle gigantesque, les ingénieurs du son doivent composer avec un sacré casse-tête. Pour sa résidence parisienne, la chanteuse canadienne bénéficie pourtant d’un allié assez inattendu : une intelligence artificielle développée par l’entreprise française L-Acoustics. Invisible pour les spectateurs, elle intervient en temps réel pour débarrasser la voix des bruits parasites. Et le résultat semble avoir convaincu les professionnels qui l’utilisent.
Une intelligence artificielle pour isoler la voix de Céline Dion
Dans un reportage publié par Bloomberg, les ingénieurs du son de Céline Dion détaillent les coulisses de cette installation. Au cœur du dispositif se trouve Source Intelligence, une technologie présentée en mai dernier par L-Acoustics.
Son principe repose sur l’apprentissage automatique. Le logiciel analyse en permanence le signal capté par le micro de la chanteuse pour distinguer sa voix des sons environnants. Instruments, bruits de foule, échos ou musique provenant des enceintes peuvent ainsi être atténués avant que le signal n’arrive sur la console de mixage.
L'entreprise annonce une réduction pouvant atteindre 40 décibels pour les sons non vocaux, avec une latence inférieure à 8,5 millisecondes. Des performances communiquées par le fabricant, qui ne constituent pas des mesures indépendantes réalisées pendant les concerts parisiens. L’intérêt ne se limite pas à rendre la voix de la chanteuse canadienne plus intelligible. En réduisant les sons parasites, le système diminue également les risques de larsen.
Denis Savage, ingénieur du son de Céline Dion depuis 38 ans, compare presque cette technologie à de la magie. Son objectif reste pourtant très concret : maintenir la voix de l’artiste parfaitement audible, quels que soient les arrangements musicaux ou les mouvements sur scène.
Derrière la prouesse, le savoir-faire d’une entreprise française
Source Intelligence ne travaille pas seule. Pour les concerts parisiens, L-Acoustics a également installé ses enceintes L1, disposées de manière à mieux contrôler la propagation du son dans la salle.
Selon les ingénieurs interrogés par Bloomberg, cette configuration permet notamment de conserver un niveau sonore sur scène jusqu’à 26 décibels inférieur à celui de la zone du public. Céline Dion peut ainsi mieux distinguer les indications et la musique diffusées dans ses oreillettes, sans subir autant de retours sonores parasites. L’ensemble du dispositif audiovisuel et acoustique représente un investissement supérieur à un million d’euros. Une installation impressionnante, mais destinée à servir sur plusieurs spectacles et tournées.
Fondée en 1984 par Christian Heil, L-Acoustics s’est imposée comme une référence de la sonorisation professionnelle. L’entreprise assemble notamment ses enceintes à Marcoussis, au sud de Paris, et emploie environ 1 100 personnes. Elle prévoit d’atteindre 400 millions d’euros de chiffre d’affaires en 2027, selon les projections de sa direction.
Avec Source Intelligence, le fabricant ajoute une nouvelle dimension logicielle à son activité historique. La technologie fonctionne exclusivement avec son processeur L-ISA Processor II et ses systèmes audio professionnels. Un choix qui renforce l’intégration de ses équipements, mais qui impose aussi aux clients de rester dans son écosystème.
D'autres artistes, parmi lesquels Harry Styles, Bruno Mars, The Weeknd et Rosalía, ont également utilisé cette technologie sur scène. Reste une question : l’intelligence artificielle pourrait-elle finir par remplacer les ingénieurs du son ? Laurent Vaissié, codirecteur général de L-Acoustics, assure que ce n’est pas l’objectif. Le logiciel automatise certaines corrections, mais laisse aux professionnels les décisions artistiques et le travail de mixage.
Une utilisation de l’IA qui tranche avec les débats sur la création musicale automatisée. Ici, pas question de composer à la place des artistes ou de recréer leur voix. Le logiciel cherche simplement à faire entendre celle qui se trouve réellement sur scène. Et dans une salle remplie de dizaines de milliers de personnes, c’est déjà un joli tour de force.

articles.title: Creadoras de OnlyFans acusan a Meta de permitirle a su IA Muse lo que les prohíbe a ellas en Instagram
articles.text:
Creadoras de contenido para adultos que trabajan en OnlyFans cuestionaron a Meta por permitir que Muse, su asistente de inteligencia artificial, mantenga conversaciones explícitas con usuarios mayores de edad mientras la empresa restringe las cuentas de creadoras reales en Instagram, según reportó Wired.
Muse es un agente conversacional que Meta lanzó hace poco más de un mes y que superó los cinco millones de descargas en sus primeras semanas. Además de organizar la agenda o responder correos, el asistente acepta sostener charlas eróticas con usuarios que confirman ser adultos.
Un vocero de Meta, Daniel Roberts, justificó la política ante Wired: “Muse es una aplicación para personas mayores de 18 años que les permite tener conversaciones de adultos, si así lo eligen, usando una máquina virtual privada y segura a la que solo ellas acceden”. Agregó que la herramienta “no bloquea un comportamiento adulto legal”.
Cuál es la molestia de las creadoras de OnlyFans
Vanniall, una creadora de OnlyFans radicada en Nueva York con más de 100 mil seguidores en Instagram, le dijo a Wired que su cuenta permanece restringida pese a no infringir ninguna norma. “No es justo que ellos puedan sacarle dinero a la gente con su agente de IA sexualmente activo, mientras no dejan que personas reales, adultas, tengan ningún tipo de sensualidad”, sostuvo.
Las normas comunitarias de Meta para Instagram y Facebook prohíben el lenguaje explícito que describa genitales, estados de excitación o encuentros, según documentó el sitio Mashable tras reproducir intercambios con Muse que incluyeron justamente ese tipo de contenido.
Otra vocera de Meta, Tracy Clayton, respondió a esa contradicción: “Una conversación privada y uno a uno entre un adulto y un agente de IA individualizado, en una plataforma restringida a mayores de 18 años, es muy distinta de la comercialización y promoción de servicios en una red social”, dijo a Wired.
Un reclamo que viene de antes
Jiz Lee, quien administra una cuenta de OnlyFans, remarcó que Instagram le marcó publicaciones para su eliminación en el pasado. Para Lee, buena parte de la censura actual a creadores se originó en la ley FOSTA-SESTA, firmada en 2018 durante el primer gobierno de Donald Trump, que modificó las protecciones legales de las plataformas de internet.
Lee también reclamó más información sobre el entrenamiento de Muse y si algún creador fue compensado por el uso de sus datos. “Hemos sido lentos para reaccionar como industria”, admitió ante Wired.
Tony Genius, otro creador de OnlyFans que también participa en películas para adultos, contó que en eventos de la industria las publicidades de agentes de IA suelen ser abucheadas por el público. Le preocupa que el contenido para adultos generado íntegramente por inteligencia artificial termine desplazando a los intérpretes humanos.
Genius cuestionó por qué Meta reservó Muse para mayores de edad en lugar de abrir un espacio equivalente para creadores reales. “Podría ser algo como Instacam”, propuso, en referencia a una versión de Instagram pensada específicamente para contenido adulto de personas verificadas.
Cómo funciona la verificación de edad
Para usar Muse, la compañía exige fecha de nacimiento y bloquea el registro de menores, además de cruzar la información con eventuales cuentas vinculadas de Facebook o Instagram. Cuando no hay señales claras de que el usuario es adulto, Meta pide verificar una tarjeta de crédito, aunque la empresa asegura que no guarda esos datos ni realiza ningún cobro.
Muse genera texto explícito pero no imágenes ni videos, a diferencia de otras herramientas de IA generativa que sí producen contenido visual sexual. Meta mantiene, por ahora, la distinción entre lo que permite puertas adentro de una conversación privada con el asistente y lo que prohíbe en las vidrieras públicas de Instagram y Facebook.

articles.title: Axonius launches AI Workforce virtual workers as AI Companion and MCP Server go live - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Axonius launches AI Workforce virtual workers as AI Companion and MCP Server go live
Asset intelligence company Axonius Inc. today added Axonius AI Workforce to its Asset Cloud platform to let security teams hand ongoing remediation work to autonomous, artificial intelligence-powered virtual workers.
AI Workforce is meant to take over follow-up work that security teams rarely have time for. A lot of that work exists because asset data ends up split across dozens of tools, and the scheduled jobs most teams rely on only catch conditions somebody thought to define ahead of time. Anything outside those rules is left for a person to sort out, Axonius says, down to working out why a single endpoint agent stopped reporting.
Two tools Axonius announced in July also moved to general availability today. The Axonius AI Companion takes plain-language questions about a customer’s environment and can act on the answer in the same conversation, opening a ticket or tagging devices when asked. Outside AI tools and agents get at the same asset data through the Axonius MCP Server, which runs over the Model Context Protocol.
The virtual workers at the center of the launch come in more than 50 types, covering security outcomes that include exposure triage, shadow AI and readiness for post-quantum cryptography. Every worker tracks a metric tied to its outcome, which is meant to save teams from building custom reports to see if anything is improving. When an asset drifts from the state it should be in, the worker responsible for it carries out the fix, and the results feed a Daily Digest that Axonius ranks by urgency.
A mode setting controls how far a worker goes on its own, and Axonius recommends a starting mode for each job based on its own best practices. In Off mode, the worker waits for approval on everything. Teams that want to watch first can use Shadow mode to preview what the worker would do, then switch to Live and let it act automatically within set guardrails. Outbound messages and changes to connected systems count as sensitive and are held for approval before they execute.
Each customer also runs a private large language model instance inside its own dedicated environment, and an audit trail marks every action as either agent-driven or human-driven.
Moshe Ben Simon, chief product officer at Axonius, said every vendor is shipping AI agents now and “the question nobody is answering is what those AI agents are acting on.” An agent that acts on one vendor’s incomplete view of an asset is going to be wrong, he said.
Axonius spent years building a platform that draws on more than 1,400 bidirectional integrations, and Ben Simon described AI Workforce as what can safely be built on top of it. The company made the same data-quality argument in April, when it launched Axonius Verified Assets on the premise that AI agents act on their inputs without questioning them.
AI Workforce, the AI Companion and the MCP Server all run on the same asset model that already powers the Asset Cloud. Axonius builds it by reconciling and deduplicating data across more than 80 asset and exposure entity types. If the software can’t verify something, it is designed to say so.
Theresa Lanowitz, principal analyst for cybersecurity at Omdia, said what stands out is how directly the launch ties autonomous remediation to a verified view of the environment. She expects that pairing, plus human oversight where it matters, to separate AI that security teams “can actually trust” from tools that merely add noise.
AI Workforce is generally available to Axonius customers now. Security engineering teams can see how many AI credits their users and the virtual workers spend, and what that costs.

articles.title: Arm fits up to 23 AGI CPU servers into a 24 kW rack
articles.text:
Arm AGI CPU crushes AMD in new agentic AI benchmark — but what does its 2x rack-level performance advantage mean for the future of x86 data centers?
Arm claims a near 2x rack-level advantage over AMD
- Arm’s AGI CPU nearly doubles AMD’s modelled rack-level performance across seven workloads
- A 24-kW rack accommodates up to 23 Arm servers under the assessment’s assumptions
- Arm’s rack-level advantage reaches 3.19x in the strongest individual workload
Arm’s AGI CPU has recorded nearly twice the modelled rack-level performance of AMD’s EPYC 9755 across seven workloads designed to evaluate agentic artificial intelligence.
The assessment, conducted by Signal65 with Arm’s cooperation, compared measured processor results before estimating performance across racks operating within a fixed power budget.
The findings rely partly on power-based modelling, while testing on final production hardware remains outstanding.
Rack density gives Arm a substantial advantage
The assessment examined workloads involving software tools, autonomous task execution, information retrieval, and support for AI model serving, including Terminal-Bench 2 and SWE-bench.
Across the seven tests, Arm’s processor achieved an average performance ratio of 1.99x, with individual results ranging from 1.43x to 3.19x compared with AMD’s EPYC 9755.
The modelled advantage partly comes from differences in server power consumption, allowing more Arm systems within the same electricity allocation.
A 24 kW rack could accommodate 21 to 23 AGI CPU servers, compared with 13 dual-socket EPYC 9755 systems.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
That configuration provides between 5,712 and 5,888 physical cores for Arm, compared with 3,328 for AMD, although the comparison depends on the rated power assumptions.
Individual server power ranges from 950 to 1,050 watts for Arm’s systems, while AMD’s dual-socket configurations carry a rated consumption of 1,700 watts.
Across workload categories, Arm recorded modelled rack-level advantages averaging 1.7x for tooling, 2.0x for agentic workflows and 2.2x for reasoning and planning.
The report also estimated that database and vector-search operations could require 30% to 35% fewer racks for equivalent processing workloads.
Faster sandbox creation and the x86 challenge
Separate testing compared Arm’s processor against AMD’s EPYC 9965 using Sandbench, which measures the time required to establish isolated execution environments.
Arm completed cold starts 45% faster, warm starts 27% faster, and its worst-case scenario under fourfold oversubscription 41% faster.
These improvements matter because AI agents frequently create execution environments while accessing services, running code, and processing information.
Faster setup can reduce delays, although the results do not demonstrate equivalent gains across all applications or complete data center deployments.
Arm executive vice president for Cloud AI Mohamed Awad said, “The industry needs to measure how well systems handle the work agents actually complete,” describing the need for workload-specific performance evaluation.
The company developed its evaluation framework with support from Fujitsu, Meta and OpenAI, while Signal65 independently verified the reported processor results.
Arm also acknowledged that further testing on final production systems would cover additional workloads and competitive comparisons.
For AMD and Intel, the findings suggest that Arm-based servers could challenge x86 infrastructure in agentic AI deployments where rack power limits constrain computing capacity.
Higher rack-level performance could let operators accommodate more AI workloads within existing power allocations.
However, the benchmark does not establish that Arm will outperform x86 across general-purpose computing or justify replacing existing servers across entire data centers.
Software compatibility, deployment costs and real-world operating conditions will influence whether the modelled advantage translates into wider adoption.

articles.title: French rioters ransack eSports team premises and are seen looting RAM sticks from PCs — Team Vitality’s ‘V.Hive’ Paris HQ was wrecked during unrest
articles.text:
French rioters ransack eSports team premises and are seen looting RAM sticks from PCs — Team Vitality’s ‘V.Hive’ Paris HQ was wrecked during unrest
Reports also highlight eSports trophies being stolen, with gaming chairs being piled up in street fires.
Leading French eSports club Team Vitality has confirmed that its Paris HQ has been smashed up, with trophies, computer equipment, and more looted over the weekend. Thankfully, no team members or staff have been hurt. The team’s V.Hive premises were attacked by criminal opportunistic looters under cover of the widespread protests in France over issues related to school funding, living costs, and government spending cuts. Other shops, public buildings, and property have been smashed, looted, and sometimes burned.
Above, you can see the confirmation of the serious, unfortunate events seen over the weekend. “Our display windows were destroyed, and our trophies and computer equipment were stolen,” lamented the post [machine translation], while being thankful that no members, staff, or fans of Team Vitality were hurt. The bulletin ends with the news that the V.Hive will remain closed for now, until after damage has been assessed. More information is promised in due course.
There are a multitude of social media posts sharing images, videos, and pointing fingers at what they see as the cause of the protests, riots, and looting. Of course, fingers point in all directions, and unfortunately there are also reports of AI-generated rage-farming media, so keep a critical eye open should you dare to doom scroll.
Of course we’ve focused on the damage and looting of Team Vitality’s HQ due to the tech angle. The compendium of video clips shared by the news organization NEXTA provides evidence of the extent of the V.Hive attack. This 30-second clip appears to show rioters hammering at and kicking in the eSports HQ’s windows, taking items from the premises, and throwing gaming chairs onto bonfires in the street.
We also see accounts like ElBuni share clips of looters brandishing what appear to be eSports trophies from Team Vitality’s HQ (embedded above). The second clip shows looters with their hands inside gaming PCs opened up on the sidewalk. It looks like the hooded and gloved looter in the video is removing RAM sticks, an easily pocketable yet highly valuable PC component, as you will all know.
This morning, the French Prime Minister has called for local and partial curfews to contain the post-demonstration rioting. Meanwhile, there are concerns that there could be copycat behavior across Europe.

Points faibles
- Formule qui peine à se renouveler.

Son écran est excellent, ses performances tiennent largement la route, son interface reste aussi complète que durable, et l’autonomie progresse malgré le retour de la puce Exynos. La partie photo se montre elle aussi convaincante. On regrette en revanche l’absence de véritable innovation, tant sur le plan matériel qu’esthétique. Le bloc photo et la nouvelle puce maison figurent parmi les principales évolutions, ce qui paraît un peu maigre et interroge sur l’intérêt de renouveler la série à ce rythme, année après année. Reste au final un haut de gamme très abouti, agréable au quotidien et sans réel faux pas, peut-être un peu trop sage pour vraiment surprendre.
