articles.title: The science of deep sleep and how Duroflex Airboost helps you get more of it
articles.text:
The science of deep sleep and how Duroflex Airboost helps you get more of it
India’s newest sleep technology is designed to enhance the N3 stage, the body’s repair shift, for better recovery, immunity, and stress resilience.
You can get enough sleep and still not get enough recovery.
We obsess over sleep duration, the “eight hours” metric, but duration alone doesn't tell the whole story. What matters just as much is depth. Deep sleep is the stage where the body does its heaviest lifting: repairing tissue, consolidating memory, and resetting the hormones that govern everything from appetite to stress. Yet for a growing number of people, deep sleep is the first thing to go missing, even when total sleep time looks normal on paper.
The different stages of sleep
Sleep isn't a single, uniform state. It cycles through distinct stages roughly every 90 minutes, each with a different job.
Light sleep (N1 and N2) acts as the transition zone; the body slows down, heart rate drops, and brain activity shifts into slower rhythms. This stage makes up the bulk of a typical night, but it's largely preparatory.
Deep sleep, or N3 stage (also called slow-wave sleep), is where the real restorative work happens. Brain waves slow dramatically, blood pressure and breathing reach their lowest points, and the body redirects energy toward physical repair, regenerating muscle, strengthening the immune system, and clearing metabolic waste from the brain.
Growth hormone release peaks during this stage, which is why it's often called the body's “repair shift”,
Rapid Eye Movement(REM) sleep stage follows, associated more with dreaming and cognitive processing than physical recovery.
Crucially, deep sleep is front-loaded into the first half of the night. If you go to bed late, cut sleep short, or microawake multiple times during your sleep, you disproportionately lose N3 stage, even if your total hours stay roughly the same.
When eight hours still isn’t enough
If you’re usually sleep-deprived, you don’t get to know it right away, since it doesn't show itself with obvious symptoms. Most of these symptoms are considered normal and ignorable, like sluggish mornings, feeling tired, and being unproductive.
But the sleep debt compounds, and it can affect your physical recovery, leading to muscle soreness, joint stiffness, and lingering fatigue. It can also affect your overall immunity, since much of the body’s repair and defence activity happens mostly during the N3 stage.
Without enough N3 stage in every sleep cycle, it becomes harder to regulate your hormones, including the balance of cortisol and growth hormone, which can affect stress resilience, appetite, and long-term metabolic health. Your cognitive sharpness also takes a hit, since deep sleep (N3 stage) also plays a role in clearing metabolic wastes from the brain overnight.
Heat discomfort, spinal misalignment, and micro-awakenings during the night can prevent the body from settling into and staying in N3, even across a full eight hours in bed.
Many people don’t realise that the frustrating part isn’t always how many hours you sleep, but how much of the right kind of sleep you’re actually getting.
Where Duroflex Airboost mattress comes in
Duroflex Airboost was engineered specifically to support quicker sleep onset and deeper sleep, positioning itself as India's newest sleep technology built around this problem.
Airboost is Duroflex's proprietary open-matrix mattress technology, built from over one lakh independently responsive fibres designed to improve airflow, movement response, and postural support.
Trusted by athletes around the world, this sleep technology is brought to Indiab for the first time by Duroflex. Airboost is accredited by the Indian Society for Sleep Research (ISSR) and recommended by doctors at the National Health Academy (NHA).
Three features built around deep sleep
1. Pressure relief from postural support
Rather than offering uniform support across the body, the mattress uses hyperlocal support built from over one lakh+ AirKnit fibres, distributing pressure according to the body's actual contours. You get the right kind of postural alignment for all types of sleepers as the individual fibres easily support every tiny pressure point across your body.
Misalignment and pressure build-up at the shoulders and hips are a common reason sleepers wake or shift position before completing a full deep-sleep cycle; proper medium-firm support like this addresses the issue at the source rather than masking it with extra foam cushioning.
2. An open-matrix core for breathability
Airboost features a 3D open-cell matrix made up of roughly 90% air, creating continuous airflow throughout the mattress that helps dissipate heat and sweat more effectively, keeping sleepers closer to a thermoneutral zone for cooler, deeper sleep. Airboost is 3X more breathable than traditional mattresses on the market.
Since body temperature naturally needs to drop to initiate and sustain deep sleep, a surface that actively supports heat dissipation removes one of the most common, and least discussed, barriers to N3 sleep.
3. Energy restoration
Each Airboost fibre responds instantly to the pressure placed on it, providing maximum rebound that makes turning and changing positions effortless. This way, the body’s energy is conserved for overnight recovery and you get to complete full sleep cycles without micro-awakenings.
Frequent, effortful repositioning is one of the quiet disruptors of deep sleep; every restless shift is a small pull away from the N3 stage. By minimizing these and micro-awakenings, this mattress helps the body stay in deep sleep for longer, uninterrupted stretches.
Airboost is accredited by the Indian Society for Sleep Research (ISSR) for delivering 30% more deep sleep(N3 stage), and is also recommended by doctors at the National Health Academy (NHA). Rather than treating sleep as one undifferentiated block of hours, their design specifically targets enhancement of N3 sleep, the stage most essential for physical repair, stronger immunity, and stress recovery.
Final thoughts
The conversation around sleep is shifting, from counting hours to increasing sleep stages. Deep sleep isn't a luxury metric; it's the mechanism behind physical recovery, immune resilience, and hormonal balance. As awareness grows, so does scrutiny of the products claiming to support it. Duroflex Airboost, a combination of engineered airflow, responsive movement support, and clinically backed deep-sleep enhancement, reflects a broader shift in the mattress category, one where design decisions are increasingly expected to be measured, not just marketed.

articles.title: Encore plus fort que la 4K : ce TV Neo QLED Samsung de 65" affiche fièrement de la 8K à 120 Hz et un prix en baisse de 265 € — Frandroid
articles.text:
En 2025, Samsung sortait sa gamme de TV QN900F qui a la particularité d’afficher non pas de la 4K, mais bien de la 8K. L’image gagne en finesse, et la marque coréenne reprend le traitement antireflet de ses écrans OLED sur une dalle LCD Neo QLED particulièrement lumineuse. Une technologie qui, mine de rien, change la donne dans les environnements lumineux. Clairement, sa place est dans un salon baigné de lumière plutôt que dans une chambre. Autre bon point, son processeur NQ8 AI Gen2 dopé à l’IA se charge de mettre à l’échelle en 8K tous les contenus qui ne sont pas dans cette définition.
Pourquoi choisir le Samsung 65QN900F
- Pour son revêtement Glare Free qui élimine la quasi-totalité des reflets gênants
- Pour la luminosité de son rétroéclairage Mini LED, adaptée aux pièces très éclairées
- Ses prestations gaming avec 4 ports HDMI 2.1 et support de la 4K jusqu’à 165 Hz
Sur Son-Vidéo.com, le Samsung TQ65QN900F est affiché à 2 649 euros. Mais avec le code HAL10 sur le site, il passe à 2 384,10 euros dans le panier.
Si, par la suite, l’offre mentionnée dans cet article n’est plus disponible, merci de jeter un coup d’œil ci-dessous afin de dénicher d’autres offres concernant le Samsung TQ65QN900F. Le tableau s’actualise automatiquement.
Un design repensé et des performances de haut vol
Si vous connaissez un peu les TV de chez Samsung, vous constaterez que ce TQ65QN900F est un modèle qui s’inspire grandement de la gamme The Frame. Ici, la marque assume un cadre biseauté en aluminium de 1,3 centimètre d’épaisseur, plutôt que de faire la course à l’invisibilité des bords. Il se pose sur des pieds avec un système de clips, avec deux positions en largeur pour s’adapter à tous les meubles, et deux hauteurs pour glisser une barre de son. C’est juste dommage qu’on ne profite pas du boîtier déporté One Connect, pourtant présent sur la génération QN900D. Toute la connectique réintègre le dos de la dalle, ce qui épaissit le téléviseur et demande un peu de gestion de câbles.
Pour l’affichage, ce TV repose sur une dalle LCD de type VA avec un filtre Quantum Dot et un rétroéclairage Mini LED. Une technologie qui n’éradique pas totalement le blooming autour des objets clairs, mais qui propose une bonne dynamique globale. Les pics de luminosité permettent d’exploiter pleinement les formats HDR10+ Adaptive et Gaming, bien que Samsung continue de bouder le Dolby Vision. Si vous êtes un gamer, vous y trouverez votre compte avec quatre ports HDMI 2.1 qui acceptent la 4K jusqu’à 165 Hz (depuis un PC, les consoles plafonnant à 120 Hz) et la 8K jusqu’à 60 Hz. Pour le reste, on retrouve l’arsenal habituel avec le VRR, le FreeSync Premium Pro et le Gaming Hub si vous êtes adepte du cloud gaming.
L’IA aux commandes de l’interface
Le TV fonctionne sous Tizen, dans sa version One UI 2025, qui est plutôt fluide et bien fournie, même si elle n’est pas aussi généreuse en applications que Google TV. Mais ce système intègre de nombreuses fonctions poussées par l’IA, comme la traduction instantanée des sous-titres, la génération de fonds d’écran ou des recherches vocales intuitives via Bixby et Alexa. Côté son, le TV ne fait pas de figuration avec un système 4.2.2 canaux de 70 watts. Il est compatible Dolby Atmos et profite de la technologie OTS+ pour suivre les objets sonores à l’écran et renforcer l’immersion spatiale. Sans oublier la fonction Q-Symphony qui permet de synchroniser le son du TV et d’une barre de son Samsung pour plus de profondeur.
Ce TV a tout de même ses compromis. Malgré sa définition 8K, encore très rare sur le marché, il se contente du processeur NQ8 AI Gen2 et fait l’impasse sur le NQ8 AI Gen3 réservé au QN990F, le pied central et le boîtier One Connect. C’est vraiment un téléviseur pour les technophiles avec un salon très lumineux en quête d’un rétroéclairage agressif et d’un traitement Glare Free qui fait bien son travail.
Vous pouvez retrouver nos conclusions et de nombreuses autres informations sur ce TV dans notre test complet du Samsung 65QN900F qui regorge de détails.
Si vous êtes vraiment en quête d’un écran 8K, vous pouvez consulter notre guide des meilleurs modèles de TV qui peuvent afficher cette définition.

articles.title: Cette peau intelligente pourrait rendre les jeux en réalité virtuelle plus immersifs
articles.text:
Pliez cette feuille de silicone conçue au MIT, et l’écran affiche presque aussitôt sa forme en 3D. Les trois chercheurs en génie mécanique qui l’ont fabriquée l’imaginent un jour cousue dans un vêtement de joueur, même si leur prototype est encore un objet de laboratoire.
Au MIT, les doctorants Qifan Yu et Nina Cao et la professeure assistante de génie mécanique Kaitlyn Becker ont glissé quatorze fibres optiques en caoutchouc dans une feuille de silicone de 16 centimètres de côté et de 5 millimètres d’épaisseur. Dans leur étude, l’écart entre la feuille réelle et sa copie numérique est inférieur à un demi-centimètre. Cousue dans un vêtement, ce type de feuille suivrait vos bras et vos jambes. Pour l'heure, au niveau de la précision, le Steam Frame de Valve, lancé en septembre, ne repère vos mouvements qu'avec ses caméras intégrées et ses deux manettes. PLeur algorithme calcule trop lentement pour un jeu vidéo et suit mal le poignet et le coude.
Du caoutchouc rugueux à la place du verre
Dans une fibre optique classique, la lumière est retenue dans un cœur en verre transparent par une gaine sombre. Plus la fibre se courbe, moins la lumière ressort à l’autre bout, et il suffit de mesurer cette perte pour estimer une courbure. Les chercheurs du MIT ont remplacé le verre par un caoutchouc souple et transparent, gainé de ce caoutchouc teint en noir, puis ils ont rendu rugueuse une seule face du cœur. Selon que la fibre plie vers cette face ou vers le côté lisse, la lumière diffuse plus ou moins, et l’équipe connaît à la fois le sens et l’ampleur de la flexion.
Les quatorze fibres sont réparties sur deux couches de sept. Chaque fibre reçoit la lumière d’une LED à une extrémité et aboutit à un capteur de lumière à l’autre. Les mesures sont ensuite collectées par une carte électronique externe, et l’algorithme de l’équipe les convertit en forme 3D.
En simulation, les chercheurs ont gagné davantage de précision en inclinant les fibres qu’en ajoutant des fibres. Ils ont aussi testé la panne de plusieurs d’entre elles. Avec trois fibres hors service sur quatorze, l’erreur simulée était inférieure à 0,3 centimètre, et elle était d’environ un centimètre, voire davantage, à partir de cinq.
Sur trois moules imprimés en 3D, l’écart entre la feuille réelle et sa reconstruction était compris entre 0,28 et 0,45 centimètre. « Les conceptions existantes, fondées sur des capteurs rigides, présentent des erreurs d’environ 1 à 2 centimètres », a précisé Qifan Yu, pour qui ce résultat est « au moins au niveau des technologies existantes ».
Un algorithme trop lent et des articulations mal suivies
Le MIT parle d’une reconstruction « presque en temps réel », mais les chercheurs obtiennent environ trois reconstructions par seconde dans MATLAB, en comptant l’ensemble de la chaîne de mesure et d’affichage. Sur le Steam Frame de Valve, lancé en septembre, l’image est rafraîchie jusqu’à 144 fois par seconde dans un mode encore expérimental. À ce rythme, la forme de la feuille ne changerait à l’écran qu’une fois toutes les 48 images environ. L’équipe envisage de remplacer le solveur généraliste du logiciel par un outil plus rapide.
Pour le MIT, la feuille est souple et extensible. D’après la description détaillée de l’étude publiée par Tom’s Hardware, la surface est entièrement souple, mais la feuille ne s’étire pas dans son ensemble. Au poignet et au coude, la peau s’étire, et l’algorithme de forme est mis en défaut par cet étirement. Les chercheurs ont donc estimé l’angle de ces articulations avec une méthode simplifiée. Un seul des auteurs a d’ailleurs réalisé toutes les démonstrations portées sur le corps.
La feuille est aussi sensible à une pression sur l’avant-bras, sans mesure calibrée de la force, et l’équipe traite cette détection à part du suivi de forme. Les fibres font aujourd’hui 1 millimètre d’épaisseur. Avec d’autres procédés de fabrication, les chercheurs pensent descendre à quelques dizaines de micromètres, soit moins qu’un cheveu, puis loger davantage de fibres dans un vêtement, par exemple pour suivre les progrès d’un patient en rééducation.
« Ces feuilles pourraient aider un kinésithérapeute à se rappeler et à comparer plus précisément le déroulement d’une évaluation aujourd’hui et celui d’il y a deux mois et des centaines de rendez-vous », a expliqué Kaitlyn Becker.

articles.title: Claude für alte Fernseher: So macht die KI Android-TVs wieder flott
articles.text:
Claude für alte Fernseher: So macht die KI Android-TVs wieder flott
Wer schon mehrere Jahre einen smarten Fernseher mit Android benutzt, wird das Problem sicherlich kennen. Nach dieser langen Zeit fühlt sich das Betriebssystem nicht mehr so flott wie am Anfang an. Der Android-TV startet langsam und manche Apps brauchen eine gefühlte Ewigkeit, um ihre Inhalte anzuzeigen. Doch das könnte dank eines KI-Workarounds bald ein Ende haben.
So räumt Claude bei Android-Fernsehern auf
Das Projekt stammt vom Entwickler Ansub Khan, der es kostenlos auf GitHub zur Verfügung stellt. Zunächst handelt es sich um eine Anleitung, wie du deinen alten Android-TV mit Claude Code in Verbindung bringst und die KI anweist, auf dem Fernseher aufzuräumen. Um die beiden miteinander zu verbinden, müssen Nutzer:innen erst den Entwicklermodus auf ihrem Smart-TV aktivieren, indem sie in den Geräteeinstellungen unter „Über das Gerät“ siebenmal mit der Fernbedienung die Build-Version auswählen.
Im Anschluss muss noch der USB-Debugging-Mode in den Entwickleroptionen aktiviert werden. Sobald du Claude Code oder Codex dann auf einem Laptop oder PC betreibst, der im selben Netzwerk wie der Fernseher angemeldet ist, kann die KI auf den Android-TV zugreifen. Für die Aufräumarbeiten gibt Khan einen sechsteiligen Prompt, den Claude Schritt für Schritt abarbeiten kann.
Braucht es eine KI für einen schnelleren TV?
Die KI soll zunächst eine Verbindung mit dem TV herstellen und dann alle installierten Apps auflisten. Dabei soll die KI schon Empfehlungen geben, welche Anwendungen ohne Probleme deaktiviert werden können, um mehr Speicher freizugeben. Dann kommt das entwickelte Tool zum Einsatz, das Khan auf GitHub bereitstellt. Es handelt sich um einen neuen Homescreen für Android TV, der deutlich aufgeräumter ist, Werbung blockiert und Animationen auf ein Minimum beschränkt. So soll die Performance optimiert werden.
Claude fragt bei jedem Schritt nach, ob User:innen die Änderungen wirklich vollziehen wollen. Möglich ist das laut Khan auf Fernsehern mit Android TV 9 oder höher sowie Google TV 14. Andere Systeme wie Samsungs Tizen-Betriebssystem oder webOS von LG können von dem Tool nicht beeinflusst werden. Bei Amazons Fire TVs funktioniert immerhin noch die Aufräumarbeit, aber der neue Homescreen wird blockiert.
Bevor du zur Tat schreitest, solltest du beachten, dass Claude natürlich Fehler bei der Umsetzung machen kann. Wenn du die Anleitung befolgst, handelst du also auf eine eigene Gefahr.
Tatsächlich kannst du diese Aktionen aber auch bei den meisten TVs selbst händisch vornehmen. Navigiere dazu in den Einstellungen zum App-Bereich und wähle bei den Anwendungen, die du vorerst nicht mehr benötigst, „deinstallieren“ oder „deaktivieren“ aus. Selbst der neue Homescreen lässt sich mit ein paar Handgriffen ohne KI installieren. Dafür benötigst du einen Mac oder Windows-PC mit der Android Debug Bridge. Eine genaue Anleitung dazu findest du auf der GitHub-Seite des Projekts in den FAQ unter „Can I install the home screen without AI?“.

articles.title: Ethereum: cuál es el precio de esta criptomoneda este domingo
articles.text:
Ether, comúnmente llamada como ethereum, es la moneda virtual #2 en cuanto a términos de capitalización de mercado, por lo que se trata de una de las divisas digitales que más despierta el interés entre los mineros (creadores de las criptodivisas).
Ethereum es una plataforma de blockchain de código abierto que se ejecuta con el uso de su moneda nativa, llamada ether o ETH, por lo que a pesar de que la gente usa estos nombres como sinónimos son cosas distintas.
Ether es un token que se utiliza específicamente en la blockchain ethereum para pagar transacciones. Este token es responsable de impulsar casi todo lo que ocurre en la red, misma que puede ser usada por cualquier persona para crear y ejecutar contratos inteligentes, que son programas de software que se ejecutan de manera autónoma y sin la intervención del usuario.
De acuerdo con el portal de Binance, la moneda digital solana actualmente cuenta con 122.1M de unidades creadas.
El costo de la criptomoneda de ethereum para este día a las 14:05 horas (UTC) es de 2391.73 dólares por unidad.
Esto quiere decir que el activo digital reportó un cambio del -1.17 el último día, así como una variación del 0.0 % en la última hora.
Actualmente, ethereum se encuentra en el lugar #2 de popularidad en el mercado digital. Cabe mencionar que el máximo histórico que ha alcanzado esta divisa digital es de 4891.7 dólares por unidad.
Cotización de la criptomoneda Ethereum
Ethereum 2.0: las claves
Tras varios meses de retraso y con el temor de que ya nunca pasaría, finalmente el 15 de septiembre de 2022 Ethereum llevó a cabo su tan ansiada fusión o actualización al nuevo nivel 2.0 con la promesa de mejorar la experiencia de los usuarios de esta criptomoneda.
“The Merge”, inglés para “La Fusión”, es una transformación en la forma en que Ethereum procesa las transacciones y en cómo se crean nuevos tokens de Ether.
Esta fusión se trata de la combinación de la cadena de bloques de Ethereum con una nueva cadena de bloques separada conocido como proof-of-stake, el cual reduce el consumo de energía de la cadena de bloques de Ethereum en un 99,9 %, según sus propios desarrolladores, lo que la vuelve más “amigable” con el ambiente al tiempo que las transacciones serían más baratas.
Sus defensores creen que la fusión hará que Ethereum resulte favorecido con respecto al máximo rival, Bitcoin, pues podría aumentar su uso.
En el proceso Proof Stake los propietarios de Ether bloquearán cantidades establecidas de sus criptomonedas para verificar nuevos registros en la cadena de bloques, ganando nuevas monedas además de su criptografía “participada”.

articles.title: Aujourd'hui, la France décolle pour Mars : le rover Idefix va rouler sur une lune où vous pèseriez 40 grammes
articles.text:
Aujourd'hui, la France décolle pour Mars : le rover Idefix va rouler sur une lune où vous pèseriez 40 grammes
Va-t-on enfin savoir comment Mars a obtenu ses minuscules lunes ? Idéfix, le rover français décollera le 19 octobre à bord de MMX, la mission japonaise. Le petit véhicule va devoir apprivoiser une gravité totalement folle pour aider à collecter des échantillons et les ramener sur Terre.
C'est l'un des décollages les plus attendus de l'année pour une mission extrêmement ambitieuse. Et la France y prend part très activement. Le 19 octobre prochain, la mission internationale MMX (Martian Moons eXploration) doit s'envoler avec comme objectif de percer enfin les mystères des deux lunes de Mars, Phobos et Deimos.
Portée par la JAXA (Japon) aux côtés du CNES, du DLR, de la NASA et de l'ESA, la mission embarque une armada d'instruments de précision et un petit rover éclaireur prénommé Idefix. Décryptage d'un défi d'ingénierie hors norme.
D'où viennent les deux petites lunes martiennes ?
En ligne de mire scientifique : trancher un débat vieux de plusieurs décennies. Phobos et Deimos sont-elles de simples astéroïdes capturés par la gravité martienne ou sont-elles nées des débris projetés lors d'un choc titanesque subi par Mars dans sa jeunesse ?
La mission MMX décollera à bord du nouveau lanceur lourd japonais H3, récemment certifié après des débuts chaotiques et quelques explosions. Les récents tirs ont été des succès rassurants (voir en fin d'article).
Le piège orbital : impossible de tourner autour de Phobos
Naviguer autour de Phobos relève du casse-tête de mécanique spatiale.
Il est techniquement impossible de placer une sonde en orbite classique autour d'une si petite lune (24 km pour Phobos et 12 pour Déimos). Sa masse minime génère un champ de pesanteur balayé par la gravité de Mars, distante de seulement 6 000 km. La zone d'attraction de Phobos ne dépasse pas quelques centaines de mètres.
Pour stationner à ses côtés pendant trois ans, les pilotes vont exploiter des orbites quasi-satellitaires (QSO). La sonde MMX tournera physiquement autour de Mars, mais calera au millimètre près sa vitesse pour “escorter” Phobos pas à pas.
Idefix : 25 kg sur Terre, 15 grammes sur Phobos
Avant que le vaisseau principal ne touche le sol, MMX va larguer Idefix, un rover de 25 kg développé par le CNES et le DLR. Pourquoi lui avoir donné le nom du petit chien téméraire d'Obélix ? La raison la plus évidente tient à une filiation avec Astérix, le premier satellite tricolore, lancé en 1965, faisant de la France la troisième nation spatiale de l'histoire.
Sur Phobos, la gravité est environ 2 000 fois plus faible que sur Terre. Les calculs sont saisissants :
- Un adulte de 75 kg sur Terre n'y pèserait que 40 grammes.
- Le rover Idefix de 25 kg sera quant à lui attiré vers le sol de Phobos comme s'il ne pesait que 15 grammes.
La moindre impulsion risquant de l'expulser dans l'espace, Idefix avancera à une vitesse d'escargot : entre 1 et 3 cm par seconde. S'il se retourne au largage ? Ses quatre jambes motorisées lui permettent de se redresser en autonomie.
Le souvenir de Rosetta et Philae
Ce scénario rappelle la mission Rosetta en 2014, où l'atterrisseur Philae avait rebondi à la surface de la comète 67P à cause d'une microgravité mal anticipée.
Idefix sert de crash-testeur pour évaluer la consistance du sol avant l'atterrissage du module principal. Mais MMX va plus loin : au lieu d'analyser les échantillons sur place, la sonde rapportera au moins 10 grammes de poussière sur Terre à l'horizon 2031. Une première.
Les instruments embarqués
Pour accomplir sa mission, le duo sonde-rover intègre le haut du panier de la technologie spatiale avec 12 instruments parmi lesquels :
Sur la sonde mère :
- MIRS : spectromètre infrarouge (CNES/Observatoire de Paris) pour analyser la composition minérale et traquer l'eau.
- MEGANE : spectromètre gamma et neutrons (NASA).
- TENGOO & OROCHI : caméras téléobjectif et grand-angle haute résolution.
- LIDAR & SAMPLER : altimètre laser et système de prélèvement de sol.
Sur le rover Idefix :
- RAX : spectromètre Raman pour l'étude cristalline des roches.
- miniRAD : radiomètre thermique.
- NavCAM & WheelCAM : caméras de navigation et optiques braquées sur les roues pour observer l'interaction mécanique avec le régolithe.
Souhaitons toute la réussite possible à cette très belle mission, qui, en cas de succès, nous réservera très certainement de superbes découvertes scientifiques.

articles.title: Pulsar Gaming Announces eS Xlite Gaming Mouse
articles.text:
Monday, October 19th 2026
Pulsar Gaming Announces eS Xlite Gaming Mouse
Pulsar Gaming Gears (AplusX Inc.), a leading developer of high-performance esports peripherals, and VAXEE Corporation, a respected innovator in gaming hardware, today announced the official launch schedule of the new Pulsar eS Xlite. This highly-anticipated product line is the result of the strategic exclusive partnership and joint development work between the two companies, aimed at delivering unparalleled innovation and performance to the esports community.
The Pulsar eS series is a unified vision for the future of competitive gear. Crafted from the absolute finest materials with flawless finishing and extreme precision, the eS Xlite is in running production and is not a limited edition, confirming Pulsar's commitment to making this reference-standard equipment widely available.Evolved Ergonomics for the Biggest Stages 
Retaining the beloved ergonomic advantages of the original Xlite, the eS Xlite introduces refined geometry to maximize grip stability and comfort. The mouse features a slimmer width that allows for an agile, secure grip, while the raised rear and rearward-shifted center of gravity provide full, stable support for the palm. This advanced shape allows the wrist to rest in a more natural, lower position, significantly reducing strain during extended tournament sessions. Additionally, the sensor position has been moved forward to perfectly align with the user's index and middle fingers, delivering highly consistent and precise horizontal tracking. 
Uncompromising Hardware & Next-Generation Performance 
Under the hood, the eS Xlite is powered by the next-generation XS2 Sensor, boasting up to 42,000 DPI, 800 IPS, and 70G acceleration. This significant upgrade ensures flawless tracking without spinouts, even during the most aggressive flick shots. The mouse fully supports an 8000 Hz (8K) polling rate in both wired and wireless modes. To drive this extreme performance, Pulsar integrated a dual-core-class MCU alongside a high-capacity 500mAh battery—delivering 2.5 times the capacity of its predecessor (200mAh) and offering up to 119 hours of continuous use at 1KHz. 
Weighing a perfectly balanced 51 g, the eS Xlite is presented in the signature Pulsar eS blue color. To guarantee hardware longevity and prevent double-clicking issues at the source, it is fully equipped with Pulsar Optical Switches. 
The Link 8K Dongle Integration
The eS Xlite signals a major milestone in competitive peripheral design with its seamless integration of the Link 8K Dongle. Functioning as an active controller rather than a passive wireless receiver, the Link 8K allows players to instantly adjust critical settings—such as DPI, polling rate, and profiles—using its built-in buttons, eliminating the need to interrupt intense gameplay by flipping the mouse or accessing software. 
Pricing & Availability 
The Pulsar eS Xlite carries a suggested retail price of $179.95 USD. The Pulsar eS Xlite is available as of today.

articles.title: DIY VR: How to build your own headset, and why you probably won't want to
articles.text:
Virtual reality is in a bit of a weird place right now. After a lot of unfulfilled promise in the 1990s, it came back strong with the 2016 release of the Oculus Rift. For a while, it looked like VR, AR, XR, the metaverse, or whatever you wanted to call it, was going to be huge. Mark Zuckerberg was certainly convinced, and even Apple got in on the hype with its Vision Pro.
But by then momentum for alternate realities of every acronym was already in steady decline, and it only dwindled from there. The rate of development of new headsets has slowed, with many companies (including Apple) scaling back or shelving their efforts. While new releases like the Steam Frame and Pimax Dream Air are still happening, many of the most interesting developments in the space these days are on the enthusiast front.
That’s right, DIY VR is a thing, and with a couple hundred dollars in components, plus many hours of your time, you too can enter the immersive world of virtual reality while also experiencing the highs and lows of soldering, firmware flashing, and 3D printing. I rode that rollercoaster myself and learned why this is still a decidedly niche movement.
An off-the-shelf VR pad keeps things semi-comfortable.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
An off-the-shelf VR pad keeps things semi-comfortable.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
The DIY VR landscape
I stumbled into this space about a year ago. I primarily use VR for sim racing to practice driving the world’s greatest cars on the world’s greatest tracks while at home in my pajamas. At that time, I was using an HP Reverb G2, a virtual reality headset built around the Windows Mixed Reality (WMR) standard.
As part of its own cooling on VR tech, Microsoft was nixing support for WMR, and I feared that I might need a new headset. (I need not have worried. Many talented folks have kept WMR headsets alive through third-party drivers like OASIS on Steam.)
That’s when I found YouTuber CNCDan’s video on building a VR headset for $150. The price was certainly compelling, and as someone with a particular set of electronics skills developed over years of disassembling and repairing pinball machines, I thought it sounded kind of fun.
That opened the door to a rich landscape of DIY VR development, complete with software tools and hardware advice on how to get started.
The best starting place is Relativty VR. This project, started in the late 2010s by Jonas Ceccon, Gabriel Combe, and Maxime Coutté, includes all the code, configurations, and guidance you’ll need to get started.
But there are others, like OpenVR Arduino HMD, Project North Star, and the full-body tracking SlimeVR. There are plenty of ways to piece together your headset. As my first attempt, I kept it simple, sticking with the Relativty software and relying on the 3D headset models provided by CNCDan as part of his build. First step: the hardware.
An Arduino, an IMU, and a set of tiny displays are all you really need.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
An Arduino, an IMU, and a set of tiny displays are all you really need.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Bill of materials
A DIY VR headset is a mixture of hardware and software, and while you can have the software ready to go in just a few clicks, chances are it’s going to take some time to get the hardware you need. That’s doubly true given the uncertainty in global shipping.
The biggest and potentially most important piece of hardware is a 3D printer. Although I’ve seen some compelling DIY VR headsets made out of repurposed VR phone holders—Google Cardboard among others—most projects fit in shells that come out of a 3D printer. If you don’t have access to one, services like Formlabs can handle it via mail order, but given the amount of tinkering here, it’s certainly advantageous to print at home.
Regardless, you need to buy quite a few things. Let’s start with the most expensive: displays. You might think a pair of panels small enough and good enough for a VR headset would be difficult to find and prohibitively expensive, and you can certainly spend a lot here, but the standard option is a set of 2.9-inch LCDs, which can be purchased with the necessary controller for about $125.
Each has a 1440×1440 resolution. They offer 150 nits of brightness and a contrast ratio of 600:1. Not exactly world-class specs, but plenty enough for this application, and though they’re pretty ugly to view from odd angles, since you’re literally going to be sticking them a few inches from your eyeballs, that’s not really an issue.
Cheap plastic lenses keep everything in focus.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Cheap plastic lenses keep everything in focus.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
The next missing piece is a sensor module containing an inertial measurement unit, or IMU. This device detects the headset’s position. You’ll want a GY-91, a sensor board that has an onboard accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, and barometer. You can find one for around $5, but buyer beware for reasons I’ll explain shortly.
Next is the circuitry that ties it all together. Some DIY VR projects call upon custom PCBs riddled with components. The Relativty project just relies on an Arduino Pro Micro, which can be bought at any number of electronics retailers for $5 or less.
You’ll also need a pair of 34 mm-diameter lenses to focus those tiny displays, some miscellaneous hardware to connect the pieces, and a nylon strap to hold the thing to your head. Oh, and a pad from an HTC Vive, because nobody wants the sharp edges of layered plastic extruded from a 3D printer rubbing against their face.
My total spend for all that came to just under $180.
Breadboarding isn’t strictly necessary, but it helps with early testing.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Breadboarding isn’t strictly necessary, but it helps with early testing.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Breadboard time
Before you break out the soldering iron and fire up your 3D printer, I suggest you start with a breadboard and some patch wires. Wiring on this project is on the simple side, but trust me when I say it will be much easier to figure out why your firmware isn’t flashing with a few components on your workbench than when they’re all crammed inside a headset.
I won’t include all the wiring details here, as it’s best to follow the guide in the GitHub above, but in general, you need to connect your IMU to your Arduino to provide both power and data.
You can also optionally connect the display controller to the Arduino for power, as suggested in the video above. That’s what I did for my testing, but be advised, this isn’t necessarily a good idea given the power requirements of the displays vs. the capabilities of the Arduino. You’re better off running a separate USB cable to the display or a USB splitter inside the headset.
Once you’ve wired everything and powered it on successfully, you’re ready to start with the software.
A legit Arduino and a bogus IMU.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
A legit Arduino and a bogus IMU.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Firmware fun
Flashing the firmware to the Arduino should be the easy part, but this is when things started falling apart for me. In theory, you install the Arduino IDE on your desktop, download the FastIMU project, connect your Arduino via USB, and then click compile. Easy.
Mine just kept failing. I got a basic error message, e:-1, again and again. After a bit of research and tinkering, I finally figured it out, and the news wasn’t good.
Although I ordered and paid for a GY-91 with an onboard 9250 IMU, and that’s what it identified as, in actuality, it was a basic, cheaper 6500 IMU, one that lacks the magnetometer.
As I learned (the hard way), this is a disconcertingly commonplace experience. Many shady electronics companies are happy to sell you the wrong component for the wrong price. The two devices are compatible and operate much the same way, but without the magnetometer, tracking performance drops substantially.
Once I updated the code to reference the 6500 I had and not the 9250 I thought I had, everything flashed beautifully, and I was instantly up and running. I calibrated my IMU through the Arduino IDE, and I was ready for final assembly.
Be extremely careful in placing your displays.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Be extremely careful in placing your displays.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Putting it all together
You can find various shells online for custom VR headsets, many of which are designed to accommodate this specific set of boards used in Relativty. I decided to use CNCDan’s files, as it looked like a clean and clever design, even allowing for adjustment of the distance between displays, known as interpupillary distance, or IPD.
That makes for a complicated assembly process, requiring numerous printed parts, a handful of threaded receivers melted therein, plus rods and screws to hold it together. You’ll also need a pair of eye boxes, each one holding a lens on one side and the display on the other.
This was where I made a painful mistake. The design’s eye boxes contain small clips, and the instructions suggest you just pop the displays in there.
This is not what you should do. The exposed LCDs are extremely fragile, and by clipping them in, I managed to break both. The small amount of pressure required was enough to shatter them, and the damage was invisible until I turned them on.
Given that, I highly recommend modifying those boxes, either by printing them without the clips or by breaking them off after the print is complete. I used a few strips of thin painter’s tape to hold mine in place.
A little tape held things secure.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
A little tape held things secure.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Getting in the game
With all the wires jammed into place, I screwed the headset together, stuck on the face pad, threaded on the head strap, and proceeded to spend about five minutes trying to get a comfortable fit. I never quite succeeded.
I booted into SteamVR’s living lounge space and was immediately discombobulated. For one thing, I was staring straight at the floor. For another, turning my head just sent the view spinning in different directions in a way that quickly threatened nausea.
I had forgotten to recalibrate the headset after mounting all the components, and my cut-rate IMU was now oriented differently than it had been when it was on my workbench.
After recalibrating and a little more firmware fiddling, I got back into SteamVR’s setup room and could tell I still had a problem. Holding my head perfectly still, I could see the perspective slowly spinning.
Additionally, the IMU axes seemed slightly crossed, so the perspective change didn’t quite match my head movement. I verified the IMU was mounted correctly in the case and recalibrated a few times with no improvement.
You can print any manner of shells for your headset.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
You can print any manner of shells for your headset.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
I soldiered on, booting into iRacing, my favorite SteamVR-compatible racing sim. Before I was even out of the pits, my perspective was drifting. I mapped the recenter view command to a button on my steering wheel, and had to reach for it quite often.
Still, the image quality was not nearly as bad as I expected. Those cheap plastic lenses work surprisingly well, and though I could make out the pixels on the displays (the dreaded “screen door” effect of VR), it didn’t bother me. Brightness and contrast were more than adequate, and the refresh rate of 60 Hz was enough for casual practice.
But sensor drift and headset comfort were real issues. Without a proper cable-routing solution, the headset kept tugging to one side, and despite the padding, it was smashing my nose and cheeks.
I’ve done hourslong endurance races in multiple mass-market VR headsets. After 15 minutes in this one, I was ready to quit.
Projects like this are never really done.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Projects like this are never really done.
Credit:
Tim Stevens
Final thoughts and future upgrades
My total outlay for this project was $239.93. But that includes the extra $62 I had to spend on a second set of displays. Avoid that expensive gaffe, and you’re looking at around $180 in components.
That makes it roughly half the cost of a Meta Quest 3S, one of the cheapest headsets on the market right now. That’s a substantial savings, but I’d certainly recommend that most people pay the extra. The tracking issues in my headset are maddening, the image quality is middling at best, and this is far and away the least comfortable headset I’ve ever worn.
All that can be fixed, though. Some projects use a MinIMU-9 IMU, which looks miles more accurate and is less likely to be faked, but it’s also substantially more expensive at $35. You can also step up to higher-quality LCDs or even tiny OLED panels that come with all the color and contrast you could ever want. There are options for onboard battery packs, wireless adapters, and of course you can spend as much time as you like designing an ultra-comfortable housing for it all.
But even if you ignore the time commitment, once you start adding those upgrades, you’re not far from the cost of that Quest, a far-from-perfect headset that still works effortlessly and comfortably out of the box.
As always with these projects, it depends on what you want. If you just want a cheap, easy, reliable headset for your next-gen immersive gaming fix, this probably isn’t it.
If, however, you want a fun project that will help you appreciate the industrial design required to make a good-looking and comfortable wearable device, this could be it. I learned a lot and, despite the frustrations, I’m glad I embarked on this journey.
That said, while I’ll keep tinkering and likely throw a few more upgrades at this thing, I can’t see it replacing my other headset for regular racing duties, deprecated though it may be.

articles.title: Hackers used a fake VPN download page to steal corporate credentials
articles.text:
Fake VPN download site steals administrator credentials to give attackers direct access to corporate networks — but delivers official signed software so victims never suspect a thing
A fake WatchGuard VPN site is stealing your passwords
- Fake WatchGuard VPN website steals administrator credentials while delivering legitimate software
- Attackers collected VPN server addresses, usernames, and passwords
- The fraudulent website rejected initial submissions to collect credentials a second time
A fraudulent WatchGuard download website stole VPN login details while supplying the authentic installation package, experts have claimed.
Security investigators at Huntress traced the activity to a lookalike domain that collected connection details before downloading the legitimate client.
The investigation began after suspicious activity involving an administrator working for a managed service provider was detected.
Fake download pages harvest user credentials
Investigators found that the user had searched Bing for a WatchGuard VPN download before visiting a deceptive website designed to resemble the vendor's official download pages.
The website, watchguard-vpn[.]net, offered a purported mobile VPN with SSL download and displayed a form requesting the server address, username, and password.
Those details matched information required by the genuine VPN client, making the request appear consistent with an ordinary installation process.
Submitting the form transmitted the information to a separate domain, watchguard-ssl[.]online, where attackers collected the credentials for potential use against the organization's network.
The malicious script rejected the first submission and cleared the fields, prompting the victim to enter the information again and potentially supplying attackers with multiple password attempts.
Huntress revealed that the operators registered the download domain on August 22, 2026, while the credential collection domain appeared on September 14.
WatchGuard had previously reported the lookalike address in January, although researchers then found no functioning mechanism directing visitors through the fraudulent download process.
Genuine software helps conceal the credential theft
After collecting the second submission, the website initiated a download from WatchGuard's official content delivery network rather than providing a counterfeit installation package.
The file was Mobile VPN with SSL client version 12.11.5, carrying a valid digital signature from WatchGuard Technologies and a timestamp dated November 4, 2025.
Huntress verified that the installer remained unchanged after signing, meaning investigators found no evidence that attackers had modified the legitimate executable.
This approach differs from campaigns that distribute tampered installers or malicious libraries, which endpoint protection products may identify through file inspection.
The authentic download also gives victims little reason to suspect their credentials have already been compromised, since installation can proceed normally afterward.
Huntress found no recorded download from the official server during the investigated incident, suggesting the user might not have completed both credential submissions.
The detection arrived 21 seconds after the malicious website loaded, allowing the security operations team to provide remediation guidance before investigators observed further escalation.
Huntress reported that the main deceptive domain was offline by October 13, although that status does not establish whether associated infrastructure remains active elsewhere.
The attack avoids many malware checks because the fake website steals VPN credentials through the browser before downloading the genuine software.
Organizations should reset compromised passwords, enable multifactor authentication, check for suspicious VPN logins, and direct employees to official software download pages.

articles.title: Attention aux cagnottes pour aider Pierre du Micromania de Nice, pillé pendant les manifestations
articles.text:
Samedi, si vous avez suivi les manifestations contre la vie chère, émaillées de pillages à Nice, Marseille ou Paris, vous êtes forcément tombé sur cette vidéo mettant en scène Pierre. Gérant du Micromania de l’avenue Jean-Médecin, à Nice, Pierre a tenu tête aux casseurs, plus nombreux que lui, pendant l’attaque de son magasin, même quand il a pris un coup de pied alors qu’il leur tournait le dos.
Pierre est devenu un symbole de résistance pour beaucoup de Français, horrifiés par certaines images qui circulent sur les réseaux sociaux. Une image résume parfaitement ce sentiment : on le voit avec une attitude pleine de confiance, juste à côté d’une affiche de Son Goku, le héros de la saga Dragon Ball. Pierre est celui qui ne s’est pas défilé face aux pillards. Il a donc reçu un immense soutien, et des cagnottes ont vite été ouvertes à son nom, sans qu’il en soit à l’origine.
Le gérant de Micromania dit n’être à l’origine d’aucune cagnotte
Sur son compte Instagram intitulé stonebrushstudio, Pierre a publié une Story le dimanche 18 octobre. Il a d’abord remercié ceux qui le soutiennent. « Les gens qui sont venus me voir en vrai, c’est adorable. Merci. Merci beaucoup. Mon équipe et moi, on est très touchés », a-t-il indiqué, avant de poursuivre : « Je n’ai pas l’habitude de m’exprimer face caméra. Ce n’est pas mon métier. Mais je me vois contraint de réagir. »
Le principal intéressé ne se voit pas en héros. « Je pense qu’il n’aurait pas fallu le faire », a-t-il reconnu auprès d’ICI Azur, avant de qualifier son geste de « bêtise ». Il a assuré s’en tirer avec « quelques éraflures ».
Il a surtout pris la parole pour évoquer le sujet des cagnottes : plusieurs ont effectivement été créées en son nom. Celle lancée par Double Pixels, par exemple, approche les 10 000 €. Dans un message publié ce lundi 19 octobre sur Leetchi, Double Pixels, qui est également une chaîne de contenu pop culture installée en Provence-Alpes-Côte d’Azur, a affirmé : « Nous avons rencontrer [sic] Pierre il est au courant pour la cagnotte, il est d’accord ! Votre soutien est énorme. » Quelques heures auparavant, l’intéressé disait pourtant : « Je ne suis au courant de rien. Personne ne m’a contacté pour ce genre de choses. Je ne suis en lien avec personne. »
Pierre n’a rien publié depuis son intervention et, dès lors, rien n’indique qu’il ait bel et bien approuvé l’initiative de Double Pixels. « Ne vous faites pas avoir. Pour le moment, rien est fait », a-t-il rappelé. En attendant que Pierre s’exprime de nouveau, pour confirmer ou infirmer son accord, on ne peut que vous inviter à la prudence concernant d’éventuelles cagnottes à son nom. Il en va de même pour des achats de certains produits sur les plateformes Leboncoin, Vinted et eBay.
Si une collecte venait à utiliser son nom pour tromper les donateurs, elle relèverait de l’escroquerie. L’article 313-1 du Code pénal punit ce délit de cinq ans d’emprisonnement et de 375 000 euros d’amende.

articles.title: 250 000 dollars d'acompte et zéro garantie : la folle condition imposée par Tesla pour le nouveau Roadster
articles.text:
On oublierait presque qu’il puisse aussi rouler au sol comme une voiture ordinaire. Capable des galipettes les plus impressionnantes qui soient, le nouveau Tesla Roadster tient véritablement de la science-fiction. La pirouette au-dessus d’un Semi ? Check. La promenade au plafond ? Check. Le 0 à 100 km/h sous la seconde ? Check. La livraison dans les temps ? Houlà, ça reste à prouver, d’autant plus que la livraison « tout court » n’est même pas garantie…
On pourrait en effet penser qu’après 9 ans d’attente, les commandes du Roadster seront enfin honorées. Quelle erreur ! Le loup se cache au paragraphe numéro 4 du contrat de réservation de la supercar volante : « vous comprenez que le Roadster est encore en phase de développement au moment de signer ce contrat et que, par conséquent, nous ne pouvons garantir ni la date de livraison de votre véhicule, ni même s’il sera livré ».
À lire aussi : le Tesla Roadster pourra-t-il rouler (et voler) en France ?
Un chèque de 250 000 $ versé… sans même connaître le prix final
En sachant qu’il faut débourser jusqu’à 250 000 $ pour effectuer la réservation, il y a de quoi l’avoir en travers de la gorge. Surtout que vous serez juste placé en liste d’attente lorsque Tesla sera enfin prêt à mettre les véhicules en production. Inutile donc d’espérer avoir l’engin dans votre garage à ce stade. D’ailleurs, le prix du nouveau Roadster n’a même pas été communiqué, ce qui n’est guère rassurant quant à l’attente se profilant.
Le même contrat stipule en effet que « le prix d’achat estimatif du véhicule, s’il est indiqué, n’est qu’une estimation. Tesla travaille encore sur les options, les fonctionnalités et les équipements du véhicule et ne peut donc pas encore confirmer le prix exact. Le prix définitif sera indiqué une fois que vous aurez configuré votre véhicule ». Le chemin est donc encore très long avant le lancement, normalement prévu pour 2028.
Pas d’interdiction de revente, mais des conditions très particulières
L’accord a beau poser des conditions assez inédites, il n’avance en revanche aucune interdiction de revente. C’est pourtant chose fréquente chez les marques lançant des modèles exclusifs imposant une attente importante. Pour éviter que le véhicule ne soit revendu uniquement pour faire de la spéculation et briser les délais aux acheteurs les plus pressés, remettre immédiatement la voiture sur le marché est alors interdit.
Ce n’est pas le cas pour le Roadster, alors même que les Cybertruck Founders Series et Model S Signature Edition ont bien été concernés par cette interdiction. Une bonne chose, même si les réservations du Roadster ne sont pas transférables. L’autre bonne nouvelle, c’est que l’acompte versé pour la réservation est entièrement remboursable si vous changez d’avis ou que Tesla soit effectivement dans l’impossibilité de livrer le véhicule. C’est bien le minimum…

Points forts
- Écran bien calibré et très lumineux.
- Présence du Snapdragon 8 Elite.
- Volet photo complet.
- Excellente autonomie.
- Expérience One UI 7.
Points faibles
- Design déjà vu.
- Téléobjectif assez décevant.
- Charge limitée à 25 W en 2025 !?
Alors oui, ce Galaxy S25 a tout d’un S24 amélioré, mais le résultat est là : le millésime 2025 surpasse le précédent. Son format compact, son écran réussi et sa puce surpuissante et économe en énergie en font un modèle aussi fluide qu’endurant. L’expérience photo gagne en précision, même si tout n’est pas parfait, notamment du côté du téléobjectif. On peut aussi regretter une puissance de charge encore limitée par rapport à la concurrence. Cependant, l’expérience offerte par One UI 7 et les nombreuses fonctions d’IA apportent un vent de modernité. À moins de posséder le modèle de 2024, cette itération est donc hautement recommandable. Samsung prouve ici que dans la tech comme en amour, il ne faut pas se fier aux apparences, et que l’important, c’est ce qu’il y a à l’intérieur.

articles.title: Angel One, Zerodha expand US stock investing access for Indian investors
articles.text:
Angel One, Zerodha expand US stock investing access for Indian investors
This reflects a broader push by Indian investment platforms to expand beyond domestic equities as retail investors seek exposure to global markets.
Angel One and Zerodha are expanding access to the US stock markets for Indian investors, as domestic brokerages look to tap into the growing demand for international equities and portfolio diversification.
Angel One has begun rolling out US stock investing on its app, allowing users to invest in US-listed stocks and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) alongside their Indian portfolios. The facility is currently available to a limited group of users, with a wider rollout expected by mid-November.
Investors will be able to buy shares of companies such as Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia, Netflix, Spotify and Toyota. The platform will also support fractional investing, allowing users to purchase a portion of a share rather than an entire unit.
Meanwhile, Zerodha has also launched US stock investing in beta, offering access to around 2,000 US-listed stocks and 1,000 ETFs through its platform. The move gives Indian investors another avenue to access global businesses, particularly in sectors such as artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and semiconductors.
The expansion follows regulatory approval from the International Financial Services Centres Authority for brokers to offer international investing through GIFT City in Gujarat.
Angel One will waive brokerage charges until December 2026. From January 2027, it will charge 0.1% per trade, subject to a minimum brokerage of $0.99. Account opening, maintenance, deposits, and withdrawals will be free, although regulatory charges, GST, and foreign-exchange conversion costs will apply.
Zerodha's offering is being introduced in beta, with brokerage and other applicable charges governed by its published pricing structure.
Investments through these platforms are subject to the Reserve Bank of India's Liberalised Remittance Scheme and applicable regulatory requirements. Angel One has also said eligible US securities will carry Securities Investor Protection Corporation protection of up to $500,000, subject to applicable conditions.
The launches reflect a broader push by Indian investment platforms to expand beyond domestic equities as retail investors seek exposure to global markets. Platforms including Groww, Upstox and INDmoney also offer routes to international investing, intensifying competition in the segment.

articles.title: Apple updates guidelines to ban nudify apps masquerading as regular apps to pass review | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Apple tightened its developer guidelines over the weekend to ban apps that use AI to create offensive content, as well as those that masquerade as regular apps to pass the App Store review process and then turn into nudify apps, or surface those features prominently.
The company updated its guidelines with strong language around AI and user-generated content, and how app developers should include enough preventative measures to moderate objectionable or offensive content.
“Apps that host user-generated content are required to filter objectionable material, give users a way to report offensive content, and let users block abusive accounts. Apps containing hidden or undocumented features are also prohibited on the App Store, including apps that misrepresent their purpose during review and only reveal harmful capabilities — such as “nudification” — after approval, a tactic commonly known as bait-and-switch,” the company said in a blog post.
Apple said that it will remove apps that add features not present in the version submitted for App Store review.
The iPhone maker has also updated the language in its legal section to reinforce that it will bar apps promoting human trafficking and exploitation of children.
Apple said last year its review process blocked over 150,000 apps from reaching users, and removed 193,000 developer accounts on account of fraud and abuse.
In July, San Francisco ordered both Apple and Google to clean up and delete nudification apps from their app stores. City Attorney David Chiu accused the companies of profiting from these apps through store fees. And in April, a Tech Transparency Project report indicated that both tech giants’ stores hosted multiple nudify apps, some of which were rated as suitable for minors.

articles.title: Cinebench world record that stood for 12 years gets toppled — OC expert scores 10.8cb in Cinebench R11.5 using an Intel Core i5 4670K at 6.3 GHz
articles.text:
Cinebench world record that stood for 12 years gets toppled — OC expert scores 10.8cb in Cinebench R11.5 using an Intel Core i5 4670K at 6.3 GHz
Overclocking enthusiasts are still having fun with Haswell CPUs and DDR3 in 2026.
You don’t need the latest and greatest PC hardware to have fun or even break overclocking world records. OC expert Luumi has demonstrated this very capably by achieving a new HWBot world record using an ancient Intel Core i5 4670K, a modest amount of DDR3, and (inevitably) a flask or two of LN2. Overclocker Luumi recently knocked the four-cores Intel Core i5 4670K Cinebench R11.5 record holder off their perch after 12 years, achieving a multicore score of 10.8 cb.
The HWBot-crowned system is built around Haswell-era Intel silicon, the Core i5 4670K to be precise. This is an unlocked 4C/4T CPU with a stock base/boost of 3.4 / 3.8 GHz, 84W TDP, with a 6MB cache and HD 4600 graphics, built on Intel’s 22nm process. You had to buy an i7 chip back in this era to get 4C/8T.
Luumi’s system hosted the CPU on an ASRock Z97 OC Formula motherboard, which was fitted with 4GB of DDR3 RAM from XPG, and fed ample power via a Corsair AXi 1600. To achieve the Cinebench R11.5 benchmark record liquid nitrogen was used to cool the 4670K, and the validation files show the CPU ran at a blistering 6,301.00 MHz.
Again, we’ll comment that this isn’t a world record Cinebench R11.5 score for any / all quad-core processors. It's just in the Core i5 4670K category. Nevertheless, it is great to see retro hardware achievements like this, 12 years later. As one other HWBot community member commented, it is brilliant to see an OC result on the HWBot homepage that involves neither an X3D CPU or RTX 5090 GPU. You don’t need the latest, greatest, most expensive, nor unobtainuim components to get featured on the online home of competitive overclocking.
Out of curiosity I decided to give ye olde Cinebench R11.5 a spin on the laptop I’m currently working on. With its 12C/24T CPU, it trounced the old-but-record-breaking Haswell desktop, of course. Even though the laptop is running in cool/quiet mode I achieved 4x the 4670K score.
Mostly I was happy that this older version of Cinebench still works on modern hardware and Windows 11 without any fuss. Some apps which were popular benchmarking staples, like 3DMark tests from DX10 and earlier eras, have issues on modern computers making the results you can wheedle out of them invalid for HWBot rankings. Luumi used Windows 7 64-bit Pro for their Haswell CPU Cinebench R11.5 testing.

Mark Tyson is a news editor at Tom's Hardware. He enjoys covering the full breadth of PC tech; from business and semiconductor design to products approaching the edge of reason.

Anyway, I still have a Haswell box, with a Refresh i3 in it. I never really used it for the intended purpose, but I have some ideas for it. Temps ran higher than I expected, so I bought a delidding tool last year to see what I could do about that. I had already lapped both the CPU and heatsink, so I was a bit surprised at how warm it still ran.

articles.title: I tested Sony’s towering Bluetooth speaker in a parking lot and I’m surprised I didn’t get any noise complaints — here’s why the new ULT Tower 7 should be your go-to for any party
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Sony ULT Tower 7 is a fantastic party speaker that serves up deep, pounding bass, clear mids and highs, and plentiful power. Mix in an impressive 30 hour battery life, attractive visual style, and versatile connectivity options, and there’s a lot to love here. Sure, the 360-degree Party Sound could be better, and the speaker isn’t the most mobile, but if you want a top-tier all-in-one party box, then look no further.
Reasons to buy
- + Gigantic bass output with clear mids and highs
- + Versatile connectivity options
- + Attractive design with fantastic lighting
- + Strong battery life
Reasons to avoid
- - 360-degree sound could be more convincing
- - Heavy and a little cumbersome to move
- - IPX4 waterproofing is just OK
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Sony ULT Tower 7 review
The Sony ULT Tower 7 is another strong entry in Sony’s refreshed ULT line, coming in with newly developed, rounded woofers for enhanced deep bass, a swathe of connectivity options for personal or professional use, and customizable lighting for highly immersive listening.
This model is the mid-sized option in Sony’s new ULT Tower lineup, sitting above the Tower 5 and below the ULT Max. It has a seven driver setup, with a single 280mm woofer, two mid-ranges, and four tweeters — including two rear-facing tweeters for Sony’s 360-degree Party Sound. It also has an impressive 420W of power meaning that it can get unbelievably loud — honestly I had to test this one outdoors for the most part, as it shook the foundations of our music testing space to its very core.
How good is the Sony ULT Tower 7? I’ve tested it for hours on end, listening to countless tunes, playing around with the light settings, and assessing its various features and functions available through Sony’s Sound Connect app. Here’s why I think it can compete with some of the very best Bluetooth speakers.
Let’s start with the most important thing of all: sound quality. The ULT Tower 7 is an excellent-sounding model, providing clarity and insight right across the frequency range, but the clear standout is the bass. It can extend all the way down to 20Hz with confidence, plating up regimented, meaty bass and even rippling sub-bass.
When tuning into First Summer by H.K., the deep, pounding bass was replicated fantastically, sounding just as dynamic, full-bodied and agile as I’d hoped. But still, vocals were textured and clear in the build up, keys and vocals were brilliantly balanced in the mid-range, and higher-pitched drums had a highly energetic, rhythmic quality.
A lot of these positive qualities were mirrored when listening to Rocking Chair by Mr. Scruff. Rich, deep bass was mesmerizing and phenomenally full-sounding, with tonally accurate keys in the mid-range and expressive drums up top adding plenty of color. In addition, guitars had a great sense of width to them, sounding as if they were playing from the corners of our testing room during my indoor assessment.
When blasting tunes from the ULT Tower 7 outdoors, I was astonished by its raw, uncompromised power. It has a maximum power output of 420W, and sound can fill large open spaces confidently, without losing low-end impact or clarity in the mids and treble. One of my colleagues could hear the speaker clearly from the other side of the parking lot in which I was testing the speaker, and let me tell you, this thing is borderline deafening (in a good way) at top volumes.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
My only criticism, sonically speaking, is that the 360-degree sound on this speaker is a bit underwhelming. When listening at less favorable angles, like the side and rear of the speaker, the experience was noticeably worse. The overall sound of my tracks just wasn’t as cohesive and balanced as I’d hoped for, and while the larger ULT Tower Max may remedy this issue, the Tower 7 is certainly outclassed for 360-degree sound by rivals like the Marshall Bromley 450.
Still, this is a fantastic sounding speaker that handles dynamics beautifully, and plates up emphatic deep bass, clear mids and highs, and a whole lot of power. The ULT Tower 7’s Sound Field Optimization — which analyzes speaker placement and background noise and accordingly adjusts sound balance across the frequency range — also means that you’re getting consistent quality in any environment.
Something else I love about the ULT Tower 7 is how easy it is to customize its audio output, thanks to its top-tier EQ options. ULT 1 is best for huge outdoor spaces, and places additional emphasis on deep bass, while ULT 2 provides a more rounded sound that focuses on delivering the most energetic, powerful sound. There’s also a Live mode if you want to replicate live recordings more faithfully, a Flat signature for a more balanced sound, and a custom 10-band equalizer which gives you more granular control over the speaker’s output.
What’s more, this speaker supports the higher-res Bluetooth codec LDAC, enabling you to get a surprisingly detailed, insightful listen from the speaker. If you’re after true lossless audio, you’re in luck too — there’s USB-C, 3.5mm, and RCA connectivity on board. This flexibility is great for professionals who want to hook up a DJ controller via RCA or casual listeners who just want to run with Bluetooth or USB-C. In addition, there’s a pair of mic ports so you can dabble in a bit of karaoke from time to time.
If you’re using the ULT Tower 7 for karaoke, there are some effects available to you in Sony’s Sound Connect app, including a voice changer, echo, and so on. There’s also a party pad for effects like a flanger and sampler, as well as playing drum sounds and robotic noises when DJing. These are easy to access, and more generally, I found the SoundConnect app to be highly user-friendly and reliable — it wasn’t filled with bugs like some rivals’ apps are.
While we’re talking about features, it only seems right to talk about battery life. The ULT Tower 7 can offer up to 30 hours of playback with the LEDs turned off, and for a party speaker in this size-category, that’s very strong indeed. That’s almost double of a rival like the JBL PartyBox 330, and means you can keep the party going well into the early hours. There’s also a Stamina mode for extended playtime, or you can use the speaker while hooked up to the mains.
Let’s move onto design now, an area where the ULT Tower 7 largely excels. It looks fantastic, with eye-catching yet tasteful lighting, an attractive rounded aesthetic, and well-sized, illuminated buttons. Even the ULT logo impressed me because it enables you to adjust volume and cycle through EQ modes swiftly — adding a functional layer here is a very nice touch. While it’s not made of the most premium materials, it’s still built to a great standard, and has a rugged yet refined appearance.
My issue with the overall build, however, is that this speaker is not as practical as it could be. At 50.3lbs / 22.8kg, it’s very heavy, and will take a fair bit of effort to move around. Yes, there are a couple of handles built-in alongside some wheels, but a model this hefty really could’ve done with a pull-out handle for easier transportation. When using the main handle on the reverse side of the speaker, I found the ULT Tower 7 to be awkward to maneuver, something that you won’t find with a lot of the JBL PartyBoxes, for instance.
I also would’ve liked to have seen slightly better waterproofing on the ULT Tower 7. IPX4 means it's safe against splashes of water, and this is essentially the standard for party speakers of this size. But some models, like the Marshall Bromley 450, provide superior IP55 protection, which also shields against dust ingress.
But anyway, let’s get down to the crucial question: is the Sony ULT Tower 7 worth the money? Well, for $649.99 / £499 / AU$799, I think you’re actually getting great quality overall. With imposing, gigantic sound, a flashy look, long battery life, and broad connectivity options, the ULT Tower 7 is more accomplished than a lot of the competition in this price-range.
It’s still a big investment, sure, but pound-for-pound, you’re getting an awful lot of functionality and great audio. If you’re looking to save a bit of cash, then I’d personally go for the Sony ULT Tower 5, but for some added oomph, you really can’t go wrong with the ULT Tower 7.
Sony ULT Tower 7 review: price & release date
- Priced at $649.99 / £499 / AU$799
- Released in September 2026
The Sony ULT Tower 7 released in September 2026, and is the mid-sized option in the new Tower lineup, sitting right between the smaller Sony ULT Tower 5 and the giant Sony ULT Tower Max. It comes in at $649.99 / £499 / AU$799, which is a reasonable price for a model with such powerful sound and fleshed-out features.
While the ULT Tower 7 is a fair bit pricier than the ULT Tower 5, it does come with the benefits of rear-facing tweeters for 360-degree sound, added power, and better battery life. It’s also priced pretty well against rivals in this size category, such as the JBL PartyBox 330 and the Marshall Bromley 450 — which you can read more about in the ‘also consider’ section.
Sony ULT Tower 7 review: specs
| Weight | 50.3lbs / 22.8kg | 
| Dimensions | 16.6 x 28 x 13.7 inches / 421 x 710 x 347mm | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 5.3, RCA, XLR (in and out), USB-A, USB-C, mic input (6.3mm) | 
| Battery life | 30 hours | 
| Speaker drivers | 1x 280mm woofer, 2x 120mm mid-range, 4x 50mm tweeters (incl. 2x rear-facing tweeters) | 
| Waterproofing | IPX4 | 
Should I buy the Sony ULT Tower 7?
| Attribute | Notes | Score | 
|---|---|---|
| Features | Versatile connectivity, LDAC support, customizable lighting, and top EQ options. | 5/5 | 
| Performance | Powerful, regimented bass, clear mids and expressive highs, but 360 sound could be better. | 4.5/5 | 
| Design | Flashy, striking look with tasteful lighting, but could do with a pull-out handle, waterproofing is OK. | 4/5 | 
| Value | Good price for the sound and expansive set of features on offer. | 4/5 | 
Buy it if…
You want premium party sound
The Sony ULT Tower 7 sounds spectacular, with extremely powerful yet regimented bass, clear mids, and expressive treble. LDAC is on-board for higher-res Bluetooth streaming, or you can use a wired connection for lossless audio, and advanced EQ settings help you get the perfect sound for any genre or environment.
You’re looking for versatile connectivity
The ULT Tower 7 is the ultimate party device with so many connectivity options. You’ve obviously got Bluetooth there, but you can also plug in a DJ controller or turntable via RCA, hook up a device over USB-C, or play music back from a USB drive. Pair that with microphone ports for karaoke shenanigans, and you’ve got everything you need in one box.
Don’t buy it if…
You’re on a budget
If you want a great party speaker but you’re on a budget, then I’d strongly recommend going for the Sony ULT Tower 5 over this model. The ULT Tower 5 is smaller, and skips on the 360 sound, but it provides almighty bass output for its size, and comes in at a tempting price of $449.99 / £349 / AU$549.
You need great 360-degree sound
While the ULT Tower 7 sounds great when facing you, its sound falters a bit from side and rear listening angles, even in spite of the 360 sound tech that Sony has included here. If you want a speaker with no real blind spots, then I’d recommend checking out the Marshall Bromley 450 or 750.

JBL PartyBox 330
The JBL PartyBox 330 feels like the ULT Tower 7’s main competitor, with a powerful party-ready sound signature, similarly eye-catching LED lighting, and a lot of shared connectivity options. While the PartyBox 330 can’t quite compete in terms of battery life, it has a pull-out handle making it more mobile, and has attractive features like karaoke support and IPX4 waterproofing.
Marshall Bromley 450
Sure, the Marshall Bromley 450 has a high asking price, but it offers the luxurious quality to back that up. It has stunning stage-light inspired LEDs, beautifully detailed and powerful 360-degree sound, and strong connectivity options to boot. Throw in top-tier battery life and solid waterproofing, and you’re looking at one of the best party speakers in this size-class. Read my full Marshall Bromley 450 review.
How I tested the Sony ULT Tower 7
- Tested outdoors and at the Future Labs music testing space
- Mainly streamed tunes over Tidal
- Tried Party Chain functionality alongside ULT Tower 5
I spent many an hour testing the Sony ULT Tower 7, using it both in our music testing space at Future Labs and outdoors. As well as testing the ULT Tower 7 on its own, I also tried using it alongside the Sony ULT Tower 5 with the Party Chain function.
For the most part, I made use of Bluetooth connectivity to stream tunes over Tidal on my Xiaomi 17 phone, which supports the higher-res LDAC codec. I started by sifting through the TechRadar reference playlist, which features tracks from a wide variety of genres, but I also made sure to bump countless tunes from my personal library as well.
More generally, I’ve spent years testing audio gear here at TechRadar, where I serve as a Senior Reviews Writer. I’ve reviewed everything from wireless headphones like the Sonos Ace Ultra to Dolby Atmos soundbar systems like the JBL Bar 1300MK2. On top of that, I’ve tested a large number of party speakers, including ULT Tower 7 competitors like the Marshall Bromley 450.

Harry is a Senior Reviews Writer for TechRadar. He reviews everything from party speakers to wall chargers and has a particular interest in the worlds of audio and gaming. Harry has a background in business tech journalism, particularly around the telecoms industry.
