Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: Un modelo de Claude resolvió en 30 minutos un misterio de la NSA que duraba 25 años
articles.text:
Un modelo interno de Claude, el asistente de inteligencia artificial de Anthropic, resolvió en menos de media hora un misterio de la criptografía que llevaba 25 años sin respuesta: el origen de las semillas numéricas que la Agencia de Seguridad Nacional de Estados Unidos (NSA) entregó para definir las curvas elípticas que hoy protegen buena parte de las conexiones seguras de internet.
Según el informe que Anthropic publicó el 16 de octubre, un empleado le pidió a un modelo de investigación interno que averiguara cómo se habían generado esos números sin darle ninguna pista previa. El modelo determinó que las semillas de las curvas P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384 y P-521 no salieron de ningún algoritmo de hash, sino de lrand48, un generador de números pseudoaleatorios incluido en las bibliotecas del lenguaje C desde los años noventa, inicializado con una marca de tiempo del sistema.
Un enigma heredado de la era Snowden
El Instituto Nacional de Estándares y Tecnología de Estados Unidos, conocido como NIST, adoptó esas curvas en el año 2000 dentro del estándar de firma digital FIPS 186-2. El organismo publicó las semillas junto con las curvas, pero nunca explicó de dónde habían salido esos números, lo que alimentó sospechas de que pudieran esconder una puerta trasera a favor de la NSA.
El criptógrafo Filippo Valsorda, quien organizó en 2023 una recompensa para quien resolviera el enigma, confirmó el hallazgo en su propio sitio y precisó que el equipo de Anthropic reclamó el premio el 15 de octubre a la 01:07:51 UTC. El dinero, de 36.864 dólares, se donará a Internet Security Research Group, la organización sin fines de lucro que opera el servicio de certificados Let’s Encrypt.
Durante años circuló la versión de que un empleado de la NSA, Jerry Solinas, había generado las semillas a partir del hash de una frase en broma, algo que él mismo narró en 2015 sin poder aportar pruebas. Solinas murió en 2023 y nunca quedó registro de esa frase ni de su proceso exacto.
Cómo llegó Claude a la respuesta
El modelo descartó esa pista desde el principio y probó un camino distinto: supuso que el programa original usaba un generador de números pseudoaleatorios típico de los años noventa y escribió un rastreador que comparó 34 combinaciones posibles de esos generadores contra los valores publicados.
Encontró que en varias semillas los bits superiores de cada bloque de 32 aparecían siempre en cero, una señal característica del generador lrand48. Según el propio informe de Anthropic, esa coincidencia tenía una probabilidad de apenas una en 5.810 de ocurrir al azar.
Para las semillas de las curvas primas, donde el generador conserva menos información de cada salida, Claude recurrió al algoritmo de reducción de retículos Lenstra-Lenstra-Lovász para reconstruir el estado interno del generador a partir de los pocos bits disponibles. El sistema corrió el generador hacia atrás hasta llegar al punto en el que se inicializó con la función srand48.
Las diez marcas de tiempo recuperadas correspondían a fechas reales entre mayo de 1997 y abril de 1998, lo que para Anthropic descarta que la coincidencia fuera casualidad. La semilla de P-256, una de las curvas más usadas en la actualidad, surgió de una corrida iniciada el 16 de agosto de 1997, en la candidata número 1.842 del generador.
Lo que el hallazgo no resuelve
Anthropic fue clara, el resultado no constituye una ruptura criptográfica ni revela una debilidad nueva en el algoritmo de firma ECDSA, que usa estas curvas. Al contrario, sostiene que el hecho de que las semillas salieran de un procedimiento simple y reproducible por cualquiera reduce el margen para que hubiera un diseño deliberado con fines de espionaje.
El informe reconoce también varios cabos sueltos. El equipo no logró explicar el origen de la semilla de la curva binaria B-163, ni cómo se generaron los puntos base de las curvas P-224, P-256, P-384 y P-521, un dato distinto de la semilla y necesario para completar cada curva.
Tampoco quedó claro por qué el programa original saltó algunas combinaciones que, según el análisis de Claude, también habrían producido curvas matemáticamente válidas. Para la curva P-256, por ejemplo, la candidata número 876 del mismo proceso también cumplía todos los requisitos, pero no fue la elegida.
El trabajo estuvo a cargo de diez investigadores del equipo de seguridad de Anthropic, entre ellos Nicholas Carlini y Steve Weis, quienes reconocieron de forma póstuma a Solinas por haber sobrellevado con humor años de sospechas sobre su posible rol en un eventual backdoor de la NSA.

articles.title: SA-founded clinical AI startup Healthleap raises $38m seed, Series A funding - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
South Africa-founded clinical AI startup Healthleap has raised US$38 million in combined seed and Series A funding as it looks to expand its offering to more conditions.
Founded in South Africa in 2022 by siblings Josiah and Jemima Meyer, Healthleap has developed a platform that screens hospital patients for conditions that often go undiagnosed.
The platform reads each patient’s full electronic health record (EHR) every morning, including notes, labs, vitals, orders and problem lists, and flags risk. It then pushes risk scores into clinicians’ existing EHR workflows, showing care teams which patients need attention first.
Healthleap has initially focused on malnutrition, but now plans to expand its offering to cover additional conditions after raising the US$38 million round. The funding came from Sequoia Capital, First Round Capital and Hummingbird Ventures, and will also be used to grow Healthleap’s engineering, sales, customer success and product teams. The platform will be expanded to cover conditions including congestive heart failure, pressure ulcers and a range of hospital-acquired infections.
“Every week, millions of patients leave hospitals with unresolved health conditions that will erode their health and cost up to 10x more to treat in the long term,” said Josiah Meyer, co-founder and chief executive officer (CEO) of Healthleap. “Our goal is to help improve care and save lives by identifying those conditions now.”
Alfred Lin, partner at Sequoia Capital, said Healthleap was focused on finding patients who are being missed and getting them the care they need.
“The impact for both patients and hospitals has been inspiring, with one hospital seeing 39 per cent more malnutrition cases identified and treated, and US$11 million in incremental revenue in a single health system,” he said.
Josh Kopelman, co-founder and partner at First Round Capital, said the firm was drawn to Healthleap’s vision of every hospital using real-time AI to spot overlooked clinical risk, improve care and unlock reimbursement revenue.

articles.title: TechCrunch Mobility: Rivian's next act | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility!
As I wrapped my TechCrunch Disrupt interview with Rivian CEO and founder RJ Scaringe, I kept circling back to one question: What does Scaringe want Rivian to become? If you look at Rivian’s moves over the past year, it’s clear that Scaringe wants the company to be much more than an EV maker. But he doesn’t want to stray completely from that mission either.
Rivian is far more vertically integrated than it was just a couple of years ago. It has developed its own AI models to power its in-vehicle assistant and is building an end-to-end automated driving stack for its passenger vehicles and future robotaxis through a partnership with Uber. It’s even developing custom silicon, a 5 nm processor in collaboration with Arm and TSMC. And then there is its $5.8 billion joint technology venture with VW Group focused on electric architecture and software.
Scaringe’s ambitions extend beyond Rivian as well, although there is always a link back. He created a micromobility skunkworks program that has since spun out into a startup called Also. And he founded an industrial robotics startup called Mind Robotics, which is now 31% owned by Rivian and counts the automaker as a prospective customer. (Scaringe announced onstage that former Ford, Apple, and Tesla executive Doug Field has been hired as president of Mind Robotics.)
Scaringe’s aspirations were on display as he talked of not only expanding the joint venture with VW to cover AI and autonomy, but also licensing Rivian’s tech to “many different brands.”
So what does Rivian look like at the end of the decade? Certainly not just a maker of electric trucks and SUVs. The term I kept coming back to was “tech supplier.”
Hear me out. Rivian is clearing a path toward licensing its electric architecture and software as well as its AI models and autonomy stack. Meanwhile, the Mind Robotics startup it partially owns is building industrial robots to not only be used in Rivian factories, but also sold to other companies. Then there’s the robotaxi business. A successful launch with Uber could open the door to more deals.
And Scaringe is already imagining how autonomy could reshape Rivian’s own vehicles.
“Where it gets really interesting is then you think beyond R2 and R3 and start to imagine the form factors that you want to build for a personally owned autonomous vehicle. You know, it opens up all kinds of design opportunities. It can create dramatically different experiences,” he said in an interview with TechCrunch. “I’m wildly excited about what the next 10 years look like in transportation because of what this enables us to dream and think about.”
Deals!
Bedrock Robotics, a startup developing autonomous driving tech for construction vehicles, is raising $600 million, Axios reported, citing sources.
Dot Ai completed its acquisition of electric vehicle car-sharing business Envoy Technologies in a $65 million all-stock transaction, according to a regulatory filing.
Evos, a startup that developed AI agents to automate work for industrial businesses, including freight brokerages, raised $9 million in a pre-seed round co-led by Uncork Capital and Field Ventures.
Mana Battery, a Colorado-based startup developing anode-free sodium batteries, raised $10.15 million in a round led by Voyager Ventures.
PlusAI, the autonomous trucking developer, and Texas Ventures Acquisition III filed a Form S-4 registration statement with the Securities and Exchange Commission —advancing its previously announced agreement to go public via a merger with a blank-check company.
Volvo is leveling up its automated driving system through an expansion of its nearly decade-long partnership with Nvidia. Neither company shared financial terms of the deal. The automaker plans to use a trio of Nvidia products to be able to offer hands-free, point-to-point driving on highways and surface streets.
Waabi, a startup developing self-driving trucks, landed a commercial partnership with carrier Warrior Logistics. Under the deal, Waabi’s self-driving trucks will move freight between Dallas and Houston.
Notable reads and other tidbits
Electric vehicle sales in the United States are showing signs of life.
Laplace Intelligence, one of 20 startups that competed in TechCrunch’s Startup Battlefield 200, is building automated red-teaming that stress-tests robots and self-driving cars.
MIT startup LNK Energies says it has created a way to convert existing heavy-duty trucks from diesel to hydrogen, slashing pollution and costs while shielding operators from price spikes.
The Paris Auto Show puts Chinese cars on center stage.
Tesla showcased its SpaceX-powered Roadster with a theatrical kickflip stunt. The Roadster used a mix of high-powered fans and thrusters to drive up an inverted ramp, spin around, and stick a landing on the pavement below. CEO Elon Musk claims the vehicle will be on the road by 2028. But will future owners be allowed to legally deploy these maneuvers on public streets? I don’t see how.
Waymo is expanding into Canada — specifically, Toronto — after receiving approval to participate in an automated vehicle pilot program. Waymo has also opened up its robotaxi service to everyone, meaning no more waitlists, in San Antonio, San Diego, and Tampa.
One more thing …
TechCrunch reporter Tim De Chant recently test drove the 2026Porsche Macan Turbo EV. His week with the EV has him questioning what a sports car is supposed to be. Read the full review.

articles.title: Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon
articles.text:
Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon
These scientists hope that fire-spotting satellites, AI tools and ancient land practices could preserve the world’s vulnerable permafrost—and the vast carbon it stores.
In the middle of an especially warm July in 2021, a wildfire ignited in a thick forest of black spruce and peeling paper birch trees on the northern campus of the University of Alaska, Fairbanks.
The blaze, possibly sparked by lightning, burned across the dry carpet of feather mosses and lichen before climbing into the crowns. By the time fire agencies responded, flames had reached 12 feet in length and sent up a 500-foot column of smoke.
A few days shy of the five-year anniversary of the Yankovich Road Fire, I followed three members of the Alaska Fire Science Consortium into the boreal forest, walking along cross-country ski trails lined by feathery field horsetail.
In 2024, the organization, which hosts presentations to keep wildfire managers abreast of new developments in fire science, helped turn the area into an educational walking trail, with interpretive signs posted along the route. About a half-mile in, the horizon opened up as we reached a sparse stand of naked, blackened tree trunks, stripped of needles and neighbors.
Hilary Shook, the coordinator of the consortium, stepped off the trail with her thaw probe, a T-shaped pointed metal rod used to detect the upper boundary of the permafrost, the ancient layer of frozen soil that underlies 15% of the land around the Northern Hemisphere and stores roughly twice as much carbon as the atmosphere.
A test of the ground just outside the burn scar hit the concrete-like layer about a foot below the surface. But as Shook applied pressure here, where the fire had burned away the moss and organic-rich topsoil that insulates the permafrost, the probe plunged at least three times deeper into the ground.
“That was an immediate effect of the fire,” said Alison York, the outgoing coordinator of the organization, who was standing nearby. “When we monitored right after, it had already thawed quite a bit.”
This rudimentary tool, offering a measure of depth from a single point in the earth, reveals an escalating problem across the far north. As climate change fuels increasingly frequent and severe fires in the planet’s northern latitudes, they’re accelerating the thawing of more and more permafrost. This allows the organic matter to break down and release powerful greenhouse gases that contribute to a spiraling climate feedback effect, propelling more warming, more fires, and the loss of still more permafrost.
Most dramatically, intensifying wildfires in Canada released more carbon than the nation’s combined fossil fuel emissions in 2023. As in Alaska, many of these megafires occur in vast remote areas where the policy is to let them burn so long as they don’t threaten human habitats. Yet if intensifying fires and warming are left unchecked, the world’s boreal forests and permafrost could increasingly transition from giant carbon sinks into massive sources of atmospheric carbon.
Now, international teams of researchers across the US, Canada, and elsewhere are scrambling to understand what’s at stake, financially as well as ecologically. They’re looking at preventive measures, like controlled burns, and studying the potential to rapidly detect and extinguish wildfires before they grow out of control. They’re even exploring what was once unthinkable: sending in human firefighters not to save lives or structures, but to protect one of our planet’s great stores of carbon.
“We need to figure out a better way to live with wildfire," says Brendan Rogers, a senior scientist at the Woodwell Climate Research Center, one of the main organizations driving the loosely collaborative research effort. “I do think that it can make a meaningful difference."
Woodwell, the University of Victoria’s Polis Institute for Ecological Governance, and the nonprofit Alaska Venture Fund are now partnering on a multimillion-dollar initiative known as North Fire to study and raise public awareness about the potential benefits of these interventions, MIT Technology Review can report.
The idea is complicated and controversial for a number of reasons. Wildfire is a natural and necessary component of healthy forest ecosystems. Preventing or suppressing fires across huge stretches of largely unmanaged Arctic-boreal forests and tundra would take vast resources. And it’s not yet clear how much of a difference such interventions would make in emissions.
Ultimately, the mere fact that researchers are considering such extreme interventions into natural systems is a grim reflection of the dangers we’ve placed ourselves in by continuing to generate more and more greenhouse-gas emissions each year. Those threats are forcing us to grapple with increasingly difficult questions that involve ever steeper trade-offs: What’s the best way to spend our finite resources and dwindling time to avoid the worst dangers of climate change? And when, if ever, is it okay to put people in possible danger to reduce broader risks to the world?
‘A massive blind spot’
Emissions from forest fires have risen 60% around the world since 2001—but they’ve nearly tripled across the boreal forests in the far north.
This stretch of the globe is warming as much as four times faster than the rest of the planet, drying out the landscape. In addition, lightning strikes that set off fires have ticked up sharply as warmer air increases the convective energy in the atmosphere, driving the updrafts that trigger thunderstorms.
In that sense, humans have already interceded in these otherwise natural ecosystems by producing the greenhouse-gas emissions that are increasing temperatures, subjecting forests to fire patterns well outside healthy historic norms.
“To me, that outweighs the existential dread of ‘Should we or should we not intervene?” says Kate Hayes, an assistant professor at Western Washington University, who is working with Woodwell to study the emissions benefits of fire interventions. “We’ve already intervened, arguably. And so from here, it’s a little bit of a Band-Aid on a bullet wound.”
The permafrost that encircles the northern latitudes, underlying large stretches of Canada, Greenland, Siberia, Scandinavia, and other Arctic nations, stores around 1.5 trillion tons of carbon, much of which froze in place millennia ago. The steady global rise in temperature, however, has already shrunk the footprint of Arctic permafrost by about 12 % since 1850, with that loss rapidly accelerating during the last 50 years.
By 2100, fire-driven thawing of permafrost could release about the equivalent of nearly 80 billion tons of carbon dioxide, under high warming scenarios. That’s more than half the emissions that fires will release from the direct combustion of vegetation, according to a January study. And it would be on top of more than 400 billion additional tons that could be released through thawing from general warming over that period.
Despite its growing contributions to climate change, only a minority of the models that have informed the UN’s major climate reports to date include the gradual loss of permafrost through warming temperatures, and none incorporate the abrupt collapse and accelerated thaw that can often occur after fires and heat waves. In light of those phenomena and other powerful and undercounted climate feedback effects, we’re almost certainly underestimating how rapidly the planet will warm up, as scientists warned in a paper earlier this year.
These warming-driven emissions are a “massive blind spot,” says Brian Buma, a senior climate scientist at the Environmental Defense Fund and a coauthor of the paper, who is working to develop tools that could help fire agencies decide which fires to prioritize.
As escalating fire and permafrost emissions become significant additional contributors to climate change, some researchers have begun to explore what it might cost to take on the responsibility of preventing them, in much the way we’ve sought to cut the pollution from power plants, vehicles, and factories.
A 2022 paper in Science Advances, led by researchers at Woodwell and the Union of Concerned Scientists, found that making greater efforts to put out boreal fires could be a cost-effective climate solution—comparable to, or even cheaper than, addressing emissions by building wind turbines, solar farms, or carbon-sucking factories.
The Yukon Flats pilot
Those economic findings were instrumental in getting more researchers to take the idea of tackling fire emissions seriously, says Peter Frumhoff, a coauthor of the 2022 paper and now a senior science policy advisor at Woodwell.
For several years now, Woodwell researchers have been in discussions with forest managers, fire agencies, Indigenous communities, and other groups across Alaska to communicate the potential of this approach.
It hasn’t been an easy sell, given the constrained resources and tightly defined mission of the federal and state agencies responsible for combating fires in Alaska. The general policy there is to allow fires in remote territories to burn unless they present a direct danger to communities.
“Those agencies are tasked with protecting life and property now, and to a lesser extent natural resources,” says Randi Jandt, a fire ecologist at the Alaska Fire Science Consortium. “But they’re not tasked to save the world.”
There was one notable early success, however.
The Yukon Flats National Wildlife Refuge is an 11-million-acre patchwork of wetlands, forests, and bogs. The foothills sit above a particular type of frozen soil known as yedoma. It’s an especially deep, ice-rich, and carbon-dense form of permafrost, composed of massive wedges of silty, wind-blown sediments frozen during the late Pleistocene, which ended about 11,700 years ago. (It also presented ideal conditions for preserving mummified remains of woolly mammoths.)
“It took kind of the last ice age to accumulate,” Hayes says. “So there’s no rapid way to re-accumulate it. We can’t really put it back.”
In 2019, the region suffered a series of devastating fires that burned some 750,000 acres. After an Alaska Fire Science Consortium meeting at which Woodwell scientists highlighted the possible climate benefits of more aggressive fire suppression, the refuge's then manager, Jimmy Fox, began exploring the possibility of putting out blazes when they threatened that permafrost, whether or not they threatened human habitations.
The early reaction was not encouraging.
“You’re going to have people jumping out of airplanes with parachutes to save frozen woolly mammoths—and maybe dying from that?” he recalls being asked.
But eventually, he persuaded managers at the US Bureau of Land Management’s Alaska Fire Service to carry out a pilot project on a 1.6-million-acre section of the Yukon Flats. They agreed to try to put out fires there if they had the resources available and believed they could contain a blaze within 72 hours.
Woodwell and its partners agreed to study how that change affected permafrost loss and fire emissions, in the hope of making the case for similar programs elsewhere.
It wasn’t clear the pilot program would survive after Donald Trump was reelected, particularly once the DOGE initiative retroactively cut the public funding for that research collaboration.
But in February, the federal government formally preserved the program and broadened its rationale to include goals like protecting habitat diversity, water quality, and air quality.
Mapping and modeling
One of Woodwell’s main tasks now is determining when and where fire agencies should step in. Crucially, excessive efforts to stamp out fires in the past have allowed the buildup of dry plant material that fuels more severe fires later.
“We’re not going after all fires all the time,” says Rogers over lunch in a sunny courtyard on the Stanford University campus, where Woodwell and EDF hosted a workshop on potential fire interventions in January. “We can’t do that. We don’t want to do that. We shouldn’t do that. So how do we prioritize our resources?”
Woodwell and its collaborators are working to answer that question by developing a map of burn risk and carbon vulnerability across interior Alaska. The plan is to eventually expand it across much of Canada as well.
These maps will highlight the locations of rich reserves of yedoma and other forms of permafrost, forecast where fires are most likely to break out in the next 10 to 15 years, and predict how they’re likely to behave and spread.
“Our ultimate goal is to get a layer that can tell us, if a fire were to occur, what areas are most vulnerable to high carbon emissions, permafrost thaw, permafrost degradation,” Rogers says.
In response to a question about potentially putting firefighters at risk, Rogers stressed in an email that it’s “a very serious issue that needs careful consideration.”
He added that early fire detection technologies, preventative fire stewardship practices, improved fire suppression planning and other measures can all help to reduce dangers to firefighters as well as communities.
‘Mild fire’
Once areas of particular risk are identified, the first option is to take measures to prevent fires there, or at least to reduce the odds that they’ll become major ones. That generally entails using heavy equipment or intentional, controlled fires to clear away vegetation that could fuel new fires, or to create fire breaks that might check their spread.
Indigenous tribes carried out what’s known as cultural burning for thousands of years to reduce fire dangers, clear land for crops, and more. The practice was widely outlawed across North America beginning in the 1800s, though those rules have loosened in recent years.
Both cultural and prescribed fires, however, remain controversial because they can burn out of control. And even if they remain contained, the fires can still produce smoke that wafts into towns.
But rushing around to put out blazes after they’ve started will never get Alaska ahead of its surging wildfire problem, says Edward Alexander, cochair of the Gwich’in Council International, which represents the Indigenous Gwich’in peoples of the Northwest Territories, the Yukon, and Alaska.
“There’s not enough money in the world for this to be a chainsaw-and-ax problem,” he says. “This country is too big up here.”
Alexander, who also serves as senior Arctic lead at Woodwell, argues that Alaska should encourage much greater use of cultural burning to reduce the risk of conflagrations and the emissions that come with them.
“We need mild fire, not wildfire,” he says.
New pilot projects
The North Fire initiative will include several additional pilot research projects, including an effort to study the potential for cultural burning to reduce climate and fire dangers near Fort Yukon, Alaska.
The plan is for a wildland firefighting crew operated by the Council of Athabascan Tribal Governments, a consortium in the Yukon Flats region, to carry out cultural burns there next spring, Rogers says.
Researchers at Woodwell and the University of Alaska, Fairbanks, will then collect and analyze data flammability, carbon levels, and permafrost over several years, in the hopes of learning more about what such interventions do.
Similarly, the Polis researchers at the University of Victoria plan to study how adding fuel breaks, by logging or switching to less flammable trees, alters fire risks in British Columbia.
The broad aim of the North Fire initiative is to accelerate research and expand community involvement “in a way that helps us scale this as a meaningful global natural climate solution on a rapid timeline,” says Erin Harrington, a partner at the Alaska Venture Fund, a philanthropy focused on environmental, economic development, and Indigenous issues.
Detecting fires from space
Other observers, including Jandt, believe the bigger opportunity to reduce fire emissions and preserve permafrost may lie in the “initial attack.” That means marshalling planes, tankers, and firefighters to stamp fires out at the first sign of them, before they’ve had the chance to turn into conflagrations.
Once fires reach a certain size, it takes much more time to contain them—and the job becomes far more dangerous.
Accelerating response times is one of the chief promises of the FireSat satellite constellation, which is expected to begin delivering fire data at least twice daily from around the world to Woodwell, a handful of fire agencies, and other early adopters by the end of this year. The system will eventually include more than 50 satellites circling the globe, equipped with high-resolution cameras and thermal sensors that can detect smaller, lower-temperature fires than existing satellite systems, down to as little as five by five meters (16 by 16 feet).
Currently, it can take days to spot fires. But once the full constellation is in place, likely in the early 2030s, FireSat should be capable of detecting and providing updated images of fires anywhere in the world every 20 minutes or less.
The first prototype satellite launched in 2025, and three operational ones went into orbit in July. The Earth Fire Alliance, the nonprofit that manages the constellation, expects to launch four more by the end of next year.
A number of similar systems are also coming online. German-based OroraTech has launched 18 of its fire-detecting satellites in the last year and a half. Similarly, Canadian agencies are planning to launch their own satellite constellation, dubbed WildFireSat, beginning in 2029.
But as these systems produce more and more detections across the globe, it’ll become increasingly essential to build tools that can filter through that information.
EDF is supporting and collaborating on several projects that could potentially help with that, and it ultimately intends to develop an AI-powered triage tool that could help fire agencies prioritize responses as FireSat and other fire-spotting tools come online.
"All of this is kind of like building the data ecosystem around FireSat, so that when they start popping out “fire start here, there, fire start here, fire start there,” we won’t be like, ‘Oh shit, there’s fires everywhere,’” Buma says. “We’ll have a framework. It won’t be perfect, obviously. We’ll have to improve it, but we’ll have the machinery to incorporate those data.”
Rapid response
But faster detections and decisions do only so much. Regions would still need to get firefighting personnel and resources to those fires fast enough to prevent them from burning out of control.
“Say we have the full FireSat constellation up and running, and it spots a fire that just broke out in one of these sort of high-priority, highly vulnerable areas,” I said to Rogers and Frumhoff during our conversation in that Stanford courtyard. “How might we deploy firefighting resources to a remote area fast enough for it to matter in that scenario?”
“I think the answer, unfortunately, is that it depends,” Rogers responded.
Ideally, he said, we would have fire management policies in place that allow for putting out fires with a high risk of producing climate-warming emissions. In addition, regions could install more firefighting personnel and resources across more operational centers, strategically placed in locations that allow them to get to those blazes fast.
Frumhoff stresses that Woodwell isn’t promoting any particular companies but says there are additional technologies “in the mix of conversations” that might help to prevent or rapidly put out fires as well.
Those possible approaches include seeding clouds to suppress lightning strikes and pre-positioning autonomous firefighting helicopters to respond rapidly to high-emissions-risk fires.
Sikorsky, a Lockheed Martin company, is developing and testing autonomous versions of the Black Hawk helicopter, equipped with thermal sensors and water tanks. It is collaborating with Rain Industries, a startup based in Alameda, California, that has developed software to track shifting conditions and steer unpiloted aircraft through the process of putting out wildfires.
The company says it has talked to fire agencies and the “broader Alaska fire community” about the potential use of its technology but declined to name any specific entities it has interacted with.
“The twin climate tipping points of the yedoma permafrost and the boreal forest, and the fact that it’s completely underresourced at the moment, from my perspective does make it an ideal use case for autonomous aircraft,” says Max Brodie, chief executive officer of Rain.
Defending carbon
Advancing technologies can only do so much if governments’ fire prevention and suppression policies don’t prioritize preserving carbon.
And that will remain a hard sell given the costs of managing extensive areas of land that nations have historically left largely alone.
The 2022 Science Advances paper estimated that additional fire suppression efforts would cost about $12.63 per metric ton of prevented carbon dioxide emissions—a number that drops when the carbon in permafrost is taken into account, according to upcoming research.
But that would still add up to about $7 billion in additional spending this decade to keep Alaska’s fire emissions at their historical levels, and another $7 billion to $50 billion over the subsequent 30 years as fire severity continues to rise.
Frumoff stresses that those figures just reflect what the researchers found it would cost to preserve the status quo, which is not necessarily what the policy goal would be.
But widening the scope of where we put out fires will inevitably create a big added cost for fire agencies that are already notoriously underfunded in the US. While Alaska produces about half the nation’s wildfire emissions, it receives around 4% of federal firefighting funds.
The US Wildland Fire Service provided a prepared statement in response to an MIT Technology Review inquiry asking whether preserving carbon could or should become a priority in certain fire management decisions. The roundabout reply suggests that this isn’t the agency’s prime concern: “Firefighter and public safety are the top priorities for the U.S. Wildland Fire Service.”
Frumhoff says it’s possible that landowners or government agencies could eventually use carbon markets to defray some of the additional costs. Woodwell has also had multiple conversations with Alaska’s federal legislators about the value of preventing catastrophic wildfires and the need to increase the “total pot” of public funding, he says.
Kicking the fire can
A few days after walking through the fire scar in Fairbanks, I drove slowly along a crumpled stretch of Stampede Road, just north of Denali National Park, where the underlying permafrost had melted without the aid of fire.
I arrived at a cramped wooden cabin to meet with Michelle Mack, a regents professor of ecosystem ecology at Northern Arizona University.
Mack studies how fire is altering ecosystems in the high northern latitudes as the region grows warmer and drier, and she sometimes collaborates with Rogers and other scientists working on the push to protect permafrost in other areas of research. But she’s unsure how much these interventions will accomplish as climate change continues.
“I’m an empiricist, and at this point, it’s not clear to me that the empirical evidence suggests that we can actually have any impact on these fires,” she says.
She expects there will be clear cases where we could and should act fast to put out fires and “keep carbon in the ground.” She points to the example of the 2007 Anaktuvuk River Fire, a massive tundra fire on Alaska’s North Slope that might have been extinguished with relative ease in its early days but was instead allowed to burn until the winter snows put it out nearly three months later. Over that time, it ripped across 400 square miles and, Mack’s research showed, released more than 2 million tons of carbon into the air.
“I feel like that’s the low-hanging fruit, something that doesn’t cost much—and that’s where the technology for detection I think is really important,” she says.
But she adds that fires in boreal forests can rapidly spread in unpredictable ways, frustrating efforts to quickly extinguish them even when they are spotted right away.
In addition, rapidly putting out a fire one season doesn’t necessarily reduce the fire risk for a given forest, so suppression may simply kick the “fire can” down the road—delaying but not preventing an inevitable loss of carbon, Mack says.
Her thinking more recently shifted “a little” after she came across an earlier modeling paper that showed some encouraging findings on the potential of early suppression to reduce the footprint of boreal fires. But she says that prevention through forest thinning, prescribed burns, and the introduction of less flammable deciduous trees to create “living fire breaks” is probably a more promising path than technology-augmented suppression.
“If we could solve this with a techno fix, that’d be great,” she says. “But what if we solved it with nature?”
‘A real difference’
Rogers, in an emailed response to Mack’s concern, said that the interventions they’re exploring, which do include both prevention and suppression, “can make a real difference.”
“I certainly agree that some fires are much easier to suppress via initial attack than others,” he wrote. “That said, until I see data showing me otherwise, I believe there is strong potential to bend the curve with management.”
EDF’s Buma acknowledges there are a number of unknowns, including how quickly agencies could act on faster detections from satellites—and how big the political obstacles will be to making necessary changes to fire management policies.
“We can’t overpromise what’s possible. We don’t know what’s possible,” he says. “It’s all new. But we’re in a new climate and have to consider trying new things.”

articles.title: This 'benchtop' nuclear fusion device could provide fuel for the next revolution in clean energy
articles.text:
This startup is developing tiny 'benchtop' fusion devices in secret to build a more efficient nuclear reactor
Stellar power here on Earth
Nuclear fusion is how stars (including our own Sun) create their energy, and scientists are hopeful it could one day be used as a clean, abundant energy solution here on Earth. There are no carbon emissions, most of the fuel required is widely available, and it's safe: if the reaction goes wrong, it simply peters out and stops.
You might have spotted the big challenge, which is trying to fit an entire star's worth of energy production inside a power plant. Two main approaches are being explored, one using magnets to create the incredibly high temperatures and pressures required, and one using lasers — which is where the startup Cambridge Heavy Industries comes in.
As TechCrunch reports, the company is currently operating in 'stealth mode' from a lab attached to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), but now seems ready to share some details about the technology it's developing. The main innovations: fusion that's more efficient and needs less room than conventional reactors.
Nuclear fusion on a tabletop
Yun Kai, co-founder and CEO of Cambridge Heavy Industries, describes the company's fusion device as "tiny" and "benchtop" sized, which means experiments can be carried out and improved upon quickly. The technology will eventually be scaled up, but the aim is to build something smaller than conventional reactor designs — the size of two basketball courts approximately, rather than a full power plant complex.
What makes the approach of Cambridge Heavy Industries different is the dual laser setup. The first laser delivers its light as concentric rings that hit the block of fuel, designed to create shock waves traveling inward that create an accelerating compression effect; the second laser then hits the wave at the perfect spot to produce the super-high pressure required for ignition and nuclear fusion.
The enclosed system effectively acts as its own self-contained, compact fuel factory, because everything is moving inwards. It's also designed around a 2D rather than a 3D setup, which means fewer angles to cover — the laser fusion setup at the National Ignition Facility (NIF) in the US uses an array of 192 lasers in three dimensions to compress its own fuel blocks, for example.
As it's smaller and more efficient, the Cambridge Heavy Industries benchtop device can get through 50–80 laser shots per day — at the NIF, it's just a handful. A relatively low amount of laser power is required, says Kai, and as dozens of experiments are being done every 24 hours, the system can be quickly analyzed and iterated over time.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
There is one big caveat: the tabletop device at Cambridge Heavy isn't doing the same job as the NIF reactor or any other reactor in development, not yet. For now, it's focused on making one of the fuels required for nuclear fusion, tritium, rather than generating electricity. The actual reactor and plant stages will come later.
What happens next
For nuclear fusion to happen, two light atoms need to be smashed together. The best combination, scientists think, will be deuterium and tritium — and while there's a lot of deuterium around, there's not much tritium at all. At the moment, most of what we have comes from older nuclear fission power plants that are being phased out.
The long-term plan is for nuclear reactors to make their own tritium alongside producing electricity, but with reactors not expected to come online until the 2030s at the earliest, there's a window of opportunity before then that Cambridge Heavy Industries is hoping to make the most of.
TechCrunch points to a recent study that suggests the tritium shortfall could be as much as 28 kilograms (62 pounds) for the industry as a whole by 2054. At today's prices that works out at around $840 million (£631 million / AU$1,209 million) worth of the isotope — a potentially lucrative market.
There's also a lot of money, potentially, in nuclear fusion in general, which is why investors are putting capital into the development of future fusion plants. It's worth bearing in mind that while nuclear fusion reactions have been produced in the lab for decades, we're not yet at the stage where they can practically produce electricity — that's still some years off.
A steady supply of tritium and more efficient, compact nuclear fusion reactors will certainly help us get there faster though, and that's what's driving Cambridge Heavy Industries. If the technology can be fully developed over the next few years, it promises to be a genuine game-changer for energy production and supply.

Dave is a freelance tech journalist who has been writing about gadgets, apps and the web for more than two decades. Based out of Stockport, England, on TechRadar you'll find him covering news, features and reviews, particularly for phones, tablets and wearables. Working to ensure our breaking news coverage is the best in the business over weekends, David also has bylines at Gizmodo, T3, PopSci and a few other places besides, as well as being many years editing the likes of PC Explorer and The Hardware Handbook.

articles.title: 300-plus local data center bans have only delayed just three US projects — bans 'much more bark than bite,' only 2.3 gigawatts of data centers are held up, versus 38 gigawatts expected online in 2027
articles.text:
300-plus local data center bans have only delayed just three US projects — bans 'much more bark than bite,' only 2.3 gigawatts of data centers are held up, versus 38 gigawatts expected online in 2027
A project-by-project audit finds most moratoriums miss the site, the permit, or the timeline.
More than 300 local data center construction moratoriums haven’t had a massive impact on planned buildouts, with only three projects at about 2.3 out of 21 gigawatts (GW) of data centers in moratorium areas likely to be delayed, with a total of 38 GW projected to come online next year, SemiAnalysis shared on X. Per-project audits of the moratoriums indicate that they tend to miss the site, the permit, or the timeline.
The crux of the report is that, while everyone thinks the moratoriums are killing the U.S. buildout, its forecast has “barely moved over the last 12 months.” This forecast includes 38 GW of U.S. data center IT capacity in 2027, which is more than double that of 2026. Of that, 22 GW is under vertical construction, and the other 16 GW is mostly financed, with site work being done. The enacted local moratoriums cover about 20 GW with only about 1.5 GW of it delayed; New York’s pause adds 0.8 GW more. “We think moratoriums COULD delay the buildout, but they just aren’t yet at scale.”
The firm defines a moratorium as a “temporary legal pause,” and almost always a “freeze on accepting new applications.” More than 400 local instruments are tracked across 17 states, the enacted ones including a few permanent zoning bans, as of September. Four states acted in under two months this summer: New York, Texas, Pennsylvania, and Oregon. To test each active restriction against the records of thousands of projects, the firm’s analysts worked alongside “an army of state-of-the-art research agents.”
Several reasons are given for moratorium ineffectiveness, starting with the fact that they don’t revoke existing approvals. Short ones may expire before later projects need approval, and litigation or equipment lead times may already set the schedule. A moratorium moves the delivery date only if every condition holds, including that it reaches the parcel, is in force, overlaps the timeline, and covers the use in a way the project can’t work around. Capacity already under construction or fully permitted is also out of reach.
For example, Michigan has 45 enacted moratoriums but effectively zero pipeline exposure, and a Google campus there sits on industrial land already zoned for data processing. The firm says SpaceX’s planned data center in Brownsville, Texas, is on land the city removed from its limits and thus out of reach of the city’s moratorium. For a moratorium that did work, a township adopted a pause before NorthPoint, in Pennsylvania, filed for its special exception, with local approval pushed to next year. The company is still pursuing it.
The 2.3 GW figure is also incomplete, as it leaves out the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) pause. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott told the TCEQ to issue no permits for data center projects. Law firm Bracewell says this applies whether a project is in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas’s (ERCOT) queue or not, and expects the pause to last until ERCOT finishes its review in mid-December. Pauses like the TCEQ’s, and how they play out, could impact buildout forecasts.
The post quotes another by The Economist’s Archie Hall, from a trip that covers Michigan and Ohio, with the reporter stating that data center moratoriums are “much more bark than bite” for the time being. He puts the bigger risk at deterring newer projects, though he guesses that affects where data centers end up more than whether they get built. His impression is that politics also plays a role, and according to the firm’s poll in August, more Americans have a negative rather than positive impression of data centers.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The analysis concludes that moratoriums would need to be “materially more widespread and restrictive” to delay the buildout. On the firm’s weekly podcast last month, Jeremie Eliahou Ontiveros, one of the report’s authors, said the firm would be worried by a strict, state-level moratorium that blocked even off-grid projects, citing Texas as an example. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, in addition to Abbott, also found ways to bypass their legislatures for pauses they control and can revoke. The next move to watch is the TCEQ’s compliance report to Abbott’s office, due Monday.

Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

articles.title: Avec sa future Koala, Fiat veut sa part de la 2 CV électrique à 15 000 €
articles.text:
Pendant le Mondial de l’Auto de Paris 2026, Citroën a attiré tous les regards avec le concept de sa future 2 CV électrique. Le genre de succès que d’autres marques aimeraient également avoir, y compris au sein du groupe Stellantis. C’est ainsi que Fiat préparerait sa jumelle de la « deuche ». Arnaud Belloni, directeur général de Fiat depuis le 1er septembre 2026, l’a confirmé pendant le salon dans des propos rapportés par le magazine britannique Autocar ce 19 octobre : « Nous préparons une petite voiture qui sera basée sur la 2 CV ».
Les deux modèles partageront la nouvelle plateforme de Stellantis, conçue pour la catégorie européenne E-Car qui doit encore voir le jour. Le nom du modèle n’est pas arrêté, mais Fiat a déposé la marque Koala. « Nous avons un Koala, un Panda et un Grizzly », a résumé Arnaud Belloni, dans la lignée des noms d’animaux (citadine Grande Panda et SUV Grizzly).
La petite Fiat est déjà aussi avancée que la 2 CV
La future Fiat doit devenir l’alternative électrique à la Panda thermique, rebaptisée Pandina. Disponible en Europe depuis près de quinze ans, elle reste la voiture la plus vendue en Italie. Fiat promet d’ailleurs de garder une petite voiture essence abordable au catalogue. Gaetano Thorel, patron de Fiat en Europe, disait plus tôt cette année chercher une solution multi-énergie.
François Leboine, directeur du design de Fiat, assure que le modèle est « aussi prêt que la 2 CV », mais que ce n’était « pas le bon moment » pour le montrer. Selon lui, Fiat ne voulait pas voler la vedette à Citroën sur son salon national.
Le style pourrait reprendre des idées d’un concours organisé cette année auprès d’étudiants italiens. Le public a voté pour l’Ippo, une citadine très carrée qui rappelle les Panda d’antan et d’aujourd’hui. En revanche, la voiture ne jouera pas la carte du pur néorétro comme la 2 CV. Arnaud Belloni parle d’une « approche très différente ». Grosso modo, évoquer le passé sans le ressusciter trait pour trait.
Une voiture taillée pour une règle pas encore votée
Fiat et Citroën misent sur la future réglementation E-Car, une catégorie réservée aux petites électriques de moins de 4,2 mètres. Stellantis et Renault la réclamaient depuis l’été 2025, et la Commission européenne l’a proposée le 16 décembre 2025 dans son paquet automobile, sous le nom de « petites voitures abordables ». Les constructeurs espèrent obtenir des règles allégées pour ces modèles, notamment sur les aides à la conduite imposées par le règlement GSR2, afin de faire baisser les prix.
La catégorie s’inspire des « kei cars » japonaises. Là-bas, ces mini-voitures limitées à 3,4 mètres et moins taxées représentent près de 40 % des ventes de voitures neuves. La version européenne serait bien plus permissive. Avec une limite de 4,2 mètres, même une Renault 5 de 3,9 mètres entrerait dans les clous.
Sauf que le texte n’est pas encore adopté par le Parlement européen et les États membres. Le calendrier laisse de la marge, puisque la 2 CV de série n’est attendue qu’à la fin de 2028.
Fiat n’a donné ni prix, ni autonomie, ni date. Le seul repère vient de Citroën, qui vise environ 15 000 euros pour sa 2 CV de 3,76 mètres, soit environ 5 000 euros de moins que l’ë-C3, affichée à partir de 19 990 euros hors aides. Pour mémoire, Fiat promettait déjà en 2023 de rejoindre le club des électriques à moins de 25 000 euros.

articles.title: De la connexion à la protection des données : comment Nordnet accompagne vos usages numériques — Frandroid
articles.text:
Une commande passée depuis son smartphone dans un train, une facture téléchargée sur l’ordinateur familial, quelques documents envoyés depuis le Wi-Fi d’un hôtel : vos données personnelles vous suivent d’un écran à l’autre. Coordonnées bancaires, identifiants, fichiers privés… vous les utilisez chaque jour, sans forcément vous demander comment elles sont protégées. Jusqu’à ce qu’un faux mail de livraison ou une page de paiement suspecte vous rappelle qu’elles valent cher.
Pour Nordnet, accompagner ces usages passe aussi par leur sécurisation. Fournisseur d’accès à Internet depuis 1995 et filiale d’Orange, l’entreprise française développe cette approche avec sa gamme Securitoo. Elle veut aider les utilisateurs à protéger les informations contenues dans leurs appareils, mais aussi à mieux préserver la confidentialité de leur navigation.
Pour répondre à ces besoins, la gamme Securitoo de Nordnet détecte par exemple les logiciels malveillants, limite le suivi publicitaire lorsque vous naviguez sur Internet et sécurise vos transactions où que vous soyez.
Avec le code FRAN60, l’abonnement annuel à Securitoo coûte 60 % moins cher la première année.
Nordnet connecte les foyers et protège aussi leurs données
Selon le Baromètre du numérique publié par l’Arcep en mai 2024, un foyer comptait en moyenne 10 équipements numériques avec écran en 2023. Smartphones, tablettes et ordinateurs en représentent à eux seuls 6,3 (y compris ceux qui ne servent plus), et tous peuvent stocker les données sensibles de la famille.
Pour protéger ces données, Nordnet propose sa gamme Securitoo, conçue pour s’adapter aux usages de chaque foyer, que l’on passe sa journée sur un ordinateur ou que l’on utilise surtout son téléphone.
Cette protection repose sur deux volets complémentaires. Le premier concerne les appareils et leur contenu : repérer un programme malveillant, détecter une tentative de fraude ou empêcher un logiciel d’accéder à des informations sensibles. Le second porte sur la confidentialité de la connexion et les traces laissées pendant la navigation.
Securitoo couvre ces deux volets avec deux offres distinctes. Chacun choisit ainsi ses protections selon ses appareils et ses usages, sans empiler des outils dont il connaît mal le périmètre.
Des protections concrètes pour les usages du quotidien
En pratique, les outils de cybersécurité de Securitoo couvrent bon nombre de situations courantes. Par exemple, si un mail vous invite à régler des frais pour débloquer un colis, il renvoie très probablement vers un site conçu pour dérober vos coordonnées bancaires.
La suite de sécurité Securitoo de Nordnet intègre des fonctions antiphishing et antifraude pour repérer et bloquer ces pages malveillantes, ainsi qu’une protection des transactions en ligne.
Autre scénario : vous téléchargez par mégarde un programme qui tente ensuite de modifier vos fichiers. L’antivirus intégré de Securitoo et son système d’analyse, baptisé Advanced Threat Defense, surveillent les activités suspectes pour détecter les menaces.
La protection contre les ransomwares vise notamment les logiciels qui cherchent à chiffrer vos documents pour vous réclamer de l’argent. L’analyse des vulnérabilités permet, de son côté, d’identifier des faiblesses dans la configuration de votre appareil et vous indique comment les corriger.
Sur les équipements compatibles, Securitoo peut aussi bloquer les accès à la webcam et au micro pour éviter qu’une application ne les utilise à votre insu. Ces fonctionnalités varient selon le système et le terminal équipé : un PC Windows, un Mac et un smartphone ne disposent pas tous des mêmes modules.
Nordnet propose également, dans sa gamme Securitoo, une offre distincte consacrée à la confidentialité de la navigation : Securitoo VPN. Elle chiffre la connexion entre votre appareil et un serveur distant, ce qui protège vos échanges sur un réseau Wi-Fi public, en France comme à l’étranger. Le blocage des traqueurs et des publicités intrusives contribue, lui, à limiter la collecte de données sur vos habitudes de navigation.
Le service s’active d’un simple bouton ON/OFF dans l’application. Une fonction de coupure automatique peut aussi bloquer l’accès à Internet si la connexion protégée s’interrompt, afin d’éviter que les échanges se poursuivent sans cette protection. De quoi mieux maîtriser sa confidentialité en ligne, sans avoir à configurer soi-même chaque paramètre réseau.
Plusieurs équipements, un interlocuteur : la proposition de Nordnet pour votre foyer
Ces protections doivent aussi pouvoir suivre les utilisateurs d’un écran à l’autre. Avec cinq licences incluses, la suite de sécurité Securitoo permet par exemple d’équiper l’ordinateur familial, deux smartphones et deux tablettes. Elle est disponible sur Windows, macOS, Android et iOS, avec des fonctionnalités qui diffèrent selon le système utilisé.
Nordnet propose cette suite à 5 euros par mois avec un paiement mensuel, ou 48 euros par an avec un paiement annuel, soit l’équivalent de 4 euros par mois pour cinq appareils. Il existe aussi une formule trimestrielle à 13,50 euros, soit 4,50 euros par mois. Le paiement mensuel est sans engagement ; en trimestriel ou en annuel, l’engagement court sur la période payée.
Pas besoin d’être abonné à Internet chez Nordnet pour en profiter : la suite de sécurité se souscrit seule, pour les résidents de France métropolitaine. Ceux qui veulent seulement protéger un smartphone ou une tablette peuvent aussi choisir Securitoo Mobile, limité à un appareil, à 2,99 euros par mois ou 29,90 euros par an.
L’offre consacrée à la confidentialité de la navigation se souscrit séparément. Compatible avec ces mêmes systèmes, elle se décline en formules pour trois, cinq ou sept appareils, à partir de 3 euros par mois, avec un paiement mensuel (sans engagement), trimestriel ou annuel. Pour sept appareils, comptez 6 euros par mois en paiement mensuel ou 57,60 euros par an. La formule annuelle revient ainsi à 4,80 euros par mois, soit moins de 70 centimes par appareil. Avec le code FRAN60, les abonnements annuels éligibles de la gamme Securitoo sont réduits de 60 % pendant un an.
Le code ramène ainsi la suite de sécurité à 19,20 euros la première année au lieu de 48 euros, et la formule de confidentialité pour sept appareils à 23,04 euros au lieu de 57,60 euros. À l’issue de cette première année, l’abonnement se renouvelle tacitement pour la même durée, sauf résiliation de votre part.
Au-delà des logiciels, Nordnet met à disposition une assistance en ligne consacrée à Securitoo, avec des guides pour installer les applications, activer les protections et prendre en main leurs réglages. Chaque foyer peut ainsi combiner la suite de sécurité et les outils de protection de la navigation selon ses appareils, avec un seul interlocuteur pour les deux abonnements et leur assistance.

articles.title: Cheaper fibre fees don't spark Nigerian infrastructure investment
articles.text:
Nigeria’s states take widely different approaches to the cost of laying fibre-optic cables. Some have waived Right of Way (RoW) fees; others charge the ₦145-per-metre benchmark, while Ogun State charges up to ₦6,600 ($4.84) per metre. Yet these differences do not neatly explain where fibre infrastructure has been built, raising questions about what else drives investment.
Administrative reforms and project-specific concessions may help offset high fees, but there is little evidence that they do so systematically. The Lagos State Infrastructure Maintenance and Regulatory Agency (LASIMRA) describes itself as a one-stop regulator for utility infrastructure, and the state has announced an online permitting system to streamline approvals for fibre, masts and towers. However, the announcement does not establish whether the system has reduced processing times or costs or removed requirements such as environmental approvals.
Ogun has also reportedly waived RoW charges for a specific 250-kilometre MainOne deployment, but that historical concession does not establish that similar incentives are generally available today. There is no verified evidence of a telecom-specific tax-break programme that explains the substantial fibre networks in these high-fee states. Without access to operators’ permits, concession agreements and investment decisions, it remains unclear whether incentives offset the charges or whether companies invest despite them.
Data from the Nigerian Communications Commission’s (NCC) Ease of Doing Business portal, published in July 2026, shows that Ogun has 4,246.48 kilometres of deployed fibre, while Kano and Rivers, which charge ₦2,754 (2.02) and ₦2,256(1.65) per metre respectively, have 4,616.71 kilometres and 4,616.01 kilometres. Delta, with a rate of ₦2,706 ($1.98) per metre, has 4,202.62 kilometres.
RoW charges are only one component of deployment costs. Trenching and duct installation also depend on ground conditions, water crossings, construction methods and access to existing infrastructure. The NCC portal’s fee and deployment indicators do not provide route-level construction costs. Broader evidence establishes why this matters: the World Bank identifies civil works as the dominant component of certain broadband deployments, accounting for up to 80% of costs in some cases.
At the other end of the spectrum, Ebonyi, which charges a ₦145 benchmark, has just 586.92 kilometres of fibre. Bayelsa, at ₦850 ($0.62) per metre, has a length of 656.87 kilometres. Jigawa and Zamfara, both of which have waived the fee, have 970.10 kilometres and 1,100.98 kilometres, respectively.
The disparity raises a critical question about closing Nigeria’s connectivity gaps: what will persuade operators to invest in places they have largely overlooked? Lower fees may reduce deployment costs, but they do not necessarily make a project commercially viable. Understanding what drives investment is essential to ensuring that these reforms extend broadband to underserved communities, rather than simply lowering costs in places where operators already intend to build.
High fees, low deployment
Sango-Ota, a major town in Ogun State. Image source: Femi Adedesin-Kuti
Ogun presents a particularly striking case. Its ₦6,600 ($4.84) per metre fee is more than 45 times the ₦145 ($0.11) benchmark. A hypothetical 10-kilometre deployment would attract ₦66 million ($48,387) in RoW charges alone, compared with ₦1.45 million ($1,063) at the benchmark rate.
Despite this high charge, Ogun has more than 4,200 kilometres of deployed fibre. Kano and Rivers also have more than 4,600 kilometres each, despite charging substantially above the benchmark. These existing networks indicate that operators have built significant infrastructure in high-fee jurisdictions, driven by commercial markets, strategic transport corridors, enterprise customers, and existing telecoms infrastructure.
The comparison with low-fee states raises the opposite question. Ebonyi’s 586.92 kilometres of fibre and Bayelsa’s 656.87 kilometres are substantially below the footprints in Ogun, Kano, and Rivers. Jigawa and Zamfara also have fewer than 1,200 kilometres despite waiving RoW charges. A waiver removes one cost from a deployment project, but it does not guarantee that expected revenue will justify construction, equipment, maintenance, and security costs where demand is limited.
The picture is not uniformly unfavourable to states that have reduced or eliminated their fees. Kaduna, which has waived RoW charges, has 4,339.85 kilometres of fibre, putting it among Nigeria’s leading states for deployment. Anambra, another zero-fee state, has 2,547.34 kilometres, while Niger has 3,383.43 kilometres.
These examples matter because they show that a zero-fee policy and a substantial fibre footprint can coexist. However, total fibre figures reflect accumulated infrastructure over time rather than recent policy impacts. A state with a large network may have attracted investment before reducing its fees, while a state with a smaller network may have introduced a waiver recently and has yet to see its full effect.
Lagos exposes a separate pricing problem
Lagos and the Federal Capital Territory complicate the argument that high right-of-way (RoW) fees necessarily deter investment. The NCC portal lists Lagos’s RoW charge at ₦850 ($0.62) per metre and the FCT’s at ₦950 ($0.70). Yet Lagos has 11,586.70 kilometres of fibre, while the FCT has 6,973.13 kilometres. Together, they account for 18,559.83 kilometres, or 18.35% of Nigeria’s reported 101,148.36-kilometre fibre network.
Their sizeable networks reflect the concentration of businesses, financial institutions, government agencies, data centres and other major connectivity users in both locations. But Lagos also exposes a problem beyond its fees: inconsistent published rates. While the NCC portal lists ₦850 ($0.62) per metre, the Lagos State Infrastructure Maintenance and Regulatory Agency (LASIMRA) lists ₦1,500 ($1.10) per metre for fibre. It also publishes a ₦50,000 ($36.66) application fee and an administrative and project-management charge equivalent to 15% of permit fees.
For operators, the discrepancy makes expansion costs harder to predict. A 10-kilometre fibre route would attract a base charge of ₦8.5 million ($6,232) at the NCC-listed rate, compared with ₦15 million ($11,000) at LASIMRA’s rate—a difference of ₦6.5 million ($4,765) before additional charges. If LASIMRA’s 15% administrative and project-management fee applies to the base fibre permit charge, it would add ₦2.25 million ($1,650). Including the ₦50,000 ($36.66) application fee, the total would reach ₦17.3 million ($12,683) before construction costs. This is an illustrative calculation, not a confirmed invoice; operators need clarity on which schedule applies.
The NCC acknowledges that rates may differ and directs operators to confirm the applicable charges with LASIMRA before making payments. “Charges may vary depending on project location and scope. Operators are advised to engage the Lagos State Infrastructure Maintenance and Regulatory Agency (LASIMRA) for updated rates and guidelines,” the commission says on its website.
The problem extends beyond the amount operators pay to the uncertainty surrounding their costs. Higher upfront fees tie up capital that could fund other deployment needs, while inconsistent rates make it harder to budget for projects and assess their commercial viability.
Lagos’s extensive fibre network shows that substantial infrastructure can coexist with high charges, but it does not establish that those charges do not affect future investment. Operators must still weigh the full cost of deployment against expected demand, particularly on less profitable routes. Clear, consistently applied fees could reduce uncertainty and improve the prospects of projects that might otherwise struggle to make commercial sense.
Fibre kilometres are not capital expenditure
The length of a fibre network offers a useful measure of deployment, but it is not a direct measure of investment. Costs vary with route conditions, excavation and road reinstatement, equipment, network design, and the extent to which operators can use existing infrastructure. A longer network does not necessarily mean more capital was invested, just as a shorter one does not automatically indicate weaker investment.
Determining whether lower RoW fees attract investment requires data that links policy changes to actual deployment. The NCC and state governments should publish annual figures on new fibre laid, along with the dates of fee changes, permit applications, approval times and operators’ state-level capital expenditure. Such data would help distinguish the effect of lower fees from other factors influencing where operators build.
A commissioner in a northern state, who requested anonymity because of concerns about the upcoming general elections, said little had changed since the state adopted a ₦145-per-metre fee. The commissioner also pointed to Nasarawa, which has waived the charge but, in the commissioner’s assessment, has yet to see an improvement in infrastructure deployment. He did not provide specific figures for operator permit applications submitted before and after the adoption of the ₦145 fee.
These accounts suggest that lower fees alone may not be enough to spur investment, although assessing their effect requires time-series data on deployment and capital expenditure.
Anambra State, meanwhile, views its zero-fee policy as a long-term investment in connectivity rather than an immediate revenue driver.
“Anambra’s zero-RoW-fee policy is a strategic investment in expanding broadband infrastructure, improving connectivity and accelerating digital inclusion,” Chukwuemeka Fred Agbata Jnr., managing director and chief executive of the Anambra State ICT Agency, told TechCabal. “We see it as an enabler of long-term digital growth, with continued efforts to deepen infrastructure deployment across the state.”
Move beyond assuming cheaper fees automatically produce more fibre. Ogun, Kano, and Rivers maintain substantial networks despite high charges, while Ebonyi, Bayelsa, and Jigawa have comparatively little infrastructure despite lower fees. High fees do not halt expansion where strong commercial demand exists, just as waivers cannot single-handedly make an unviable market profitable.
For state governments, the real test is whether lower fees are followed by faster approvals, newly laid fibre, greater capital investment, and expanded connectivity beyond major urban centres. Until states systematically track and report new construction following policy changes, fee reductions remain an input into investment policy—not proof that investment has actually increased.
South Africa’s spam calls reached 17.5 billion in the first half of 2026. Now, the government wants companies to prove they have checked who they call before they press send.
The National Consumer Commission (NCC), South Africa’s consumer watchdog, launched a National Opt-Out Registry on Wednesday that will allow consumers to pre-emptively block unwanted direct marketing.
The registry is part of a sweeping government effort to tackle South Africa’s growing spam-call problem. Marketers will have to register with the system and cleanse their lists every month before running campaigns. Fintechs, banks, telcos, insurers, retailers and other digital businesses will need to build consumer opt-outs into their marketing systems.
Truecaller’s 2026 South Africa Spam Report found that there were 17.5 billion spam calls between January and June, 25.2% higher than the same period in 2025. Spam short message service (SMS) messages also jumped 58.9% to 3.7 billion
The numbers help explain why the NCC is moving beyond asking consumers to ignore or block unwanted messages and is instead imposing obligations on the companies that send them.
Parks Tau, the Minister of Trade, Industry and Competition, said the growing sophistication of spam and scams required a stronger regulatory response.
“South Africans are becoming more alert, but alertness alone cannot substitute for a proper regulatory backstop,” Tau said at the launch. “Scam and marketing networks are becoming more sophisticated, using spoofing and artificial intelligence to reach consumers.”
The registry gives effect to Section 11 of the Consumer Protection Act, which gives consumers the right to block unwanted direct marketing communication. Tau believes the issue relates to data and privacy, as more companies rely on personal information to reach potential customers.
“Section 14 of our Constitution guarantees everyone the right to privacy. A person’s phone number, email address and time are not raw material to be harvested and traded without their consent,” he said.
For companies, however, the challenge will be translating that principle into their existing marketing systems.
The NCC said direct marketers have been able to register on the registry since September 15 and have until December 2026 to complete their registration. They will then have five months, from December to April 2027, to cleanse their marketing lists and prepare to interface with the system at no cost.
From May 2027, registered consumers will be able to pre-emptively block direct marketers from contacting them.
The registry means companies will have to account for it before launching campaigns, potentially requiring changes to customer databases, campaign-management tools, and internal compliance processes.
“This is a momentous occasion for consumers who have for years been flooded with unwanted direct marketing,” Hardin Ratshisusu, the NCC’s Acting Commissioner, said. “The National Opt-Out Registry will promote responsible direct marketing, ensuring consumers are protected from unwanted direct marketing through spam calls, texts, e-mails and other electronic communication.”
The NCC said the phased rollout will give businesses time to prepare and that it will publish further guidance while running a consumer education programme.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. articles.title: Is your marketing AI tool driving profit or just noise? CleverTap co-founder Anand Jain weighs in
articles.text:
Is your marketing AI tool driving profit or just noise? CleverTap co-founder Anand Jain weighs in
At TechSparks 2026, CleverTap co-founder Anand Jain explained why marketing teams must move beyond basic generative AI productivity tools and adopt autonomous, real-time decisioning systems that drive genuine business profit.
Most marketing teams today use AI to save time on tasks such as drafting emails, creating image variants, and summarising long documents. However, Anand Jain, Co-founder and Chief Marketing Officer of CleverTap, a customer engagement and marketing automation platform, says basic tools that do these jobs rarely improve company profits.
In a masterclass on marketing strategy at TechSparks 2026, Jain urged leaders to look beyond simple shortcuts.
“We are going to talk about how you go from using AI for fun and games all the way to using AI to generate actual business results," he said.
While creating content using AI makes the job faster and saves time, Jain questioned whether it truly drives growth, asking, “Is it actually going to impact business results or it is just more of the same?”
Traditional digital campaigns usually operate on a push model wherein companies decide what they want to sell instead of understanding what consumers want to buy. Whereas, a local shop assistant in an offline channel remembers a customer’s personal taste, notices immediate reactions, and suggests items tailored to their budget and style. Digital marketing must adopt a similar mindset.
“Not what I want to sell, (but) what my customer wants to buy. So you flip this around,” Jain said.
Instead of broadcasting generic promotions to large groups, modern marketing engines should interpret live customer actions to match individual needs.
This approach marks a shift towards the highest level of AI maturity, known as 'real-time decisioning'.
Marketing technology generally progresses through three stages. Level 1 focuses on basic time-saving tasks, Level 2 covers experimentation such as A-B testing (comparing two ad versions to see which works better), and Level 3 achieves true automated decisioning.
“You start with productivity, then you do experimentation, and the hardest thing is decisioning. When you actually are building an entire system for a party of one and that one person could be one out of several million that show up on your app or your website,” Jain noted.
Instead of bombarding users with discount codes, decisioning offers gentle helpful steps first, such as establishing brand trust or explaining product benefits.
Real-time decisioning relies on a single data hub that combines a customer’s historical profile with their immediate live actions. Traditional A-B testing usually stops after selecting one fixed winner, but decisioning uses reinforcement learning, a smart system that learns continuously from user responses and adjusts offers on the fly.
Furthermore, instead of relying only on propensity scoring (calculating how likely someone is to buy), decisioning uses uplift modelling. This method identifies the specific nudge, message, or channel needed to encourage an individual user to take their next positive step.
As automated systems manage campaign delivery across thousands of message options, the role of the marketer shifts from execution to strategic direction. Rather than manually drafting creative variants, marketers define high-level goals and establish strict operational limits.
“Your job is to create budget guardrails, brand guardrails, regulatory guardrails. Do not use the word 'free' if you are offering something, if you are a bank,”Jain emphasised.
By establishing clear boundaries, marketing leaders empower smart decisioning engines to work independently, keeping brand messaging safe while driving genuine commercial profit, he added.
Edited by Swetha Kannan

Un buen ejemplo lo tenemos en el Xiaomi TV F Pro (2026), que ahora mismo ha bajado en Amazon hasta los 129,01 euros con un doblete de descuentos:
