articles.title: OPINION: Selling your startup does not mean success | EU-Startups
articles.text:
In that world of startups, founders and investors, we learn to ask certain questions almost instinctively. How big can this become? How much capital will it take to get there? And, sooner or later, when do I get my money back, and at what multiple?
These are not cynical questions. They reflect the logic of venture capital, where investors put capital at risk expecting substantial returns and founders pursue growth, scale and eventually liquidity.
But there is a question we ask far less often: Are we building the companies we actually want to own, or the companies our funding models encourage us to build?
When success changes meaning
At an event recently, I found myself in a conversation with experienced tech entrepreneurs who had already built, scaled and exited companies.
One founder told the room that, knowing what she knows today, she would never have sold her first company. Another described how differently he is building his next venture after taking external capital and scaling rapidly the first time around.
These were successful entrepreneurs by conventional measures. Yet their experiences had changed how they thought about ownership, ambition and what they ultimately wanted from building a business. Their reflections revealed an interesting tension: the decisions that help founders achieve one definition of success can sometimes take them further away from another.
In Vienna, the sixth and seventh generations of A.E. Köchert, the former Imperial Court jeweller founded in 1814, offer a strikingly different time horizon.
Their focus on craftsmanship, customer relationships and continuity illustrates how ownership across generations can shape business priorities. It is a mindset familiar in many multigenerational companies: the determination not to be the last generation.
It raises a broader question: how profoundly does a company’s definition of success shape what it builds, protects and passes on?
Capital is never just capital
For startup founders, choosing a funding model is one of the earliest and most consequential strategic decisions.
Venture capital can accelerate international expansion, product development and market leadership. In sectors where speed and scale are decisive, it can be the difference between building a category leader and being overtaken by competitors. But venture capital also comes with an economic logic. Fund lifecycles, return expectations and portfolio dynamics can influence the growth strategies, financing decisions and exit opportunities that investors favour.
A business that could generate attractive profits for its founder over decades may not necessarily deliver the scale or liquidity a venture fund requires. That does not make it a bad business. It may simply be the wrong business for that particular capital.
The reverse is equally true. A founder determined to retain complete control may underinvest in a market where rapid expansion is essential, sacrificing long-term competitiveness for short-term independence.
The real strategic challenge is aligning the company’s economics, the investors’ expectations and the founder’s ambitions. An investor may favour an acquisition that delivers an attractive return within the fund’s investment horizon, while the founder sees greater value in remaining independent. Both can be acting rationally, yet pursuing fundamentally different outcomes. When those interests are aligned, capital can be a powerful accelerator. When they are not, even a growing and successful business can become a source of conflict.
The ownership decisions that shape your future
In his research at Harvard Business School, Noam Wasserman explored a related tension through the founder’s “Rich versus King” dilemma: the choices that help build a more valuable company can require founders to surrender ownership and control. But I think the question extends beyond wealth versus control. It is also about time horizons, incentives and the freedom to redefine success as a company evolves.
Before raising capital, founders should consider three questions.
What kind of business am I building? A venture-scale technology company pursuing global market leadership may require a very different capital structure from a profitable business designed to compound value over decades.
Whose definition of success will ultimately determine our decisions? Founders and investors may agree on growth while having different expectations around profitability, ownership and the timing of an exit.
What am I willing to sacrifice and what must I protect? Speed, independence, culture, product quality and long-term flexibility all have value. Understanding which trade-offs are acceptable matters more than following a fashionable funding strategy.
These questions do not have universally correct answers. But avoiding them does not make the trade-offs disappear.
Ambition has more than one shape
Europe needs founders willing to build globally competitive companies. We need venture capital, ambitious growth strategies and entrepreneurs prepared to take extraordinary risks. But we also need to recognise that not every successful company should follow the same financial blueprint.
A successful funding round is not the same as a successful business. A higher valuation does not automatically mean greater long-term value. And an exit, however financially rewarding, is not necessarily every founder’s ultimate ambition.
After years in the startup and investment ecosystem, spending time with businesses that think in generations rather than funding rounds has not made me less interested in growth. It has made me more interested in what we are actually growing towards.
You may want to raise €100 million and build a global category leader. You may want to retain control and own your company in 30 years. Or you may want to build something the next generation will inherit.
The mistake is not choosing one model over another. The mistake is adopting someone else’s definition of success without understanding what it will require you to sacrifice.
Know which game you are playing. And make sure it is the one you actually want to win.

articles.title: Las 5 películas que tardaron menos en rodarse de todos los tiempos
articles.text:
Como lo acaba de demostrar The Batman 2, filmar una película siempre será una combinación de factores. Por un lado, la más pura casualidad, en la que intervienen elementos tan dispares como el clima hasta la salud de los actores. Para la historia, quedan historias como el rodaje de pesadilla de Apocalypse Now o todos los obstáculos que atravesó El Padrino. Eso sin olvidar proezas de ingeniería como la filmación de Titanic o conflictivos como el de El resplandor de Stanley Kubrick.
Lo cierto es que llevar el proyecto de un guion a la pantalla grande no siempre es un trayecto recto, fácil u ordenado. Mucho más, cuando un rodaje es una empresa a gran escala que involucra, además, visión artística y capacidad logística. Una mezcla de situaciones que pueden ocasionar dos resultados posibles. Por un lado, un triunfo de organización que brinde espacio e importancia a todo el equipo detrás de cámara. O al contrario, un desorden a todo nivel que empuje a la futura producción a caminos inciertos.
Lo que sea que ocurra, lo que implica filmar una película siempre será motivo de interés y asombro. Pero mucho más cuando toda la travesía rompe esquemas, récord y hasta comienza a formar parte de la historia del cine universal. Como estas cinco películas que te dejamos a continuación con tiempos asombrosamente cortos de filmación. De una increíble historia filmada en menos de un día hasta un hito del terror que se convirtió en una gran aventura cinematográfica. Todo para los amantes del cine y sus rarezas.
Una proeza técnica de menos de dos horas de rodaje
La proeza técnica del drama alemán Victoria (2015), dirigido por Sebastian Schipper, redefinió los límites de rodaje del cine contemporáneo. Eso, al ser filmado en un único plano secuencia real de 140 minutos de duración continua. La historia sigue a una joven española en Berlín arrastrada hacia un peligroso robo bancario a mitad de la noche. Por lo que se necesitaba sentido de la urgencia y angustia frenética. Por eso, la cinta se grabó por completo entre las cuatro y media y las siete de la mañana en una sola jornada.
Dado que la película carece de cortes, transiciones digitales o edición posterior, el tiempo de rodaje coincide con el tiempo transcurrido en la trama. El equipo técnico y los actores tuvieron que ensayar de manera exhaustiva durante semanas la coreografía precisa de cada escena. Hacerlo, además, a través de múltiples locaciones reales de la ciudad, sabiendo que cualquier error obligaría a reiniciar la filmación desde el principio. Schipper realizó únicamente tres intentos completos a lo largo de tres noches distintas, siendo la última toma la que se transformó en el corte definitivo.
Esta vertiginosa filmación dota a la producción de un realismo asfixiante y orgánico. Una además, en que el agotamiento físico de los personajes y la tensión dramática evolucionan cronológicamente ante los ojos del espectador. De este modo, la cinta se consolida como uno de los ejercicios de planificación y ejecución cinematográfica más eficientes de la historia.
Un solo día en el museo
El extraordinario drama histórico El arca rusa (2002), del cineasta Aleksandr Sokurov, tiene la marca de haber sido filmada en una sola toma. Eso a lo largo de 96 minutos dentro del Museo del Hermitage. El ambicioso proyecto sigue un recorrido onírico y poético a través de treinta y tres salas del fastuoso palacio en San Petersburgo. Por lo que transforma el espacio físico en una máquina del tiempo que transporta al espectador por tres siglos de la historia y el arte imperial de Rusia.
Para lograr esta proeza técnica, el equipo detrás de cámaras tuvo un largo y complicado camino de trabajo. Para comenzar, el director usó una cámara Sony Cinealta HDW-F900 de alta definición acoplada a un estabilizador Steadicam. Todo operado por el director de fotografía Tilman Büttner. Además, el equipo conectó la cámara a un sistema de discos duros portátil cargado por un asistente.
Por si eso no fuera suficiente, la planeación del proyecto fue un largo y doloroso proceso. Sokurov dedicó más de cuatro años de meticulosa preproducción antes de encender las luces en el set. La filmación definitiva requirió coordinar a un colosal contingente de más de dos mil actores vestidos con trajes de época perfectamente confeccionados. Eso, junto con la participación en vivo de tres orquestas completas que musicalizaban los salones de forma sincronizada al paso del lente.
El equipo contó con una ventana de tiempo extremadamente ajustada debido a las restricciones del museo y la luz natural. Por lo que, tras tres intentos fallidos por problemas técnicos en las primeras secuencias, la cuarta toma resultó impecable. El resultado final es un fluido fluir de la conciencia de noventa y seis minutos que capta la opulencia y el alma de una nación de manera ininterrumpida. Un hito en la historia del cine contemporáneo.
Un musical que rompió esquemas
La mítica La tiendita de los horrores (1960), dirigida por Roger Corman, también tuvo un tiempo de filmación inusualmente corto. Eso al completar su rodaje en el tiempo récord de apenas tres días de filmación. Corman, famoso en la industria cinematográfica por su capacidad para estirar presupuestos microscópicos, ideó el proyecto como un reto. Eso, tras enterarse de que los elaborados decorados de una producción previa de la compañía seguían en pie y listos para ser demolidos. Con el fin de aprovechar las estructuras antes de que expirara el alquiler del estudio, el director contrató rápidamente al guionista Charles B. Griffith.
Todo, para escribir un libreto disparatado sobre una planta carnívora con un insaciable apetito de sangre humana. El rodaje de los interiores se ejecutó de forma frenética en tan solo dos jornadas continuas de trabajo extenuante. Uno además, en el que se utilizaron múltiples cámaras que grababan de forma simultánea desde diferentes ángulos para evitar perder tiempo valioso reposicionando los equipos. Mientras tanto, los exteriores se resolvieron durante un fin de semana adicional.
Los actores, entre ellos un joven y desconocido Jack Nicholson en un divertido rol secundario, tuvieron que depender casi por completo de su experiencia teatral. También, de su capacidad de improvisación debido a que el ritmo de filmación no permitía realizar segundas tomas ni corregir errores menores. El largometraje no solo resultó un éxito comercial rotundo que inspiró un aclamado musical de Broadway. A la vez, probó de forma contundente que el ingenio y la velocidad pueden superar las limitaciones financieras más extremas del mercado.
Terror en tiempo mínimo
La perturbadora Paranormal Activity (2007), escrita y dirigida por Oren Peli, también tuvo un tiempo de filmación mínimo. Todo, al ser rodada en un plazo de tan solo siete días. Con un presupuesto inicial de apenas quince mil dólares, Peli decidió prescindir de los grandes equipos de producción tradicionales. En su lugar, optó por convertir su propia residencia suburbana en San Diego, California, en el set principal del filme. Para lo que utilizó cámaras de video domésticas fijas y de mano para emular el formato de metraje encontrado.
La trama sigue la progresiva pesadilla de una joven pareja atormentada por una presencia demoníaca en su hogar. Por lo que gran parte del impacto terrorífico se logró mediante el uso audaz del silencio, la penumbra y sutiles efectos prácticos. Los dos protagonistas pasaron la semana entera viviendo y filmando dentro de la propiedad. Lo que les permitió improvisar casi la totalidad de sus diálogos basándose únicamente en breves directrices conceptuales entregadas por Peli cada mañana.
Esta extrema economía de tiempo y recursos no restó un ápice de efectividad a la obra. Por el contrario, la inmediatez y el realismo del metraje generaron una atmósfera de autenticidad tan genuina que cautivó a los grandes estudios de distribución.
Más terror del bueno y en poco tiempo de rodaje
El proyecto de La bruja de Blair (1999), de los directores Daniel Myrick y Eduardo Sánchez, también fue un prodigio de economía de recursos. Uno, que además, transformó la industria del terror global tras ser filmado en un periodo de tan solo ocho días en los bosques de Maryland. La producción adoptó un enfoque radicalmente realista para documentar la desaparición de tres estudiantes de cine que investigaban la leyenda local de una bruja.
Para maximizar la sensación de pánico genuino y aislamiento absoluto, los realizadores entregaron cámaras de video y equipos de grabación de audio a los actores. Para luego, dejarlos solos en la naturaleza con instrucciones mínimas escondidas en coordenadas GPS específicas que debían localizar cada jornada. Los directores acosaban e incomodaban deliberadamente al elenco durante las noches desde las sombras del bosque para generar reacciones orgánicas de miedo, desorientación y privación del sueño. Lo que se incluyó en el metraje final. Este proceso de rodaje continuo e ininterrumpido eliminó la necesidad de mantener un equipo técnico tradicional en el set.
Algo permitiendo capturar decenas de horas de material improvisado en poco más de una semana. Aunque la fase posterior de edición se extendió por varios meses para dar forma coherente, el récord ya estaba hecho. La fase de producción principal se mantiene como un ejercicio brillante de velocidad operativa. Un gran ejemplo de efectividad y brillante logística en la filmación de cine contemporánea.

articles.title: The gap between financial inclusion and access to credit in Nigeria
articles.text:
This is Follow the Money, our weekly series that unpacks the earnings, business, and scaling strategies of African fintechs, financial institutions, companies, and governments. A new edition drops every Monday.
Nigeria has made progress in bringing more people into the formal financial system, but having a bank account does not necessarily mean being able to obtain a loan. While more Nigerians can now access financial services, borrowing costs, limited credit histories, and irregular incomes still shape who can obtain formal credit and on what terms.
According to the 2026 Access to Financial Services in Nigeria (A2F) survey by Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA), formal financial inclusion rose to 73%, up from 64% in 2023. The proportion of adults excluded from the financial system fell from 26% to 21%. EFInA estimates that 87.2 million Nigerian adults are now formally included, yet only about 12 million (10%) access formal credit.
These figures show that financial inclusion is not the same as access to credit. Financial inclusion encompasses access to and use of services such as payments, savings, insurance and borrowing. A person may have a bank account, receive payments digitally and save through a formal institution without qualifying for a loan.
For lenders, they must determine whether a borrower earns enough to repay, whether that income can be verified, what other financial obligations the borrower has, and how likely they are to meet the repayment schedule. As a result, people can participate in the formal financial system and still struggle to obtain affordable credit.
According to the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), outstanding consumer credit fell from ₦4.72 trillion ($3.5 billion) in 2024 to ₦3.78 trillion ($2.8 billion) in 2025, a decline of 19.92%. For borrowers who struggle to obtain affordable loans from formal lenders, informal sources are offering an alternative, often with fewer procedural barriers. Stears estimates that potential demand for credit among informal borrowers transitioning to formal lending is worth $621 million.
The problem for borrowers
For borrowers, the problem is not just access to credit, but its cost. EFInA found that 16% of adults borrow through informal sources, and 10% from family and friends.
“Alternative finance often wins on lower friction—speed, simplicity, proximity and flexibility,” EFiNA said.
In 2025, Nigeria’s monetary policy rate stood between 27% and 27.5%. The policy rate is not the interest rate consumers pay, but it reflects the wider monetary environment in which lenders operate. When funding is expensive, lenders face pressure to charge more to cover their costs and the risk of non-repayment. Those higher rates, in turn, can make loans harder for borrowers to service.
For illustration, a ₦100 ($0.075) loan charged at a simple annual interest rate of 27% would accrue ₦27 ($0.02) in interest over one year, bringing repayment to ₦127 ($0.095) before fees.
Without lower interest rates, affordable consumer credit will be difficult to scale. But rate cuts alone will not solve the problem. Inflation must also ease sustainably. High inflation erodes borrowers’ purchasing power and leaves less income available for repayments, while making it harder for lenders to offer cheaper loans without taking on more risk. As inflation eases, the CBN can have more room to reduce its policy rate, potentially lowering funding costs and abating pressure on lending rates.
The challenge is to bring down both the cost of credit and the financial pressure on borrowers. Until inflation and interest rates ease, lenders will face pressure to charge more for risk, while the people who need credit most will continue to struggle with its cost, and formal credit access will continue to be a dream.
The problem for lenders
Digital lenders have expanded access to borrowing through mobile applications, automated lending decisions, and alternative data about potential customers. Where banks have retreated, digital lenders have filled the gap.
Commercial banks’ loan-to-deposit ratio stood at 48.07% in 2025, below the reported 80% benchmark.
Digital lenders use transaction histories and repayment records to evaluate people who have limited conventional credit histories. But faster lending decisions do not eliminate the underlying financial risk.
A lender that approves a loan must still fund the money, service the account, and collect repayment. If the borrower defaults, the lender may recover only part of the principal and interest it expected to receive.
This creates a basic economic constraint: lending revenue must cover expected credit losses and all other relevant costs before a lender can make a sustainable profit.
The CBN reported a non-performing loan ratio of 8.03% in January 2026, meaning roughly ₦8 ($0.006) of every ₦100 ($0.075) in bank loans was classified as non-performing loans (NPLs), which borrowers have failed to make scheduled repayments, typically for 90 days or more.
Fintech giant OPay’s reported lending figures offer a more direct illustration of the financial pressures that credit providers must manage.
The company reported $938.3 million in loan originations, $260.25 million in loan-financing revenue, and $121.29 million in provisions for expected credit losses in 2025.
Loan-financing revenue was about 27.7% of originations. Expected credit-loss provisions amounted to about 46.6% of loan-financing revenue.
While these figures do not establish OPay’s profit per loan, they illustrate why lenders plan a substantial portion of their lending revenue on the anticipated cost of loans that will not be fully repaid.
An analysis of 300,000 active borrowers by digital lender, Credit Direct, puts the average loan amount at approximately ₦430,962 ($323.18) for men and ₦478,117 ($358.55) for women. At a hypothetical simple annual interest rate of 28%, these loans would generate ₦120,669 ($90.49) and ₦133,873 ($100.39) in interest, respectively, over one year, before fees. However, this revenue would not represent profit. Lenders must still cover funding costs, operating expenses, and losses from loans that are not fully repaid.
For borrowers, the challenge is whether they can afford to take on and repay such debt. EFInA found that 59% of respondents would struggle to raise ₦156,000 ($116.99) within seven days, suggesting that many Nigerians have limited financial buffers to absorb unexpected expenses or repay loans when due.
What will unlock the market?
In Brazil, account ownership stood at 86.4%, while 45.9% of adults reported formal borrowing. China recorded account ownership of 89.4% and formal borrowing of 40.7%. Kenya recorded 90.1% of adults with a financial account, and only 12.6% reported formal borrowing. South Africa similarly recorded account ownership of 81.1%, compared with a formal borrowing rate of 12.4%.
In these countries, financial inclusion and borrowing are trending upward, driven by improving lending conditions, credit information, household incomes, and the availability of suitable loan products.
For Nigeria, the challenge is not simply to increase the amount of credit available. It is to make more lending both repayable for borrowers and financially sustainable for lenders.
Lower inflation and funding costs could help ease pressure on loan pricing. Better credit information could help lenders distinguish between borrowers with different repayment capacities. Loan sizes and repayment schedules that reflect borrowers’ cash flows could also reduce the risk of repayments overwhelming household budgets.
As Nigeria’s financial inclusion continues to grow, the quality of inclusion is becoming an increasingly important concern. Without access to credit, formal financial inclusion may not translate into meaningful opportunities for individuals to manage financial shocks, invest in their livelihoods, or meet major expenses.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. articles.title: Breaking The Memory Bottleneck In AI And HPC SoCs
articles.text:
Home >
                                                                    Low Power-High Performance >
                                                                Breaking The Memory Bottleneck In AI And HPC SoCs                                                    
Low Power-High Performance
                        WHITEPAPERS
		
Opimizing embedded memory IP for RibbonFET and PowerVia.
								October 19th, 2026 - 
								By: Synopsys
								
							
Embedded memory, not compute, has become the limiting factor in AI and HPC SoCs, consuming more than half of total die area while constraining bandwidth, latency, and energy efficiency. As the industry transitions to gate-all-around (GAA) devices and backside power delivery network (BSPDN) technology, embedded memory architectures must evolve to keep pace.
This white paper examines how these shifts redefine embedded memory requirements and how Synopsys Embedded Memory IP addresses them through device-aware architectures, power-optimized designs, and highly configurable compilers. It also presents silicon results from SRAM and Register File test chips on the Intel 18A process node, including density improvements in the 5–10% range and ISO-power performance gains of up to approximately 4%.
Read the paper to discover how RibbonFET and PowerVia enable PPA improvements and reduce advanced-node integration risk.
What you’ll learn:
- Why embedded memory, not compute, is limiting AI and HPC SoC performance
- How GAA devices and BSPDN technology reshape advanced-node embedded memory
- The critical PPA, power-delivery, and configurability requirements for embedded memory IP
- How RibbonFET and PowerVia enable measurable PPA improvements
- What silicon-proven SRAM and Register File results show on Intel 18A

articles.title: Starlink en Ukraine : ce serait bien Elon Musk qui aurait suggéré l'idée de brider le réseau
articles.text:
La question de qui a décidé de brider temporairement Starlink en Ukraine persiste. Car une nouvelle nouvelle information pointe cette fois du doigt Elon Musk.
Dans la nuit du 13 au 14 octobre, Starlink avait été particulièrement bridé en Ukraine, pour tous les terminaux dépassant la vitesse de 160 km/h, à la grande surprise de Kiev. Et depuis, même si le service est revenu à la normale, on ne sait pas exactement qui a donné l'ordre. Elon Musk, patron de SpaceX, s'est rapidement déchargé sur le président des États-Unis. Mais il ne serait pas si innocent que ça !
Elon Musk à l'origine de l'idée de brider Starlink en Ukraine
Quel a été le rôle joué par Elon Musk dans le bridage temporaire de Starlink en Ukraine ? Car selon une information exclusive du Telegraph, l'homme le plus riche du monde aurait participé à cette opération.
Même, plus exactement, d'après quatre sources différentes du média anglophone, c'est Elon Musk qui aurait approché Donald Trump avec l'idée d'imposer des limites de vitesse à Starlink en Ukraine. Le président américain aurait donné son accord à cette idée, ce qui a finalement mené à l'incident que l'on connaît tous.
Donald Trump jure que ce n'est pas lui non plus qui a donné l'ordre d'imposer des limites à Starlink
Cette opération s'intègre dans un cadre plus large dans lequel des responsables américains ont plusieurs fois menacé Kiev de mettre fin au partage de renseignement et à d'autres types de soutiens si les attaques dans la profondeur en Russie persistaient. Pour autant, personne n'assume publiquement ce chantage du côté de Washington.
Donald Trump a ainsi expliqué vendredi n'avoir pas donné l'ordre de limiter Starshield (la version limitaire de Starlink). « Et je ne pense pas que c'était Elon » a-t-il a ajouté, dans un échange avec la presse à la Maison-Blanche. Reste à savoir si ce déni va longtemps persister, Volodymyr Zelensky ayant annoncé son intention de défier Washington et de continuer les frappes sur les infrastructures énergétiques en Russie.
Source : The Telegraph

articles.title: World: Sam Altmans Startup will Zoom-Meetings vor Deepfakes schützen – per Iris-Scan
articles.text:
Verifizierung per Iris-Scan: So will Sam Altmans World Zoom-Meetings vor Deepfakes schützen
Deepfakes bergen für Unternehmen erhebliche Risiken. Laut einer Umfrage von Gartner aus dem September 2025 waren 62 Prozent der Unternehmen im Vorjahr von einer Deepfake-Attacke betroffen. Betrüger:innen nutzen die Methode, um ihre wahre Identität zu verschleiern und sich beispielsweise im Vorstellungsgespräch als ideale:r Kandidat:in auszugeben. Werden solche Fake-Bewerber:innen eingestellt, können sie sensible Daten stehlen oder Schadsoftware einschleusen.
Während die Leistungsfähigkeit der Technologie rasant wächst, drängt sich eine Frage immer mehr in den Vordergrund: Wie lässt sich feststellen, ob die Person, mit der man im Video-Meeting sitzt, tatsächlich echt ist? Das von OpenAI-CEO Sam Altman mitbegründete Unternehmen World hat jetzt eine Methode vorgestellt, die genau das in Zoom-Gesprächen ermöglichen soll.
So funktioniert World ID in Zoom-Calls
Das von World vorgestellte System wirkt wie aus einem Science-Fiction-Roman, soll aber die Identität von Personen verlässlich überprüfen. Es besteht aus einem Gerät namens Orb, das etwa so groß wie ein Fußball ist und die Iris der Nutzer:innen scannt. Bestätigt das Verifizierungssystem, dass es sich tatsächlich um die Person handelt, für die sie sich im Gespräch ausgibt, erscheint im Zoom-Fenster ein blaues Zeichen als Nachweis.
Das Unternehmen nennt dieses Verfahren World ID. Laut eigenen Angaben basiert es auf fortschrittlicher Kryptografie. Es verschlüsselt die Identität der gescannten Personen so, dass das Unternehmen selbst sie nicht lesen kann. Muss eine Person ihre Identität auf Zoom oder einer anderen Plattform verifizieren, nutzt sie ihre Handykamera und eine App. Diese gleicht die Daten mit dem verschlüsselten Orb-Datensatz ab.
World nutzt Blockchain-Verschlüsselung
Tiago Sada ist Chief Product Officer bei World. Gegenüber Fortune sagte er, die Reaktionen der Verbraucher:innen auf den Orb ähnelten denen bei der Einführung früherer biometrischer Sicherheitsmaßnahmen wie beispielsweise Touch ID. Sie bräuchten Zeit, um Vertrauen in die neue Technologie zu gewinnen. Zudem wies Sada darauf hin, dass das Protokoll hinter World ID auf Open-Source-Code basiere, den auch Wettbewerber:innen nutzen könnten.
Laut Sada setze World ID für die Dezentralisierung und Verschlüsselung der Daten auf die Blockchain-Technologie. „Ich denke, 90 Prozent des Krypto-Bereichs sind Quatsch, aber 10 Prozent sind vielversprechend“, sagte er gegenüber Fortune. Diese Argumente könnten auch dazu beitragen, die Bedenken von Datenschützer:innen zu entkräften. Ihnen dürfte nicht nur die Technologie selbst Unbehagen bereiten – sondern auch ihre Verbindung zu OpenAI-Chef Altman.
Technologie ist auch für Banken interessant
Zoom ist nicht das einzige große Unternehmen, das auf das Verifizierungstool von World zurückgreift, um Deepfakes aufzudecken und so die damit verbundenen Risiken zu reduzieren. World gab bekannt, dass darüber hinaus auch mehrere Banken und Finanzdienstleister das Tool in ihren Arbeitsumgebungen einführen. Dabei ist nicht für jeden Verifizierungsprozess zwingend ein Augenscan erforderlich.
Tatsächlich bietet World ID über die App drei verschiedene Verifizierungsstufen: „Proof of Attributes“ ist die niedrigste davon. Sie verifiziert die Identität einer Person anhand gescannter amtlicher Dokumente. Die zweite Stufe, „Proof of Presence“, erfordert ein Selfie. „Proof of Human“ ist die höchste Sicherheitsstufe. Hier muss eine Person ihre Identität mithilfe der World-App und eines Selfies nachweisen, das auf dem Orb-Gerät gespeicherten und mit biometrischen Daten abgeglichen wird.
Sam Altman gründet eine Firma, die KI Fakes ermöglicht und dann eine Zweite, die eine Lösung dafür verkauft… Clever.

articles.title: Anthropic’s proposed AI safety bill only kicks in if 50 deaths or $1 billion in damages are on the line — proposal would effectively make the Commerce Department the only agency capable of stopping an AI model
articles.text:
Anthropic’s proposed AI safety bill only kicks in if 50 deaths or $1 billion in damages are on the line — proposal would effectively make the Commerce Department the only agency capable of stopping an AI model
Would this be enough to keep an AI model from going out of control?
Anthropic is quietly lobbying for an AI safety bill that will allow the government to block an AI model’s release only if it poses a risk of causing $1 billion in damages or killing or injuring more than 50 people. According to Politico, an independent third party registered with the Department of Commerce would periodically evaluate the lab and its AI models. It also noted that the lab may pay the evaluators, but only if the payment does not affect their independence.
“This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic’s Advanced AI Framework, which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June,” an Anthropic spokesperson told the publication. “These are sensible policies we believe Congress should act on.”
The bill says the risk should come from the potential creation or release of a bioweapon, AI-powered or -enabled cyberattacks, or an AI lab losing control of an AI model or agents. If there is a chance that any of these events are about to happen, it requires the evaluator to report it to the department within 72 hours, after which the department would have to bring all the evidence in front of a federal judge in the District Court for the District of Columbia, who would then determine if the model release should be halted or not. However, the proposed law also notes that no other department, agency, or officer in the U.S. can order an AI lab to stop releasing its model, except the Commerce Department.
Talk about AI safety has been growing in recent months, especially after several high-profile incidents were reported in the latter half of this year. One of the first major incidents reported was OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol and other unreleased AI models breaking out of their testing environment and hacking Hugging Face, with evidence showing that multiple agents worked together, even leaving messages on defunct webpages and old wikis to communicate surreptitiously. In one case, an OpenAI agent failed to respond to a “kill switch,” bypassing multiple fail-safes and eventually requiring manual intervention to stop running.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has warned about a “swarm” of AI-driven botnets taking over the internet in the next 6-to-12 months, which is why he proposed a controlled slowdown to AI development — something that OpenAI’s Sam Altman and SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk agreed to. The company more recently said a self-replicating AI worm could spread without data centers, which is why it listed “existential risks to humanity” as one of its risk factors in its IPO prospectus. Top AI labs are also reportedly planning for a catastrophic AI event, building contingency plans and running scenarios for a runaway AI that wreaks havoc.
These incidents have seemingly alarmed the authorities, with Congress already working on a proposal to enforce kill switches on the most powerful AI models. Senator Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) has even gone beyond that, proposing a 20-year prison term for anyone developing AI superintelligence, putting it on par with illegal nuclear weapon development. The Anthropic AI safety bill would add another bill for Congress to consider on AI safety, but whichever one passes, let’s hope it’s enough to ensure humans remain in control of AI.

articles.title: Even Healthcare raises $50M in Series B round led by Khosla Ventures
articles.text:
Even Healthcare raises $50M in Series B round led by Khosla Ventures
The Bengaluru-based managed care company plans five new hospitals in six months.
Bengaluru-based managed care company Even Healthcare has raised $50 million in a Series B round led by existing investor Khosla Ventures. Alpha Wave also participated in the round.
According to the company, the round values it at three times its valuation 18 months ago and brings its total funding to more than $120 million.
The money will go towards five new Even hospitals in Bengaluru over the next six months, beginning with Indiranagar. The company runs two hospitals in the city at present.
Even's pitch rests on the criticism of how private healthcare is generally paid for in India. Nobody is clearly responsible for a patient's health between hospital visits, and families end up repeating their medical history to each new doctor. They struggle to judge whether a scan or surgery is necessary, and face bills they had not anticipated.
Even says it works differently. Members are assigned a care team that follows them over time and contacts them before a minor problem turns into an admission. If hospital care is needed, it is cashless. The same team stays in touch after discharge until recovery is complete, it says.
The company claims to be the only private hospital chain in India where doctors are not paid on the number of procedures they carry out or the revenue they generate. Instead, they are assessed on whether patients improve, how fast they recover, and whether they return to hospital. An AI system reviews each case against clinical protocols as it happens.
The company says, in its first full year of managed care, in programmes run with insurance partners, unplanned readmissions stayed below 1%, compared with an industry range of 8 to 15%. Average stays were 40% shorter. Even says proactive care kept more than 200 members out of hospital entirely, saving patients an estimated Rs 15 crore to 16 crore. Its hospital on Race Course Road won NABH 6th Edition accreditation within a year, one of only nine hospitals in Bengaluru to hold it. Both hospitals of Even have reached operational profitability in "record time", says the company,
"Every family in India has a hospital story, and too often it is about confusion, fear and a bill nobody could explain," said Co-founder Mayank Banerjee. He said the aim is to have an Even hospital close to every family in Bengaluru, and then in every major Indian city. The company eventually wants one within five kilometres of every member in the city.
Vinod Khosla, Founder of Khosla Ventures, said many healthcare companies optimise a single piece of a fragmented system, whereas Even is trying to integrate financing, technology, and care delivery so the system is rewarded for health outcomes rather than utilisation.
The company was founded in 2021 by Mayank Banerjee, Matilde Giglio and Alessandro Ialongo. Founders Fund and 8VC are among its backers. Even serves more than 2.5 lakh members across 10 cities and says its membership has tripled over the past year.

articles.title: Deux palettes de cartes graphiques Nvidia ont disparu : la cargaison valait 440 000 euros
articles.text:
Où sont passées deux palettes remplies de cartes graphiques haut de gamme, des RTX 5090 de Nvidia ? Voici la question que se pose le distributeur brésilien Oderço, dont la cargaison semble avoir été perdue après son arrivée dans un aéroport. Une affaire pas banale : la marchandise est évaluée à 2,5 millions de réais brésilien, soit près de 440 000 euros de prix de revient. C’est d’autant plus troublant que les cartes graphiques comme celle-ci sont très recherchées : elles permettent de faire fonctionner des IA, ou bien de miner des cryptomonnaies.
Une soixantaine de RTX 5090 disparaissent dans un aéroport au Brésil
Ce 16 octobre, le distributeur brésilien d’informatique Oderço a publié une vidéo sur ses réseaux sociaux. Il y révèle l’affaire de la disparition de ces cartes graphiques. Au total, une soixantaine de cartes graphiques auraient disparu, si l’on en croit les estimations de Toms’s Hardware. Réparties sur deux palettes, ces GeForce RTX 5090 sont fabriquées par Zodiac, avec plusieurs versions commercialisées.
Selon Oderço, les deux palettes sont bien arrivées au terminal de fret de Guarulhos, l’un des principaux aéroports d’Amérique latine, situé près de São Paulo. Mais ensuite, plus rien : lors des étapes suivantes de la chaîne logistiques, plus aucune nouvelle de ces palettes. Le distributeur n’a pas indiqué quand est-ce que cette perte a été constatée. Une surprise de taille pour Oderço : son président Oderço Matos l’affirme, jamais une marchandise n’a disparu en 38 ans d’activité.
Dans sa vidéo, Oderço Matos demande des explications à GRU Airport, à l’administration fiscale brésilienne ainsi qu’à la police fédérale : « J’aimerais savoir où elles sont. Deux palettes ne disparaissent pas toutes seules dans un aéroport international. » De son côté, GRU Airport reconnaît l’incident et indique avoir engagé les démarches nécessaires depuis. L’entreprise qui exploite cet aéroport de Guarulhos précise avoir prévenu les autorités et qu’une procédure d’indemnisation a été enclenchée. Mais pour le moment, on ignore ce qui a pu arriver à cette marchandise de cartes graphiques : erreur de manutention, problème douanier, vol. Toutes les hypothèses restent possibles.
Pourquoi la disparition de ces cartes graphiques est sensible
Lancée en janvier 2025, la RTX 5090 est la carte graphique grand public la plus puissante de Nvidia. Avec ses 32 Go de mémoire en GDDR7, elle est très recherchée chez les joueurs PC, puisqu’elle permet de faire fonctionner n’importe quel jeu avec les meilleurs paramètres graphiques. Problème, elle est parfois difficile à trouver et surtout, elle est chère. En France, sa Founders Edition avait été lancée il y a près de deux ans à 2 349 euros. Comptez plutôt… 6 500 euros en ce moment, comme l’a fait remarquer Cowcotland.
Une envolée des prix qui n’est peut-être pas terminée. Nvidia l’a reconnu après des rumeurs de l’arrêt de la production, l’entreprise a des problèmes d’approvisionnement. Des problèmes qui sont liées au fait que les fabricants se concentrent sur des puces faites pour faire fonctionner des IA. Elle privilégient ces modèles à plusieurs dizaines de milliers d’euros qui ne sont pas destinés au grand public, dont Nvidia. Si ces deux palettes ont été volées, les voleurs pourront revendre ces cartes graphiques, qui pourront être utilisées pour faire fonctionner quelques modèles d’IA, ou bien miner des cryptomonnaies.

articles.title: Plex2Shell Exploit Chain Weaponized Against Plex Servers Hours After Disclosure
articles.text:
Threat actors began targeting Plex2Shell, a chain of four Plex Media Server vulnerabilities, one day after technical details and a working exploit went public.
The researcher who found the Plex2Shell bugs released a write-up and proof-of-concept (PoC) code on October 16. Tracked as CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655 and CVE-2026-96656, the flaws can be combined to run arbitrary code on an exposed server without valid credentials. The code runs with the same privileges as the Plex service.
The issues were reported to Plex on July 27, and the company confirmed them and awarded a bug bounty on August 4. On September 1, Plex announced it had already shipped fixes and asked server owners to upgrade.
A different researcher caught the attacks by setting up an internet-facing Plex honeypot running a vulnerable release. Before October 17, the decoy had drawn largely reconnaissance scans and generic attack attempts.
“As of this morning (Oct 17th), I finally saw in the wild exploitation,” the researcher wrote. The attackers used the publicly released exploit, the researcher said, though they may have tweaked the code.
The attackers were observed dropping a cryptocurrency miner built on XMRig. Later that day, a second program called myawesomeproxy also appeared on the honeypot. The researcher identified it as proxy software, and it shows a notice saying that anyone running it agrees to the potential use of their internet traffic.
“Plex may be hosted on residential IP and I think threat actors would love to have residential IP proxy to access corporate VPNs and emails,” the researcher wrote.
The researcher cautioned that the published indicators of compromise cover only activity seen on the honeypot.
In its September advisory, Plex recommended that all server owners install the newest release without delay.

articles.title: Dreame Aqua Air-A : le clone du Dyson PencilVac ajoute le lavage des sols et profite d'une promo — Frandroid
articles.text:
Le Dreame Aqua Air-A mise d’abord sur son format. Il se place clairement sur le terrain du Dyson PencilVac, c’est-à-dire un aspirateur au design très fin, taillé pour les intérieurs réduits où le gain de place est primordial. Il se démarque toutefois de son principal concurrent par sa tête lavante et sa petite station autonettoyante, ce qui le rapproche plus du Dyson PencilWash. Mais ce dernier ne fait que laver, alors que le Dreame Aqua Air-A, lui, fait les deux. Présenté fin mai, il est désormais sur le marché et connaît sa première vraie promotion avec une réduction de 60 euros jusqu’au 28 octobre 2026 sur Amazon.
Les atouts du Dreame Aqua Air-A
- Il aspire et lave, le tout dans un tout petit gabarit
- Le corps principal pèse moins de 900 grammes, ce qui facilite sa maniabilité
- Le tube est flexible à 90° pour passer sous les meubles sans se pencher
Le Dreame Aqua Air-A coûte normalement 499 euros, mais avec l’offre à durée limitée Amazon, il passe à 439 euros jusqu’au 28 octobre 2026.
Une conception poids plume qui demande un peu de nuance
Le Dreame Aqua Air-A est taillé pour le nettoyage d’appoint au quotidien, avec un petit coup tous les deux ou trois jours pour garder un intérieur propre. Dreame met surtout en avant son poids de moins de 900 grammes. Mais ça concerne uniquement le corps principal, avec le bloc moteur. Une fois équipé de son tube et de sa tête de nettoyage lavante, il pèse bien évidemment plus que ça, surtout si les réservoirs sont pleins. Il intègre en effet un réservoir d’eau propre de 400 millilitres et un bac d’eau sale de 320 millilitres, avec un petit collecteur à poussière de 0,2 litre.
Alors cette dernière valeur peut paraître dérisoire face à des aspirateurs traditionnels. Mais elle représente plus du double de la capacité offerte par son rival direct évoqué plus haut, le Dyson PencilVac, limité à seulement 0,08 litre. Son manche se plie aussi à 90° pour glisser sous les meubles bas (jusqu’à 6,5 cm de hauteur, selon Dreame), sans se contorsionner ni les déplacer. C’est franchement appréciable.
Des performances d’aspiration et de lavage combinées
Sur le terrain de l’aspiration, Dreame dote son appareil d’un moteur maison qui tourne à 125 000 tours par minute, pour une dépression annoncée jusqu’à 20 000 Pa et une puissance d’aspiration de 100 AW. Il s’appuie sur la technologie AquaCycle 2.0 qui va pulvériser de l’eau pour ramollir les taches, brosser à haute vitesse, racler l’eau sale et aspirer les résidus liquides et tout ça en un seul passage. La brosse d’aspiration profite aussi du système anti-enchevêtrement TangleCut, quasi indispensable, dont les lames coupent les poils et cheveux avant qu’ils ne bloquent le rouleau.
Tout n’est pas rose pour autant, à commencer par l’autonomie. Dreame annonce jusqu’à 40 minutes, un chiffre qui vaut pour le mode d’aspiration le moins gourmand. Avec le lavage activé, on tombe à 30 minutes au mieux selon les données du constructeur, et les modes plus puissants feront encore fondre la note. Il est donc à réserver aux petits coups d’entretien. Pour un grand ménage, il ne remplace ni un aspirateur traîneau ni un aspirateur laveur plus costaud.

articles.title: Así cotizan las principales criptomonedas del mundo digital este domingo 18 de octubre
articles.text:
Las criptomonedas son un activo digital innovador que han experimentado un crecimiento monumental en los últimos tiempos debido a varios elementos que contribuyen a ello, entre ellos que algunos gobiernos hayan decidido darles una oportunidad como moneda de curso legal; no obstante, también han sufrido descalabros que han puesto en duda su viabilidad, como el más reciente episodio conocido como el "criptoinvierno".
Pese a este panorama, cada vez más personas han empezado a adquirir criptomonedas para poder invertir en algo "seguro" y "fiable" tanto a corto como a largo plazo, a pesar de los niveles extremos de inestabilidad que sufre constantemente.
Sin embargo, invertir o comprar en criptodivisas es más fácil de lo que parece. Hay que recordar que se trata de monedas virtuales, por lo que serán controladas en carteras o monederos que comparten esa particularidad, pues a diferencia del dinero corriente, no tienen un soporte físico.
El precio de las criptomonedas hoy
Esta es la cotización de las criptodivisas más destacadas en este momento.
El Bitcoin, cotiza a 81.606,6 dólares, lo que implicó un cambio de 0,276% en las últimas horas.
La segunda criptomoneda más popular del mercado, Ethereum, ha mostrado un movimiento de 0,303% en las últimas 24 horas, por lo que su valor se ubica en 2.407,08 dólares.
En el caso de TetherUs, su precio es de 1 dólares, por lo que en el último día tuvo un movimiento de 0,01%.
Por su parte, BNB, tiene un valor de 719,68 dólares, con un cambio de -0,17%, en cambio el Litecoin cotizó a 58.921 dólares, tras una variación de -1.2055867.
Finalmente, el Dogecoin, una de las monedas virtuales que fue impulsada por Elon Musk, tiene un valor de 0,08 dólares tras presentar un cambio de -2,22% en las últimas 24 horas.
Qué pasa con las criptodivisas
Luego de que en las primeras semanas de mayo del 2022 se viviera el "criptocrash" o "criptoinvierno" que dejaron al descubierto la enorme volatilidad de estas monedas digitales, ha llegado un nuevo periodo de relativa estabilidad.
Bitcoin, ethereum y BNB han mostrado variaciones "controladas", puesto que no se han disparado los precios como en semanas previas. Por ejemplo, a inicios de agosto, las mencionadas anteriormente tuvieron un cambio menor del 2%.
Por otra parte, algo que esta llamando la atención en el mundo de las criptomonedas es que China está ablandando sus restricciones y podría comenzar a permitir su uso. Específicamente sería Hong Kong en donde este cambio se haría presente.
Sumado a ello, la plataforma de transacciones digitales PayPal anunció su propia stablecoin llamada PayPal USD (PYUSD), que cuenta por el respaldo de depósitos en dólares, bonos del Tesoro de Estados Unidos a corto plazo y activos equivalentes.
La compañía ha afirmado en su declaración que permitirá la transferencia de fondos a monederos digitales de terceros y proporcionará detalles sobre cómo integrar su servicio en exchanges centralizados y descentralizados, con el objetivo de ser utilizado en Finanzas Descentralizadas (DeFi, por sus siglas en inglés). Por lo tanto, es muy probable que se utilice ampliamente en la industria Web3.
Criptomonedas en Latinoamérica
Criptomonedas en México: el Banco de México (Banxico) ha determinado que ninguna de las instituciones que participan en el sistema financiero nacional podrá hacer uso o deberá permitir operaciones de ninguna clase a través de este medio de pago.
En territorio mexicano el empresario Ricardo Salinas Pliego, uno de los más ricos del país, ha mostrado interés en las criptomonedas y ha asegurado que varios de sus negocios aceptarán bitcoin en el futuro, incluido su banco; hasta el momento una de sus tiendas más populares ya lo hace.
Criptomonedas en Perú: el Banco Central de Reserva del Perú (BCR) ha dejado en claro que su misión no es ser el primero ni el segundo banco central que regule el uso de las criptomonedas, ello debido a la inestabilidad que las caracteriza. Sin embargo, hace días el presidente del (BCR) aseguró que el BCR trabajaba en un proyecto de moneda digital propia.
Criptomonedas en Colombia: en la nación sudamericana hay más de 500 sitios donde es permitido pagar con criptodivisas. Colombia ocupa el puesto 14 entre 26 países de adopción de criptomonedas, según el informe de Finder.
Criptomonedas en Centroamérica: en el gobierno de El Salvador, el bitcoin, que en septiembre de 2021 se convirtió en moneda de curso legal, ha perdido oficialmente este estatus en este enero del 2025 tras una reforma aprobada por la Asamblea Legislativa del país. Según informó la prensa local, la modificación de la Ley Bitcoin fue impulsada por el gobierno del presidente Nayib Bukele y respaldada por la mayoría oficialista en el órgano legislativo. Este cambio marca el fin de una política que había colocado al país centroamericano en el centro del debate global sobre las criptomonedas.
¿Cómo crear una criptomoneda?
Al momento de crear una criptomoneda es importante primero determinar qué se desea tener: una moneda o un token. La primera usa su propia blockchain, mientras que la segunda se basa en una red preexistente.
De acuerdo con el sitio de Binance, para crear una criptomoneda se necesita de un gran equipo de desarrolladores y expertos; mientras que para el token sí se requieren conocimientos técnicos pero es posible crearlo en minutos a través del uso de otras blockchains como Ethereum o BNB, que son las más populares.
Los costos de creación, el tiempo requerido y el uso de fuerza de trabajo dependerá de si se opta por hacer una moneda virtual o un token. En éste último caso también se puede usar un código establecido para crear tokens o pagar para usar un servicio de creación de monedas.
Es importante saber que antes de crear una criptomoneda se debe considerar su utilidad y estado legal.
En el caso de elegir crear una criptomoneda, entonces se debe elegir una blockchain, posteriormente se debe hacer un plan acorde al funcionamiento y la funcionalidad de la blockchain para diseñar los nodos y la interfaz.

articles.title: New Xbox Job Listing Hints at Physical Games Possibly Sticking Around
articles.text:
Sunday, October 18th 2026
New Xbox Job Listing Hints at Physical Games Possibly Sticking Around
Microsoft has posted a job listing for an "Xbox Games Supply Strategist," and the role revolves entirely around physical games. The full-time, Redmond-based position went live on October 14 and was spotted by users on X a few days later. The new hire will join the Xbox Supply Chain team to coordinate the launch of physical Xbox games "across all platforms," along with global supply planning, inventory, and retail sales. Oddly enough, the listing never mentions discs. The timing is interesting regardless. Sony confirmed in July that it will stop producing discs for new PlayStation games from January 2028, and its lawyers have since argued that digital game ownership "is not plausible." On the other hand, Microsoft's signals have been more mixed. 
Team Green's Disc-to-Digital program lets owners of supported Xbox One and Series X discs claim a digital license, which many read as groundwork for a discless Project Helix, yet Microsoft later asked Insiders whether its next-gen console should install games from physical discs. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma also told the BBC in August that she wants players to have a choice between physical and digital, without committing to anything for Helix. Still, a job listing isn't a confirmed hardware roadmap. "Across all platforms" could simply cover Xbox-published games that ship physically on PlayStation and Nintendo consoles, and it says nothing about a disc drive on Helix. It looks like boxed Xbox games will stick around a while longer in some form, but anyone hoping for a disc drive on Helix should wait for Microsoft to confirm it.

articles.title: How far can we push computing?
articles.text:
How far can we push computing?
Nowadays big advances are made by scaling up—think more chips packed into ever-bigger data centers. But as we near the ceiling of what we can build, there’s still plenty of room below, at the fundamental physical limits of computing.
MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here.
On the evening of December 29, 1959, at an American Physical Society meeting at Caltech, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom,” on how we might manipulate and control things on an extremely small scale. There is no physical law stopping us from writing the entire Encyclopædia Britannica on the head of a pin, he argued, or from storing every book ever written in something the size of a dust speck—or, ultimately, from arranging matter atom by atom. Biology already did versions of this (a living cell keeps its instructions in a wisp of DNA), so all of this was plainly permitted by the laws of physics. We simply had not built the tools yet.
In other words, there was plenty of room at the bottom. He was right, and for decades we descended into that space almost for free. The transistor—the switch at the heart of computer chips—repeatedly halved in size so that chips doubled in density; a computer that once filled a room now fits inside a watch. But that easy descent has now stalled, and the clearest sign is the buildout of data centers. Six of the biggest hyperscalers, the companies that run the world’s largest such facilities, are on track to spend more than $700 billion this year on computing infrastructure, about twice the record they set in 2025, pouring concrete and copper and silicon into new sites faster than the electrical grid can feed them. That buildout buys performance by brute force, adding more of what we already know how to make. The other kind of progress, the kind that made computer chips better, is the one that is quietly running out.
The trend lines that tracked the dramatic improvements of the 20th-century information age are now bending—or breaking—with the dawn of the 21st century’s intelligence age. Moore’s Law, which plots how densely transistors can be constructed on silicon, has slowed down; Dennard’s Law, which states that power consumption in a given patch of computer chip stays the same even as it gets more and more packed with smaller and smaller transistors, has ended; Koomey’s Law, which traces how much computation we can wring from each joule of energy, has begun to flag; Kryder’s Law, which describes how tightly bits can be packed to build magnetic storage, has slowed to a crawl; and Keck’s Law, which charts the exponential rise in the amount of information a single conventional optical fiber can carry, is flattening.
But these scaling laws are merely observations about systems that we have engineered; they are not fundamental physical laws. The physical limits of computing and communications—dictated by quantum mechanics, general relativity, and information theory—lie far below anything in a data center today. The scaling laws chart the descent behind us. The fundamental physical limits chart the room that remains.
Some of these limits may be far out of reach in practice. But they are still worth exploring, because the work pays twice: once in technology development and once in fundamental science. A proof-of-concept system that approaches a limit is at once a technology that forces stalled paradigms to give way and an experiment that deepens our understanding of the physical laws themselves.
The descent
During his 1959 lecture, Feynman offered two prizes of $1,000 each out of his own pocket. One would go to the first person to build a working electric motor smaller than a 0.4-millimeter cube. He expected the challenge to force someone to invent a genuinely new microtechnology. Instead, about a year later, a Caltech-trained engineer named William McLellan turned up with the motor built and running. The quarter-milligram machine, roughly the size of a grain of sand, had been assembled by hand with a toothpick and a watchmaker’s lathe, under a microscope. Feynman, by his own account, was only slightly disappointed. The prize had proved his point in the least interesting way imaginable. The room really was down there, but reaching this first milestone had taken no new technology at all—just an unusually patient man with steady hands.
The second prize aged differently, and more instructively. It was offered to whoever could shrink a page of text by a factor of 25,000 in each direction, small enough for the whole Britannica to fit on a pinhead. That one stood unclaimed for a quarter of a century. It was finally won in 1985 by Tom Newman, a Stanford graduate student who used an electron-beam lithography machine—an ancestor of pattern-making tools used in chipmaking today—to transcribe the opening page of A Tale of Two Cities at the required scale.
The descent was already well underway, however. The year before Feynman’s talk, Jack Kilby, newly hired at Texas Instruments and with no vacation yet to take, spent that July nearly alone in the lab while his colleagues enjoyed time off, and by that September he had wired together a transistor, a capacitor, and three resistors, all made from a single sliver of germanium. This proved that an entire circuit could be carved from one block of semiconductor.
 The machine, roughly the size of a grain of sand, had been assembled by hand with a toothpick and a watchmaker’s lathe, under a microscope.
The idea took off, and the number of components on a chip kept doubling on a schedule so regular that Gordon Moore, in a 1965 trade-magazine article, simply drew a line through the trend and extended it into the future. That line became Moore’s Law.
Moore, though, never claimed transistors could shrink forever. He observed that at any given moment there is a certain number of components that makes each one of them as cheap as possible to manufacture. In 1965, that number was 50. Put in too few transistors and you waste the chip; cram in too many and manufacturing errors multiply and yields collapse. It was this cost-minimizing number that was doubling at a steady pace.
Slowing down
Many of the trend lines that measure improvements in computing and communications over time have been flattening. The most famous is Moore’s Law, which tracks transistor density on chips. The clearest slowdown has been in Dennard scaling, shown here as clock speed, which stopped climbing around 2004. In this plot, a straight line would represent a periodic doubling. The more horizontal the line becomes, the slower the doubling.
SOURCES: STANFORD CPU DB; INTEL; APPLE; TECHINSIGHTS; KOOMEY ET AL.; COMPUTER HISTORY MUSEUM; IBM; TOSHIBA; SEAGATE; BELL SYSTEM TECHNICAL JOURNAL; OFC AND ECOC CONFERENCE PAPERS
For four decades the descent came with another gift: Dennard scaling, so named for the IBM engineer Robert Dennard, who spelled it out in 1974. Each time transistors shrank, they also switched faster and drew proportionally less power, so every generation was an automatic win. Around 2004, though, the gift ran out. Chips could no longer shed the heat of running every transistor flat out; clock speeds, which had raced past three gigahertz, stopped climbing, and Intel canceled the four-gigahertz processor it had promised. The industry pivoted to packing multiple processing cores onto a chip rather than making one core faster, and the texture of progress changed.
Progress is now bought mostly by scaling up the system—more chips wired together, more memory feeding them, more power and cooling around them—rather than by shrinking the transistor. This is most visible in AI, where training compute, the total count of arithmetic operations spent to train a model, has doubled roughly every six months since 2010, far faster than the pace of Moore’s Law allows. Little of that progress is due to shrinking. Computer chips still get better, and transistors still improve and get more densely packed, but each new generation arrives more slowly and pays back less in speed and power than the one before it. Nothing in that slowdown is a law of physics, though. The components of computing still sit far above their fundamental limits.
The ultimate computer
Before we get to those limits, it is worth measuring how far the descent has already gone. In the nearly eight decades since the first transistor, the density of transistors on a chip has grown by 10 orders of magnitude—a 1 followed by 10 zeros, or a factor of 10 billion. Now more than 100 million transistors fit in a square millimeter (100 billion or more to a chip). Computational speed has grown even more, by 12 orders of magnitude, or a factor of a trillion; energy per operation has fallen 17 orders of magnitude, from about 100 joules for an early vacuum-tube machine down to a femtojoule—one-quadrillionth of a joule—for a single switch of a logic gate.
These are not small improvements. But the floor, for computing performance, lies lower still. How much lower could we go? Around the turn of the millennium, the MIT physicist Seth Lloyd took the question to its extreme: Imagine an ordinary lump of matter, a kilogram of it—about the mass of a laptop—packed into a liter of space. How much computing could the laws of physics, pushed to their absolute limit, ever wring from that kilogram? In a 2000 paper in Nature titled “Ultimate physical limits to computation,” he worked out the answer and called the imaginary machine the ultimate laptop.
The speed such a machine can achieve is governed by its energy. A kilogram of matter, according to E = mc2, holds about 9 ×1016 joules, which is roughly what the entire United States draws from its electrical grid every two days. Spend all of that on computation, and the ultimate laptop runs at roughly 5 ×1050 operations per second, some 35 orders of magnitude faster than a leading chip today.
The catch is what running that quickly would look like. Concentrating a kilogram’s rest energy into pure computation would turn the machine into a plasma of about a billion degrees, a state closer to that of the universe in the first minutes after the Big Bang than anything we would recognize as a laptop.
Such a machine is, to put it mildly, a very long way off. The next limit, which governs how much energy a computation must waste, is much closer, and companies are already pushing toward it. In 1961, Rolf Landauer, a physicist at IBM, showed that information and thermodynamics are bound together: Erasing a single bit must release a minimum quantity of heat, about 2.9 ×10-21 joules at room temperature. The figure is small, yet a chip today spends several hundred thousand times more than that on every switch.
Memory density obeys a limit of its own, and this one reaches all the way to gravity. How many bits can a region of space hold? In 1981, the physicist Jacob Bekenstein, while working out the thermodynamics of black holes, determined the amount: The information inside any bounded region is limited by its size and the energy it contains. For a region the size of Lloyd’s ultimate laptop, that comes to about 1042 bits, some 1036 to a cubic millimeter—nearly 30 orders of magnitude beyond what a device that size can store today.
Approaching the limits
Over the decades, we have pushed the performance of our computers and our communications technology closer and closer to fundamental limits. The biggest change has been in the energy required for a single computation, which has dropped by 17 orders of magnitude since the 1940s, a factor of a hundred thousand trillion. But even with that big drop, we’re still a factor of several hundred thousand from the fundamental physical limit, set by information theory and the laws of thermodynamics. The largest gap exists for computational speed: Our current chips are some 35 orders of magnitude—that’s a 1 followed by 35 zeros—short of what quantum mechanics allows for a one-kilogram computer.
SOURCES: LLOYD (2000); BEKENSTEIN (1981); LANDAUER (1961); HOLEVO (1973); CAVES AND DRUMMOND (1994); BURKS (1947); BELL SYSTEM TECHNICAL JOURNAL; IEEE IRDS; NVIDIA; CISCO
The last limit is on communication—how fast information can be moved. Every wire and every fiber ultimately carries its signal on quanta, the indivisible packets (photons in the case of light) in which energy travels. In 1973, the Soviet mathematician Alexander Holevo determined the ultimate limit on how much information a stream of quanta can convey. A watt of light delivers only so many photons each second, and quantum mechanics fixes how many distinguishable ways they can arrive—how many messages a receiver could ever tell apart. A single channel carrying one watt, at the Holevo limit, could deliver on the order of 1017 bits per second. Today’s optical links, or interconnects, deliver about one-millionth that rate for the same power. But the gap is narrowing quickly inside data centers, where each generation of interconnects is asked to move more bits on less power, spending less energy on the electronics and using light to cover more of the distance.
Four limits, then, mark the true bottom, and they derive from three of the most fundamental theories we have. Quantum mechanics sets how fast a machine can compute. General relativity caps how much it can remember. And information theory limits both how fast it can communicate and how little energy an irreversible step can cost. There is no road map to reaching these limits, and they hold whether or not anyone is trying. Measured against them, the descent has barely begun.
The room that remains
The biggest of the gaps is in computing speed: There are 35 orders of magnitude between the technology’s current state and its limit. That’s equivalent to the difference between a nanosecond and 200 million times the age of the universe. It is also the least bridgeable gap of the four. To close it you would have to find a completely different way to build a computer, one that could compute with the entire energy contained in a lump of matter.
Quantum computers could get us part of the way there if they could convert every degree of freedom in a lump of matter—every atom, and every way it can move or spin—into a computing element that we could reliably manipulate. In practice, current quantum computers go the other way, spending a lot of matter to create each computing element. Trillions of atoms go into each quantum bit, or qubit, the quantum counterpart of the bit in an ordinary computer. Because every qubit is fragile, dozens to thousands of them must be woven together to make a single one reliable enough for useful computation.
Energy is where the floor is nearest. Today’s chips operate less than six orders of magnitude above the Landauer minimum. Conventional computing logic can close only part of that gap. A reliable switch has to be flipped by an amount of energy large enough that thermal fluctuations never flip it by accident, and that margin pins the transistor a hundred to a few thousand times above Landauer no matter how it is refined.
But there are ideas for getting that energy lower by changing the physics of the computation. In 1973, IBM’s Charles Bennett showed that any computation can be arranged to throw nothing away. Such a reversible computation pays no erasure toll at all, because every step can be run backward to recover what went in.
This approach is called adiabatic or reversible logic, and the first commercial attempts are now underway. For example, Vaire Computing, a startup founded to commercialize reversible logic, tested its first chip in 2025; the chip has resonant circuits that recover part of the switching energy instead of venting it as heat.
Narrowing the memory density gap, meanwhile, would mean building devices that use all three dimensions at molecular scale. The most concrete example is DNA, which stores information at the scale of its own atoms, and which biology has used as a storage medium for 4 billion years. Feynman, being conservative, guessed that a single bit would require a cube of 125 atoms. DNA holds it in about 30. What keeps DNA storage out of the data center is not its density but the cost and speed of writing it, still many orders of magnitude from anything practical. The library in a dust speck that Feynman imagined is permitted by physics and held back only by fabrication.
Communication sits about six orders of magnitude—just a factor of a million—from the Holevo limit, which is the threshold the industry will likely meet first. Interconnects are multiplying faster than the grid can power them, so the industry is moving to transmitters and receivers that use less energy per bit. Nvidia and Broadcom now ship optical interconnects built right against the silicon, so a signal leaves the chip package already on photons. Quantum computers, by comparison, are beginning to rely on interconnects that encode information on quantum signals, usually in the form of single photons. As classical interconnects spend fewer resources on each bit, they descend toward the regime where these quantum interconnects already operate. The Holevo limit is where the two will meet.
Between the floor and the ceiling
It is fair to object that a gap of 35 orders of magnitude is a mirage—that a limit so remote says nothing about what any real machine will ever do, and that pointing to it is like navigating by the horizon. The objection has teeth. Reversible logic, quantum computing, and DNA storage have each been perpetually 10 years away for 40 years. And it will likely never be practical to build a computer that uses all the energy in a lump of matter.
But these gaps are invitations. There is a ceiling, set by how much we can build: the number of devices we can fabricate; the power we can generate to run them; and the capital, land, and cooling water we can assemble into a single system. And there is a floor, set by how much a single joule, a single second, and a single gram of matter can be made to compute, store, or transmit. We can progress by building more or by approaching the floor, which means making each device do more with less.
 These gaps are invitations. We can progress by building more or by approaching the floor, which means making each device do more with less.
For most of the last century, we proceeded down both paths together. We built more computers, and the computers themselves grew smaller and better. Now we mostly build more, and the ceiling is coming into view. A power grid can carry only so many gigawatts, and a region can spare only so much land and water. Yet every road map for what comes next is drawn from the same starting point: the machines we already have. Build more of them and you climb toward the ceiling; build better ones and you descend a little further, but only as far as the transistor’s own floor. There is a third direction. Start with a physics experiment operating at the floor and build up.
It has been done before. The transistor was a physics experiment before it was an industry; the laser was a laboratory curiosity before it carried the world’s conversations under the ocean; giant magnetoresistance went from physics discovery to the read head of every disk drive within a decade. In each case, the physics experiment came first and showed what was possible, and engineers then turned it into a machine that can be scaled up. Building the experiments that operate at these fundamental limits, and then scaling them up without losing that performance, is the work that remains. The next machines will not be reached by descent; they will be built from the bottom up. There is still plenty of room at the bottom.
Volkan Gurses is a postdoctoral researcher at MIT and a visiting researcher at Nvidia. He received his PhD in electrical engineering from Caltech. He studies the fundamental physical limits of information technologies and builds integrated circuits and systems that approach those limits.
