articles.title: DeepSeek made its name with cheap AI models. Now it’s undercutting search API rivals, too.
articles.text:
DeepSeek made its name with cheap AI models. Now it’s undercutting search API rivals, too.
Not content with challenging the major frontier AI labs with lower-cost models, Chinese AI company DeepSeek is setting its sights on the search API market.
On Saturday, the company announced it has opened up its internally developed search engine to outside developers through two new APIs, Search and Fetch, allowing them to retrieve live web search results and webpage content for use in their own apps and agents.
Both services cost $0.75 per 1,000 successful requests, and developers can use them independently of DeepSeek’s AI models.
The launch also came alongside DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, a minor update to the V4.1 Flash model the company released in September.
Why AI agents need web search
Large language models (LLMs) are trained on data collected up to a certain point in time, meaning they can’t always answer questions about recent events, updated documentation, or any other kind of dynamic information. By supporting live web search, models can retrieve current information from the internet, which supplements their responses.
For developers building AI agents, this is particularly important. A coding agent, for example, might need to consult the latest software documentation, investigate a recently disclosed vulnerability, or otherwise check that a particular library has been updated.
Until now, developers using DeepSeek’s models had several ways to provide this functionality. They could connect their applications to third-party search services, or use DeepSeek’s existing search functionality through its model API.
Indeed, when DeepSeek open-sourced its agent harness in August, it included web search among its capabilities. The Harness supported interchangeable search providers, including Exa, Perplexity and DeepSeek itself. However, accessing DeepSeek’s native search through the Harness required an additional model request, with each search running as a separate call to a DeepSeek model, according to the Harness documentation, introducing extra latency and token costs.
The new APIs are designed to simplify that process. Developers can now call DeepSeek’s Search endpoint directly to retrieve ranked web results, including titles, URLs, snippets and summaries, while the Fetch endpoint retrieves the contents of individual webpages in Markdown format.
“Neither requires a separate model request, meaning developers can integrate DeepSeek’s search capabilities into applications powered by competing AI models, too.”
Neither requires a separate model request, meaning developers can integrate DeepSeek’s search capabilities into applications powered by competing AI models, too.
DeepSeek develops an in-house engine
For much of the past two years, DeepSeek has relied on outside providers to power web search, even as it was building its own.
For context, in March 2025, Chinese business publication National Business Daily reported that DeepSeek had integrated the search API of Bocha, a Chinese AI search startup based in Hangzhou. Bocha’s CTO, Weng Rouying, noted that DeepSeek had been using its service prior to the chatbot’s surge in popularity earlier that year.
DeepSeek’s own February 2025 privacy policy, meanwhile, also acknowledged its reliance on third-party search services, naming Microsoft’s Bing as an example of an external API provider.
“Behind the scenes, the company has also been laying the groundwork for its own search infrastructure.”
Behind the scenes, the company has also been laying the groundwork for its own search infrastructure. In January this year, Bloomberg reported that DeepSeek was recruiting engineers to build a multilingual AI search engine, according to job ads listed by the company. The planned capabilities reportedly extended beyond text searches to include images and audio.
Fast-forward some nine months, and the company says its internally developed search engine, dubbed DeepSeek Search, already handles hundreds of millions of requests daily, and maintains an index containing hundreds of billions of webpages.
According to its October 17 changelog, the engine supports multilingual searches and uses filtering mechanisms designed to identify search spam, low-quality AI-generated material, and attempts to manipulate search rankings.
DeepSeek has disclosed relatively little about the underlying architecture, or how it builds and maintains its index. It’s also not clear whether the company has entirely replaced its external search suppliers across the board.
A growing market for AI search
Building a search engine is no trivial undertaking. It requires the infrastructure to crawl webpages, maintain an index of their contents and rank results, while continuously updating that information as the web changes. For years, that meant developers who wanted raw search results for their applications largely turned to Google and Microsoft, the two companies with web-scale indexes of their own.
Now, however, a growing number of companies are investing in their own search infrastructure, increasingly with AI applications and agents squarely in mind. Brave, for example, operates an independent index of more than 40 billion webpages, which it says is maintained through its own crawler and other discovery mechanisms. AI search company Exa, meanwhile, has also developed its own crawling and indexing infrastructure.
Perplexity has similarly invested in proprietary search infrastructure, including building its own crawling and indexing systems. Another competitor, Parallel, says it has built its search infrastructure from the ground up, including the crawling, indexing, query processing and ranking components.
Cloudflare is also entering the market from a different angle. Earlier this month, the company launched a Web Search API through its AI Gateway, allowing developers to access search results from serveral providers through a single interface. The service, currently in beta, uses Ceramic as its default provider and charges customers at each provider’s published API rates, without additional markup.
“DeepSeek, for its part, is competing aggressively against the incumbents on price.”
DeepSeek, for its part, is competing aggressively against the incumbents on price, although it’s not strictly the cheapest option available. Ceramic.ai, which provides keyword-based web search for AI agents, charges $0.25 per 1,000 queries on its pay-as-you-go plan.
Still, DeepSeek’s $0.75 per 1,000 successful searches compares favorably with many others, including Parallel’s Turbo and Fast search services and Perplexity’s Fast Search API, both of which charge $1 per 1,000 searches. Meanwhile, Exa charges $4 per 1,000 Instant Search requests, while Brave charges $5 per 1,000 searches. Other notable players include Tavily, a search API provider for AI agents that European AI infrastructure company Nebius acquired in February. Tavily charges $8 per 1,000 basic searches on its pay-as-you-go plan.
It’s worth noting that the various services differ in terms of retrieval capabilities, result limits and performance, so the prices aren’t necessarily entirely comparable. But they provide some useful benchmarks for DeepSeek’s move into the search infrastructure space.
The emergence of these alternatives also comes as Google and Microsoft have withdrawn longstanding search API offerings. Microsoft retired its Bing Search APIs in August 2025, while Google has closed its Custom Search JSON API to new customers, with existing users required to migrate by January 1, 2027. Both companies continue to provide search functionality through their respective AI platforms, including Grounding with Google Search for Gemini and Grounding with Bing Search for Microsoft Foundry agents. These services allow AI models operating within their respective platforms to retrieve web information and generate answers with citations.
Standalone APIs such as DeepSeek’s give developers direct access to search results, which they can use with AI models and applications of their choosing.
Developer reaction and the fine print
The announcement has sparked considerable discussion among developers about pricing and whether the new APIs offer much beyond existing search integrations. On Reddit, one user welcomed the cost in particular. “I don’t think any other search provider comes close to the price that DeepSeek is offering,” they write.
Others questioned what the announcement would ultimately change for users already accessing web search through third-party tools. One Reddit user notes that they are already using DeepSeek with the Hermes AI agent, which could search the web. Another user responded that those who had already configured their own search tools might see little immediate benefit from the new APIs.
A similar discussion emerged on Hacker News, where one developer questions the need for paid search APIs when free, self-hosted alternatives such as SearXNG were available. Another commenter argues that businesses have additional requirements, citing “reliable latency, data processing guarantees” and the potential risk of exposing sensitive company information through search queries.
For businesses weighing DeepSeek’s APIs, that last point carries an extra dimension. DeepSeek’s privacy policy states that it collects, processes and stores personal data in China, and that it generally keeps user inputs for as long as an account remains open. The Search and Fetch documentation, however, doesn’t say how long search queries specifically are retained.
The discussions highlight the differing needs of individual developers and businesses, particularly when it comes to cost, reliability, and handling large numbers of requests. And while DeepSeek’s pricing is certainly competitive, there are some practical restrictions worth considering.
According to its API documentation, Search and Fetch requests are each capped at five per second per account, although individual searches can return up to 50 results without increasing the request price. DeepSeek also only bills for requests that return results, so failed calls, empty searches, and timeouts are free.
DeepSeek is temporarily waiving Search and Fetch charges for server-side tool calls made through DeepSeek Harness, Claude Code, and Codex when using its API. That is very much a temporary arrangement, however, one that ends on October 31, when the standard per-request charges take effect. Direct calls to the standalone APIs are already billable, according to DeepSeek’s announcement.

articles.title: Données d’élèves et de parents en vente : deux services éducatifs français visés par le même pirate
articles.text:
Près de cinq millions de comptes d’une application de révision et plus de 286 000 dossiers d’élèves de lycée sont proposés à la vente par le pirate Angel_Batista. Nomad Education et Inter-Etab n’ont pas confirmé la fuite, mais les échantillons contiennent des données d’enfants et de leurs parents.
Angel_Batista a mis les deux fichiers, à quelques minutes d’intervalle, sur un forum cybercriminel. FrenchBreaches a relevé les 4 852 437 lignes de comptes Nomad Education et, pour 250 dollars, les 286 773 dossiers d’élèves d’Inter-Etab. Cyberattaque.org a pour sa part passé au crible les extraits fournis par le vendeur, un millier de comptes d’un côté et 1 030 fiches scolaires de l’autre. Nomad Education propose des fiches et des quiz de révision aux élèves de tous niveaux, tandis que des lycées gèrent avec Inter-Etab les stages et les épreuves en contrôle continu. Entre des comptes récents d’enfants et des dossiers vieux d’une dizaine d’années, les familles ne courent pas le même risque d’un fichier à l’autre.
Des enfants chez Nomad Education, des parents chez Inter-Etab
Dans l’extrait Nomad, chaque ligne contient une adresse e-mail et un nom d’utilisateur, et 869 comptes sur 1 001 indiquent une date de naissance. Selon Cyberattaque.org, 323 de ces titulaires étaient mineurs au 17 octobre, dont 16 enfants de moins de 13 ans. Le plus jeune a 6 ans. Les lignes examinées ne contiennent ni mot de passe ni coordonnées bancaires, mais 254 d’entre elles comportent un jeton de connexion. Grâce à ce jeton, Nomad Education garde un élève connecté sans lui redemander son mot de passe, et 138 des jetons de l’échantillon expirent après le 17 octobre, certains en 2027. Un éditeur peut toutefois révoquer un jeton à tout moment, quelle que soit sa date d’expiration. Le vendeur a d’ailleurs reconnu qu’environ 500 000 adresses de sa base sont des adresses de remplacement ou masquées par Apple. Il y a donc moins d’élèves concernés que de lignes annoncées.
Chez Inter-Etab, les parents sont presque partout. Sur 1 030 dossiers, 1 018 mentionnent au moins un responsable légal, avec dans 998 cas le numéro de portable d’un parent. Chez Climb Up, où un pirate a mis en vente cette semaine les fiches de 151 000 clients, parents et enfants apparaissaient aussi ensemble. Les dossiers Inter-Etab proviennent de neuf établissements, dans les académies de Strasbourg, Créteil, Dijon, Toulouse, Grenoble et Lyon, et la base vient plus probablement d’un système commun à plusieurs lycées que du piratage d’un seul établissement, estime Cyberattaque.org. Les fiches datent en grande majorité de 2016, avec des modifications jusqu’en 2019, et les anciens élèves, nés entre 1994 et 2003, sont aujourd’hui majeurs. La mise en vente « ne prouve pas qu’Inter-Etab a été compromis récemment », souligne le site. Toutes les fiches contiennent aussi un champ « pass », le plus souvent une chaîne de dix caractères, et personne ne peut dire s’il s’agit de vrais mots de passe.
Identifiants volés et faux messages scolaires
Nomad Education et Inter-Etab n’ont donné aucune explication publique sur l’origine des fichiers, et Angel_Batista ne précise pas comment il les a obtenus. Plus tôt dans l’année, en racontant ses méthodes d’intrusion à ZATAZ, il a expliqué que les « stealers » étaient son « passe-partout ». Avec ces logiciels espions, souvent glissés dans des programmes piratés, il récupère les identifiants enregistrés sur l’ordinateur d’un salarié, puis se connecte aux outils internes de l’entreprise. Quand ZATAZ lui a demandé ce qui l’aurait arrêté, il a cité la double authentification, mise en place depuis sur la plateforme interministérielle Resana. Il suffit parfois d’un compte légitime. Début octobre, un autre pirate a aspiré 140 000 profils de l’École 42 depuis l’intranet de l’école, à partir d’un compte utilisateur doté d’un accès normal.
Avec le nom d’un élève et le portable de sa mère, un escroc peut envoyer au nom du lycée un SMS crédible pour réclamer un paiement ou une mise à jour de dossier. Les numéros de 2016 ne sont pas tous valables, mais les noms et les liens de parenté sont toujours exacts dix ans plus tard. Un élève inscrit sur Nomad Education peut de son côté recevoir, à son vrai nom, un faux e-mail de réinitialisation de mot de passe.
La CNIL et Cybermalveillance.gouv.fr ont mis en ligne début octobre un guide de réaction après une fuite. Recevoir une alerte « ne signifie pas que mes données ont déjà été utilisées de manière frauduleuse », rappellent les deux organismes. Si votre enfant utilise Nomad Education, vous pouvez changer son mot de passe et ouvrir directement l’application, jamais un lien reçu par e-mail. Si vous êtes passé par un lycée équipé d’Inter-Etab vers 2016, mieux vaut changer tout ancien code encore utilisé ailleurs. Seul Nomad Education peut vérifier, sur ses serveurs, si les 138 jetons encore valides sur le papier permettent toujours d’entrer dans un compte d’élève.

articles.title: Exploited Fortinet Bug Linked to Stealthy FortiGate Implant in Telecom Hack
articles.text:
A suspected state-sponsored threat actor exploited multiple Fortinet vulnerabilities in an attack against a telecommunications organization, Palo Alto Networks reports.
The intrusion, attributed to UNC5820 (tracked by Palo Alto Networks as CL-STA-0954), occurred in September 2024 and resulted in long-term access to the victim’s environment.
Initial access was obtained through the exploitation of a critical remote code execution (RCE) bug in FortiManager, tracked as CVE-2024-47575 and patched in October 2024 as a zero-day.
Shortly after the patches were rolled out, Mandiant warned that UNC5820 had been exploiting the flaw, named FortiJump, since at least June 2024.
A fresh report from Palo Alto Networks shows that UNC5820 also exploited CVE-2025-61624, a path traversal vulnerability affecting multiple Fortinet products, as part of the same intrusion.
Impacting FortiOS, FortiPAM, FortiProxy, and FortiSwitchManager and patched in April 2026, the security defect could allow authenticated attackers to write or delete arbitrary files. Fortinet flagged its exploitation as a zero-day at the time of disclosure.
On Friday, the US cybersecurity agency CISA added CVE-2025-61624 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list, urging federal agencies to patch it immediately.
UNC5820 appears to have exploited the path traversal as a zero-day to deploy a previously unknown FortiGate implant dubbed PeerStitch.
The ARM64 malware resides in memory, avoids opening listening ports or initiating outbound network connections, and communicates through the traffic generated by legitimate processes on the appliance.
As part of the observed attack, UNC5820 exploited FortiJump to access a central FortiManager instance, registered a rogue Virtual FortiGate appliance, and exfiltrated a configuration archive containing details on FortiManager, more than 500 managed FortiGate firewalls, and the victim’s network.
UNC5820 exploited CVE-2025-61624 to gain root access to the underlying firewall operating system, dropping a script to initiate the PeerStitch deployment.
Written in C, the implant acts as a ‘one-shot process memory patching injector’ targeting the central system and traffic logging, and the IKE/IPsec VPN service daemons in FortiOS to create a covert, memory-resident communication bridge between them and bypass default FortiOS security validations.
As part of the attack, the threat actor was also seen impersonating FortiManager in FortiGate-to-FortiManager (FGFM) communications to issue commands from external infrastructure and “took extensive measures to eliminate forensic artifacts”.
According to Palo Alto Networks, UNC5820 asserted the management identity either by terminating the authentic FortiManager’s session by exploiting CVE-2024-26008, or by reusing exfiltrated secrets and authenticating as the legitimate FortiManager.
“The discovery of the PeerStitch implant demonstrates the increasing technical maturity of edge-device malware. By operating as a one-shot injector, avoiding persistent disk artifacts and building a covert inter-process communication bridge inside process memory, the attackers achieved sustained persistence while evading traditional monitoring,” Palo Alto Networks notes.

articles.title: Top 10 videos más vistos en YouTube Chile hoy
articles.text:
Aunque redes sociales como Facebook e Instagram están apostando cada vez más por los videos, lo cierto es que YouTube sigue siendo el rey al ser la segunda página más visitada en el mundo sólo por detrás del buscador Google.
YouTube tiene presencia en 104 países y está disponible en 80 idiomas, por lo que no sorprende que en dicha plataforma puedas encontrar un video de BTS, pasando por videos de terror hasta llegar a contenido educativo sobre cómo resolver una ecuación.
La plataforma estadounidense, surgida en el año 2005, se ha convertido en la biblioteca digital de videos más grande del mundo y prueba de ello es que a ella se suben más de 500 horas de contenido cada minuto, al día son vistos 5 mil millones de videos y las ganancias se estiman en 15 mil millones de dólares al trimestre.
Ante estas cifras podría ser un tanto difícil perderse las novedades o los clips que están siendo los más populares, es por eso que YouTube cuenta desde 2018 con diversas listas en donde se pueden consultar los artistas más escuchados, los videos más vistos y cuáles son las tendencias del día en tiempo real.
Acá el listado de los 10 nuevos videos que están en tendencia
1. Déjate Llevar (Remix)Artista/canal: Mateo on the Beatz, Jere Klein, simonpizarro y El Bai
2. VuelveArtista/canal: Anuel AA
3. No Lo Pienses TantoArtista/canal: Lucky Brown y Tobal Mj
4. Koke Nunez & Ignacio Ormazábal - Buen Vino (Video Oficial)Artista/canal: Koke Nuñez
5. LE DEBO CONFESARArtista/canal: Alanys Lagos
6. Kidd Voodoo - SENSACIONESS (Video Oficial)Artista/canal: Kidd Voodoo
7. Desde Que Te TengoArtista/canal: Carín León
8. Bulin 47 X Kevin Wai - Dame Hombro (Video Oficial)Artista/canal: Bulin 47 Oficial
9. BbY WOWArtista/canal: KAROL G, rusowsky y Judeline
10. 7 MaravillasArtista/canal: Gino Mella, Jairo Vera y Ag Daddy
Los inicios de YouTube
YouTube vio la luz en febrero de 2005, cuando tres antiguos empleados de la compañía de Paypal ―Chad Hurley, Steve Chen y Jawed Karim― se unieron y la crearon luego de que experimentaran dificultades para compartir entre sí un par de videos tras asistir a una fiesta.
El dominio fue activado el 14 de febrero de 2005 y casi un mes después, el 23 de abril, fue cargado el primer clip a la plataforma que llevaba por nombre “Me at the Zoo”. Fue cuestión de tiempo para que todo el mundo comenzara a cargar contenido y a compartir los enlaces a través de otras redes sociales como MySpace.
Una de las grandes empresas que vio el potencial de YouTube fue la marca Nike, que subió una publicidad protagonizada por Ronaldinho, lo que hizo que otras grandes compañías voltearan a ver a YouTube y se sintieran atraídas.
Tal fue la gran acogida de los internautas por YouTube que para diciembre de 2005 la plataforma pasó de las 50 millones de visitas al día a 250 millones de visualizaciones luego de que un canal subiera el clip musical Lazy Sunday, transmitido originalmente por Saturday Night Live.
Para el año siguiente, en el 2006, el sitio fue comparado por el gigante del internet, Google, por un valor de 1650 millones de dólares. En ese entonces eran visualizados 100 millones de videos al día y 65 mil clips se añadían a diario. También firmaron acuerdos con disqueras para poder reproducir videos musicales.
YouTube: entre la cultura popular y la política
Desde que fue puesto en marcha, YouTube fue un sitio que llegó a hacer una revolución no sólo en internet, sino también en la forma en la que los usuarios miran contenido. Muestra de ello el reconocimiento que la revista Time le otorgó en noviembre del 2006 al ser nombrado el “Invento del Año”.
Convertido en el mejor medio de difusión, el gozar de tanta popularidad también ha metido a sus dueños en aprietos como cuando albergar peleas escolares o en donde hay bullying, clips relacionados al terrorismo, narcotráfico u otros temas considerados delicados por su contenido íntimo o por mostrar delitos como asesinatos y más.
Para Estados Unidos uno de los temas más delicados es el de los tiroteos escolares, por lo que YouTube ha estado más de una vez en el ojo del huracán por alojar contenido filmado por los atacantes, como fue el caso de la masacre de Virginia Tech, cuando Cho Seung-Hui, el atacante, subió previamente a los hechos un discurso.
Más recientemente, tras el surgimiento de la pandemia del coronavirus, también ha surgido inquietud sobre cómo la plataforma permite la monetización de contenido que puede ser engañoso y riesgoso para la población.
Aunque no todo es malo, pues a través de dicha plataforma muchas personas han podido ser reconocidas por su talento, como fue el caso de Susan Boyle, quien participó en el programa Britain’s Got Talent cuyo extracto subido a YouTube logró que la mujer pasara a ser una completa desconocida a una de las personas más viralizadas, famosas y aclamadas del internet.

articles.title: La psicología dice que las personas que dejan el móvil boca abajo no es para ocultar nada; en realidad, es una táctica para evitar distracciones
articles.text:
Una comida, dos personas. Antes de que llegue la primera ración, uno de los comensales gira su teléfono y lo deja sobre el mantel con la pantalla hacia abajo. Hay quien lo interpreta como desconfianza, pero la explicación es otra: quiere librarse de las notificaciones y las llamadas entrantes y de la presión constante de estar disponible en todo momento. Al fin y al cabo, es solo una interpretación, y no se apoya en ningún experimento científico que estudie sus motivaciones.
Lo que sí han estudiado los experimentos es el efecto de tener el móvil a la vista.
En la Universidad de Essex, Andrew Przybylski y Netta Weinstein realizaron un experimento con parejas de desconocidos que hablaban entre ellos durante diez minutos con un teléfono o un cuaderno sobre una mesa cercana.
En su trabajo, publicado en el Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, el teléfono se asoció con una menor cercanía y una conversación de menor calidad y, en un segundo experimento, con una menor confianza y empatía, aunque solo cuando hablaban de algo personal: con un tema trivial no hubo diferencias. Después, otro grupo de científicos, ya fuera del Reino Unido, llevó la comparación a conversaciones reales.
Shalini Misra, de Virginia Tech, observó 100 conversaciones reales entre dos personas en entornos informales. Aquellas que tuvieron lugar sin ningún dispositivo a la vista salieron mejor valoradas. “En presencia de un dispositivo móvil hay menos contacto visual”, resumía la investigadora.
Matt Johnson, profesor en la Hult International Business School, recopiló varios de estos trabajos en su artículo ‘The Psychology of the Face-Down Phone’ (la psicología del móvil boca abajo). Según los experimentos que recoge, no hace falta usar el aparato para que afecte a la atención, y cuanto más difícil es la tarea, más pronunciado es el efecto.
También repasa los experimentos de Elizabeth Dunn (Universidad de Columbia Británica): en grupos de tres a cinco personas sentadas en una cafetería, quienes tenían el teléfono sobre la mesa (¡cualquiera podría hacer esto!) se sintieron más distraídos y disfrutaron mucho menos del encuentro.
¿Y qué ocurre con la práctica de poner el móvil boca abajo?
El experimento más conocido sobre el tema es el de “pérdida cognitiva” (“brain drain”) de Adrian Ward y sus colegas de la Universidad de Texas en Austin, en el que 520 estudiantes realizaron una serie de pruebas de memoria y razonamiento. El móvil se situaba o en otra habitación, o en el bolsillo o el bolso de los participantes, o sobre la mesa, donde se les indicaba que lo pusieran boca abajo en un sitio marcado del escritorio.
Fueron las personas que lo dejaron sobre la mesa las que obtuvieron los peores resultados en las pruebas. Según el trabajo, publicado en 2017, la mera presencia del propio smartphone reduce la capacidad cognitiva disponible, aunque no se use ni se piense en él.
Quienes lo dejaron en otra habitación obtuvieron los mejores resultados, mientras que los del bolsillo o del bolso obtuvieron resultados intermedios. Girar el móvil lo quita de la vista, pero el cacharro sigue ahí. En un segundo experimento del mismo trabajo, el efecto se mantuvo con el teléfono apagado del todo, algo que se repasaba en mayo de 2026.
¿Son suficientes las pruebas?
No del todo. Una réplica directa del experimento hecha en la Universidad de Western Ontario, publicada en Acta Psychologica en octubre de 2022, encontró que el efecto no se repetía: no hubo diferencias entre tener el móvil sobre la mesa, en el bolsillo o fuera.
Sin embargo, un equipo de la Universidad de Augsburgo juntó 22 estudios en un metaanálisis publicado en Behavioral Sciences en septiembre de 2023 y sí encontró el efecto, sobre todo en pruebas de memoria y atención, más débil en tareas sencillas y más fuerte en los estudios hechos en Asia que en los de Europa y Norteamérica.
Además, se aconseja precaución al sacar conclusiones sobre quien deja el móvil boca abajo, porque puede hacerlo por razones muy variadas: educación, costumbre o pura comodidad.
Cómo hacer que el gesto sirva para algo más
La forma más sencilla de que girar el teléfono tenga sentido es que lo silencie. Esta opción está disponible en los teléfonos Pixel de Google, en la función Silenciar al girar, que llegó a los Pixel 2 en noviembre de 2019 con una actualización de Bienestar digital y activaba el modo No molestar al poner el teléfono boca abajo.
Los propietarios de iPhone no tienen esta función incorporada, pero los modos de Concentración se pueden activar a mano o programar para que se enciendan solos a una hora concreta. Esto último es útil si la comida o la reunión tiene una hora fija.
Por último, no existe ningún ajuste, ni en iPhone ni en Android, que elimine la distracción de tener el móvil cerca durante una comida o una reunión. En el experimento de la Universidad de Texas en Austin, lo que mejor funcionó fue dejar el teléfono en otra habitación; la réplica de Western Ontario no encontró esa diferencia, y el metaanálisis de Augsburgo sí encontró el efecto, sobre todo en memoria y atención.

articles.title: NestJS 12: ESM Packages, Standard Schema Validation and Native Observability
articles.text:
NestJS, the TypeScript framework for building server-side Node.js applications, has released version 12, a major release that moves its core packages to ESM, adds first-class Standard Schema validation, rebuilds the CLI and introduces an official observability SDK. It follows April's roadmap, and creator Kamil Myśliwiec's announcement on X has passed 1,100 likes and 66,000 views.
The ESM change is the headline, largely because it asks so little of existing teams. Core packages now ship as ESM, but CommonJS applications keep working through Node.js require(esm) support, which is why v12 requires Node.js 20.19+ or 22.12+. nest new now asks whether to generate a CJS or ESM project, with ESM projects defaulting to Vitest and oxlint, while Rspack replaces webpack as the monorepo bundler. Developer Anton Chapala's preview benchmarks found no meaningful startup or memory gains from ESM, concluding it "is a massive cleanup of tooling and configuration debt" rather than a performance upgrade.
Day-to-day ergonomics change most around validation. Route decorators such as @Body(), @Query() and @Param() accept a schema option taking any Standard Schema compatible object, so Zod, Valibot and ArkType work without third-party wrappers once the new pipe is registered.
class-validator remains the documented default. Blogger iiaku argued that building on a spec rather than on Zod directly "keeps the choice in my hands while removing the boilerplate", though a commenter on ByteIota's preview coverage noted that types must still be annotated by hand because Nest continues to rely on legacy TypeScript decorators.
The most debated addition is @nestjs/observe, which hooks into Nest's own lifecycle through a new instrument option instead of patching the HTTP server, reporting traces in terms of controllers and providers. APM vendor Scout Monitoring acknowledged the richer context but warned the SDK is "NestJS-only", lacks cross-stack correlation out of the box and risks "vendor lock-in at the framework level". A new nest deploy command, forwarding to the Mau platform, points the same way towards first-party services.
The NestJS Observe dashboard, source: Trilon
Upgrading from v11 means installing the latest CLI with npm i -g @nestjs/cli@latest and running nest upgrade, which moves every @nestjs/* package to v12, bumps TypeScript to v6 and applies mechanical changes such as the GraphQL Playground to GraphiQL switch and the NATS v3 client swap.
It deliberately does not convert projects to ESM, Vitest or oxlint. The migration guide covers the rest, including lifecycle hook ordering and Joi v18.
One GitHub issue prompted docs noting AWS Lambda runtimes need --experimental-require-module, while others report path aliases breaking under ESM and Fastify middleware exceptions hanging. The follow-up v12.1 has since added built-in cookies, CSRF protection and security headers.
NestJS is an open-source, MIT-licensed framework for building efficient and scalable server-side applications with TypeScript. It combines an Angular-inspired module and dependency injection architecture with Express and Fastify support, and has more than 76,000 stars on GitHub.

articles.title: Elon Musk promises to give every child in America a free SpaceX share next year
articles.text:
What just happened? Elon Musk makes a lot of big promises, not all of which come to pass, but it's hard to see how he'll renege on this one. The world's richest person says he will give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in America next year, adding that "this will be the first of many."
Musk explained the plan on his X platform. He didn't elaborate, so we don't know details such as what ages will qualify for a free share, how he intends to distribute them, and exactly when the giveaway will take place in 2027.
 – Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 19, 2026
It's estimated that Musk would be required to give a share to around 72 million people under the age of 18. SpaceX's share price is currently $146, so that would represent stock worth about $10.5 billion.
Musk certainly has plenty of SpaceX shares to hand out. The company's SEC filing in August showed he owned 6.42 billion shares as of June 30, including shares held in trusts for which he acts as trustee, restricted stock, and shares that could be issued upon exercising options.
Musk's announcement comes soon after Anthropic, xAI's rival, said it would commit 5% of its shares to a fund that will make donations for the "public good." The company later said that the fund could also receive another 2% of the firm's shares at its board's discretion. Anthropic's IPO could value the firm at more than $1 trillion
Musk responded to the Anthropic announcement by writing "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public. This is what I will be doing."
The moves also echo the thinking behind Trump Accounts, the tax-advantaged investment accounts for children that give eligible US citizens born between 2025 and 2028 a $1,000 government-funded head start. Families, employers, and other donors can add money, which is invested in funds tracking US stocks to help children build wealth as they grow up.
There's already a SpaceX connection to the program. The company's chief operating officer, Gwynne Shotwell, has pledged more than $320 million of her own SpaceX stock to help fund Trump Accounts for over two million children.

articles.title: Aproveite: Nintendo Switch 2 entra em oferta relâmpago no Mercado Livre • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Aproveite: Nintendo Switch 2 entra em oferta relâmpago no Mercado Livre
Switch 2 com proposta multiuso e acesso a jogos exclusivos da Nintendo recebe raro desconto de 15% no Pix, mas promoção acaba ao meio-dia de hoje!
O Switch 2 está saindo por apenas R$ 3.814 no Pix no Mercado Livre. O mais recente console da Nintendo, que possui uma proposta de múltiplo uso e acesso a jogos exclusivos, recebe desconto de 15% sobre o preço original de R$ 4.499.
Embora não seja o menor preço histórico, esta é uma rara chance de adquirir o console por um preço menor, mas corra (mesmo!): a oferta relâmpago acaba ao meio-dia desta segunda-feira (19).
O destaque do Switch 2 é sua proposta como console híbrido. Assim como seu antecessor, o sistema mais vendido da Nintendo, ele pode ser usado conectado à TV por meio da dock, como portátil com os Joy-Cons conectados, ou como semiportátil apoiado sobre uma mesa.
Sua tela LCD de 7,9″, usada nos modos portátil e semiportátil, conta com resolução Full HD e taxa de 120 fps. Quando ligado à dock, o sistema suporta 4K a 60 fps ou 120 fps em 1080p e 2K, com HDR10 em TVs compatíveis, oferecendo uma experiência gamer fluida.
O hardware interno inclui um chip Nvidia T239 customizado, 12 GB de RAM e 256 GB de armazenamento expansível com cartões microSD especiais. Os Joy-Cons podem ser usados como um mouse quando apoiados em uma superfície, e a dock traz uma porta Ethernet nativa para conexões de rede mais estáveis.
O Switch 2 suporta boa parte da biblioteca do Switch original, e tem acesso a inúmeros games de franquias exclusivas da Nintendo, como Mario, The Legend of Zelda, Pokémon, Donkey Kong e Metroid, indisponíveis em sistemas concorrentes.
Sua bateria de 5.200 mAh resiste a até 6 horas de uso, segundo a fabricante. A dock é capaz de carregar o sistema quando usado como console de mesa, sem interromper a jogatina.
O Switch 2 (apenas R$ 3.814 no Pix) tem acesso ao Nintendo Switch Online, serviço que oferece jogos em rede e benefícios exclusivos para assinantes, como games clássicos de sistemas legados da companhia centenária de Quioto.
Aviso de ética: ao clicar em um link de afiliado, o preço não muda para você e recebemos uma comissão.

Calibre-aware, short-resilient via insertion for signoff-ready physical design.

Physical design teams face challenges with via resistance, electromigration and routing density. Calibre DesignEnhancer Via (DE-Via) automates the insertion of additional vias, ensuring DRC-clean layout modifications.
This shift-left methodology improves via robustness early in the design cycle, reducing late signoff iterations. DE-Via identifies short-prone regions, avoiding insertion in those areas to maintain productivity and visibility into unresolved issues.

articles.title: 3 razones para ver 'Avatar: Los Siete Refugios', la nueva secuela de 'La leyenda de Aang'
articles.text:
Llega por fin a España Avatar: Los Siete Refugios, la nueva serie secuela de La leyenda de Aang y La leyenda de Korra. La franquicia se expande por primera vez en diez años con su tercer proyecto de animación. Una nueva historia que promete muchísimo potencial, tanto por sus protagonistas como por la manera en la que va a profundizar en el lore y la mitología de la saga.
Por el momento, Avatar: Los Siete Refugios cuenta con una recepción buenísima. En Rotten Tomatoes, tiene una puntuación perfecta del 100% entre los críticos y un sólido 81% en el marcador del público. El proyecto apunta muy alto y puede confirmarse como uno de los mejores estrenos de animación del año en televisión.
Tras su llegada a Estados Unidos, Latinoamérica y otros territorios en Paramount+ hace unos días, Avatar: Los Siete Refugios se estrena en España el 17 de octubre a través de SkyShowtime con el lanzamiento de sus tres primeros episodios. A partir de ahí, llegarán tres episodios nuevos cada semana hasta completar los 13 que tendrá esta primera temporada. Y por si aún tienes dudas, a continuación te dejamos 3 motivos imprescindibles para ver la serie.
Un mundo nuevo
En Avatar: Los Siete Refugios, la franquicia nos lleva 225 años después de los acontecimientos de la serie de Avatar: La leyenda de Korra y prácticamente 300 años después de Avatar: La leyenda de Aang. Evidentemente, por tanto, lo que nos encontramos es un mundo muy cambiado. Algo que, gracias a su intro, se nos explica rápidamente. Durante la era de Korra, algo terrible sucedió en el mundo terrenal y en el mundo de los espíritus.
Un cataclismo que provocó la caída de las Cuatro Naciones y del que se culpa (¿injustamente?) a la propia Avatar. Ahora, en un planeta absolutamente hostil, la humanidad solo habita en siete refugios separados entre sí. Son asentamientos dispersos y, probablemente, con características y formas de vida muy distintas. En Avatar: Los siete refugios solo hemos visto Ellora, en mitad del desierto. Allí, los maestros de los cuatro elementos son reclutados, sin importar su edad, para la Brigada de Maestros. Además, podemos intuir que el control de los elementos se ha deteriorado
¿Dos Avatares?
Lo más atractivo e interesante, además de saber qué ha sucedido en el mundo, es que por primera vez en Avatar: Los Siete Refugios tenemos a dos Avatares. Primero conocemos a Pavi, una niña coja y huérfana que vive por libre en el desierto y se cuela cuando puede en Ellora. Pero al final del primer capítulo, como intuíamos gracias a los tráileres, se nos descubre que tiene una hermana gemela, Nisha, que también es capaz de controlar los cuatro elementos.
Por tanto, esta es la primera vez en el ciclo Avatar en la que existen dos personas con este inmenso poder. Y aunque aún no lo tenemos claro, es muy probable que la propia serie nos descubra que no es simple casualidad. Es lógico pensar que hay una razón por la que Pavi y Nisha han recibido los poderes del Avatar. Y quizá tenga que ver con ese cataclismo que asoló el mundo durante la era de Korra. Además, será interesante ver cómo se desenvuelven en un mundo que ya no considera al Avatar como su salvación sino como su principal amenaza.
La nueva era de Avatar
Un último motivo de peso para ver Avatar: Los siete refugios es que esta serie abrirá de par en par el camino para el futuro de la saga. La leyenda de Aang se emitió entre 2005 y 2008, mientras que La leyenda de Korra lo hizo entre 2012 y 2014. Ahora, más de una década después, la franquicia vuelve a ponerse en marcha. Y los planes son bastante prometedores y ambiciosos.
Por lo pronto, sabemos que Avatar: Los Siete Refugios tendrá cuatro temporadas que ya han recibido luz verde por parte de Paramount. Y, además, la compañía anunció hace unos días que ponía en marcha otra serie más, titulada Avatar Kuruk: Wave of Chaos (La ola del caos). Será una precuela de Aang, concretamente de tres generaciones antes que el pequeño maestro del aire. En este título se seguirá la historia de Avatar Kuruk, perteneciente a la Tribu del Agua. Sucedió al Avatar Yangchen y precedió a la Avatar Kyoshi. Aún no tiene fecha de estreno pero está oficialmente en desarrollo.

articles.title: Vibe coding is turning the music gear world upside down
articles.text:
If you spend any time on r/synthesizers or watch a lot of synth videos on YouTube, you’ve probably noticed the explosion of custom firmware for hardware synthesizers, samplers, and grooveboxes. What unites almost all of them is that they were made possible by increasingly sophisticated vibe coding tools.
Vibe coding is turning the music gear world upside down
LLMs have led to an explosion of custom firmware and hacks for synths, samplers, and grooveboxes.
These sorts of custom firmware were exceedingly rare in the pre-LLM days, and required both deep expertise and an incredible investment of time. It could take weeks or months to add a simple feature like velocity sensitivity to a Korg Volca. Now, hobbyist hackers are able to turn Temu synths into full-fledged grooveboxes in a matter of days.
Elektron’s budget-friendly Model:Cycles, Digitone, Octatrack, and Digitakt have all gained new capabilities with Claude’s help. Roland’s SP-404 MKII, Ableton’s Push 3 and Move, Akai’s MPC Live and MPC One, as well as the vintage MPC 2000, Novation’s Circuit, Arturia’s MicroFreak, and even Zoom’s 14-year-old Multistomp pedal line have all seen new custom firmware released in the last month or so.
Leading the charge is a tiny $70 Yamaha DX-7 clone: the M-Vave FM-1. It was already on its way to being the synth of the summer. The dirt-cheap price and faithful recreation of classic FM tones made it incredibly popular with first-time synth buyers, hobbyists, and synthfluencers alike. Inevitably, someone wondered how far they could push the hardware and, with the help of AI, kickstarted an arms race.
The FM-1 now has dozens of custom firmwares available. Many of the most popular — Felucca, Sloop, and x0x — list Claude as a contributor on their GitHub page or include explicit disclosures about their use of AI. Baudgirl is also suspected to have been created with the assistance of AI, but the developer did not reply to a request for comment.
What started as a surprisingly good, but basic DX-7 clone now supports a variety of synth engines, including virtual analog, sample playback, multi-track sequencing, and a variety of UI designs.
It’s not terribly shocking that someone was willing to risk bricking a $70 Temu synth. Generally, the gear that has benefited from this surge of vibe-coded custom firmware is older or more affordable.
Roman Rusinov, who posts on Reddit as themanro and releases music under Farlow, set his sights on the Zoom MS-70CDR. It’s a budget multi-effects pedal from 2012 that has a reputation for punching above its weight, making it a staple of affordable synth setups. He started by learning about ZDL, a project that reverse-engineered the Multistomp format, allowing for the creation of custom effects. He eventually coaxed the pedal into running NAM A2 Lite captures and custom impulse responses (IRs), turning it into a full-fledged modeler capable of emulating vintage amps.
“I was already using AI for some work stuff and figured this would be a great case to try learning some vibe-coding fundamentals and get a project going,” he told The Verge. “There was a lot of trial and error of finding the limitations of the hardware and software.” He says he’s thrilled to be part of a broader movement. “Somehow it all lined up with all these other projects pushing the boundaries of older hardware and breathing new life into it. I love that,” he said. “If you own the hardware, you should be able to do whatever you want with it.”
18nelli, the developer behind Modded Cycles, was similarly motivated by a desire to revitalize some forgotten gear. “I had an Elektron Model:Cycles that left me feeling frustrated,” he told The Verge. He said that it felt designed “just to push us to buy their more expensive gear.” But recent AI advances made him believe he could add features to the groovebox, which hasn’t had an official update since May 2021.
So he opened up his Cycles, documented all the parts, and started working with Claude Code to implement his first hack — six-track audio over USB. That has since exploded into a community project with multiple mods contributed by others, several standalone custom firmwares, and even the ability to turn your Model:Cycles into a Model:Samples. “I think not using LLMs would have been counterproductive,” he said. “I probably would have spent a massive amount of time and energy on just a single feature, whereas my real goal is to actually create and make music with amazing mods.”
Modded Cycles has certainly been one of the more frantic projects out there. I recently watched as five firmware updates hit the announcements channel on its Discord in one day. 18nelli has since said he plans to pause adding new features and slow development to polish the existing code and stomp out some bugs.
New mods and firmwares hit the web almost every day now. If there’s a favorite piece of gear in your arsenal that you wish had one killer feature, there’s a chance it might end up on a GitHub page sooner than later. Heck, if you just wish your pocket synth could play NES ROMs, that’s also a distinct possibility.
Of course, there is some risk here. These firmwares are often less thoroughly tested than the manufacturer’s official one. The response to the modding scene has varied from company to company, with many choosing to remain silent. Elektron banned links to custom firmware from their forums. In a statement posted on its official forums, the company said, “We would always warn against modifications to our firmware and/or machines that could brick them … Something that looks like a simple change in isolation can lead to major problems elsewhere, particularly when a later official OS arrives, and can confuse users about which features are officially available on our machines.”
Others, like M-Vave, seem to be embracing the movement. It recently announced FM1 Open, an open-source firmware with additional features, plus a development kit and a firmware-flashing tool for the community.
The response to music gear that uses AI and vibe coding has been mixed. Devices like the Polyend Endless have sparked some ire. And music-making subreddits are awash in people complaining about vibe-coded plugin slop. But so far the community has been less hostile to vibe-coded firmware. Maybe, in part, because breathing new life into old instruments helps keep their Gear Acquisition Syndrome (GAS) in check.

articles.title: DJI’s first battery-swapping dock gets drones recharged and back in the air in under 45 seconds — but 'Dock 4' has no FCC clearance for U.S. sale
articles.text:
DJI’s first battery-swapping dock gets drones recharged and back in the air in under 45 seconds — but 'Dock 4' has no FCC clearance for U.S. sale
No more half-hour recharges, ideal for safety and rescue.
DJI has delivered a battery-swapping drone dock, the Dock 4, with an automated 25-second swap this week, according to a company press release. The dock bypasses the normal recharging process, which would take about 30 minutes, and DJI promises a turnaround of under 45 seconds from landing to takeoff. The drone-in-a-box solution is the first of its type by the company, although not in the industry, and is aimed at applications like emergency response but is not FCC-authorized or for sale in the U.S.
The company emphasizes the safety angle, pitching the Dock 4 as a “dock-as-a-first-responder (DFR)” solution. Its product page calls it “Always There, Always Ready.” Swapping the battery takes less than half a minute, and the drone is back in the air within 45 seconds of landing. The dock also charges two 925 g battery packs, rated at 260 Wh for 400 cycles, at once, estimated to take 27 minutes to get each from 15% to 95%.
The packs also double as backup power, rated at about 4.5 hours each, in sequence. Additionally, with at least two packs loaded, the dock is able to continue swapping even when grid power is lost, although backup power doesn’t charge the packs. This configuration should enable a drone to handle back-to-back calls even in less-than-ideal circumstances. The new dock, 66 kg bare, also has the same 400 x 400 mm mounting holes as the Dock 3, but it only works with the Matrice 5TD drone and requires the DJI O4 Ground Station.
The Matrice 5TD drone is rated for almost an hour of forward flight, measured from 100% to 0% at 15 m/s and with no payload, with a few minutes less of hover time. It can move at up to 21 m/s, or 47 mph, but only in “FlyTo” tasks. It carries three 50 MP cameras: wide, 70 mm equivalent medium telephoto, and telephoto at 252 mm equivalent, which DJI calls 11x. It also has 1280 x 1024 native thermal and 2560 x 2048 in DJI’s UHR infrared mode, color night vision without a spotlight, and a laser rangefinder up to 3,000 m.
For sensors, it has rotating LiDAR, mmWave radar facing forward, up and down, and six-direction vision, and DJI says it is capable of detecting power lines at night. On-board AI allows for the detection of 17 object types, “such as cars, boats, or animals,” and DJI FlightHub 2 can search the feed by text or image and send alerts. The dock and drone are rated for temperatures from minus 40 degrees to 50 degrees Celsius (minus 40 to 122 degrees Fahrenheit) with IP56 and IP55 ratings, respectively. The drone is rated for winds up to 12 m/s, or about 27 mph.
For payload, the drone carries up to 450 g across three mounts for a speaker, spotlight, and parachute. The previous model, the Dock 3’s Matrice 4TD, has a lower-resolution 640 x 512 thermal camera, a 168 mm telephoto, a shorter 1,800 m laser range, and is only good down to minus 20 degrees Celsius (minus 4 degrees Fahrenheit). The drone upgrades are nice, but the new dock capabilities are the real selling point, especially for the intended applications. Currently, DJI partners in China are taking orders for a kit with the Dock 4, Matrice 5TD, and O4 Ground Station at 167,999 yuan, or about $25,000, for the hardware alone.
The new dock and drone sound great for other markets, but DJI’s own spec sheet has no FCC figures. This is likely because the FCC added all foreign-made drones and their critical components to its Covered List in December of last year. New models can’t get FCC authorization or be sold in the U.S. unless the Department of War or the Department of Homeland Security determines they don’t pose a security risk. DJI sued the commission earlier this year.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
A separate FCC proposal published in August could pull previously authorized foreign drones that carry LiDAR or thermal sensors from sale, along with previously authorized docking stations. The FCC’s docket shows no final order on it as of Oct. 17, and the proposal would give sellers 180 days after Federal Register publication to stop importing and marketing covered gear.

articles.title: The LiberNovo Omni Pro delivers peak office chair performance
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The LiberNovo Omni Pro took an already outstanding chair, the LiberNovo Omni, and made it even better, making it worth upgrading even for those who already have the LiberNovo Omni, which is impressive. The chair is spectacular. It will work wonders for most.
Reasons to buy
- + Lives up to the 'Dynamic' branding
- + Great build quality
- + Comfortable
- + Built-in airflow cooling seat
- + OmniStretch Massaging
Reasons to avoid
- - Electronic warranty is only 2 years
- - Expensive
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
For the last 160 days, I've used this chair as my primary desk chair. I spend about 8 to 9 hours a day, 5 to 6 days a week. If you've followed any of my other reviews, you know that I work across several workspaces, but this one is my primary for this season.
Previously, I had the Lenovo Omni here, and I loved it. There are a few things, like build quality and a few other areas, that, if it were a perfect chair, I wouldn't see problems with. Then Lenovo, without anyone asking, dropped the Omni Pro, and my goodness, this thing answers and checks all those boxes.
I sit in this chair all day long, and I have zero comfort issues. Every time it gets too warm, which it normally does, I can turn on the fan. If it gets way too warm, I can turn on the cooling aspect as well. I need to lean back to look under my desk to relax, and I can do so fully flat.
If I just need a little tension resistance so I can lean back against my desk while sitting and working, I can do that as well. The arms are great, and the adjustability is great. Really, the only thing I wish for is adding more features. I can't find anything wrong with this chair from my testing, making it one of the best office chairs - if you can afford it.
LiberNovo Omni Pro: Price and Availability
You can buy the LiberNovo Omni Pro direct from the company here. List price is $1299 / £1,369. However, at time of review, it's down to $1,109 / £1,191. That's a premium price comparable with Herman Miller and Steelcase seats. Whether that's good value really depends on whether you want a chair with all the bells and whistles, or one with a strong design and engineering heritage.
The Omni Pro chair comes in three different bundles: One with the chair, one with chair and footrest, and the premium which includes chair, footrest, and spare battery for the seat.
LiberNovo Omni Pro: Unboxing and First Impressions
First of all, I was so excited for this year that I didn't even have time to sign up, but luckily I did. Time: literally less than a minute, start to finish.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
LiberNovo spares no expense on the shipping box for this chair and the RMD to make assembly very simple. Yes, there's a unique actuator screw that I need to connect, and I have to do that for other chairs, but even with that, there are only 7 screws total, 1 multi-bit screwdriver, and very clear instructions.
Some chairs have 7 screws just for the base, so does this: 7 screws maximum made me smile.
LiberNovo Omni Pro: Design and Build Quality
I absolutely love this chair's design. I know it's not for everybody, but I've worked with people who do like the look of this chair. They think it looks futuristic or isn't their style, which I understand, but for me, this pairs beautifully with my Parsons standing desk and all my gear.
In my testing so far, I've had zero durability or reliability issues. The material still looks like new. Well, I don't typically eat at this desk. The few crumbs that have fallen on this chair wipe off easily, too. I don't usually get stuck in the fibers, but if there were crumbs, you could easily knock them out or wipe them off.
The unique-looking bionic flex backrest is almost like it is designed to fit your back, with multiple sections that cover its curvature and adjust and bend as you move the lumbar support in and out with the buttons.
The five allowed recline positions, more than the last chair, are spectacular and well placed. I occasionally use the 105 mode when I need to lock in. I usually set my chair super, super tight with the crank wheel, then lock it at 115 or 125 so that, if I want to push back, I can stop there easily.
Occasionally, if I want, I kick it all the way back to 160 and use the massaging function, which is, of course, yet another spectacular bonus of this chair.
LiberNovo Omni Pro: In use
I've been sitting in this chair for over 160 days. During that time, I've spent an embarrassing amount of time here.
So far, I'm thrilled with how comfortable it is. Wow, it's breathable, especially as the weather gets warm, and it's supportive. I haven't had any fatigue or pain after a day of sitting in the chair.
Yes, this chair is incredibly cushy, but it also feels like it lives up to the hype. I've only had to charge the battery a few times. I like the backrest features.
I really haven't sent one I like, and I occasionally will use the massaging function. I do, however, use the fan and even the cooling feature regularly. They work great, especially I run hot - if you're the same, it's practically worth the price of admission alone.
LiberNovo Omni Pro: Final verdict
This chair is genuinely just about everything I wish a chair could have (within reason) and lives up to the hype. It's not just a chaotic rush of ads you've seen; it's also a spectacular seat that I don't see myself swapping out at this desk for a long time.
What's funny is that, since I work in an office space where I have several coworkers and other people that come through, I've had friends, coworkers, and some of my employees try my chair and then immediately turn around and wish that had one.
They find times to come and sit in it while I'm away, of course. Everyone has mentioned how much they love it. So, it's not just me. And I totally understand that feeling.

articles.title: Cabinet approves Go-Delhi Foundation to help young innovators, startups
articles.text:
Cabinet approves Go-Delhi Foundation to help young innovators, startups
Delhi is home to nearly 21,000 startups recognised by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade.
The Delhi government has approved setting up Go-Delhi Foundation with a corpus of Rs 50 crore to empower young innovators and startups, said a CMO statement on Sunday.
The approval was given in a recent Cabinet meeting chaired by Chief Minister Rekha Gupta, sanctioning the fund to help turn ideas into products and take them to market.
Delhi is home to nearly 21,000 startups recognised by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT).
The foundation aims to promote startups, innovation and entrepreneurship in the capital while providing young people, researchers and entrepreneurs with integrated support to turn their ideas into practical products and successful enterprises.
The government has also committed an initial budget outlay of Rs 50 crore for the foundation. Through the Go-Delhi Foundation, these resources will be brought together on a common platform, with a focus on developing new enterprises, attracting investment and creating employment opportunities, said the Delhi CMO statement.
Gupta said the foundation would help startups and micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) access product engineering, prototyping, laboratories and testing facilities. It would also provide technical guidance, mentorship, incubation, business support and opportunities to connect with investors, helping turn early-stage ideas into market-ready products.
The initiative would support entrepreneurs at different stages, from product development and testing to certification preparation and market access. Its aim is to reduce dependence on scattered facilities for different needs and make it easier to set up and grow enterprises in Delhi, she added.
The government departments would be able to bring their real-world challenges to Delhi's innovators through the foundation, Gupta said and added that the products and technologies developed to address these challenges could be tested through pilot projects, with successful solutions taken forward for adoption.
This would give government departments an opportunity to access new technologies and practical solutions, while allowing startups to demonstrate the usefulness of their products, she added.
The foundation will also work with industry, educational institutions, investors and other partners. It will adopt a hub-and-spoke model, delivering programmes through existing facilities and partner institutions across Delhi, the statement said.
The foundation will be established as a not-for-profit company under Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013, and will function under the Delhi government's Department of Industries, it added.

articles.title: Anthropic wants AI models blocked only if they threaten over $1 billion in damage or more than 50 deaths or serious injuries
articles.text:
Winners & losers: Anthropic is pitching a draft AI safety bill to lawmakers. That might sound like a good thing, but there are some eyebrow-raising sections. One of them is that the government should be able to block the release of a new AI model, but only if it has the potential to cause at least $1 billion worth of damage or kill or seriously injure more than 50 people. It seems causing $999 million worth of damage and killing 49 people isn't really a problem.
Politico obtained the confidential draft of the proposal, which a company spokesperson said included "sensible policies we believe Congress should act on."
The headline provision would allow the government to block only models that could cause at least $1 billion worth of damage or kill or injure 50 or more people.
Moreover, the risk posed by the model must stem from the creation or release of a biological weapon, the model evading its developer's controls, or a cyberattack. Politico notes that the language mirrors California's AI laws, including SB 5, which was signed last year.
The bill proposes that independent evaluators, registered with the Commerce Department, periodically evaluate the lab and its frontier models. It's also noted that the lab may pay the evaluators, but only if their independence remains unaffected.
If an evaluator discovers these alarming-sounding potential risks in an AI model, they are required to report their findings to Commerce within 72 hours of completing their assessment.
The Commerce Department would then have to present the evidence before a federal judge in the US District Court for the District of Columbia, who would decide whether the model's release should be stopped. The proposal also states that no other US department, agency, or office could suspend the model's development, deployment or internal use.
"This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic's Advanced AI Framework, which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June," the Anthropic spokesperson added.
There have been plenty of concerns over the runaway pace of AI development recently. Following the numerous incidents of AI agents going rogue and hacking other companies, an Anthropic researcher resigned with a warning that AI could end the human race. The company even highlighted these risks in its preliminary IPO prospectus.
Lawmakers have been proposing AI safety rules in the wake of these incidents. Bernie Sanders wants to ban superintelligence and sentence developers who ignore the rules to 20 years in prison. There was also President Trump's Joint Commitment On Frontier Responsibilities, though that "morally binding" agreement relies largely on tech companies policing themselves.

articles.title: Dreame's clever self-heating portable espresso machine heats its own water, takes pods or grounds — and looks remarkably like Count Binface
articles.text:
Hot to go: I tried Dreame's clever portable espresso maker, which heats its own water and accepts three different types of coffee pods — plus grounds
Dreame is well known for making some of the best robot vacuums and hair stylers around, but it also has a sideline in coffee machines — and they're every bit as good as the rest of its appliances. This week I'm testing its new portable espresso machine, the Dreame Ecceluxe Go, and I think this pint-sized brewer is going to be my new favorite travelling companion.
Of course, there's no shortage of travel-friendly coffee makers available, from the classic AeroPress to the hand-pumped Wacaco Nanopresso. The problem is, they all need to have hot water on hand, which isn't always feasible. Who wants to set up a camping stove and kettle for one drink — and who has the patience?
The Ecceluxe Go eliminates that problem by heating the water itself. It's a smart idea: a single shot of espresso only needs a tiny amount of water, so a portable Li-ion battery and compact heating elements are sufficient to bring it to temperature.
The device comes in a classy carry case that holds the machine itself (about the size of a small thermos) and a collection of adapters for brewing three different types of coffee pods or grounds. Whether you prefer Nespresso Classic, Dolce Gusto, ESE (Easy Serve Espresso), or freshly ground beans, the Ecceluxe Go has you covered.
Each adapter twists onto the bottom of the brewer, and a flexible cap lifts off the top to reveal a small water reservoir with fill lines to help you add the correct amount. All done? Open the little legs on the bottom of the adapter, place the whole assembly on top of the clear coffee cup supplied in the box, and you're ready to begin.
The only control on the Ecceluxe Go is a small touch-sensitive LED display. Hold your finger against this for three seconds to power it on, then select one of its two programs. P1 is for brewing with cold or ambient-temperature water, and P2 is for brewing with water that has already been heated. Once you've made your selection, wait three seconds and coffee-making will commence.
The brewer's miniature water tank contains a temperature sensor, and as it heats, you'll see the temperature displayed on its little screen (in centigrade) start to climb. This will take a couple of minutes (it's using a very small heating element), but once the water's good and hot, it will be forced through your coffee preparation of choice, and you'll have a delicious shot of espresso to enjoy, wherever your adventures have taken you.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
I'm testing the Ecceluxe Go with all four coffee types for my full review, which will be published in a couple of weeks, and so far I'm impressed. The flavor is milder than usual, but still tasty and well-suited to drinking as a plain shot.
Dreame doesn't currently have a release schedule for the Ecceluxe Go in the UK, but it's scheduled to arrive in the US, Portugal, and Spain by the end of the year.

Flock camera locations revealed on MapQuest’s new Surveillance Layer — users can now see placement and direction of known license plate readers from multiple companies
Time to download the app.
MapQuest, a long-time online mapping and navigation service that predates Google Maps, just released an app update that added a new Surveillance Layer. The company said on Bluesky that it plots the locations of known license plate readers on the map and that it covers devices from Flock, as well as other companies like Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), Genetec, Axis Communications, Axon, Leonardo (ELSAG), Neology, Rekor, PlateSmart, Ubicquia, Verkada, and other brands.
The Roads Have Eyes! 👁️ Turn on the Surveillance Layer in Map Options to see known license plate readers from Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), Genetec, Axis Communications, Axon, Leonardo (ELSAG), Neology, Rekor, PlateSmart, Ubicquia, Verkada, and other outdoor surveillance cameras.
— @mapquest.com (@mapquest.com.bsky.social) 2026-10-18T02:31:11.890Z
It’s unclear how the app developers found all this data, but it is similar to the Flock Surveillance Map that one security researcher built using Flock’s own data. Beyond showing each camera's location, it also indicates the direction it faces, allowing anyone who doesn't want to be captured by an automatic license plate recognition (ALPR) system to avoid known cameras, if possible.
While cities and police forces argue that systems like these help keep people safe by making it easier to track potential criminals, many people say that they’re a massive invasion of privacy, citing multiple incidents of police officers abusing the system and administrative mistakes, like one resulting in the detention of an innocent car reviewer. This is why some cities whose constituents have complained have started removing them.
A Canadian YouTuber built a “Flock-like” camera that tracked police vehicles and was visited by officers who, in an ironic twist, raised privacy concerns. These are the exact concerns critics have about ALPRs, especially when they connect to a wider federal or national system that lets police officers from another city or state track vehicles without a warrant. It’s unclear how police would react to this functionality, but many police departments have previously complained when Waze released a 2015 update that let users report officers' locations.
This new MapQuest feature can help you get around known ALPR camera locations. But if your destination has heavy camera coverage, you’ll have no choice but to pass through one and be detected, unless someone in the neighborhood has put a “Flock Sock” on one of them.

Jowi Morales is a tech enthusiast with years of experience working in the industry. He’s been writing with several tech publications since 2021, where he’s been interested in tech hardware and consumer electronics.

articles.title: From Macro to Micro, and Back - EE Times
articles.text:
Looking at this year’s Nobel prizes, I was struck by how many of them explain the behavior of a large system through its smallest parts.
Four different Nobel prizes, one common theme
The medicine prize went to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel for optogenetics. Hegemann and Nagel found that a protein from green algae could make cells respond to light, and Deisseroth put its gene into neurons, so researchers can switch specific brain cells on and off with a flash of light. For the first time, neuroscientists could test what an individual neuron does and how groups of neurons produce memories, feelings, and behavior.
The chemistry prize went to Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai for their work on chirality, the property of molecules that come in two mirror-image forms, like our left and right hands. Living organisms use only one form of each, and the long-standing puzzle was how that happened. Soai found a reaction in which a minuscule imbalance between the two forms amplifies itself, which the Nobel Committee described as the first time anyone had created chirality from non-chiral molecules since the dawn of life. It is a striking example of micro shaping macro, since a tiny imbalance between individual molecules, amplified by feedback, ended up determining a property of all life on Earth.
The physics prize went to Francis Halzen for his decisive contributions to IceCube, a detector spanning a cubic kilometer of ice at the South Pole. Neutrinos barely interact with matter, so they cross the universe unimpeded and are extremely hard to catch. IceCube’s light sensors wait for the rare flash of a single neutrino interaction, and from those individual events physicists learn about cosmic sources too distant to observe by any other means.
Finally, the economics prize went to Robert Hall and Michael Woodford, with a citation that says it outright: “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation.” After the Keynesian models seemed to fail in the oil crises of the 1970s, they helped rebuild models of the whole economy from the decisions of individual, forward-looking households and firms. Those models are now used by central banks and governments around the world.
How does this map to chip design?
All four prizes move from micro to macro, explaining a system through its parts. That is also how we have traditionally designed chips, bottom-up: from transistors to logic, from logic to blocks, and from blocks to a full system-on-chip.
In fact, chip design depends on abstraction. We characterize the smallest devices, package them into building blocks with well-defined behavior, and then stop thinking about what is inside. The next level uses those blocks the same way, all the way up to the system. Each level hides the details of the one below, and that hiding is what lets relatively small teams of engineers deliver a chip with billions of transistors.
Our design flow also runs top-down, of course. We start from a specification and work our way down to the physical implementation. But we descend the same ladder we climbed, one rung at a time, accepting the abstractions at each rung as given. A goal at the system level, such as performance per watt, never really sees the low-level choices that might serve it best, because the layers in between filter them out. To cope with the scale and complexity, we pay a margin of lost optimality that is hard to even measure. So it seems natural to ask what our field can take from these prizes, and in particular whether AI might help us cross these layers in both directions.
A glimpse from 2024
In hindsight, the 2024 chemistry prize previewed what AI can do here. It was shared between Demis Hassabis and John Jumper, for predicting a protein’s structure from its sequence, and David Baker, for designing new proteins starting from the shape and function he wanted. The first is micro to macro and the second macro to micro, and AI made both practical.
It is worth noting who led the first. Hassabis co-founded DeepMind, which Google acquired in 2014, and he is now chair of Google DeepMind and chief scientist of Alphabet. Since this was a chemistry prize, some eyebrows were raised that half of it went to computer scientists, and that same year the physics prize went to John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton for their work on neural networks. This says something about how hard such methods will be pushed into other fields, ours included.
Reaching through the layers
AI is already automating individual steps of the chip design flow, and that is useful. The bigger change, IMHO, could come from being able to move between levels in both directions, testing a system-level objective directly against low-level choices without passing through every intermediate abstraction.
Micro to macro would let us predict, quickly and with reasonable accuracy, how a small change near the bottom of the stack ripples up to the power, performance, and area of the whole chip. Conversely, macro to micro would let us ask which low-level changes would best achieve a system-level target, and get useful candidates back. Together, they would turn abstraction layers from walls into something closer to windows.
It is worth being precise about where we are. Today, AI models can learn the behavior of one level well enough to serve as fast stand-ins for slow simulations, and they can propose designs across one or two levels in fairly bounded problems. Research is pushing toward models that link several levels at once, so a change at the bottom can be traced to its effect at the top. Reasoning freely across many levels of a full chip, in both directions, remains speculative.
The price of skipping layers
There are good reasons for caution. The first is that the downward direction is much harder than the upward one. Many different low-level configurations can produce the same system behavior, and some of them produce it only under the conditions you happened to test.
The second will be familiar to anyone in our industry. Abstraction is also a contract, and a layer with a clean, well-defined interface is a layer you can verify. Verification already consumes a large share of the effort on any chip, and if AI optimizes across those boundaries, we may lose the very structure we rely on to prove that a design works. IMHO, verification, more than generation, will decide how far this can go.
The third brings us back to the economics prize. Hall and Woodford’s work was needed because earlier models, built on statistical relationships between aggregate numbers, broke down when conditions changed. This is a word of warning about the limitations of AI models, which are themselves based on a limited set of training data, and statistical in nature. They can be excellent within the range they were trained on and badly wrong outside it. Moving across scales with learned models will require some caution.
A different role for abstraction
If this works, even partially, the role of abstraction in chip design changes. We would still need layers, because engineers need them to think, to divide work across teams and to verify results. But they might become a view we choose for a given question rather than a limit on what the design can reach. Designers could then spend less time on the hand-offs between levels and more on objectives and the tradeoffs that matter. Most importantly, we might reach levels of optimization that are out of reach today.
When Francis Halzen was asked what IceCube might reveal, he answered, as quoted by The Economist, “The real excitement is that I cannot answer that question yet.” I feel similarly here, so I will end with a question rather than a prediction. What happens when we no longer have to choose between thinking about the system and thinking about its smallest components?
