articles.title: Top 10 videos más vistos en YouTube España hoy
articles.text:
YouTube ha adquirido una importancia sin precedentes en el mundo moderno y en su momento se convirtió en un fenómeno que llegó a revolucionar la forma en que se consume el contenido audiovisual.
Antes de su existencia el acceso a este tipo de clips estaba limitado a canales de televisión tradicionales y producciones de gran presupuesto, sin embargo, YouTube ha permitido que cualquier persona con una cámara y una conexión a internet pueda hacer y compartir sus propios clips, lo que ha beneficiado a la aparición de una amplia cantidad de canales que brindan desde contenido educativo hasta de entretenimiento.
La plataforma también ha funcionado como un trampolín para artistas emergentes, músicos, comediantes y cineastas independientes, quienes han encontrado en YouTube una audiencia global y la posibilidad de obtener reconocimiento sin pasar por los canales tradicionales de la industria del entretenimiento.
YouTube tiene presencia en 104 países y está disponible en 80 idiomas, lo que la ha llevado a convertirse en la biblioteca digital de videos más grande y prueba de ello es que a ella se suben más de 500 horas de contenido cada minuto, al día son vistos 5 mil millones de videos y las ganancias se estiman en 15 mil millones de dólares al trimestre.
Ante estas cifras podría ser un tanto difícil perderse las novedades o los clips que están siendo los más populares, es por eso que YouTube cuenta desde 2018 con diversas listas en donde se pueden consultar los artistas más escuchados, los videos más vistos y cuáles son las tendencias del día en tiempo real.
Aquí el listado de los 10 videos que están en tendencia en YouTube España
1. Bulin 47 X Kevin Wai - Dame Hombro (Video Oficial)Artista/canal: Bulin 47 Oficial
2. VuelveArtista/canal: Anuel AA
3. Judeline - La Falda (Official Video)Artista/canal: Judeline
4. JukiarArtista/canal: Quevedo y Clarent
5. PARADIXEArtista/canal: Pirlo, El Americano 4KT y Feid
6. RETRICAArtista/canal: Lucho RK
7. Olivia Rodrigo - expectations (feat. Chappell Roan) (Official Music Video)Artista/canal: Olivia Rodrigo
8. Bicho raroArtista/canal: Estopa
9. 0 AMIGOS cap. 5 - YOLAMASCARAArtista/canal: YOLAMASCARA
10. Miki Núñez, The Tyets - Raquel Sans (Official)Artista/canal: Miki Núñez
El éxito de YouTube
YouTube vio la luz en febrero de 2005, cuando tres antiguos empleados de la compañía de Paypal ―Chad Hurley, Steve Chen y Jawed Karim― se unieron y la crearon luego de que experimentaran dificultades para compartir entre sí un par de videos tras asistir a una fiesta.
El dominio fue activado el 14 de febrero de 2005 y casi un mes después, el 23 de abril, fue cargado el primer clip a la plataforma que llevaba por nombre “Me at the Zoo”. Fue cuestión de tiempo para que todo el mundo comenzara a cargar contenido y a compartir los enlaces a través de otras redes sociales como MySpace.
Una de las grandes empresas que vio el potencial de YouTube fue la marca Nike, que subió una publicidad protagonizada por Ronaldinho, lo que hizo que otras grandes compañías voltearan a ver a YouTube y se sintieran atraídas.
Tal fue la gran acogida de los internautas por YouTube que para diciembre de 2005 la plataforma pasó de las 50 millones de visitas al día a 250 millones de visualizaciones luego de que un canal subiera el clip musical Lazy Sunday, transmitido originalmente por Saturday Night Live.
Para el año siguiente, en el 2006, el sitio fue comparado por el gigante del internet, Google, por un valor de 1650 millones de dólares. En ese entonces eran visualizados 100 millones de videos al día y 65 mil clips se añadían a diario. También firmaron acuerdos con disqueras para poder reproducir videos musicales.
Las polémicas de YouTube
Desde que fue puesto en marcha, YouTube fue un sitio que llegó a hacer una revolución no sólo en internet, sino también en la forma en la que los usuarios miran contenido. Muestra de ello el reconocimiento que la revista Time le otorgó en noviembre del 2006 al ser nombrado el “Invento del Año”.
Convertido en el mejor medio de difusión, el gozar de tanta popularidad también ha metido a sus dueños en aprietos como cuando albergar peleas escolares o en donde hay bullying, clips relacionados al terrorismo, narcotráfico u otros temas considerados delicados por su contenido íntimo o por mostrar delitos como asesinatos y más.
Para Estados Unidos uno de los temas más delicados es el de los tiroteos escolares, por lo que YouTube ha estado más de una vez en el ojo del huracán por alojar contenido filmado por los atacantes, como fue el caso de la masacre de Virginia Tech, cuando Cho Seung-Hui, el atacante, subió previamente a los hechos un discurso.
Más recientemente, tras el surgimiento de la pandemia del coronavirus, también ha surgido inquietud sobre cómo la plataforma permite la monetización de contenido que puede ser engañoso y riesgoso para la población.
Aunque no todo es malo, pues a través de dicha plataforma muchas personas han podido ser reconocidas por su talento, como fue el caso de Susan Boyle, quien participó en el programa Britain’s Got Talent cuyo extracto subido a YouTube logró que la mujer pasara a ser una completa desconocida a una de las personas más viralizadas, famosas y aclamadas del internet.

articles.title: Sangue tipo B tem mais risco de diabetes, mas hábitos pesam mais
articles.text:
Uma revisão científica publicada em 2024 identificou uma associação entre o sangue tipo B e o risco de desenvolver diabetes tipo 2. O resultado surgiu de uma análise abrangente de estudos sobre grupos sanguíneos e saúde, que avaliou centenas de possíveis relações com diferentes doenças.
A pesquisa apontou que pessoas com sangue B positivo ou negativo apresentam, em média, risco 28% maior de desenvolver a doença do que indivíduos com outros tipos sanguíneos. Os autores, porém, ressaltam que essa relação não explica a causa do diabetes nem permite prever quem terá a condição.
Apenas uma associação apresentou evidências convincentes
Liderada pela epidemiologista Fang-Hua Liu, do Hospital Shengjing da Universidade Médica da China, a equipe analisou 51 revisões científicas que, juntas, investigaram 270 possíveis relações entre tipos sanguíneos e problemas de saúde.
Essas revisões reúnem resultados de pesquisas anteriores para identificar padrões que talvez não apareçam em um único estudo. Os pesquisadores, então, verificaram se as conclusões eram consistentes, se havia participantes suficientes nas pesquisas e se os resultados poderiam ter sido influenciados por falhas ou distorções. Também avaliaram a possibilidade de que as associações desaparecessem em estudos futuros.
A maioria das relações analisadas não apresentou evidências suficientemente fortes para ser considerada confiável. A única que passou por todos os critérios mais rigorosos foi a associação entre o sangue tipo B e o diabetes tipo 2, em comparação com os demais tipos sanguíneos.
“Até o momento, a associação entre esses grupos sanguíneos e os resultados de saúde humana permanece controversa”, escreveram os pesquisadores.
O resultado é relevante justamente porque restringe a conclusão a uma relação sustentada por evidências mais consistentes. Isso não significa, contudo, que o tipo sanguíneo B cause diabetes.
Como os grupos sanguíneos são definidos?
O sangue é classificado em oito grupos principais pela combinação do sistema ABO com o fator Rh. No primeiro, a presença ou ausência de determinados antígenos — moléculas que podem desencadear uma resposta imunológica — diferencia os tipos A, B, AB e O. O fator Rh indica se o sangue é positivo ou negativo.
Pesquisas anteriores investigaram se essas diferenças poderiam estar relacionadas à predisposição a doenças. Apesar disso, os mecanismos que explicariam a associação entre o tipo B e o diabetes ainda não foram estabelecidos.
Uma pesquisa de 2025 levantou a hipótese de que o microbioma intestinal, formado pelos microrganismos que vivem no intestino, possa participar dessa relação. A possibilidade ainda exige investigação e não foi demonstrada pela revisão de 2024.
O que pesa no risco de diabetes?
O aumento de 28% no risco associado ao sangue tipo B é inferior ao observado em relação a alguns hábitos e condições de saúde. O consumo diário de 50 gramas de carne processada está associado a um risco 37% maior de desenvolver diabetes tipo 2. Já o sedentarismo pode elevar esse risco em 112%. O excesso de peso também está entre os principais fatores que favorecem o desenvolvimento da doença.
Esses percentuais não devem ser interpretados como previsões individuais nem como medidas diretamente equivalentes em qualquer situação. O risco de desenvolver diabetes depende de diferentes fatores, e a associação com o grupo sanguíneo não substitui a avaliação das demais condições.
Publicado na revista BMC Medicine, o estudo amplia o conhecimento sobre possíveis relações entre características do sangue e doenças. Ainda são necessárias novas pesquisas para esclarecer por que o tipo B aparece associado ao diabetes tipo 2 e qual é a relevância dessa relação na prática.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: Tenstorrent secures $1.5 billion USD at $6.2-billion valuation to challenge GPU dominance
articles.text:
Canadian-founded, United States (US)-based AI infrastructure company Tenstorrent announced today that it has closed $1.5 billion USD ($2.1 billion CAD) in Series E funding to fuel its global expansion plans.
The equity round, which was led by new US investors Trace Capital and Innovation X, gives Tenstorrent a post-money valuation of $6.2 billion USD (almost $8.8 billion CAD), more than twice the $2.6 billion USD mark that Tenstorrent was valued at when the company closed its nearly $700-million USD Series D in late 2024. Since then, Tenstorrent has begun shipping its Galaxy servers commercially.
“The future of compute is open, scalable, and owned by the people building on it.”
Jim Keller, Tenstorrent
Tenstorrent plans to use this capital to fund volume manufacturing of those Galaxy servers, the development of next-generation hardware and intellectual property (IP), and hiring, as it looks to compete with Nvidia and other established AI chipmakers and challenge traditional graphics processing unit (GPU) dominance in AI with an open-source approach it claims is cheaper, more scalable, and easier to customize.
“We built one architecture and sell it at every size,” Tenstorrent CEO Jim Keller said in a statement. “The future of compute is open, scalable, and owned by the people building on it.”
A Tenstorrent spokesperson told BetaKit over email that Canadian investors also participated in the round, but declined to share specific names. Tenstorrent’s existing Canadian backers include Export Development Canada, Toronto’s Georgian, and the Healthcare of Ontario Pension Plan. Montréal-based early Tenstorrent investor Real Ventures sold its stake last year, returning the entirety of its $88-million third fund.
The Tenstorrent spokesperson also declined to share any more details regarding the structure of its Series E, including whether it involved any secondary capital, or disclose Tenstorrent’s total funding to date.
RELATED: US chip giant AMD to acquire Taalas
Founded in 2016 in Toronto by former AMD employees Ljubisa Bajic (who went on to build Taalas, which AMD recently agreed to acquire), Ivan Hamer, and Milos Trajkovic, Tenstorrent is developing what the company describes as “a general-purpose AI platform” for running large language models, video models, and image models.
The firm builds and sells AI compute “at every level,” from single cards and workstations to racks and superclusters, providing the hardware necessary for AI training and inference. Tenstorrent’s customers include chip designers, sovereign infrastructure providers, and inference platforms. The company also licenses its AI and RISC-V IP to clients who want to own and customize their silicon, including LG and Samsung.
Tenstorrent is betting that the future of AI inference is open-source, and views its software as a differentiator compared to competitors. “We built a scalable, open-source software stack because we believe customers want flexibility and control,” the Tenstorrent spokesperson said, adding that, “AI models keep changing, so hardware has to run whatever comes next.”
Tenstorrent’s clients and partners include FinTech firm Virtu Financial, data centre provider Equinix, and AI companies like ai& and Smallest.ai.
Keller, a renowned chip designer who also previously worked at AMD as well as Apple, Intel, and Tesla, took over for Bajic as Tenstorrent CEO in 2021. Tenstorrent quietly relocated from Canada to the US in 2023, moving its headquarters from Toronto to Santa Clara, California, to raise more money from American investors and prepare for an eventual initial public offering (IPO) on the Nasdaq or New York Stock Exchange.
RELATED: AI chipmaker Tenstorrent closes nearly $700-million USD Series D at $2.6-billion valuation
Despite this, Tenstorrent has retained a strong presence in Canada; Toronto remains its largest office, housing 200 of its 1,000 employees. The company also still makes a number of its parts at Vexos Canada’s Markham site.
This summer, The Information and Bloomberg reported that Tenstorrent has drawn takeover interest from larger US chipmakers Intel (Keller’s previous employer) and Qualcomm. While Keller told EE Times that he has met with the CEOs of both firms to pitch them on Tenstorrent’s hardware IP, he said an IPO remained the company’s target at that time.
The Tenstorrent spokesperson declined to comment on those reports, the status of those discussions, or the company’s IPO ambitions.
Last year, Tenstorrent made an acquisition of its own, snapping up Blue Cheetah Analog Design to bolster its in-house chip design capabilities, reportedly explored another fundraise, and shed 7.5 percent of its workforce amid a shift from enterprise to developer sales.
UPDATE (10/19/26): This story has been updated to note that Real Ventures sold its stake in Tenstorrent last year.
Feature image courtesy Tenstorrent.

articles.title: The Maeving RM2 is high-style electric riding with a few compromises
articles.text:
There’s a fast-growing category of two-wheeled electric vehicles splitting the difference between high-end scooters and entry-level motorcycles, fresh bikes with avant-garde style but approachable performance.
The Maeving RM2 is high-style electric riding with a few compromises
It’s ultra-smooth and looks fantastic, but a few rough edges keep it from greatness
The Maeving RM2 is high-style electric riding with a few compromises
It’s ultra-smooth and looks fantastic, but a few rough edges keep it from greatness
I’m talking about offerings like the Infinite Machine P1 and BMW CE 02, similar concepts but with wildly different attitudes. Among this class, the Maeving RM2 stands out. It has a distinctly retrofuturistic flair, bringing together the vibe of classic British motorcycles like the Triumph Bonneville or Royal Enfield Continental GT, just without the literal vibes caused by internal combustion.
Quite the contrary, in fact. The RM2 is one of the quietest, smoothest motorcycles I’ve ever ridden. It also has an innovative solution to a common electric motoring problem. Unfortunately, its rough edges make the $10,995 asking price feel a bit extravagant.
Power for one
UK-based Maeving was founded in 2018 and currently has three motorcycles in its stable: the RM1S, the moody Blackout edition, and the RM2. All are based on the same basic drivetrain and battery technology, with similar power output and range.
The difference is the layout. The RM1S and Blackout offer a solo seat, while the RM2 has a longer saddle and beefier frame that lets you invite a friend along for a ride.
A lightweight friend, anyhow. The RM2 features a 15-horsepower, 193-pound-foot electric hub motor integrated into the rear wheel. That’s more torque than the beefiest of muscle motorcycles, so it gets off the line reasonably well. However, that anemic power figure means it struggles to pick up speed.
It’s officially rated for up to 70mph, but in its most powerful mode it barely clipped over 63mph with me holding the throttle wide open for as long as I dared.
If I put my chest on the tank and tucked in my elbows it crept up a few points to 67mph, but to hit 70 I had to wait for the road to pitch down into a valley. On the climb back out I struggled to maintain 60. (For reference, I weigh 172 pounds.)
That’s not the kind of performance that would make me feel comfortable riding with a passenger on the back. Power, then, is not the RM2’s forte, but that isn’t to say it’s lacking charm.
Smooth operator
While I do love the sound of many motorcycles, I’ve lately come to adore the serenity of riding electric. I’ve thrown a leg over plenty of electric bikes over the years, but none offered the peace and quiet of the RM2.
The hub motor design means there’s absolutely no drivetrain noise at all. Most electric motorcycles rely on chains or belts to send power to the rear wheel, and even the quietest add some sort of commotion to your commute. On the RM2, all I can hear is the wind.
Well, the wind and a persistent buzz from the front fender whenever I hit a bump. As many vehicle manufacturers have learned, the outright silence of an EV means that noises formerly drowned out by the white noise of internal combustion can suddenly become quite annoying.
That sadly wasn’t the only thing rattling on the RM2 I tested. The left bar-end mirror was so loose I was worried it might fall off, and the front wheel seemed to chatter over every asphalt imperfection, creating an unsettled feeling from the nonadjustable front fork.
Overall, the bike’s suspension just didn’t seem up to the task. Bigger bumps launched me out of the saddle so harshly that I got in the habit of standing up when approaching obstacles. And that’s despite my test machine having the $995 upgraded shocks at the back.
Practicalities
That rear suspension has more to do thanks to the weight of the hub motor. But mounting it there frees up room within the RM2’s frame, creating a delightfully simple look and keeping weight low: just 320 pounds. Combine that with a seat height of 30.5 inches and you have a wonderfully easy machine to ride.
The traditional engine spot in the frame is filled by a forward-leaning battery unit. Press a button on the left grip and the battery door swings open, exposing a pair of removable packs. Each has its own button to release it from the bike, then just swivel out the integrated handle and carry it inside to charge under your desk.
That’s the theory, anyway. In practice, you’ll have to hit that button a few times, as it never worked for me on the first try. Likewise, the bike often didn’t recognize when I’d closed the door again, showing an error code on the digital dash until I’d opened and slammed the door a few times.
Each of the 2.73-kilowatt-hour packs weighs 36 pounds and features an uncomfortably thin plastic handle. Want to feel what it’s like to carry one? Fill a 5-gallon bucket three-quarters of the way to the top with water, then lug it up to your office or apartment. While great in concept, it’s not something I’d want to do regularly.
Sadly, you might have to if you don’t have access to outside charging. The RM2 is officially rated for 80 miles on a charge, but I think the only way you’d hit that is by keeping to the bike’s default ride mode, limited to 45mph. In Sport mode, I averaged roughly 50 miles per charge.
If you don’t want to carry those packs around, you can charge the bike directly via a connector on the side. Sadly, it’s proprietary and only works with the included charger. Maeving does offer an adapter for charging on a standard SAE J1772 connector, but that costs a whopping $440 and doesn’t increase charging speed.
The good news is there’s room to store that charger right on the bike. What looks like a fuel tank is actually a locking storage compartment. It’s the perfect size for a quick run to pick up some milk or takeout from your local Thai place.
Charmingly flawed
The RM2 certainly has a lot of room for improvement, but at the end of my time with the thing, I was still quite charmed. It’s such a good-looking, easy-riding machine that I wanted to hop on it for every errand I had to run.
Well, every errand that didn’t take me on the highway or more than 25 miles away from home, anyway. I wouldn’t trust the RM2 to go any farther, and with an 80 percent charge taking four hours on the standard charger, road-tripping is out of the question.
And then there’s the cost. The Maeving RM2 starts at $10,995, but when you add the matte paint, upgraded suspension, and carbon fiber fenders of my test bike, you’re looking at $13,275. For that money, you could buy two Royal Enfield Continental GT motorcycles, and as much as I love electric motoring, that’s a tough financial pill to swallow.
Photography by Tim Stevens / The Verge

articles.title: Google Adopts Pyrefly for Faster, More Accurate Python Type Checking
articles.text:
Google has replaced its long-standing Python type checker, Pytype, with Pyrefly, an open-source tool originally developed by Meta. The decision was driven by Pyrefly's advantages, including faster and more accurate type checking, and lower infrastructure costs.
As Python’s typing system evolved rapidly, Pytype faced fundamental challenges. Because it operated by analyzing compiled bytecode rather than source ASTs, keeping pace with modern typing PEPs became an increasing maintenance burden due to bytecode instability across Python releases.
According to Google’s internal benchmarks, Pyrefly is approximately 10 times faster than Pytype, reduces incremental rebuild latency by up to 98%, and cuts peak compute cost for Python type checking by more than 80%. Google also reported a 90–99% reduction in type-checking time along clean-build critical paths, substantially "eliminating a long-standing development bottleneck".
One of Pyrefly's key strengths, Google explains, is its strong conformance to Python's typing specification, passing approximately 97% of tests in the conformance suite. Pyrefly is also actively supported by the community, which helps it keep pace with new syntax, and its diagnostics provides more actionable feedback, including inline code annotations that pinpoint the root cause of errors and, in some cases, suggest fixes.
The community has responded with interest to Google's announcement. While most commenters agreed that Pytype performs worse than Pyrefly, others debated Pyrefly's relative merits compared with Ty and Mypy. Gushys noted that
Pyrefly is much more mature. Its already at past 1.0, has similar performance speed to ty, and is a proven tool. ty just isn't quite there yet.
WindHawkeye observed that "Mypy is much faster in large setups than people think. It still has the fastest incremental type check", to which BeamMeUpBiscotti replied that
Mypy 2.0 is supposed to be up to 5x faster on large projects for cold checks, but the newer generation of type checkers can be up to an order of magnitude faster than even that.
Commenting on the announcement on LinkedIn, Python developer Amirrea Azadmher offered a different perspective, arguing that a type-checker's value is not is not merely in saving 30 seconds in CI pipelines, but in how it improves the edit-check loop during development. He also noted that:
If you're evaluating Pyright vs Pyrefly vs mypy right now, don't trust someone else's monorepo numbers. Measure cold and warm times on YOUR tree, and score diagnostics quality beside throughput — a fast checker that floods you with noise still costs more than a slower one that points at the real break.
Meta open-sourced Pyrefly last year. Pyrefly is designed for high performance and implemented in Rust to maximize efficiency. According to Meta, it can check 1.8 million lines of code per second on large codebases, making it possible to perform typechecking on every single keystroke.

articles.title: EA Sports FC 27 review: come for The Grounds, stay for Career
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
EA Sports FC 27 is a slightly confusing entry in EA’s long-running football franchise. It plays well, Ultimate Team has some neat new features, and Career mode is refreshingly challenging (particularly off the pitch). But The Grounds isn’t anywhere near as revolutionary as it could’ve been, and the FC art style is still crying out for some FIFA-era soul.
Reasons to buy
- + The new transfer system in Career is a big change, for better or worse
- + Streamlined SBCs are a great addition to FUT
- + Meaningful gameplay improvements
Reasons to avoid
- - The Grounds feels underbaked
- - Please, EA, add some color to your menus
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
I’ll say one thing for EA Sports FC 27: it’s not the same game as EA Sports FC 26.
That reads like a compliment — and in some respects, it is — but where previous entries in EA’s long-running football simulator series shipped with minor improvements and equally minor frustrations, FC 27 takes bigger swings that flip between successful, insignificant, and occasionally experience-worsening in their execution.
Platform reviewed: PS5
Available on: PS5, Xbox Series X|S, Nintendo Switch 2, PC
Release date: Early Access: September 18, 2026 | Full release: September 25, 2026
I wish I could package that sentiment into a neat metaphor (‘a mixed bag’ is too hackneyed), but I can’t — so here’s the Cliffs Notes version of my review:
EA’s shiny new mode, The Grounds, is a hollow imitation of NBA 2K's The City. Ultimate Team is objectively better than it was in FC 26, but is still geared towards card-collecting youngsters and time-rich YouTubers. Career mode is the best it’s ever been, but is oddly prone to breakage by the same new features that make it better. And the overall FC gameplay experience is more challenging than before, but more rewarding as a result.
Still with me? I’ll run through each of those mini-verdicts as you read on, but you get the idea: EA Sports FC 27 is immense fun in parts, dull in others, and a generally quite confusing entry in a series that rarely changes so much from one year to the next. But hey, change is good... right?
Around The Grounds (and out again)
This year’s big new addition to the FC franchise is The Grounds — an ‘open-world’ reimagining of the series’ Clubs mode in which you can compete with friends or randoms in both stadium- and street-based challenges.
I put ‘open-world’ in quotation marks because The Grounds is not so much a free-roam experience as a third-person menu-hopping one. The idea of exploring three “cultural hubs of football” sounds cool, but in reality, these hubs are little more than poorly rendered maps populated by lifeless NPCs (non-player characters), Riddler Trophy-style Drop Kick Targets, and PvP waiting areas.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
The game modes available within The Grounds are fun enough — there are traditional 11v11 matches, FIFA Street-style cage matches, and more casual mini-games like the basketball-inspired Bucket Ball — but the ‘open-world’ aspect of the experience adds little beyond longer wait times (because you now have to travel from A to B on foot) and the ability to customize your pro’s wardrobe with licensed clothing. At a price, of course.
I won’t lie: I did have a good time building my pro and was excited to get out into The Grounds’ virtual world. But once I’d played a handful of matches and completed enough Alex Hunter-ordered errands to buy myself a cool headband (Kylian Mbappé, Paulo Dybala, and Chloe Kelly are the other ‘mentors’), the novelty of this new open-but-actually-closed game mode quickly wore off.
With enough friends in tow, I can imagine The Grounds being a lot of fun, and I don’t criticize EA for trying something genuinely new with FC 27. I’m just not sure The Grounds actually is all that new — it’s more like Clubs with an extremely elaborate menu system.
Players for points
Opening Ultimate Team (FUT) for the first time in FC 27 feels like walking into a nightclub sober. You’re immediately hit with a barrage of menus, cards, and checklists, which is a frankly disorienting experience until you remember that this is exactly what FUT has been like for several years now.
Still, once you get over the customary nausea, there are some genuinely neat improvements to be found in this year’s edition of EA’s most popular (and profitable) mode.
My favorite addition is Streamlined SBCs (Squad Building Challenges). These are essentially SBCs that swap the starting XI puzzle aspect for a cumulative target score — each player in your club has a value, and you need to exchange enough players to reach that score. You don’t need to worry about formations, positions, or chemistry; instead, Streamlined SBCs are purely a numbers game.
Traditional SBCs are still present and correct in FC 27 — I personally enjoy the challenge of completing the weekly Marquee Matchups SBC — but with Streamlined SBCs, EA has acknowledged that most players aren’t fussed about the puzzling they require. Streamlined SBCs are for those who, understandably, want to snag the SBC reward in as little time as possible. But I appreciate that EA has kept both SBC types in the game.
The Gallery is a less meaningful but otherwise harmless addition to FUT. It’s a sticker book-style card-collection feature that tracks every player who’s ever passed through your club and encourages you to curate these players into graded sets. Doing so earns you trinkets and cosmetics (boring), but also Gallery Tokens (less boring), which can be spent on special Hall of FUT players like Loïc Rémy, Adebayo Akinfenwa, and Marouane Fellaini.
Honestly, the Gallery interface is as dizzying to navigate as everything else in FUT, but at least there are tangible player rewards to be gained from taking the time to understand it. I just wish The Gallery were available in the FC 27 Web App, so I could kill time grading cards while on my evening commute, and not while playing FC 27 proper.
Jockey down the line
It’s a little hard to give a comprehensive verdict on gameplay in FC 27, since EA is tweaking the mechanics all the time, but broadly speaking, the biggest gameplay changes apply to defending and set pieces.
On the former, there’s now less AI assistance, so computer-controlled players on your team (i.e., those you haven’t switched to yet) won’t auto-tackle an opponent, meaning you’ve got to be quicker on your L1/LB draw and smarter with your tackle timing. Jockeying is faster for all players as a result, which also makes the Jockey PlayStyle less overpowered than it was in FC 27.
As someone who’s better at defending than attacking, I’m all for these defensive changes — and the redesigned corner kicks system also puts more importance on defenders in this year’s game.
There’s now a longer pause between the taking of a corner kick and the ball’s arrival in the box, and — finally! — you get manual control over player positioning within the box itself. This change means corners are now skill-based rather than luck-based, which is absolutely what they felt like before (even if EA would never say so).
I spend most of my time playing the Authentic gameplay preset in Career mode, which is a different kettle of fish entirely, but for those who play Competitive in FUT, I’d say defending and corner kicks have seen the most noticeable tweaks in FC 27.
Skilled dribblers now ride challenges more effectively, too, but this isn’t such a significant gameplay tweak in my experience — but then again, I haven’t played too many online matches in FUT, which is where you’re likely to come up against the dribble-happy duo of Ousmane Dembélé and Lamine Yamal. I’ll pray for your controller.
The Art of the Deal
After fulfilling my testing-time obligations in The Grounds and Ultimate Team, I couldn’t wait to dive into FC 27’s refreshed Career mode. And judging by the view counts on EA’s YouTube Deep Dives for the game (the Career Deep Dive has the most views by a margin of over 1 million ), there’s a good chance that you, too, are more interested in FC 27’s slower-paced managerial simulator than any of its other modes.
The big changes this year apply to transfers. The awkward 3D negotiation scenes have been replaced with FIFA 13-style 2D negotiations, primarily because there’s a lot (and I mean a lot) more negotiating to be done in FC 27.
Previously, you’d offer a sum of money for a player, and if the selling club accepted your price, you’d then negotiate personal terms with the player in question. That was it. Two steps. You could pretty much buy any player for any club if you had the funds to do so.
In FC 27, transfer negotiations are far more realistic — for better and worse.
Now, if you’ve got your eyes on a player, you first have to send an inquiry to determine whether their current club is willing to sell them. The players themselves can also reject your advances if they’re simply not interested in joining your club — regardless of the money you might’ve been prepared to pay them and their club. If you’re rejected, you won’t be told the reasons why, but EA says player decision-making is based on tactical fit, club finances, form, historical rivalries, and long-term club philosophy.
And trust me: you will get rejected a lot. Or at least I was while playing as Everton. I couldn’t convince 80% of my transfer targets to even come to the negotiating table, and even when I did get close to signing a target, they’d invariably be stolen at the last minute by a bigger rival (Newcastle, for instance, accepted my offer for Harvey Barnes, but Barnes rejected me to join Chelsea on deadline day. Mercenary!).
Actually being able to score from corners and free-kicks using carefully positioned target men, thanks to the revamped set-piece system.
If you do get to the negotiation stage, there are some nice new ways to structure deals, including with transfer instalments, agent fees, and performance-based bonuses. But I was honestly surprised by how difficult it was to sign players generally.
You can make transfer negotiations easier — they’re set to strict by default when you start a save — but actually, after the initial difficulty shock, I came to enjoy the challenge. Sure, I didn’t get most of my initial transfer targets, but that struggle made my eventual signings — Patrik Schick, Lucas Bergvall, Dan Ballard, and Raúl Asencio on loan — feel more rewarding as a result. It also felt very Everton to be rejected or outbid so frequently.
One big negative, though, is that players are absolute prima donnas in FC 27 Career mode — and their stinking attitudes can sometimes present a real headache.
It’s entirely possible that large groups of players hand in transfer requests at the same time because, as per the new minutes system, a player with 41% or higher stamina expects to play. If they don’t, they get annoyed and request a transfer. That (sort of) makes sense, but it’s particularly problematic if you like to simulate lots of matches, as the computer will only play high-stamina players (think 70% stamina and above).
I’ve seen some streamers complain that the game’s liberal transfer request system has ground their Career saves to a halt, and even if you can appease your unruly squad, it’s not particularly enjoyable to feel like virtual players are managing you, rather than the other way around.
Unexpected Events are back in FC 27, too, and these random scenarios — like Abrupt Retirement or Urgent Family Leave — can similarly disrupt the flow of a season.
I’m all for being tested as a manager, but Career mode feels particularly patience-testing this year — it’s more rewarding in places, sure, but it would be nice to play five straight matches without an injury, a mutiny, or an unmissable family funeral.
Dynamic Overall is a more positive addition to Career mode in FC 27. It’s essentially a dynamic rating system that causes player ratings to fluctuate throughout the season instead of staying fixed. Form, morale, and fitness can all make a player’s rating go up or down, and transfer values are impacted by big changes in rating.
In my Everton save, Tyler Dibling played so well so consistently that his rating went from 74 to 83 in a matter of months — that seems ridiculous on paper, but it’s actually representative of how player values change drastically in real life. Good feature!
Should you play EA Sports FC 27?
Play it if...
You've always wanted a more challenging Career mode
The redesigned transfer system has a huge impact on the realism and difficulty of Career mode in FC 27.
You can't resist FUT's shiny player cards
FC 27 makes it easier than ever to unlock special player cards in FUT via Streamlined SBCs, while The Gallery gives you a place to show off your collection.
Don't play it if...
You want an open-world footballing experience
Yes, The Grounds is 'open-world' to some extent, but it's more like an elaborate menu system than an enjoyable place to explore and engage with.
You want an arcade-style Career mode 
Career mode is more feature-packed than ever in FC 27. Its difficulty can be lowered, but it's no longer an arcade-style experience.
Accessibility features
Like its predecessors, EA Sports FC 27 offers a comprehensive suite of accessibility options, including settings for subtitles, button remapping, color blindness, and increasing the size of the player indicator. It also features a dedicated High Contrast Mode for low-vision and cognitively disabled players.
All of these accessibility options can be found in a dedicated Accessibility Settings tab. The game has six difficulty levels — Beginner, Amateur, Semi-Pro, Professional, World Class, Legendary, and Ultimate — and features support for 21 languages.
How I reviewed EA Sports FC 27
I played EA Sports FC 27 for a month, having received the game a few days ahead of its official Early Access release on September 18. During that time, I had access to all modes and features and was able to compete against real-world players who also had early review access to the game.
I played on PS5, using a standard DualSense controller, on a Samsung QN95A Neo QLED 4K TV. I’ve played every EA Sports football title since FIFA 13, and also reviewed FIFA 22, FIFA 23, EA Sports FC 24, EA Sports FC 25, and EA Sports FC 26 for TechRadar Gaming.
First reviewed: October 2025.
Axel is TechRadar's Phones Editor, reporting on everything from the latest Apple developments to newest AI breakthroughs as part of the site's Mobile Computing vertical. Having previously written for publications including Esquire and FourFourTwo, Axel is well-versed in the applications of technology beyond the desktop, and his coverage extends from general reporting and analysis to in-depth interviews and opinion.
Axel studied for a degree in English Literature at the University of Warwick before joining TechRadar in 2020, where he earned an NCTJ qualification as part of the company’s inaugural digital training scheme.

articles.title: A Composable Thermal Solver For Heterogeneous 2.5D/3D-IC Packages (Cadence, Notre Dame)
articles.text:
Researchers at Cadence Design Systems and the University of Notre Dame published “A Composable AI-Accelerated Iterative Solver for 3D-IC Thermal Modeling.”
Abstract:
“Accurate thermal analysis of heterogeneous 2.5D/3D-IC packages is essential yet computationally prohibitive. A single full-package FEM simulation can take hours, while AI-based surrogates treat the entire stack as a monolithic prediction target and must be retrained whenever the die count or topology changes. To address this limitation, this work proposes Domain-Decomposed AI-Accelerated Iterative Solver for Thermal Analysis (DAIST), a composable thermal solver that decomposes the global package simulation into block-level subdomain problems, replaces subdomain solvers with neural operators, and couples them through iterative exchanges of interfacial temperature and heat flux. This local-to-global architecture eliminates the topology lock-in of monolithic models: block-level neural operators can be directly reused in unseen package assemblies without retraining. The iterative coupling strategy further provides a controllable accuracy-runtime tradeoff, where the iteration budget can be adjusted to trade accuracy for runtime. Evaluated on a multi-chiplet system and an advanced packaging system, DAIST achieves up to 178× speedup over traditional FEM solvers with mean temperature errors of 0.068% and 0.323%, respectively, while demonstrating cross-topology reuse of block-level models across structurally distinct package assemblies.”
Find the technical paper here. October 2026
Li, Yixing, Jiahang Zhou, Zhiyu Zeng, and Xin Ai. “A Composable AI-Accelerated Iterative Solver for 3D-IC Thermal Modeling.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2610.02461 (2026).

articles.title: « La partie émergée d'un iceberg » : après les frigos, quels appareils risquent aussi de se faire pirater ?
articles.text:
Entre le 11 et le 12 octobre 2026, des pirates ont compromis les systèmes de réfrigération de plus de 700 supermarchés français. Intermarché, Netto, Super U, Carrefour, Monoprix ou encore E.Leclerc ont été touchés. En pleine nuit, les températures sont montées jusqu’à 50 °C, obligeant les magasins à jeter tous leurs produits frais et surgelés. Les géants de la grande distribution évoquent des pertes de plusieurs millions d’euros à travers tout le pays.
Pour arriver à leurs fins, les pirates, dont l’identité est inconnue, ont exploité une faille connue des contrôleurs de froid Danfoss et Dixell, dont une grande partie était accessible sur Internet sans protection. Comme l’a montré une expérience des chercheurs de Claroti, il est très facile de lancer l’attaque, notamment en se servant de Claude, en moins de 30 minutes. Si un frigo se retrouve aussi facilement entre les mains de cybercriminels, d’autres appareils du quotidien sont-ils aussi vulnérables ? On a posé la question à une poignée d’experts.
À lire aussi : Cyberattaque nationale – pourquoi les pirates s’attaquent maintenant aux supermarchés ?
Nos objets connectés dans le viseur
Pour Bruno Laureti, directeur des systèmes d’information et associé chez EBS Group, tous les objets connectés sont dans le viseur des pirates. « Au même titre que les entreprises, les particuliers possédant des équipements connectés (frigos, chaudières, pompes à chaleur, caméras…) sont des cibles pour les hackers », prévient l’expert. Le parc d’objets connectés dans le monde ne cesse d’ailleurs de grossir. On dénombrait 18,8 milliards d’objets connectés fin 2024 sur Terre, et pourrait en dénombrer près de 40 milliards d’ici 2030, selon les données du cabinet spécialisé IoT Analytics.
Les particuliers sont même souvent plus exposés que les entreprises. En effet, ils sont « rarement équipé de solutions de sécurité professionnelles » et sont rarement dotés de « la connaissance pour mettre à jour ses équipements connectés ». En clair, vous êtes une cible plus facile à pirater qu’un supermarché, ou une entreprise quelconque.
Sans grande surprise, les cybercriminels s’intéressent surtout aux appareils connectés qui brassent énormément de données, comme des « vidéos, listes de courses, données de santé ». C’est le cas d’une balance connectée par exemple, qui stocke énormément de données de santé sur son propriétaire. En général, l’objectif n’est autre que de « récupérer de la donnée qu’il puisse revendre sur le dark net ». Ces données peuvent être revendues à prix d’or sur des marchés criminels, notamment à des pirates désireux d’orchestrer des arnaques en ligne, des tentatives d’hameçonnage ou encore des opérations d’extorsion.
Un objet vulnérable comme porte d’entrée
Au-delà d’un simple vol de données, un seul appareil connecté vulnérable peut servir de tremplin vers le reste du réseau. « Un objet anodin peut servir de porte d’entrée, à partir du moment où le pirate peut installer un bout de code de compromission », avertit Bruno Laureti.
Contacté par 01net, Oded Vanunu, responsable de la recherche sur les vulnérabilités chez Check Point, abonde dans le même sens, avec plusieurs exemples à l’appui. Dans le cadre d’études réalisées sur des objets connectés estampillés LG, ses équipes ont « démontré comment les vulnérabilités des plateformes de gestion centralisées pouvaient permettre à des attaquants de prendre le contrôle des appareils connectés ». La plupart des objets connectés se pilotent en effet à partir d’une plateforme centrale, généralement sur le cloud. Si un pirate trouve une faille dans cette console centrale en ligne, il n’a pas besoin d’attaquer chaque appareil séparément. Il prend le contrôle d’une maison connectée complète avec une seule faille. Selon Check Point Research, 54 % des organisations sont visées chaque semaine par une tentative d’attaque sur leurs objets connectés.
Un effet domino
Le problème est le même dans les entreprises, au sein desquelles les équipements s’accumulent. On y trouve bien souvent un système de climatisation, de contrôle d’accès, des alarmes, et des automates. En miroir des frigos compromis récemment en France, de nombreux appareils industriels sont obsolètes, vulnérables, ou exposés sur Internet.
Charles Bouesnard et Louise Durantin, experts chez mc2i, redoutent d’ailleurs un effet domino à la suite de la cyberattaque nationale contre les supermarchés français. « Si un hacker peut prendre le contrôle d’un frigo, il peut potentiellement pivoter sur le réseau du magasin », explique le duo, et viser ensuite « les systèmes logistiques (entrepôts automatisés), les caisses en libre-service ou la domotique (lumière, son, serrures intelligentes) ». En d’autres termes, un frigo exposé peut servir de porte d’entrée vers d’autres équipements.
« La partie émergée d’un iceberg »
Dans ce contexte, Nadim El Sakaan, enseignant-chercheur en cybersécurité à l’Efrei, avertit que « les systèmes frigorifiques ne sont que la partie émergée d’un iceberg bien plus gros ». Les mêmes failles béantes se retrouvent dans « les systèmes de gestion technique des bâtiments, les infrastructures de traitement d’eau, les automates de l’industrie agroalimentaire, les équipements biomédicaux connectés ». Bruno Laureti s’attend particulièrement à des attaques « plus impactantes dans le domaine hospitalier ».
Une fois qu’une faille a été débusquée sur un appareil, elle peut être recyclée pour pirater d’autres équipements analogues. En clair, une vulnérabilité dénichée sur un frigo connecté peut servir à s’attaquer à d’autres objets connectés, ce qui peut aboutir à un effet boule de neige. L’essor de l’intelligence artificielle générative, et de modèles de langage comme ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini ou Muse, facilite évidemment la tâche des pirates à la recherche d’équipements vulnérables. Pierre Jacob, directeur général adjoint chez Magellan Sécurité, pointe d’ailleurs du doigt « la facilité croissante à générer des armes cyber grâce à l’IA ».
Pour contrer les pirates inspirés par la cyberattaque contre les frigos, les chercheurs recommandent de changer systématiquement les mots de passe par défaut, d’installer les mises à jour sur tous les objets connectés, et de ne pas exposer inutilement un appareil sur Internet. Oded Vanunu recommande d’« identifier les interfaces de gestion exposées à Internet, supprimer les accès distants inutiles d’appliquer une authentification forte » sur tous les équipements.
« Aux prémices » des cyberattaques
Idéalement, il faudrait que tous les équipements connectés, que ce soit des frigos, des climatisations ou des caméras, disposent d’une véritable politique de sécurité, estime Bruno Laureti. Trop souvent, ces appareils sont oubliés par les personnes en charge de la sécurité informatique. Bruno Laureti appelle donc les prestataires, « par exemple les frigoristes », à s’associer avec des spécialistes de l’informatique sans tarder. Selon lui, « nous ne sommes qu’aux prémices de ce type de piratage ».

articles.title: FMCG firms grapple with input cost inflation in Q2, brace for margin pressure
articles.text:
FMCG firms grapple with input cost inflation in Q2, brace for margin pressure
Input-cost pressures intensified in the September quarter, reversing some of the moderation seen in the preceding quarter, which squeezed margins even as companies absorbed part of it to protect consumer demand during the festive season.
FMCG companies face sustained margin pressure in the second half of the current fiscal year, as rising input costs squeeze profitability, with firms weighing post-Diwali price hikes against the risk of hurting consumer demand, particularly in price-sensitive mass-market and rural categories.
Input-cost pressures intensified in the September quarter, reversing some of the moderation seen in the preceding quarter, which squeezed margins even as companies absorbed part of it to protect consumer demand during the festive season.
The increase has been uneven across commodities, with crude-linked derivatives, packaging materials, palm oil and sugar emerging as key pressure points, said Naveen Malpani, Partner and Consumer Industry Leader at Grant Thornton Bharat.
"In rupee terms, palm oil prices were approximately 21% higher year-on-year in September, while sugar prices remained around 18% higher year-on-year despite correcting 8% month-on-month," he said.
Higher costs have not been fully offset by price increases and operational efficiencies, putting pressure on operating margins, Malpani said.
"Pre-results analyst estimates projected operating-margin compression of approximately 45 basis points year-on-year across a group of major consumer staples companies, with some estimates indicating declines of up to 150 basis points for the companies covered," he said.
Companies operating in mass-market categories had limited room for aggressive price increases due to affordability concerns, making cost optimisation, procurement efficiencies and calibrated pricing crucial to protecting profitability without hurting demand.
"The sector should therefore prepare for continued margin pressure through H2, with recovery contingent on actual commodity movements rather than an assumption that the cost cycle has peaked," Malpani added.
Parle Products Chief Marketing Officer Mayank Shah told PTI that rising inflation was a major concern for the FMCG industry, which is "definitely worrisome".
However, he also said companies were trying to absorb a bit of "margin shock" by offsetting higher input costs through efficiency improvements and cost cuts rather than immediately raising prices.
Shah said demand remained robust across urban and rural India as companies refrained from passing on the entire increase in costs to consumers.
However, he indicated that price increases could be considered after the festive season, depending on the movement of agricultural commodity prices and the broader geopolitical situation.
“Most decisions on price hikes would be taken only post festive season… So, you may see some sort of thing happening from December onwards,” Shah said.
Companies are also looking at reducing discounts and advertising expenditure to manage costs, Shah said, adding that protecting demand remained a priority.
Nestle India Chairman and Managing Director Manish Tiwary also acknowledged the issues last week and said "rising inflation, particularly food inflation" is a "reality".
In its commodity outlook, Nestle India said coffee and wheat prices were expected to remain range-bound, while sugar and edible oils would stabilise at elevated levels in the December quarter.
Cocoa remained volatile because of weather-related crop concerns in key producing regions, while milk prices had strengthened seasonally but were expected to ease with the arrival of flush supplies, it said.
Moreover, this inflationary environment poses a challenge for FMCG companies in the second half of FY27, when festive-season demand gives way to the need to sustain consumption momentum and restore profitability.
"Outlook for H2 FY27 remains cautious," said Malpani, adding, " Companies may continue to face cost pressures, with any meaningful margin recovery dependent on commodity prices easing and earlier pricing actions flowing through.
The risk is particularly relevant for packaged foods, home and personal care products and other categories exposed to edible oils, crude derivatives and agricultural commodities.
The potential strengthening of El Niño conditions during October-December also adds uncertainty to the outlook for agricultural production and food prices. Its impact on Indian agriculture, however, will depend on broader ocean-atmosphere conditions and regional weather patterns, and higher food inflation is a risk rather than a certainty.
The impact on consumer demand will be another key factor to watch. While price increases can support value growth, they may not translate into higher underlying volumes if consumers cut purchases, shift to cheaper brands or opt for smaller packs.
“If food inflation rises or rural incomes weaken, consumers may trade down to lower-priced brands, choose smaller packs, reduce purchase frequency or defer discretionary purchases. The uneven monsoon and potential El Niño impact add uncertainty to rural purchasing power,” he said.

articles.title: F5 releases out-of-band patches for critical NGINX vulnerabilities
articles.text:
F5 has released out-of-band security patches to address multiple NGINX web server flaws, including three critical-severity vulnerabilities that can let attackers execute code on vulnerable systems.
The three critical vulnerabilities were found in the ngx_http_v3_module (CVE-2026-15176 and CVE-2026-97205) and the NGINX map directive (CVE-2026-93479).
Remote attackers without privileges can exploit them to launch denial-of-service (DoS) attacks or gain code execution on NGINX systems with non-default configurations.
Successful exploitation causes a heap-based buffer overflow or use-after-free in the NGINX worker process, leading to crashes or a restart. However, attackers may also be able to "execute code on systems with Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) disabled or when the attacker can bypass ASLR."
F5 released security patches for multiple NGINX software products affected by these two vulnerabilities, including NGINX Plus, NGINX Open Source, NGINX Ingress Controller, NGINX Gateway Fabric, and NGINX Instance Manager.
Security teams and admins who can't immediately install these security patches can mitigate CVE-2026-15176 by not using the 'alias' directive in a location block or the $request_filename variable, and CVE-2026-97205 by disabling asynchronous file I/O (AIO) or Server Side Includes (SSI).
CVE-2026-93479 can also be mitigated by using named captures instead of unnamed captures and limiting their use to the block with the regex match.
While F5 has not yet flagged these security issues as exploited in the wild, cybercrime and nation-state threat groups have often exploited vulnerabilities in F5 products in recent years.
For instance, attackers have targeted F5 security flaws to breach corporate networks, map internal servers, hijack devices, deploy data-wiping malware, and steal sensitive documents from victims worldwide.
Since November 2021, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged eight F5 vulnerabilities as actively exploited, four of which have also been abused in ransomware attacks.
One year ago, in October 2025, F5 also disclosed that state-sponsored threat actors breached its systems in August 2025 and stole source code and information on undisclosed BIG-IP security vulnerabilities.
F5 is a Fortune 500 tech company that provides cybersecurity, application delivery networking (ADN), and other services to over 23,000 customers, including 80% of the Fortune Global 500 and 48 Fortune 50 companies.
Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked
Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.

articles.title: Vous pensez bien faire en cachant votre box internet mais vous ruinez votre réseau Wi-Fi
articles.text:
Comment retrouver toute la vitesse de votre Wi-Fi sans changer de matériel
Si vous cachez votre box internet au fond d’un meuble pour préserver la déco de votre logement, sachez que qu’il s’agit une mauvaise habitude qui sabote malheureusement la qualité de votre réseau Wi-Fi.
Design disgracieux, câbles emmêlés et voyants lumineux qui clignotent dans le salon, telle est la vision que l’on se fait de nos box internet. Comme elles s’intègrent rarement bien dans notre décoration intérieure, beaucoup préfèrent les cacher dans un meuble, ni vu ni connu. Pourtant, si cette astuce permet de garder un salon visuellement épuré tout en protégeant le boîtier de la poussière, elle ruine littéralement les performances de votre connexion sans fil.
Les espaces clos étouffent votre réseau Wi-Fi, et donc sa vitesse
Contrairement à une idée reçue, les ondes Wi-Fi ne traversent pas la matière par magie. Votre routeur émet des fréquences radio dans toutes les directions à partir de ses antennes internes, et lorsque vous l’enfermez dans un meuble, ces ondes se heurtent immédiatement à une première barrière physique avant même d’atteindre le reste de votre logement. Le bois épais, le verre, le métal des charnières ou le plâtre absorbent et réfléchissent alors une grande partie du signal au point de le détériorer
Le problème s’aggrave avec les réseaux modernes. Si la bande des 2,4 GHz parvient tant bien que mal à franchir les obstacles, les fréquences de 5 GHz et 6 GHz, qui offrent les débits les plus rapides, sont extrêmement sensibles au moindre blocage. En plaçant votre box dans un placard, vous bridez instantanément sa portée et sa vitesse dès le premier centimètre parcouru.
À cela s’ajoute le piège des interférences directes. Un meuble TV regorge souvent d’autres équipements électroniques comme une console de jeux, un amplificateur ou une multiprise. Cette concentration d’appareils crée un brouillard électromagnétique qui perturbe la diffusion du signal dès la sortie de la box, provoquant des ralentissements et des coupures incessantes sur vos appareils connectés.
L’emplacement idéal pour profiter d’un débit maximal
Pour tirer le meilleur parti de votre box Internet fibre, la règle d’or est de libérer votre équipement en le laissant à l’air libre. L’emplacement parfait se situe dans une zone centrale de votre habitation, afin que le signal puisse couvrir toutes les pièces de manière équitable. On vous conseille donc de positionner votre boîtier bien en évidence sur le dessus d’un buffet ou sur une étagère ouverte dans votre salon.
La hauteur joue également un rôle déterminant. Ne posez jamais votre routeur à même le sol, car les ondes se heurteraient à vos meubles et se perdraient dans le plancher. Privilégiez une installation à environ un mètre de hauteur pour favoriser une diffusion fluide dans tout l’espace de vie.
Enfin, accordez à votre box un minimum d’espace vital. Éloignez-la des murs porteurs très épais, des grands miroirs qui agissent comme des boucliers réflecteurs, et même des aquariums, l’eau étant l’un des pires ennemis des fréquences radio. En lui offrant cet espace dégagé, votre connexion retrouvera instantanément toute sa vitesse.

articles.title: GL.iNet Comet Q GL-RMQ1 Review A Single USB Type-C Cable Remote KVM Device with Tailscale
articles.text:
The GL.iNet Comet Q GL-RMQ1 is a new class of remote KVM devices, and it has something really neat. It is designed to be a single-cable solution. Plug a USB Type-C cable into a device with a Type-C port that supports video, and that is the only cable you need. WiFi handles network connectivity, and the built-in Type-C cable powers the unit, carries the video feed, and sends keyboard, mouse, and remote media to the remote system. One of the neat functions is that, along with being able to control many PCs, you can also connect phones and tablets using this solution.
Here is an Amazon affiliate link to where we bought ours.
GL.iNet Comet Q GL-RMQ1 Hardware Overview
The unit itself has a large 1.8″ touchscreen on its face, but it is like a puck design rather than many of the KVM units that are very boxy. What it is not, however, is small.
On the rear of the unit, you can see cooling vents, rubber feet, and an integrated USB Type-C cable.
That integrated Type-C cable is not huge, but it is nice to grab the unit and have the cable ready. It does, however, mean that if you wanted a Type-A connection, or a Type-A and HDMI, for example, the convenience is not there.
We plugged it into the Bosgame M5 since that was next to the step, and it is something you can see that is really important here. If you plug it into a system, then it has to boot. If you go from off to on, some systems boot faster than the GL-RMQ1, so that makes it hard to get into the BIOS.
Once it boots, the little touchscreen is very useful. You can see the IP address, along with the KVM and video connectivity status. You can also set up the unit, for example, by selecting a WiFi SSID and entering a password. Once the initial setup is done, you can then manage it via a browser.
Something important is that there is another Type-C port. This is a power input, which makes sense since many devices you connect to only have a single Type-C port.
Then there is one more accessory in the box, a little protector that is bright orange. We bought two of these and got the same color. Our guess is that this will eventually get a Sharpie marker on it to help quickly label these with a hostname so we know which is which.
Here is the protector installed.
Next, let us get to using the GL.iNet Comet Q.

articles.title: Pendant que l'iPhone Duo est en rupture, le Galaxy Z Fold8 de Samsung baisse de prix
articles.text:
Apple a ouvert les précommandes de l’iPhone Duo le vendredi 16 octobre. Le stock prévu pour le lancement de son tout premier smartphone pliable est parti en quelques minutes. Sur le site d’Apple, les nouvelles commandes ne sont plus livrées qu’à partir du 25 janvier 2027, alors que la sortie officielle est prévue le 23 octobre 2026. Apple parle d’une demande « extraordinaire ». Si vous espériez un iPhone pliable pour Noël, c’est mal parti.
Samsung propose des pliables au format livre depuis 2019, et son Galaxy Z Fold8 est sorti cet été. Lui est disponible tout de suite dans la boutique de RED by SFR, où il passe à 1 699 € au lieu de 1 999 € si vous souscrivez à un forfait sans engagement à 12,99 € par mois.
Il est également disponible au prix de 1 799 € sur Boulanger.
Que vaut le Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 ?
Points forts
- Format est parfait
- Compact fermé, grand déplié
- Très fin et léger
- Autonomie coriace grâce au silicium-carbone
- Il ne laisse pas indifférent
Points faibles
- Il manque un zoom optique
- Haut-parleurs moyens
- Quelques erreurs ergonomiques
- 2 000 euros, c’est cher
Le Galaxy Z Fold8 est un smartphone qui s’ouvre comme un livre. Fermé, il présente un écran externe de 5,5 pouces pour consulter vos notifications ou répondre à un message. Ouvert, il offre une dalle de 7,6 pouces au format 4:3, proche d’une petite tablette, sur laquelle deux applications peuvent s’afficher côte à côte. Ses deux écrans montent à 120 Hz : l’image se rafraîchit 120 fois par seconde, ce qui rend le défilement plus fluide.
Samsung a beaucoup travaillé sur le poids. Avec 201 grammes et 4,5 millimètres d’épaisseur une fois ouvert, le Fold8 est le Fold le plus léger jamais vendu par Samsung. Le Fold8 Ultra pèse 215 grammes. Il embarque un Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy, une puce Qualcomm adaptée par Samsung. Selon le constructeur, sa batterie de 4 800 mAh tient jusqu’à 26 heures en lecture vidéo, et la recharge filaire monte à 45 watts, mais le chargeur n’est pas fourni dans la boîte.
Pour la photo, le module arrière associe un grand-angle et un ultra grand-angle de 50 mégapixels. Le Fold8 n’a pas de téléobjectif, réservé au modèle Ultra, ce qui limite le zoom. Sa certification IP48 le protège de l’eau, mais face à la poussière, elle ne couvre que les particules de plus d’un millimètre. Un détail à garder en tête si vous le glissez souvent dans une poche pleine de sable au retour de la plage.
Face à l’iPhone Duo, le Fold8 gagne sur le poids : le pliable d’Apple pèse 254 grammes, soit 53 grammes de plus. L’iPhone Duo est en revanche certifié IP68 et protégé contre la poussière fine. Les deux téléphones ont le même format, avec un grand écran de 7,6 pouces, et aucun des deux n’a de téléobjectif.
À ce prix, le Galaxy Z Fold8 est-il une bonne affaire ?
La remise est plus intéressante chez RED by SFR : le Galaxy Z Fold8 passe à 1 699 €, soit 300 € de moins que son prix de lancement de 1 999 €, à condition de souscrire à un forfait sans engagement à 12,99 € par mois. Chez Boulanger, le smartphone pliable est également disponible à 1 799 €, soit une économie de 200 € sans condition de forfait.
Le calendrier joue aussi en faveur de Samsung. Si vous n’avez pas précommandé l’iPhone Duo dans les premières minutes, il ne vous sera pas livré avant fin janvier, et il coûte 2 339 € en version 256 Go, soit 640 € de plus que le Fold8 chez RED by SFR, ou 540 € de plus chez Boulanger. Si c’est le format pliable qui vous intéresse plus que l’écosystème Apple, le Fold8 est disponible dès aujourd’hui et Samsung en est à sa huitième génération de Fold. L’offre de RED by SFR est particulièrement intéressante si vous acceptez de souscrire à son forfait, tandis que Boulanger permet de profiter d’une réduction sans cette condition. De quoi s’offrir un pliable récent avant les fêtes tout en conservant quelques centaines d’euros pour les accessoires.

articles.title: Deux palettes de cartes graphiques Nvidia RTX 5090 ont disparu à l'aéroport de São Paulo.
articles.text:
C’est une affaire dont Nvidia se serait bien passée. Cette semaine, le distributeur brésilien Oderço a indiqué que deux palettes de GeForce RTX 5090 de marque Zotac, arrivées à l’aéroport international de Guarulhos, près de São Paulo, se sont tout simplement volatilisées. Un incident inédit pour l’entreprise, rapporte VideoCardz.
Une cargaison estimée à 440 000 euros
Le nombre exact de cartes graphiques disparues reste à déterminer, mais Oderço Matos, président du distributeur brésilien, estime la valeur de la cargaison à environ 440 000 euros pour lui. « En 38 ans, aucune de nos cargaisons n’avait disparu, jusqu’ici », explique-t-il. Si la piste du vol est envisagée, aucune hypothèse n’a pour l’heure été confirmée. Ni GRU Airport, la société qui exploite l’aéroport international de Guarulhos, ni la police fédérale brésilienne, ni l’administration fiscale ne se sont exprimés sur l’affaire. Par ailleurs, le distributeur n’a communiqué ni la date d’arrivée de l’envoi ni son numéro de suivi, précise VideoCardz.
Une carte à prix d’or
La GeForce RTX 5090 est aujourd’hui la carte graphique la plus puissante pour les joueurs. Dans un marché où les industriels accaparent les ressources, la carte graphique pourrait finir par échapper aux mains des joueurs pour se diriger dans celles des professionnels. Un manque de disponibilité qui se traduit par une augmentation stratosphérique du prix de la carte. Initialement disponible au prix exorbitant de 2 349 euros, la carte coûte au moins 4 900 euros en France.
    Pour aller plus loin
Nvidia retire la RTX 5090 de sa boutique américaine, et la carte frôle déjà les 10 000 euros en Europe
            
De quoi attiser les convoitises. Avec une telle valeur marchande, ces cartes graphiques représentent une véritable manne financière pour quiconque parviendrait à mettre la main dessus. Pour l’instant, les joyaux de Nvidia manquent toujours à l’appel.

articles.title: Anthropic Acquires Confidential AI Startup Opaque Systems
articles.text:
Anthropic has acquired Opaque Systems, a company that developed technology for using sensitive data in AI systems while keeping it protected by the underlying hardware.
Opaque announced the deal last week, saying its team is joining Anthropic. Financial terms were not disclosed.
Opaque started as a research project at UC Berkeley’s RISELab a decade ago. Its founders include Ion Stoica, co-founder of Databricks and Anyscale, and Raluca Ada Popa, an encryption and systems security researcher who now works at Google DeepMind. Aaron Fulkerson joined as CEO in October 2023.
The company turned its confidential computing research into technology used in production AI deployments. Over time, it broadened that work beyond protecting data and models.
“As AI evolved, so did the problem we set out to solve. Protecting data and models was no longer enough. Organizations also needed a way to independently verify how AI systems and agents behaved,” Opaque said.
“That led us to expand our work from confidential AI to verifiable AI: replacing trust assumptions with cryptographic evidence of what ran, where it ran, and under what policies,” the company added.
Opaque also worked with the wider community on open projects that address trust and security for AI agents and models. These include the Agent Governance Toolkit, TRACE, Confidential MCP and Weight Custody Manifest.
Opaque this year raised a $24 million Series B round at a $300 million valuation. The company listed Anthropic among its customers, alongside ServiceNow and Accenture.
Opaque’s website now states that its team “is joining Anthropic to carry our work forward, and Opaque Systems is winding down its operations.”
The company has not said what the wind-down means for its existing customers.
