articles.title: Un écran QD-OLED 280 Hz sous les 360€ : l’AOC Agon Pro est en promo ce weekend
articles.text:
L’AOC Agon Pro AG276QZD2 descend à 359,90 € chez Amazon, son plus bas prix relevé sur la plateforme. Cet écran QD-OLED QHD à 280 Hz vise les joueurs sur PC, avec deux réserves : une dalle brillante et une référence partagée avec une ancienne version à 240 Hz.
Dans la gamme Agon Pro d’AOC, l’AG276QZD2 associe une dalle QD-OLED de 26,5 pouces, une définition QHD et une fréquence de 280 Hz. Amazon le vend à 359,90 € au lieu de 399 €, son prix médian sur 90 jours. La remise reste modeste, mais ce tarif est le plus bas observé sur Amazon pour ce modèle selon l’historique de camelcamelcamel.
L’offre s’adresse d’abord aux joueurs sur PC qui veulent profiter du contraste de l’OLED sans viser les modèles les plus rapides. Darty le propose à 418,46 €, et la Fnac, au même prix, n’en avait plus en stock en ligne lors de notre relevé.
L’AOC Agon Pro AG276QZD2, écran QD-OLED QHD à 280 Hz, est affiché à 359,90 € au lieu de 399 € chez Amazon, son prix médian des trois derniers mois.
Pourquoi choisir l’AOC Agon Pro AG276QZD2 ?
- Le contraste de l’OLED : Chaque pixel s’éteint individuellement, ce qui donne des noirs profonds, utiles dans les jeux sombres comme devant un film. Il est certifié DisplayHDR True Black 400 et couvre 98,5 % du DCI-P3 selon AOC.
- Une image très réactive : Les 280 Hz et le temps de réponse de 0,03 ms annoncé en gris à gris limitent le flou de mouvement dans les jeux rapides. La compatibilité Adaptive Sync et G-Sync Compatible évite les déchirures d’image.
- Un pied complet : Réglable en hauteur sur 130 mm, inclinable, orientable et pivotable à 90°, il permet de trouver la bonne position sans acheter de bras. La fixation VESA 100 x 100 accueille aussi un bras existant.
Des FPS rapides aux soirées films, ce qu’apporte cette dalle
En jeu compétitif, les 280 Hz profitent aux joueurs dont le PC sort déjà un nombre d’images par seconde élevé, dans les FPS ou les jeux e-sport. La QHD sur 26,5 pouces offre une bonne finesse sans réclamer la puissance qu’exige un écran 4K. Hors du jeu, les noirs de l’OLED servent aussi les films et les séries, et deux haut-parleurs de 5 W dépannent sans casque. Avec deux HDMI et deux DisplayPort 1.4, une console trouve sa place à côté de l’ordinateur.
Le profil type est celui d’un joueur sur PC qui installe l’écran dans une pièce dont il maîtrise l’éclairage. Les tests publiés relèvent en effet une dalle brillante, qui renvoie les reflets face à une fenêtre ou sous un plafonnier, malgré le traitement antireflet annoncé par AOC. Pour de longues journées de bureautique aux éléments fixes, la garantie de trois ans couvre le marquage de la dalle, sous réserve de suivre les consignes d’entretien d’AOC. L’absence de port USB-C le rend en revanche moins pratique pour brancher un ordinateur portable d’un seul câble.
Face aux autres écrans QD-OLED en QHD
L’AG276QZD2 n’est pas le seul QD-OLED QHD à 280 Hz du catalogue AOC. Dans notre comparatif des meilleurs écrans PC gamer, mis à jour fin septembre, le Q27G4ZD reprend une fiche très proche et s’affichait alors autour de 330 €. L’Agon Pro garde pour lui un second DisplayPort, utile pour brancher deux ordinateurs, ce qui justifie l’écart seulement si vous en avez l’usage. Pour l’e-sport au plus haut niveau, le même comparatif met en avant des dalles OLED à 480 Hz, comme le LG UltraGear 27GX790A.
✅ Les points forts
- Dalle QD-OLED QHD à 280 Hz et 0,03 ms annoncé
- Pied réglable en hauteur, inclinable, orientable et pivotable
- Deux HDMI, deux DisplayPort 1.4 et un hub USB
- Garantie de trois ans incluant le marquage de la dalle
- Plus bas prix relevé sur Amazon pour ce modèle
❌ Les limites
- Dalle brillante sensible aux reflets dans une pièce lumineuse
- Aucun port USB-C pour un ordinateur portable
- Même référence qu’une ancienne version à 240 Hz : vérifiez le carton à la livraison
- Remise de 9 % seulement sur le prix médian
Darty affiche encore l’AOC Agon Pro AG276QZD2 à 418,46 €, quand Amazon, vendeur direct de l’offre, le propose à 359,90 €.
À 359,90 €, l’AOC Agon Pro AG276QZD2 rend le QD-OLED à 280 Hz accessible sans sacrifier la connectique ni l’ergonomie. La baisse est faible en pourcentage, mais elle porte l’écran à son plus bas niveau sur Amazon et sous le prix pratiqué par Darty. Pour un joueur sur PC qui joue surtout le soir ou dans une pièce peu exposée, l’équation tient bien.
Un point mérite votre attention : la même référence a d’abord été vendue en 240 Hz, et c’est bien la version 280 Hz que décrit la fiche Amazon. Vérifier la mention sur le carton à la réception évite toute mauvaise surprise. Si vous travaillez face à une fenêtre, ou si le second DisplayPort ne vous sert à rien, le Q27G4ZD de notre comparatif mérite un regard avant de trancher.

articles.title: KI kann uns falsche Erinnerungen einreden
articles.text:
MIT-Forscherin warnt: KI könnte bei Menschen falsche Erinnerungen erzeugen
Einer im Frühjahr 2026 veröffentlichten Studie zufolge vertrauen Menschen KI-generierten Antworten oft zu schnell und überschätzen die Kompetenz von KI-Systemen. Die Forscher:innen kamen zu dem Schluss, dass Menschen zu viel Vertrauen in KI-Empfehlungen setzen könnten, selbst wenn das System unsicher oder fehleranfällig sei.
Falsche Erinnerungen durch KI
Ein aktuelles Experiment der MIT-Forscherin Pattie Maes schlägt in eine ähnliche Kerbe. Demnach könnten KI-Systeme bei Menschen falsche Erinnerungen erzeugen, wie die Professorin vom MIT Media Lab gegenüber der Washington Post erklärte.
Im Rahmen des Experiments zeigten Maes und ihr Team 200 Teilnehmer:innen 24 Fotos. Auf diesen waren etwa eine Hochzeit, eine Straßenszene oder ein Rennen zu sehen. Anschließend bekam ein Teil der Gruppe dieselben Bilder noch einmal zu sehen. Für die anderen hatten die Forscher:innen von KI veränderte Versionen parat.
Gedächtnistest zeigt Gefahr
Dort waren etwa die Gesichtsausdrücke verändert oder Militärpersonal hinzugefügt worden, wie fr.de schreibt. Auch hatte die KI wohl Hinweise zum Klimawandel ergänzt. Bei dem folgenden Gedächtnistest zeigte sich, dass bei denjenigen, die von der KI veränderte Fotos zu sehen bekamen, die Zahl der falschen Erinnerungen stieg.
Und das war noch nicht alles. Die betroffenen Teilnehmer:innen waren von diesen falschen Erinnerungen auch noch überzeugter. „Ich halte das alles für grundsätzlich sehr gefährlich“, so Maes.
Gerichte und Geschichte manipulierbar?
Die Forscher:in spielt damit unter anderem auf Gerichtsverfahren an, bei denen Richter:innen auf möglichst korrekte Erinnerungen angewiesen sind. Schon jetzt ist klar, dass Erinnerungen von Zeug:innen leicht verzerrbar sind. Und auch die Geschichtsschreibung hängt von Erinnerungen ab.
Auf einer KI-Konferenz im schwedischen Malmö sind Forscher:innen Mitte Oktober 2026 der Frage nachgegangen, was passiert, wenn KI beginnt, sich in das menschliche Gedächtnis einzumischen. Nicht nur Maes Forschungsarbeit, sondern weitere Studien deuten daraufhin, dass KI verzerren kann, woran Menschen sich erinnern.
KI-Ideen versus menschliche Gedanken
In einem Fall etwa sahen die Teilnehmer:innen ein Video über ein Verbrechen. Diejenigen, die dazu später von einem generativen KI-Chatbot befragt wurden, hatten dreimal so viele falsche Erinnerungen. Auch die Grenzen zwischen den eigenen Gedanken und jenen von Maschinen scheinen zu verwischen. Ganz zu schweigen davon, dass Erinnerungen an Ereignisse eingepflanzt werden könnten, die es nie gab.

articles.title: Alienware AW3226Q Tandem WOLED 32-Inch Review
articles.text:
The Dell Alienware AW3226Q is the cheapest 4K OLED gaming monitor yet to offer an RGB stripe subpixel layout. This display uses the latest generation of Tandem WOLED technology, including the much sought-after RGB stripe configuration, but costs just $700. That makes it one of the cheapest 4K OLEDs overall, and by far the most affordable way to get this type of WOLED panel.
The AW3226Q uses a variant of the 32-inch 4K panel we recently reviewed in the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCWM. That Asus model features the flagship version of this 2026 panel, with a 240Hz refresh rate and a 1080p 480Hz dual mode. The Alienware variant reduces the refresh rate to 165Hz at 4K and omits dual mode entirely, but otherwise retains the same core panel technology, including the glossy screen coating.
Now, while the Asus model is being sold at a whopping $1,400, Dell's model costs just half as much at $700. Yes, the refresh rate is reduced, but the overall package is substantially cheaper. In fact, despite offering newer panel technology, the AW3226Q launches at the same price as discounted, previous-generation 165Hz QD-OLED and WOLED monitors, making for an interesting comparison.
Other specs of interest include a DisplayHDR True Black 400 certification, Dolby Vision support, and the usual adaptive sync and variable refresh rate capabilities, in this case branded as both FreeSync Premium Pro and G-Sync Compatible.
RGB Stripe: Subpixel Layout and Text Clarity
Before getting into the results, here's a quick recap of what this panel offers and why the RGB stripe layout matters.
In 2026, LG Display offers two main variants of Tandem WOLED technology. One retains the white subpixel, which has been the standard configuration for LG panels for years, resulting in an RGWB subpixel layout. The other uses a pure RGB stripe, a new configuration for 2026 that matches the traditional subpixel arrangement used by LCD panels, delivering similarly excellent text clarity.
Despite omitting the white subpixel in the RGB version, both are still WOLED panels, as the W in WOLED refers to the underlying white-light emission technology, not the presence of a white subpixel.
The main benefits of RGB stripe include full compatibility with subpixel font rendering, resulting in the best text clarity you can currently get from an OLED display, and much higher color brightness than RGWB panels. There's also significantly reduced gray banding, leading to better overall screen uniformity.
However, as with most things, there are trade-offs. Removing the white subpixel leads to lower peak white brightness than RGWB panels in both SDR and HDR content, as we'll explore later in this review. It also results in worse efficiency in certain situations. Which option is better ultimately depends on your priorities, and that's why LG Display offers both variants.
One of the biggest selling points of RGB stripe is text quality, and text certainly looks excellent on the AW3226Q. That's thanks to a combination of the RGB stripe layout and glossy screen coating. The latter eliminates the slight haze associated with matte surfaces, improving the perceived sharpness of fine details like text. Compared to a typical IPS LCD, most of which use matte coatings, the AW3226Q actually looks better when displaying text.
However, we're talking about a relatively high pixel density here at 140 PPI. While RGB stripe is the best subpixel layout for text clarity, it doesn't have a huge advantage over other OLED layouts, such as triangular RGB on QD-OLEDs or RGWB on conventional WOLEDs.
The high pixel density tends to mask the artifacts associated with these other layouts, so unless you're particularly sensitive to issues like color fringing, there's a good chance you won't notice much difference between an RGB stripe WOLED and a QD-OLED.
Screen Coating: It's Glossy
The AW3226Q uses the same type of glossy screen coating we've seen on other glossy WOLED monitors. Dell doesn't have a specific brand name for this coating, unlike Asus with its "TrueBlack Glossy" branding, but the results are essentially the same.
The screen maintains excellent black levels across a variety of environments, including brighter rooms, without the purple tint or raised blacks associated with QD-OLED panels. This is a key advantage of glossy WOLED over glossy QD-OLED: WOLED panels like this maintain meaningfully deeper blacks under moderate ambient lighting.
The trade-off is reflectivity. Glossy WOLED has a more pronounced mirror-like finish and is more likely to reflect your surroundings than QD-OLED. Which option works best depends heavily on your setup. If lights or sunlight from a window hit the display directly, those reflections will be more noticeable on WOLED, so avoiding direct light sources is particularly important.
HDR Performance and Configurations
As with other RGB stripe WOLEDs we've tested, HDR performance is one of the more interesting aspects of this display. All the fundamentals are here: perfect black levels, per-pixel lighting control, and effectively infinite contrast. OLED can display bright pixels directly alongside dark ones without blooming or zone bleed, making it an excellent technology for HDR.
However, unlike previous WOLEDs with a white subpixel, the new RGB stripe models perform quite similarly to QD-OLEDs in HDR, for better and sometimes for worse. This extends to the HDR configurations, with the AW3226Q offering three main modes similar to those found on QD-OLED monitors. Dell provides several additional options, but we'll focus on the best configurations.
The first is DisplayHDR True Black, which offers broadly accurate EOTF tracking in both bright and dark content. In other words, the screen generally delivers the brightness levels requested by HDR content. However, peak brightness is limited to just 400 nits, a significant trade-off. We also observed some panel dimming in bright scenes, though it wasn't huge.
The second option is HDR Peak 1000, which behaves similarly to the peak brightness modes found on QD-OLED monitors. It unlocks the panel's full brightness potential, reaching up to 1,000 nits for small highlights while maintaining good accuracy in dark scenes.
The downside is panel dimming in bright scenes. When the display encounters content with a high average brightness level, it can reduce the brightness of every pixel by roughly half. This makes bright scenes look noticeably dimmer than intended, reducing the impact HDR should deliver in these situations.
The third option is HDR Peak 1000 Bright, which attempts to correct this behavior by boosting brightness in brighter scenes for more accurate EOTF tracking. Unfortunately, it also raises the brightness of dark content, making those scenes considerably brighter and less accurate than they should be. Like the regular Peak 1000 mode, it retains access to 1,000 nits of peak brightness.
There are positives and negatives to Dell's approach. Having all three configurations gives users plenty of choice over how HDR content looks, but there's no single mode that delivers accurate performance in both bright and dark scenes. Bright content generally looks best in True Black or Peak 1000 Bright, while darker scenes are better served by the regular Peak 1000 mode. This isn't entirely Dell's fault. Panel limitations force manufacturers to make these compromises, and we've seen similar behavior across many QD-OLED and RGB stripe WOLED monitors.
There are a few other details worth mentioning. By default, Dell uses display-side tone mapping to provide a gradual brightness roll-off when HDR content exceeds the panel's capabilities. The roll-off varies depending on the peak brightness metadata sent to the display and generally does a decent job of preventing highlight clipping. However, it can also limit brightness in certain situations.
Compared to other HDR monitors, both Peak 1000 and True Black deliver decent accuracy in dark scenes. The AW3226Q performs better than the PG32UCWM, which only offers a boosted brightness configuration, and ends up similar to QD-OLEDs like the MSI 321UPX.
In bright scenes, True Black is somewhat underwhelming compared to the equivalent HDR mode on the Gigabyte MO32U24. Meanwhile, Peak 1000 suffers from significant inaccuracies caused by panel dimming, though its behavior is comparable to other OLED monitors with similar limitations.
Color accuracy is decent without being exceptional. Performance is comparable to the AW3926QW, while color space coverage reaches a respectable 78% of Rec. 2020. That's slightly higher than the PG32UCWM and in the same ballpark as 32-inch 4K QD-OLED monitors. Color volume is also higher than on the Asus model and comes very close to QD-OLED, though it still trails slightly. This is one area where RGB stripe WOLED has a significant advantage over previous-generation WOLED panels.
HDR Brightness
Starting with synthetic HDR brightness tests, the AW3226Q reaches 260 nits at full screen, matching first-generation QD-OLED panels and previous-generation WOLEDs.
That's 13% brighter than the PG32UCWM, although it falls short of the AW3926QW, which currently delivers the highest full-screen brightness we've measured from an RGB stripe WOLED. There's also a gap to the latest 2026 QD-OLED panels, such as the Gigabyte MO32U24 and Asus PG32UCDM3, which reach 300 nits or more, around 15% brighter than the Alienware.
Brightness at a 10% window was disappointing on our unit, reaching just 430 nits. That's 16% below the PG32UCWM when comparing peak modes, and also behind previous-generation QD-OLEDs.
Performance recovers with a 2% window, where the AW3226Q manages to exceed 1,000 nits, similar to current QD-OLED offerings. However, WOLEDs with a white subpixel, such as the XG32UCWMG, can achieve higher brightness in this test. Dell's 39-inch AW3926QW ultrawide also gets brighter despite using largely similar technology.
Moving to real-scene brightness, the AW3226Q struggles in its True Black configuration. We recorded an average of just 291 nits, which is 23% behind the 2024-generation QD-OLED panel used in the MSI 322URX in its True Black mode. It's also more than 30% behind the newer 2026 panel found in the MO32U24 using its HDR mode. It's difficult to recommend True Black on the Alienware because it simply isn't very bright, rarely reaching 400 nits in our tests.
Peak 1000 is better, but still somewhat underwhelming. Compared directly with the RGB stripe WOLED panel in the PG32UCWM, the Asus was 8% brighter on average. However, the Asus uses a boosted brightness configuration that avoids panel dimming at the expense of accuracy in dark scenes. The AW3226Q performs much better in that regard.
A typical 32-inch 4K QD-OLED from 2024, such as the MSI 321UPX, is also 13% brighter on average when comparing peak modes. Both panels exhibit similar brightness behavior across individual tests, but the QD-OLED generally comes out ahead.
The reality is that this RGB stripe WOLED panel isn't especially bright in HDR and suffers from many of the same weaknesses as QD-OLED. It's certainly not unusable, reaching over 850 nits in real-world scenes and up to 1,000 nits in smaller highlights, but peak brightness is clearly not one of its strengths.
Dolby Vision
The AW3226Q also supports Dolby Vision, which is enabled by default but can be disabled through the OSD. There are no additional configuration options, and brightness is limited to around 450 nits, similar to the True Black HDR mode. When connected to a Windows PC, the monitor generally operates in Dolby Vision mode, switching to HDR10 when compatible content is detected. This involves a brief black screen as the display changes modes.
For the most part, this works reasonably well. The monitor correctly switches to HDR10 in many games, allowing users to take advantage of brighter configurations such as Peak 1000. However, HDR10 detection isn't always reliable, and the display sometimes remains in Dolby Vision mode. We encountered this behavior when watching HDR YouTube videos in Chrome, for example.
For Windows users, we'd generally recommend leaving Dolby Vision disabled. Very few PC games support it, and none have been released recently. Some streaming services may use Dolby Vision, but for gaming, sticking with HDR10 avoids unnecessary mode switching.
Dolby Vision becomes more useful when connecting other devices. Many media players support Dolby Vision playback through streaming apps, while the Xbox Series X also supports Dolby Vision gaming. Even then, the limited brightness of Dell's Dolby Vision implementation means HDR10 may sometimes be the better option.
Motion Performance
Motion performance is one of the key differences between this 165Hz OLED and most competing models, which offer 240Hz refresh rates. An important consideration when buying an OLED, especially one with a lower refresh rate, is that motion clarity is directly tied to refresh rate.
At the same refresh rate, two OLED monitors will look virtually identical in motion clarity, so the refresh rate you'll actually use matters more than the monitor's maximum capability. For example, a 240Hz OLED and a 165Hz OLED running a game at 120 FPS with a 120Hz refresh rate will deliver essentially the same experience.
Higher refresh rate OLEDs become beneficial when you can take advantage of their additional headroom. Running at 240Hz produces a clearer image than at 165Hz, with better smoothness and responsiveness. However, if you play most games below 165 FPS, the benefits of a 240Hz model will be relatively small.
This raises the question of how much you're sacrificing by choosing a cheaper 165Hz model. In our opinion, higher refresh rate variants are best suited to multiplayer gaming. If you play a lot of fast-paced competitive titles where motion clarity and low input latency are priorities, 240Hz is the better choice. For story-driven games, 165Hz is often more than sufficient for an excellent experience.
However, 165Hz monitors have less headroom for future GPU upgrades and frame generation. With frame generation enabled, you generally want to stay within the monitor's refresh rate ceiling to avoid tearing. On a 165Hz display using 2x frame generation, the maximum base rendering rate before exceeding that ceiling is approximately 82 FPS. In other words, even with frame generation, you're limited to the input latency characteristics of a game running at around 80 FPS, plus any additional frame generation overhead.
On a 240Hz display, that base rendering rate increases to 120 FPS, which provides a more responsive experience. This is a potential limitation of 165Hz displays, even for single-player gaming.
Input lag is as expected, with a processing delay below 1ms. Our latency measurements combine processing delay and refresh lag to provide a useful indication of overall responsiveness.
The fastest 240Hz OLEDs lead the charts, while 144Hz and 165Hz models generally sit further down due to their lower refresh rates. That's ultimately the main difference between the AW3226Q and faster OLED alternatives: the lower refresh rate results in somewhat higher latency.
SDR Performance
The AW3226Q performs quite well out of the box in SDR grayscale testing. An average Delta E of around 5 is better than usual, with very good color temperature and reasonable gamma tracking. However, like many wide-gamut monitors, it doesn't enable sRGB emulation by default, so colors appear oversaturated out of the box.
Default Color Performance
There are two ways to achieve more accurate SDR colors: the dedicated sRGB mode in the OSD or Windows Auto Color Management (ACM). The latter produces reasonably accurate results, but Dell's built-in sRGB mode is even better, although it locks several settings and offers limited customization.
Default ACM Color Performance
Despite those restrictions, the sRGB mode is outstanding. Grayscale calibration is nearly perfect across the board, while saturation performance is excellent, with fantastic adherence to the Rec. 709 color space.
sRGB Mode Color Performance
A ColorChecker Delta E ITP average of just 1.53 is the sort of performance we typically see after a full manual calibration, making additional calibration unnecessary for most users.
Compared to other monitors we've tested, the AW3226Q ranks among the very best for sRGB accuracy. A handful of models deliver similarly impressive results, but that ColorChecker score is particularly exceptional. Across 202 sRGB modes we've tested over the years, the AW3226Q ranks third overall, with Dell monitors occupying all three top spots.
SDR brightness is largely as expected given the full-screen HDR results. The AW3226Q reaches 254 nits with a full-screen white image, putting it on par with 2024-generation QD-OLED panels. Most OLEDs fall within this range, with only the latest models, such as 2026 QD-OLEDs, pushing into the 300-nit territory. We still consider 250 nits sufficient for most users. Minimum brightness is also very good, and Dell uses a uniform brightness configuration in SDR mode.
Uniformity
Uniformity is an interesting aspect of the AW3226Q. Thanks to the new RGB stripe Tandem WOLED design, gray uniformity has improved significantly compared to previous WOLED panels, something further helped by the lower 165Hz refresh rate.
There's minimal dirty screen effect when viewing dark grays and virtually no dark gray banding. This makes the AW3226Q a better option for productivity work, particularly in applications with gray backgrounds, than previous WOLED displays.
However, the panel isn't without uniformity issues. In its settled state, the edges are dimmer than the center, creating a mild vignette effect that we don't typically see on QD-OLEDs or even other WOLED panels. This is reflected in the higher Delta E measurements around the edges. The PG32UCWM exhibited similar behavior to some degree, although it's more noticeable on our Alienware unit. By comparison, QD-OLED panels typically deliver better edge-to-edge uniformity.
This issue is further exacerbated by dynamic edge dimming through a system called CPC, or Convex Power Control. CPC dims the edges of the screen during dynamic content, including gaming, making the vignette effect more pronounced than our static uniformity measurements suggest. The effect can be difficult to spot while gaming, as the constantly changing imagery tends to hide uniformity problems. We also didn't notice any saturation issues around the edges of this display.
CPC is an OLED care feature designed to reduce the risk of burn-in, but unfortunately, Dell provides no option to disable it. In fact, the AW3226Q offers no user control over its OLED care settings. On several competing monitors from brands like Asus and MSI, users can adjust these features, including disabling edge dimming to restore better panel uniformity. With the Alienware, you're stuck with Dell's default configuration.
Finally, full-screen white power consumption came in at 94 watts, similar to QD-OLED alternatives and 6 watts lower than the PG32UCWM. However, removing the white subpixel makes the AW3226Q less efficient than the previous-generation RGWB WOLED panel used in the XG32UCWG. Gaming power consumption is considerably lower, averaging a very manageable 42 watts in our test.
Ports, Features and Design
The AW3226Q comes with a standard selection of ports, including one DisplayPort 1.4 with DSC, two HDMI 2.1 ports supporting the full 48 Gbps bandwidth with DSC, and a three-port USB 5 Gbps hub.
The USB hub is quite convenient, with one Type-A port on the back, another Type-A on the bottom edge, and a USB-C port alongside it. The USB-C connection supports data and 15W power delivery, but not DisplayPort Alt Mode.
All display inputs support the full 4K 165Hz at 10-bit through DSC. One of the HDMI ports also supports eARC, which could be useful in certain setups. There's a 3.5mm audio jack, but no built-in speakers.
Dell has included several features in the OSD, controlled through a directional toggle on the rear of the display. These include multiple picture presets and color controls, a dark stabilizer, picture-in-picture mode, and RGB lighting controls. Most gaming-specific features are grouped under AlienVision, which allows you to display crosshairs and apply color filters to selected areas of the screen.
Unfortunately, Dell offers virtually no control over its OLED care features. Dell has implemented the usual protections, including pixel shifting and automatic dimming in certain situations, but these features are always enabled and cannot be adjusted or disabled. On the positive side, Dell continues to offer a three-year warranty covering burn-in.
As for the design, the AW3226Q follows Alienware's recent aesthetic, although this model has a darker, almost black finish rather than the dark blue used on earlier versions. It's a relatively minimalist design that isn't overly "gamery," and I think it looks great. Build quality and surface finishes are also good, despite most of the exterior being plastic.
The Alienware logo on the rear features some RGB lighting, although it's fairly subtle on this model. Ergonomics are good, with height, tilt, and swivel adjustments, along with a compact, squarish base that doesn't occupy much desk space and still allows you to place items on top of it.
The front looks excellent, with uniform bezels and that attractive glossy finish. I also love that Dell has abandoned the curve here. The AW3226Q uses a standard flat panel, unlike the original 32-inch QD-OLED AW3225QF, which featured a curved display.
A Great OLED Faces Tough Competition
Overall, the Dell Alienware AW3226Q is a bit of a mixed bag. There are certainly aspects of this monitor that I really like, but whether we'd recommend buying it depends on a few factors. The 32-inch 4K OLED market is extremely competitive, especially on pricing, making it difficult for the AW3226Q to stand out even at its $700 MSRP.
Let's start with the good stuff. This monitor gives you a brand-new RGB stripe WOLED panel with an excellent glossy finish for half the price of the Asus PG32UCWM we recently reviewed. The main sacrifice is refresh rate, dropping from 240Hz to 165Hz, along with the removal of dual mode support. Otherwise, performance is very similar, making Dell's offering a much more affordable way to access this panel technology.
And there are good reasons to go for an RGB stripe WOLED. Performance is quite similar to QD-OLED, including excellent color brightness and good gray uniformity, but it also addresses some of QD-OLED's weaknesses.
While color fringing isn't a major issue on 32-inch 4K QD-OLEDs, the RGB stripe layout eliminates it thanks to a subpixel arrangement better suited to text rendering. The glossy coating is another significant advantage, delivering deeper blacks across more lighting conditions without the reddish-purple tint associated with QD-OLED.
Dell has also done an excellent job in a few areas. The sRGB mode is outstanding, with near-perfect SDR calibration. We also appreciate having all three main HDR configurations available. Dolby Vision and HDMI eARC are welcome additions that aren't available on every competitor.
As for downsides, HDR brightness in particular is somewhat disappointing. Panel dimming in bright HDR scenes used to be something you could avoid by choosing WOLED over QD-OLED, but the new RGB stripe WOLED panels exhibit similar behavior.
Between panel dimming and the limitations of this new RGB stripe design, the AW3226Q is actually less bright in HDR scenes than first-generation 32-inch 4K QD-OLED panels released more than two years ago.
So, should you buy the AW3226Q?
The first comparison worth making is against similarly priced 165Hz QD-OLED monitors using the original 2024 panel design. Models like the Asus XG32UCDS can typically be found for around $700, exactly the same price as the Alienware. So at price parity, the Alienware AW3226Q is the better buy. Panel performance is similar except for slightly lower HDR brightness. However, the Tandem WOLED panel has superior screen coating, which avoids the raised black issue, and its RGB stripe layout, which is better suited to text rendering.
What holds us back from giving the AW3226Q a broader recommendation is that 4K 240Hz OLED monitors aren't much more expensive, and sometimes cost exactly the same. In recent weeks, 32-inch 4K 240Hz QD-OLEDs have regularly been available for around $750, with recent sales bringing models like the MSI 321UPX down to $700.
That puts the AW3226Q in a more difficult position. For the same $700, or perhaps a $50 premium, you can get a 240Hz QD-OLED with broadly similar panel performance. Instead of comparing two OLED technologies at the same price and refresh rate, you're now weighing the advantages of RGB stripe WOLED against a substantially higher refresh rate. Do you prioritize the better motion clarity, responsiveness, and headroom of a 240Hz monitor, or the superior screen coating and text clarity of the AW3226Q?
It's a tough choice. If you really dislike the raised blacks and reddish-purple tint of QD-OLED, this Tandem WOLED is a better fit. But for most gamers, we would pick the 240Hz option.
Of course, pricing varies by region and it's also worth noting that we're comparing discounted prices for QD-OLED monitors that have been on the market for months against the launch MSRP of a brand-new product. Dell could easily make the AW3226Q a more compelling option with a price adjustment. At $700, it's a good monitor facing some very strong competition. At a lower price, it could become a much easier recommendation.

articles.title: Los despidos sin indemnizar ni justificar se disparan tras la reforma laboral y ya suman casi 3,2 millones
articles.text:
Los contratos indefinidos también pueden durar semanas; durante el periodo de prueba la empresa puede, con carácter general, acabar con la relación laboral sin tener que indemnizar y sin acreditar una causa. Su uso ha ido en aumento desde la reforma laboral de 2022; las bajas que se acumulan están en torno a los 3,2 millones, según Colpisa.
La información puede recogerse en la tabla de la Seguridad Social: en el periodo comprendido entre enero de 2022 y agosto de 2026 se registran 3.188.254 bajas por no superar la prueba con contratos indefinidos; los datos de 2026 son provisionales.
Hay que tener en cuenta lo antecedente: en 2025 se registraron 723.763, frente a los 75.004 de 2021, lo que son casi diez veces más. Si lo comparamos con 2019 (justo antes de la pandemia), las cifras fueron de 132.534, y el último año completo multiplica esa cifra por 5,46.
Nosotros ya hablamos del repunte de estos ceses. La dificultad que esto plantea se encuentra en que un contrato indefinido no tiene fecha de finalización; sin embargo, es algo que no impide que pueda terminar durante la prueba. Para quien ha cambiado de trabajo, tal posibilidad puede afectar a la estabilidad prevista por el contrato y a la protección por desempleo.
Una empresa puede prescindir de un trabajador porque no se ha adaptado al puesto, pero también (y aquí entra la picaresca) puede utilizar la prueba para una necesidad temporal. Las estadísticas que conocemos no permiten calcular cuántas de estas bajas son fraudulentas, ni adjudicarlas todas ellas a una causa única.
El Real Decreto 723/2026, publicado en el Boletín Oficial del Estado (BOE) y en vigor desde el 5 de octubre, refuerza la obligación de las empresas de facilitar información escrita sobre el periodo de prueba. Su régimen general sobre relaciones laborales de más de cuatro semanas exige comunicar por escrito la duración concreta de la prueba y las obligaciones para realizarla, aunque mantiene la posibilidad de terminar el contrato durante ella sin una indemnización automática.
También debe indicarse la función que se desempeña, diferenciando entre salario base y complementos, y exponer con claridad el cálculo de las cantidades variables de la remuneración, así como la jornada, los turnos de trabajo y las vacaciones. Si se utilizan algoritmos para tomar decisiones sobre las condiciones laborales, se informará de su existencia y sus reglas de funcionamiento. En el caso de contratos anteriores al 5 de octubre, la información pendiente puede solicitarse y deberá remitirse en treinta días hábiles.
Para nuevas contrataciones, la comunicación de estas condiciones se realizará antes del inicio del trabajo; puede incorporarse al contrato o a un documento adicional en papel o formato electrónico. La información ya facilitada al trabajador, si está completa y la tiene en su poder, no tiene que repetirse.
La prueba tiene sus límites
Es necesario saber que existe una precisión a la hora de aceptar seis meses de prueba. El artículo 14 del Estatuto remite en primer lugar a las disposiciones del convenio colectivo; si este no establece otra duración, se impone, para los técnicos titulados, un plazo máximo de seis meses y, para el resto de los trabajadores, de dos meses. En las empresas con menos de 25 trabajadores, el máximo es de tres meses para quienes no son técnicos titulados.
El Estatuto también establece que, cuando se han desempeñado las mismas funciones anteriormente en la misma empresa, el pacto de prueba es nulo, cualquiera que haya sido la modalidad de contratación anterior.
Asimismo, el Estatuto garantiza el derecho a la protección frente a la extinción por embarazo o maternidad, salvo que concurran motivos no relacionados con el embarazo o la maternidad. Y cuando el trabajador esté en prueba, tendrá los derechos y obligaciones correspondientes al puesto de trabajo, salvo los relativos a la resolución del contrato; la ausencia de obligación de indemnizar no exime a la empresa de la obligación de abonar el salario por el trabajo realizado.
La concreción de la duración de esta prueba no es una obligación descubierta en octubre de 2026, y la sentencia 551/2025 del Tribunal Supremo, de 5 de junio de 2025, publicada en el BOE, recuerda su doctrina. La remisión a un convenio colectivo que no fija una duración concreta, sino únicamente un límite superior, no basta. Si el convenio estipula una duración exacta, la remisión puede ser válida.
Esa sentencia recuerda además que el objetivo de la prueba es comprobar la idoneidad del trabajador para el puesto de trabajo, dejando claro que la libertad para decidir no ampara decisiones discriminatorias ni vulneraciones de derechos fundamentales.
Si el periodo de prueba resulta inválido o el cese es discriminatorio, el trabajador podrá impugnar la extinción. El artículo 103 de la Ley reguladora de la jurisdicción social establece un plazo de veinte días hábiles para presentar la demanda por despido; las normas de este capítulo se aplican también a la impugnación de otras decisiones empresariales de extinción, con las especialidades necesarias. Se trata, por tanto, de un plazo de caducidad; merece la pena revisar el contrato y la notificación de la baja para evitar que se pierdan los días.
El riesgo al cambiar de trabajo
La prestación por desempleo merece una aclaración independiente. El Servicio Público de Empleo Estatal incluye entre las situaciones legales de desempleo el cese por no superar la prueba a iniciativa del empresario y establece condiciones sobre cómo terminó el empleo anterior. Que la empresa acabe con la relación laboral con un trabajador en periodo de prueba no significa que este se vea privado automáticamente de todos los derechos a la prestación por desempleo.
Debe reunir los requisitos correspondientes a la prestación que solicite. Existe, no obstante, una excepción notable en el caso de aquellos que abandonan un trabajo para incorporarse a otro. El SEPE explica en la pregunta frecuente sobre la baja voluntaria que, si la segunda empresa acaba con la relación laboral por no superar la prueba antes de que haya transcurrido un plazo de tres meses desde esa salida voluntaria del empleo anterior, no se podrá optar por la prestación por desempleo. La causa y la fecha en que se produjo el cese del primer trabajo pueden ser decisivas.
La tendencia continúa, desgraciadamente. Las bajas de trabajadores con contratos indefinidos por no superar la prueba, registradas entre enero y agosto de 2026, ascendieron a 505.065, frente a las 478.268 de los mismos meses de 2025: un aumento del 5,6 %. Eso sí, se trata de datos provisionales y anteriores a la fecha de entrada en vigor del decreto.
Imágenes | Wikimedia Commons con edición

articles.title: Gemini 4 Argon vs. Claude Opus 5.5: Half the price and about half as accurate
articles.text:
Gemini 4 Argon vs. Claude Opus 5.5: Half the price and about half as accurate
When Google announced Gemini 4 Argon to a small group of testers on September 30, it came with a benchmark table that put Argon ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 on 14 of 18 tests. Those include DeepSWE (77.9% vs. 74.2%) and GraphWalks at 256K to 1 million tokens (84.2% vs. 66.8%). Two weeks later, on October 13, Google opened Argon to paid Gemini API developers.
To its credit, Google also showed where Opus 5.5 wins. Opus leads on the other four benchmarks, including Terminal-bench 4.0 (66.4% vs. 57.4%), which tests agentic work in a command line.
Google is also undercutting Anthropic on price, at least for now. Through November 30, Argon costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, half the price of Opus 5.5. On December 1, it rises to $4 and $20, matching Opus. That gives developers about six weeks to decide whether Argon is better or just cheaper.
That gives developers about six weeks to decide whether Argon is better or just cheaper.
Benchmarks don’t always match real work, and a half-price window only matters if the model matches the competitor on quality. To see whether Argon is better or just cheaper (for now), I tested both models head-to-head on three hard tasks from categories where Google claims a lead.
The tests
I ran each test once per model through OpenRouter, on Google’s and Anthropic’s own servers, at default reasoning settings. A script graded every answer against keys I built and verified before testing either model. The answer key adds more scoring areas to help ensure the quality and thoroughness of each test.
- Bug hunt – A 3,500-line Python library with 14 planted logic bugs and five decoys. Each model reviewed the code, then fixed what it found.
- Billing spec – A spec for a subscription billing engine, graded by 80 hidden tests on daylight saving, month-end dates, and rounding. A follow-up added two currencies and 20 more tests.
- Long context – A fake wiki of 400 services with scattered dependencies, at three sizes. Each model answered three graph questions with planted traps.
Bug hunt
This one was a tie. Both models found all 14 bugs, including four that only show up when you follow a value across three or more files. Neither flagged a decoy. In the follow-up, both fixed all 14 bugs without breaking any of the 93 existing tests.
Argon was cheaper. Its review cost averaged 1 cent per bug found, compared to Opus’s 2.4 cents, an average I calculated from the per-call total rather than measured per bug. Argon would still come out cheaper at its full Dec. 1 price, because it used fewer tokens.
- The numbers:
  - Review
    - Argon 53,031 in, 3,964 out, $0.15, 43.0 s.
    - Opus 64,572 in, 4,053 out, $0.34, 38.9 s.
  - Fix
    - Argon 54,923 in, 24,292 out, $0.35, 186.6 s.
    - Opus 66,465 in, 34,263 out, $0.95, 219.8 s.
Billing specs
Here’s where accuracy began to differ between the two models. Opus passed all 80 hidden tests, then all 100 after the currency follow-up. Argon passed 11 of 80, then 20 of 100.
Argon didn’t fail the majority of the tests because its logic was bad. It failed because it made a small mistake early on. Its code passed an extra argument to Python’s `datetime.combine()`, which raises an error, and most of the module depends on that helper. When I corrected that one line myself, Argon scored 80/80 and 100/100. I kept the official scores as graded but wanted to explain what happened, not just list the scores, on this one.
Overall, Argon was cheaper, but the difference between Opus and Argon pricing will disappear once the lower-cost period ends, though Argon’s lower token use would still make it cheaper on this test.
- The numbers:
  - Build
    - Argon 3,907 in, 3,727 out, $0.05, 54.1 s.
    - Opus 5,236 in, 7,763 out, $0.18, 63.0 s.
  - Follow-up
    - Argon 8,881 in, 4,673 out, $0.06, 41.5 s.
    - Opus 11,807 in, 7,267 out, $0.19, 51.9 s.
Long context
Each vendor counts tokens differently. My 500K document came to 549,483 tokens on Argon and 784,087 on Opus. My 900K document came to 1.4 million tokens on Claude’s tokenizer, so Anthropic’s API rejected it. I added a third document of about 600K tokens, the largest that both models could fit.
Both models answered two of the three questions perfectly at every size they ran. The split came on the blast radius question, which asks for every service that goes down when one fails. The answer is 33 services.
Opus got all 33 at 500K and 32 at 600K, with no wrong entries. At 500K, Argon got 20 right and 8 wrong; at 600K, 19 right and 16 wrong; and at 900K, 23 right and 2 wrong. At 600K and 900K, it treated a dependency as removed after the wiki reinstated it. Unlike the billing bug, this wasn’t a small slip. Argon got the reasoning wrong at every size. This is a big red flag.
Unlike the billing bug, this wasn’t a small slip. Argon got the reasoning wrong across the entire answer. This is a big red flag.
Another thing I noticed is that Argon raced through this long-context test. Argon answered quickly without showing any step-by-step work, and Opus took longer because it reasoned first. This shows up in token usage. Opus used over 5,000 tokens, most for reasoning, vs. Argon’s 243-425. That likely connects to Argon’s wrong answers, though I can’t prove the cause from one run.
Argon was cheaper here, but it’s not worth using it on a similar task, as it was largely inaccurate and sloppy.
- The numbers:
  - 500k
    - Argon 549,483 in, 264 out, $1.10, 24.2 s.
    - Opus 784,087 in, 5,532 out, $3.25, 68.3 s.
  - 600k
    - Argon 652,492 in, 425 out, $1.31, 32.4 s.
    - Opus 935,332 in, 5,158 out, $3.84, 69.1 s.
  - 900K
    - Argon 982,367 in, 243 out, $1.97, 41.5 s.
    - Opus not run.
Results
| Test | Gemini 4 Argon | Claude Opus 5.5 | 
| Bug hunt review | 14 of 14, 0 false positives | 14 of 14, 0 false positives | 
| Bug hunt fix | 14 of 14, 93 of 93 tests kept | 14 of 14, 93 of 93 tests kept | 
| Billing spec | 11 of 80 | 80 of 80 | 
| Billing follow-up | 20 of 100 | 100 of 100 | 
| Blast radius, 500K | 20 of 33, 8 wrong | 33 of 33 | 
| Blast radius, 600K | 19 of 33, 16 wrong | 32 of 33 | 
| Blast radius, 900K | 23 of 33, 2 wrong | Rejected, over 1M tokens | 
| Total tokens in / out | 2,305,084 / 37,588 | 1,867,499 / 64,036 | 
| Total cost | $4.98 | $8.75 | 
| Total time | 423.3 s | 511.0 s | 
My results didn’t match Google’s benchmarks. Argon tied Opus on code review and fixing at under half the cost. It lost the spec test over one bad line of code, and it missed or invented services on every long-context blast-radius question.
What do I think?
Based on these tests, I wouldn’t use Argon. Yes, it was cheaper and as accurate as Opus on the bug hunt, but after working with it on the other tests, I wouldn’t unquestioningly trust Argon on any task.
I wouldn’t unquestioningly trust Argon on any task.
Opus 5.5 is one of Anthropic’s leading models, and Artificial Analysis’s independent index ranks it at 58, ahead of Argon’s 53.
While Google is working hard to catch up, it hasn’t yet.

articles.title: Stockholm’s Vessla exits stealth with €2.94 million to bring AI agents to property management | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Vessla, a Stockholm-based AI startup building an agentic operating system for real estate, has emerged from stealth with €2.94 million ($3.3 million) pre-Seed funding.
The funding round was more than 2× oversubscribed and was led by Seedcamp. Other investors joining the round include Inception Fund, Tiny VC, operators from Lovable and OpenAI, founders Lukas Saari of Tandem Health and Fredrik Hjelm of Voi and Pit, alongside a number of angel investors.
“Property operations combine recurring work with complex processes and exceptions that require judgment. Vessla is building for both. The Vessla team has expertise in developing bleeding edge AI applications, and their experience from deploying those in high-stakes enterprise settings play a big role in why they are seeing such interest from leading players in the industry in such a short time,” said Felix Martinez, Partner at Seedcamp.
Founded earlier this year, Vessla is trying to solve a familiar but persistent problem facing property management: information is scattered across multiple systems, and connecting them falls on people. It says a single maintenance request can require checking property records, contacting a supplier, updating a work order, and following up on an invoice, each step carried out in a different system,
To solve this dependence on discrete systems, Vessla layers its AI agents across those existing systems, equipping them with the relevant context and operating rules to carry out tasks reliably. However, it also ensures that decisions that require human judgement are handled by people responsible for making them.
In addition to AI agents, the startup is building an operating system that spans entire property portfolios, connecting leasing, building operations, and investment planning. Vessla says property teams set priorities and retain decision-making authority, while agents identify opportunities to grow rental income, reduce operating costs, and help coordinate and execute work across the portfolio.
“We believe AI will fundamentally change how property companies operate, from maintenance and costs to leasing and rental income. The hard part is making it work at scale across the systems and processes those companies already rely on. That is what we are building. As AI takes on more of the execution, people’s judgment, relationships and responsibility become even more important,” said Orman Gazvini, CEO of Vessla.
The founding team of the startup has a deep and varied expertise in building and deploying autonomous AI systems in demanding enterprise environments. Gazvini previously advised major software companies at McKinsey and worked on strategy and M&A at Pophouse.
Kasper Janehag, CTO of Vessla, began his career in the space industry and contributed to NASA’s Mars 2020 mission, before leading enterprise-scale AI transformations at QuantumBlack, McKinsey’s AI division. Chief scientist Arash Dabiri brings hands-on experience building and evaluating agentic AI applications from Andon Labs and QuantumBlack. The broader team also brings experience from Legora, Stanford, and Netlight.
“AI can look impressive in a demo. The real test is whether it can handle the messy, consequential work of a complex business. That requires deep integrations with vast amounts of context, rigorous evaluation and clear limits on what agents can do. We are building Vessla to meet that standard across entire property portfolios,” said Janehag.
The company is already working with some of the largest commercial and residential property owners and operators in the Nordics. While it didn’t specify how it plans to use the funding, since it is coming out of stealth, the funding will likely be used to scale its solution.

articles.title: Qué es Windows RE y por qué puede salvarte cuando Windows no funciona correctamente
articles.text:
A todos nos ha ocurrido alguna vez que Windows no arranca como debería. El ordenador se enciende, pero no vemos el escritorio como sería lo normal. O sí aparece en pantalla, pero apenas podemos hacer nada. Las aplicaciones se abren muy despacio o se niegan a abrirse, entre otras situaciones extrañas. ¿Qué hacer para solucionarlo si Windows no funciona? Si reiniciar no basta, prueba con Windows RE, una herramienta a la que pedir ayuda y que viene integrada en tu sistema operativo.
Por lo general, si al encender tu ordenador las cosas no van del todo bien, simplemente con reiniciar debería volver todo a la normalidad. Pero, por desgracia, no siempre es así. Puede que hayas instalado algo que no deberías, o que una aplicación se ha actualizado y esa actualización estaba en mal estado… Por muchas razones, Windows no funciona cuando antes sí lo hacía.
En el mejor de los casos, basta con deshacer los cambios que hiciste el día de antes. Desinstalar alguna aplicación, buscar nuevas actualizaciones, hacer algo de limpieza entre los archivos o pasar el antivirus. Pero no siempre es así. En ocasiones es necesaria una ayuda mayor. Pero no siempre es necesario acudir a un USB de arranque con Windows o probar suerte con Linux. Antes de formatear o reinstalar Windows, prueba suerte con Windows RE, el salvavidas del sistema que deberías conocer aunque no tengas que utilizarlo jamás.
Qué es Windows RE y para qué sirve
Windows RE, también abreviado como WinRE, significa Windows Recovery Environment, traducido como Windows entorno de recuperación o entorno de recuperación de Windows. Y su nombre nos da una pista de para qué sirve. Para recuperar Windows en caso de mal funcionamiento. Microsoft lo describe como “un entorno de recuperación que puede reparar las causas comunes de los sistemas operativos que no se pueden arrancar”.
Basado en el entorno de preinstalación de Windows, conocido como Windows PE, es un modo de Windows pensado para cargar solamente aquello necesario para así diagnosticar y arreglar cualquier problema del sistema. No hay que confundirlo con el modo seguro de Windows, lo que antes se conocía como modo a prueba de fallos, aunque sus funciones son similares. Básicamente, arreglar Windows si no funciona evitando que tengas que reinstalarlo desde cero. Algo que te llevaría mucho más tiempo y que, en ocasiones, te hará perder datos, configuraciones y archivos importantes.
Por lo demás, Windows RE viene instalado en Windows 10 y Windows 11. Y cuenta con una selección de herramientas con las que probar suerte e intentar arreglar tu sistema operativo. En el mejor de los casos, la reparación será automática. Pero, llegado el caso, tendrás a tu disposición las opciones necesarias para encontrar una salida a ese problema que te impide utilizar Windows porque no funciona correctamente.
Qué puede hacer por ti Windows RE
Al iniciar Windows, si se produce algún problema relacionado con el inicio de la máquina, el propio sistema deja un aviso para el próximo arranque. Y al iniciar el PC de nuevo, si el cargador detecta ese aviso previo, inicia Windows RE en lugar de Windows como suele ser habitual. De esa manera, la herramienta se encarga de “diagnosticar y reparar automáticamente una instalación de Windows que no se puede iniciar”.
Cuando se carga el menú de Windows RE, puedes hacer varias cosas:
- Continuar. Sirve para “salir y continuar con Windows 11” en caso de que ya hayas resuelto el problema o de que hayas accedido a este menú por accidente.
- Apagar el equipo. Apaga tu ordenador.
- Usar un dispositivo. Si las soluciones que te propone Windows RE si Windows no funciona no son suficientes, puede que debas acudir a una unidad USB externa para reparar el sistema “desde fuera”.
- Solucionar problemas. Aquí es donde está todo lo que necesitas de Windows RE.
Dentro de Solucionar problemas encontrarás las siguientes opciones:
- Restauración a un momento dado. Es la solución más sencilla. Si algo hiciste o pasó para que Windows no funcione correctamente, puede que volver atrás en el tiempo lo arregle. Windows crea puntos de restauración de manera automática. Restaurar tu equipo a un punto anterior tal vez resuelva el problema. El inconveniente es que tal vez no tuvieras activada la opción de crear puntos de restauración.
- Restablecer este equipo. Esta solución de Windows RE es más eficaz pero también te llevará más tiempo. Consiste en volver a instalar Windows. En el proceso puedes elegir si quieres “mantener o quitar los archivos personales”. Lo bueno es que no necesitarás un disco de instalación. Lo malo es que el proceso es largo. Y puede que tengas que volver a instalar alguna app o reconfigurar algo de Windows a tu gusto.
- Opciones avanzadas. No pierdas la esperanza. Aquí hay más soluciones para arreglar Windows si no funciona del todo bien.
Soluciones para reparar Windows si no funciona
Las opciones avanzadas que encontrarás en el menú de Windows RE que hemos visto antes son las siguientes. Utiliza solamente aquellas que entiendas y conozcas bien. Tocar por tocar no siempre es recomendable. Y puede que empeores la situación. Algunas de esas opciones también las encontrarás en Configuración de Windows. En concreto, en la sección Recuperación, dentro de Sistema.
- Recuperación rápida de equipo. Viene a ser el diagnóstico y reparación automáticos que Windows RE activa si detecta algo raro durante el inicio. Si no se activa automáticamente, puedes activarlo tú mismo desde ahí y ver si arregla el problema.
- Desinstalar las actualizaciones. Si el problema de Windows está en una actualización, desinstalarla resolverá el asunto. Por desgracia, es algo más habitual de lo que debería.
- Configuración de inicio. Te permite elegir entre una lista de opciones de inicio para ayudarte a diagnosticar el problema. Entre las opciones encontrarás el modo seguro de Windows, que es otra manera de arreglar Windows si ni funciona y no puedes acceder al escritorio con normalidad.
- Configuración de firmware UEFI. Si tienes algún problema con el arranque UEFI y su firmware, aquí podrás retocar su configuración. Asegúrate de que sabes lo que estás haciendo.
- Símbolo del sistema. Te da acceso a la línea de comandos de Windows. Está pensado para usuarios avanzados que conocen los comandos necesarios para realizar tareas de diagnóstico y reparación desde ahí.
- Restaurar sistema. Es similar a la opción de Restauración a un momento dado, pero sirve para elegir manualmente el punto de restauración guardado. Como vimos antes, si no activaste los puntos de restauración porque ocupan espacio en el disco, no te servirá de nada esta herramienta.
Y, para terminar, además de estas opciones de Windows RE, si haces clic en Ver más opciones de recuperación, podrás restaurar una imagen de Windows. Para ello, habrás tenido que crearla con anterioridad. Así que si no te suena de nada, tampoco te servirá para reparar Windows.
Iniciar Windows RE si Windows no funciona
Como vimos antes, puede que Windows RE se cargue automáticamente para realizar un diagnóstico y reparación del sistema si ha detectado algo con anterioridad. Así que en estos casos no tienes que hacer nada. Si no es así y necesitas reparar Windows, entonces hay dos maneras principales de acceder al menú de Windows RE y ver todas las herramientas que hemos explicado.
El método corto consiste en pulsar el botón del menú Inicio, hacer clic en el icono de Encendido y, manteniendo pulsada la tecla Mayúsculas, hacer clic en Reiniciar. Así, en vez de realizar un reinicio normal, activarás Windows RE en su lugar. También puedes activar Windows RE desde la línea de comandos utilizando el comando shutdown /r /o /f /t 00.
El método largo consiste en abrir Configuración de Windows. Lo encontrarás en el menú Inicio o pulsando las teclas Windows + i. Una vez ahí, ve a Sistema. Entra en Recuperación. Fíjate en la sección Opciones de recuperación. Ahora haz clic en el botón Reiniciar ahora, al lado de Inicio avanzado. De esta forma, Windows se reiniciará y se abrirá el menú de Windows RE. Si no encuentras la ruta concreta, puedes usar el buscador.

articles.title: AWS Introduces Preview of Well-Architected Agent
articles.text:
AWS recently announced the preview of the Well-Architected Agent, a service that analyzes environments against Well-Architected best practices and provides prioritized recommendations across cost, security, performance, and reliability. The AI agent can also suggest remediation steps and review infrastructure-as-code before deployment.
The AWS Well-Architected Agent correlates resource configurations, utilization metrics, application topology, and declared business goals to prioritize recommendations at the resource, application, and architecture levels, including trade-off analysis and remediation through CLI commands, IaC changes, and automation. The agent can also review Terraform and CloudFormation IaC before deployment. Channy Yun, lead blogger at AWS, writes:
It automatically correlates utilization metrics, resource configurations, and application topology, and analyzes against Well-Architected best practices across 65+ AWS services. It generates recommendations aligned to your declared business goals, delivers implementation packages with every finding, and surfaces cross-pillar trade-offs making it simpler to remediate the findings.
The Well-Architected Agent starts with an agent profile defining the accounts, regions, optimization pillars, and business goals. It then scans resources in the configured accounts and generates prioritized recommendations at the resource, application, and architecture levels for review and remediation. The agent analyzes infrastructure across cost optimization, security, resilience, and performance, and can also review IaC templates on demand.
The Well-Architected Agent uses application context and business goals to prioritize recommendations by impact and effort, providing findings at the resource, application, and architecture levels, including cost impacts and IaC changes. Yun adds:
You can also configure API access to integrate recommendations directly into your existing development and operations workflows. To interact with the agent programmatically, including calling APIs and searching documentation, try the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI coding tool.
Some practitioners have questioned trusting an AI agent with architectural recommendations, while others point to practical challenges in prioritizing recommendations based on business goals. Nicolas Payette, founder and CEO of Specira AI, writes:
Genuinely curious where the agent reads those goals from, because in most enterprises nobody ever wrote down whether a given workload should trade cost for resilience, and that's exactly the call a recommendation has to make.
Alex Kargin, senior data engineer at Silicon Army, warns:
The part I’d watch is the jump from recommendations to automation-ready fixes. Cloud optimization is full of tradeoffs. Saving money can hurt resilience, and improving performance can increase cost.
While the agent represents an evolution of the popular AWS Well-Architected Tool for evaluating cloud architectures, AWS warns that its AI-generated recommendations may contain errors or incomplete information and should be evaluated in the specific context with appropriate oversight and safeguards. In his newsletter, Corey Quinn, chief cloud economist at The Duckbill Group, writes:
"Evaluates your environment as an experienced cloud architect would," is now being offered through the magic of AI® to accounts that can't get a solutions architect on the phone. If this thing works, what are 5,000 undifferentiated AWS "Partners" left to do?
The agent is currently available only in three US regions, although workloads from any region worldwide can be onboarded. Furthermore, it is available only to customers with a Business Support+ plan or higher.

articles.title: Ofertas do Dia: iPhone 15, iPad Air M3, Eufy e Lenovo i7

articles.title: AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
articles.text:
AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München
- Summary:
- A new study reveals that people draw a surprisingly sharp line between human consciousness and artificial intelligence, even when both behave identically. Researchers found that participants considered even the most responsive AI less conscious than the least responsive human. Yet when asked about "awareness" instead, people judged humans and AI much more similarly.
- Share:
Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a new study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).
As artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading users, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common. These behaviors often lead people to describe AI as though it can think, feel, or make decisions for itself. But does behaving like a human actually convince people that a machine has consciousness?
New research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.
How Scientists Tested Perceptions of AI Consciousness
Published in the journal Cognition, the study was led by Dr. Louis Longin of LMU's Chair of Philosophy of Mind, working alongside Dr. Bahador Bahrami, Professor Ophelia Deroy, and other researchers.
"Whereas previous studies have typically asked general questions about whether AI actually has mental states, our study is the first to directly compare how people attribute the same mental states to AI and humans behaving in exactly the same way, under identical circumstances," says Longin.
"We may be using mental terms to refer to AI, but this may only be because we lack better words," says Ophelia Deroy, philosopher and a senior author of the study. "After all, AI is trained to act and speak like a human, so these descriptions seem natural."
To investigate how people judge consciousness, the researchers conducted experiments involving nearly 1,100 participants. One group read brief descriptions of artificial agents that showed different levels of responsiveness to their environments. For example, some agents reacted to sounds or recognized the emotional states of others.
Another group encountered the same situations, except the characters were described as humans rather than AI systems. Participants then evaluated how conscious or aware each character seemed to be of its surroundings.
A Surprising Gap Between Human and AI Consciousness
The experiments revealed that responsiveness influenced how participants judged both humans and artificial intelligence. Characters that reacted more actively to their surroundings were generally considered more conscious and more aware.
However, a striking difference emerged when participants evaluated consciousness specifically. Even the most responsive AI was rated as less conscious than the least responsive human. In other words, identical behavior did not lead people to assign the same level of consciousness to humans and machines.
The results changed considerably when participants were asked about awareness instead. For this characteristic, judgments of humans and AI followed largely similar patterns, suggesting that people interpret awareness and consciousness in fundamentally different ways.
"There is a growing worry in public discussion that people will see AI behaving in a human-like way and start treating these systems as if they had human-like mental states," says Longin, lead author of the study. "We found something much more nuanced: People are quite willing to say that an AI notices things and is aware of its surroundings. But they clearly draw a line when it comes to the term 'consciousness'. People consistently attribute less consciousness to AI than humans -- even when their behavior is identical."
Although people sometimes describe AI as conscious when discussing its actions, the findings indicate that they still distinguish between artificial systems and human minds.
Why One Word Changes How We Perceive AI
The researchers believe the difference between consciousness and awareness offers an important insight into how people understand artificial intelligence.
Awareness is a relatively neutral term that can describe an agent's ability to detect and respond to information in its environment. Consciousness, however, carries deeper implications about subjective experience and what it means to have an inner mental life.
Because awareness focuses more directly on observable behavior, people appear comfortable applying it to both humans and AI. Consciousness carries a different meaning, leading people to judge the two much less similarly.
The findings also highlight why the language used to discuss artificial intelligence matters, particularly as AI systems become increasingly capable of producing convincing human behavior.
"Our study teaches us lessons for how we communicate about AI," says Bahador Bahrami, who is also a senior author of the study and an expert in social neuroscience. "Companies and journalists often reach for hyped descriptions of AI models, and credit them with intentions, plans, or even moral conscience and hesitation. What our study shows is that everyday judgments are much more discriminating: People do not simply put AI and humans on the same mental scale. But the boundary also depends on which terms we use. For more neutral descriptors such as 'awareness', the distinction can largely disappear. That makes our choice of language important."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Louis Longin, Jurgis Karpus, Nadine Meertens, Bahador Bahrami, Ophelia Deroy. AI is not as conscious as humans: Essentialism in mental state attributions to artificial systems. Cognition, 2027; 278: 106733 DOI: 10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106733
