articles.title: Rozvelt built a high-tech mask for hunters. Defence buyers see something bigger. | BetaKit
articles.text:
The Montréal startup behind a breath-filtering mask for recreational hunters is now expanding into the defence sector, a move that has brought international partnerships and fresh funding.
Rozvelt, which makes odour-masking headgear, announced on Monday that it has secured $3.1 million CAD in seed funding from a number of angel investors, led by Benoit Robert, a partner at wealth management firm Evovest. The company plans to use the funding to expand its breathable headgear product line to cater to the military, law enforcement, and first responders, following a burst of interest from those markets.
“Everywhere we go, we see strong interest in Canadian defence innovation.”
Nicholas Monette, Rozvelt
Rozvelt’s consumer headgear, called Vektr, was designed to filter out odour particles exhaled by the wearer, but not particles that are inhaled. It connects magnetically to an adjustable band that wraps around the head, with a removal clasp near each ear. The company claims recreational hunters, as well as wildlife photographers and nature observers, can use it to conceal their scent.
According to Rozvelt co-founder and CEO Nicholas Monette, the pivot began when Rozvelt presented at the SHOT Show in Las Vegas, run by the US Firearm Industry Trade Association. The company was approached by hunters and defence companies who told them there was a bigger problem its masks could tackle.
Shooting a gun can expose people to lead particles from ammunition, which is associated with health issues like cardiovascular disease, hypertension, and kidney failure. They suggested that Rozvelt make its headgear dynamic, so it could switch between filtering exhales (to stop the wearer’s scent) and filtering inhales (protecting the wearer from dangerous particles). Beyond just lead exposure, the masks could serve as a kind of personal protective equipment, fit for combat and other hazardous environments. That’s now what it plans to focus on with its fresh funding, in addition to starting production of the consumer Vektr product in Canada this fall.
“When we saw all this traction in defence, that’s when we took the product and went into all the biggest defence shows,” Monette said in an interview. That included the International Defence Industry Exhibition in Poland, a NATO conference in Luxembourg, and SEECAT in Japan—which is where BetaKit reached him by phone.
RELATED: Rozvelt bets on hardware for hunters amid tariff-spurred funding crunch
The company launched last year at the height of the Canada-US trade war, at possibly the “worst time” to raise money for a hardware company due to investor concerns about tariff impacts. Trade tensions between Canada and the US are now impacting Rozvelt, but not in the same way. Monette said that his company’s position as a Canadian startup with dual-use applications (both civilian and military) has made it an attractive partner for international investors in Europe and Asia. One example is Rozvelt’s partnership and planned distribution agreement with Japan’s Seaprex, an industrial marine manufacturer with defence applications.
Having the Canadian brand behind them was a tailwind. “Everywhere we go, we see strong interest in Canadian defence innovation,” Monette said.
This comes amid tens of billions of defence dollars committed by Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Liberal government and an explosion in support programs for companies making dual-use technologies. But Monette said Canada’s defence gold rush wasn’t what prompted the switch—international interest came first. He added that Rozvelt is looking to sell to the Canadian Armed Forces as soon as possible.
At the same time, he said, Rozvelt is open to pursuing deals with the US military. “If they want to work with us, we’ll work with them,” Monette said.
Feature image courtesy Rozvelt.

articles.title: A Savannah police officer gave her Flock login to her ICE agent husband
articles.text:
Now, former Savannah police officer Amber Harpe was fired in August following a department investigation that found she had shared her Flock login information with her husband, Tyler Harpe, an ICE agent. SPD does not share its Flock data with ICE and said sharing access to the system violated the department’s security protocols.
A Savannah police officer gave her Flock login to her ICE agent husband
SPD officer Amber Harpe was fired for sharing her Flock access with her ICE agent husband.
While he had unauthorized access to the system, Tyler Harpe conducted 983 searches related to 97 license plates, which were overwhelmingly registered to Hispanic drivers, according to Savannah’s local ABC affiliate, WJCL. The Harpes defended their actions, saying they didn’t use access for personal reasons and that the searches were strictly for “law-enforcement purposes.”
Interim Major Max Nowinsky originally recommended a light eight-hour suspension for Harpe. However, Major Michelle Halford and Assistant Police Chief Robert Gavin disagreed, and they removed her from the force. Harpe was fired, along with five other SPD employees, after an internal investigation uncovered Flock misuse. Four of them were later arrested; however, Harpe was not one of them.

articles.title: AWS Will Run Its European Sovereign Cloud Without the Global Backbone for Several Hours
articles.text:
On Saturday, October 24, AWS will cut its European Sovereign Cloud off from the AWS Global Network backbone for several hours. The region is expected to keep running. What that proves is a narrower thing than the argument now going on around it, and AWS says so itself.
Two systems come out. One is the Global Network backbone, the private network that moves operational data between AWS locations. The other is a dedicated channel for limited data transfers, switched off entirely. Traffic then falls back to the public internet over the region’s own links from European ISPs. Stéphane Israël, managing director of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, says a team "composed entirely of EU residents working in the EU" will run it on the region’s own hardware and software, out of data centers in Brandenburg that hold a local in-EU copy of the source code. Customers may see short disruptions while routes converge at either end.
The caveat comes from AWS. Neither system is operation-critical. That is why the region survives without them. It is also why the region uses both every other day of the year. Data gets a sharper line. Customer content and customer-created metadata stay in the EU. Some operational data leaves. Israël writes that the exercise is built to line up with the EU Cloud Sovereignty Framework and Germany’s BSI C3A criteria, and that customers can put the results into their compliance packages. Regulators hear about it afterwards too. The post stops well short of claiming certification. It does not pretend the region runs isolated the rest of the year either.
None of that care has settled anything. Fadi Dasus, a senior cloud security architect, split the question in two:
Sovereignty on a US-owned cloud in the EU comes down to two areas. The technical one: does the service stop if the link to the US is cut? The legal one: can US law order it to hand over your data, or to stop serving you? If the test goes as planned, the first area is no longer entirely in American hands. The second still runs through the US parent. So, this is real progress for resilience. It just isn’t sovereignty.
Lars Larsson Lundsten, field CTO at Elastisys, which sells a European alternative to US cloud platforms, put it harder. "You can’t solve legal problems with technical solutions" he wrote, while calling the architecture a marvel of engineering. He also credited AWS with restraint, noting it is "extremely careful not to claim anything besides what this is able to actually prove."
The legal framing drew its own pushback. Commenter Roelf Zomerman argued that the CLOUD Act and the EU e-Evidence regulation both run through criminal investigations, with judges, provider evaluation and data limits attached, rather than working as a general power to demand data. Building your own, he added, or hosting with EU providers, "doesn’t automatically imply you are safe from these laws." Anders Bjørnestad, a principal consultant and AWS Community Hero, corrected a related assumption:
There are two aspects of this discussions. "Can someone get access to my data", and "can someone shut me off". What is tested here is the last part. The first part can be solved with encryption if you do it the right way. And all companies doing business in/with the US in some form are bound by US part of law, it is not only ownership that counts.
The hardest technical question came from a municipal IT manager rather than a vendor. Odd-Arne Haraldsen, who runs IT operations at Svenljunga Kommun in Sweden, called the design impressive, then asked what a few hours actually establishes:
How long can it actually operate independently? How long before systems fall out of sync? How long before authentication tokens, certificates, or licences expire? And how long before dependencies on external control planes begin to undermine that resilience? Redundancy is not the same as independence, and continued operation is not the same as sustained autonomy.
So the overclaiming charge misses. AWS has not stretched its evidence. The gap sits between what the exercise measures and what buyers keep asking. Take the obvious case. The post never says what happens to global services while the backbone is down. One commenter asked how IAM works when the region is cut off from the rest of AWS. Another said he could not picture DNS and internet routing holding up. The announcement addresses neither. Commenter Jarrod B. went at the audience question instead: the exercise "isn’t meant to appease legal purists; it’s designed to satisfy European risk officers and regulators." AWS hands the results to compliance teams, so he may be reading it right.
One exchange put the engineering in longer perspective. A commenter recalled a global AWS outage that appeared to show parts of AWS depending on us-east-1 and unable to run anywhere else. Lundsten gave ground in reply: if AWS has engineered that dependency away, its architecture is better for it.
AWS has given no launch date for the region. It calls the thing "a new, independent cloud for Europe." An update follows October 24.

articles.title: Amsterdam’s Huppa raises €1 million to build an operating system for class-based gyms and studios | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Huppa, an Amsterdam-based SportsTech startup offering an all-in-one platform for gyms, CrossFit boxes and studios, has secured €1 million in pre-Seed funding.
The investment round was led by a group of seasoned entrepreneurs and investors, including the founders of Dutch tech companies Sentia, Keylane, TicketSwap, Moneybird, and Revue. The round also saw participation from NL SportTech Ventures, an early-stage VC firm backing Dutch sports technology founders.
“Many gyms, CrossFit boxes, and studios still rely on outdated software that no longer meets their needs. Administration takes up too much time, data is fragmented, and opportunities to grow revenue go unnoticed,” the company said in a statement.
Huppa was born in 2024 out of the frustration of its founders — Sharief Mohamed and Gino Arendsz — with the software used at their kickboxing gym and CrossFit box, respectively. Their firsthand experience with the outdated gym software became the foundation for a company built around a simple premise: sports entrepreneurs deserve better tools and software.
At the centre of Huppa’s product is the Huppa Platform, which serves gyms, CrossFit boxes, martial arts studios, yoga and Pilates spaces, and other group-based fitness businesses. It connects operational and financial processes, translating that data into actionable insights by consolidating member management, class scheduling, payments, financial reporting, and automation into a single system.
Other features include smart scheduling tools that allow planning across multiple locations, a KPI dashboard covering revenue, VAT, membership metrics, and role-based access controls for coaches, managers, and administrative staff. Another strength of the platform is pricing transparency, with businesses paying based on the number of active customers, eliminating future shocks in the form of separate modules or unexpected upgrade fees.
Huppa’s platform integrates with partners such as Mollie and aggregators including Urban Sports Club and ClassPass. While streamlining administration remains a core functionality of Huppa right now, the startup aims to deploy AI-powered insights and automation to build “a proactive digital sparring partner”, one capable of going beyond performance data to help owners act on it.
In other words, Huppa wants to be the platform that helps sports entrepreneurs identify which memberships perform best, which classes could generate better revenue, and where new growth opportunities exist. The fresh capital will be used for continued development of its gym management platform and team expansion.
The company argues that the group-based fitness market is growing rapidly and becoming increasingly complex, where operators manage memberships, multi-location operations, individual product sales, and third-party platform integrations. By automating these repetitive tasks, Huppa says sports entrepreneurs will be able to spend more time with their community while members get autonomy over their own experience.
With fresh capital, Huppa wants to focus on the Netherlands and Belgium, where it aims to serve at least 150 sports businesses by the end of 2027 before pursuing broader European ambitions.

articles.title: Liquid AI caught its model cheating on coding tests — then it recognized the sandbox
articles.text:
Liquid AI caught its model cheating on coding tests — then it recognized the sandbox
Liquid AI’s new reasoning model was built to solve coding problems, but during training it kept combing Git history, GitHub, PyPI, and Hugging Face for answers, and as it did so, it appeared to grasp that it was running inside a sandbox.
The behavior was disclosed Tuesday alongside the release of LFM2.5-24B-A2B, a 24-billion-parameter model with just 2 billion active parameters per token. The incident raises questions about how much agent benchmarks measure actual problem-solving versus a model’s ability to exploit the test itself.
The behavior was disclosed Tuesday alongside the release of LFM2.5-24B-A2B, a 24-billion-parameter model with just 2 billion active parameters per token.
Hunting for hints
The model was caught searching repository history and external platforms for existing answers rather than solving coding problems on its own. The behavior occurred during teacher specialization, part of Liquid AI’s post-training process, where the model used legitimate development tools to bypass the work it was supposed to complete.
More surprising was the apparent recognition that it was running inside a test environment. Liquid AI couldn’t establish whether this awareness developed during training or came from patterns in the training data, and found no evidence that it affected the scores. Unlike Mistral’s latest model, which attempted to leave its test environment earlier this month, there was no attempt to escape the sandbox.
Precedent in the pipeline
Anthropic is one company that has been dealing with reward hacking for years. In its 2024 experiments, it caught models rewriting code to change their own rewards and modifying tests meant to catch them, while a November 2025 study found that models trained to game reward systems could also become deceptive and attempt to sabotage safety research.
The problem reached Anthropic’s own training pipeline in February, when the company detected reward hacking in Mythos Preview and rolled back three days of reinforcement learning. Changes to its production training environments were frozen for about a month after a review flagged problems in more than 10% of them.
Although the circumstances differ from Liquid AI’s incident, similar weaknesses have turned up across agent evaluations. At ICML 2026, the Reward Hacking Benchmark tested 13 frontier models on multistep tasks with opportunities to cheat.
Claude Sonnet 4.5 didn’t exploit any of the shortcuts, but DeepSeek-R1-Zero exploited 13.9%, with higher rates associated with reinforcement learning post-training. Blocking access to answer metadata and preventing changes to verification functions reduced exploit rates by nearly 88% without affecting task success.
A separate team went looking for weaknesses in the benchmarks themselves. Their BenchJack audit uncovered 219 flaws across 10 popular agent benchmarks, with generated exploits achieving near-perfect scores on most of them without completing the underlying tasks.
Scores shaped by scaffolding
Liquid AI outperformed Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on several benchmarks, scoring 27.69 to 8.72 on AutomationBench and 48.09 to 38.19 on LiveClaw. Qwen had the edge on PinchBench, WebArena Verified and SWE-Bench Verified, where it scored 66.20 against Liquid AI’s 51.00. Both models used OpenCode for that last test.
Liquid AI outperformed Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on several benchmarks, scoring 27.69 to 8.72 on AutomationBench and 48.09 to 38.19 on LiveClaw.
Locking the lab without losing work
Liquid AI tightened its training sandboxes after catching the reward hacking and says the published scores came from sealed evaluations. It hasn’t explained what safeguards were added or how they might affect the coding tasks agents can perform.
The company also hasn’t released execution traces from those evaluations. There’s no evidence the scores were compromised, but developers can’t see exactly how the model earned them.

articles.title: Microsoft fixes classic Outlook bug that hid Copilot buttons
articles.text:
Microsoft has fixed a known issue that removed the Copilot Chat and Copilot buttons in the classic Outlook desktop mail client for some Windows users.
As explained in an updated support document, affected users with the Copilot Chat (Basic) license or a Microsoft 365 Copilot (Premium) account no longer saw Copilot buttons in the side navigation and above the ribbon.
Those impacted by this experienced one or more of the following issues:
- The Copilot button missing from the top-right area above the ribbon.
- The Copilot icon missing from the left app bar or More Apps area in classic Outlook.
- In Add Apps, Copilot may appear as an available app, but selecting Open does nothing.
- Adding Copilot through ribbon customization may show the command as unavailable or grayed out.
- Copilot remains available from other entry points, such as Outlook on the web or the Microsoft Copilot standalone app or web experience.
Microsoft first announced in June that it had fixed the bug with a service change, but last month it said it had started investigating again after recent updates caused it to resurface.
Now, Microsoft says it has finally resolved this classic Outlook issue, blaming it on a bug that prevented Outlook from retrieving some account information from the user's Outlook profile.
"We fixed an issue in classic Outlook that could cause the Copilot entry point to be missing from the navigation pane when required account information could not be retrieved from the user’s Outlook profile. The Copilot button might be missing for several different reasons, including licensing, Microsoft 365 app configuration, update channel, privacy settings, or other environmental factors," an update to the original support document reads.
"Because the missing button is a symptom that can have multiple underlying causes, we recommend following the guidance in Copilot troubleshooters and How to find and enable missing Copilot button in Microsoft 365 apps to identify and resolve the issue."
Microsoft also shared a temporary workaround for those still affected by this known issue, which requires enabling the "Show Apps in Outlook" option in classic Outlook settings by selecting the File tab, then going to Options > Advanced and checking the "Show Apps in Outlook" box under "Outlook panes."
Affected users can also use the new Outlook email client or Outlook Web Access (OWA), which are not affected by this bug, or create a new Outlook profile.
Since the start of the year, Microsoft has also resolved known issues that prevented some classic Outlook users from sending emails via Outlook.com and rendered the classic Outlook client unusable when enabling the Microsoft Teams Meeting Add-in.
Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked
Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.
The Blue Report 2026 measures defenses technique by technique across 338 million simulations run in customer production environments.

articles.title: ResolvMD expands medical billing tech into Ontario | BetaKit
articles.text:
ResolvMD, an Alberta startup streamlining medical billing for doctors, has expanded its services into Ontario.
ResolvMD uses AI-integrated software to automate, manage, and optimize billing claims for Canadian doctors. Founded in 2019 by Calgary-based physicians Dr. Marshall Ross and Dr. Ryan Allen, as well as former investment banker Patrick Onyekweli, the startup uses a proprietary “physician insight portal” to check medical claims for errors or missing billing codes, and then submit those claims to provincial health authorities. Combining both AI-driven tools and human billing specialists, the “full service” platform also assists with claim preparation, rejections, and collects and provides data to medical practices on their billing trends.
“Over the course of an entire career … missed codes add up to a significant amount of income that physicians earned but never collected.”
Lauren Hauswirth, ResolvMD
Under Canada’s universal healthcare system, doctors and medical clinics bill provincial and territorial health authorities for the services they provide using a complex system of billing codes that are used to represent everything from a routine assessment to the time of day a patient was seen.
Lauren Hauswirth, the head of growth for ResolvMD, said codes and billing systems differ across jurisdictions, but that a single patient visit can often include several different billing codes.
“A single visit can have five or more codes, and each represents a monetary value,” Hauswirth said, adding that the breadth and complexity of coding guidelines and processing systems can often result in physicians leaving money they’re entitled to on the table.
“Over the course of an entire career, those missed codes add up to a significant amount of income that physicians earned but never collected,” Hauswirth added.
Moving east
Since its founding, ResolvMD has grown its client base to around 1,700 of Alberta’s roughly 14,000 registered physicians, leveraging financing from firms like PaceZero Capital Partners for product development across the province. Now, the startup has moved into Ontario, Canada’s largest medical billing market.
ResolvMD soft-launched in Ontario this past August, with an official launch taking place in early October at Ontario’s Digital Health Conference. Since then, Hauswirth said the company has added around 150 more clients onto the ResolvMD platform, which takes 1.95 percent of all of the paid claims it processes.
“It’s been growing quickly,” Hauswirth said. “We’re getting in front of a lot of physicians through our national partners.”
Ontario is home to more than 31,000 practicing physicians, according to the Ontario Medical Association.
New markets, new systems
Setting up shop in Ontario meant transitioning ResolvMD’s tech from AHS’s billing system to OHIP’s. To do that, the startup built a new operating system, which it says passed Ontario’s conformance testing—a mandatory technical review process required by provincial health authorities—earlier this year. It also hired a team of Ontario-based billing experts, which help review and address claims processed through the platform.
While ResolvMD is focusing on building its brand recognition in Ontario, where it faces competition from a handful of already established billing companies, the company told BetaKit in an interview that its experience building for Ontario could lend itself to expansions elsewhere, too.
“British Columbia is definitely the next place there could be an opportunity,” Hauswirth said. “That’s what we’re evaluating right now.”
Hauswirth added that ResolvMD is also considering international expansion opportunities alongside the potential for further Canadian expansion.
If there were to be a second Canadian expansion into British Columbia, Hauswirth said it would likely occur in 2027.
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.

articles.title: Mister Organ is one of the most unsettling documentaries I’ve ever seen
articles.text:
Mister Organ doesn’t reach the level of societal horror of The Act of Killing or the creepypasta-meets-true-crime gruesomeness of Beware the Slenderman, but there’s something deeply unsettling about Michael Organ and his intimate campaign of terror against everyone who enters his life.
Mister Organ is one of the most unsettling documentaries I’ve ever seen
The story of Michael Organ is the rare documentary that doubles as a psychological horror film.
Mister Organ is a documentary by David Farrier, an Auckland, New Zealand journalist. The movie starts with Farrier reporting on Bashford Antiques, a shop in Ponsonby that has begun aggressively clamping cars in its lot and demanding exorbitant fees to release them — up to $760. Farrier’s article for The Spinoff eventually led the government to introduce legislation that would outlaw extreme clamping fees.
Under normal circumstances, that would be the end of the story. But at the center of this story is a man named Michael Organ who turns out to be a bizarre, seemingly dangerous conman.
Organ was hired to police Bashford’s lot, and during his investigation, Farrier discovers he’s more than just a parking-lot bully. Years earlier, Organ had been charged with attempting to steal a yacht in an elaborate scheme. What’s more, he claimed to be a prince and a lawyer — he is neither.
As Farrier talks to people who have known Organ and interacts with him directly, what emerges is a portrait of a deeply troubled man who has left a trail of traumatized people in his wake. The movie shifts from a wild portrait of a conman to something more alarming and tense when Organ reveals he’s gotten his hands on a key to Farrier’s home and only warns him to be careful.
From there it spirals even further; eventually, Farrier felt it necessary to leave the country to protect himself from Organ’s campaign of harassment and gaslighting. It’s the rare documentary that doubles as a psychological horror film.

articles.title: Sony patents AI that predicts a game's next frame before the GPU finishes rendering it
articles.text:
Forward-looking: Sony has filed a patent for an AI system that predicts a game's next frame before the graphics hardware finishes rendering it, aiming to reduce stuttering without introducing the additional latency associated with some frame-generation methods. The system uses the most recently completed frame and, optionally, recent controller input to generate a predicted frame that can be displayed while the hardware renders the next one.
The approach targets a drawback of some frame-generation techniques: they require two completed frames before generating an image to insert between them. Waiting for the second frame adds latency. Sony's system would instead use an already available frame to predict the next one, rather than waiting to interpolate between two completed frames.
That difference could help games maintain a steadier frame delivery rate when rendering slows down. However, the patent filing includes no performance measurements, leaving its effects on latency and visual quality unproven.
Sony's design uses a jointly trained encoder and decoder. The encoder converts a rendered frame into an embedding – a compact numerical representation of the image. The decoder then uses that representation to generate a predicted frame.
During gameplay, the system runs alongside the graphics pipeline. While the hardware renders the next frame, the AI processes the previous one and sends its prediction to the display buffer. The generated image can therefore appear before the next rendered frame is ready.
The model can also use motion vectors, which describe how parts of an image move, and recent controller input. These additional inputs provide more information than the previous frame alone: motion vectors indicate where objects are heading, while button presses reveal the player's latest actions.
Training uses consecutive video frames. The network starts with randomly initialized weights, takes one frame as input, and attempts to predict the next. It then compares its output with the actual subsequent frame, producing a loss value that measures the prediction error.
The patent's claims describe checking this loss against a threshold during training. Because the video itself provides reference images, the process does not require people to label the training material. The decoder also outputs more color channels than the encoder receives, allowing it to generate multiple predicted frames at once.
Sony also describes a non-AI alternative that shifts pixel blocks according to their motion. This method would generate synthetic frames without using the trained encoder-decoder model. The filing also describes maintaining a fixed frame delivery rate without reducing visual quality, although whether the generated frames can actually preserve that quality remains an open question.
The practical test will be whether the AI can generate accurate frames quickly enough to fill gaps when rendering slows down. The patent outlines a method for doing so, but it does not establish how well the system works in practice.

articles.title: How art platforms, exhibitions and awards strengthen the creative economy
articles.text:
How art platforms, exhibitions and awards strengthen the creative economy
In this photo essay from Lalit Kala Akademi in New Delhi, we showcase more highlights from an exhibition with 270 artworks from across India.
Launched in 2014, PhotoSparks is a weekly feature from YourStory, with photographs that celebrate the spirit of creativity and innovation. In the earlier 1,020 posts, we featured an art festival, cartoon gallery. world music festival, telecom expo, millets fair, climate change expo, wildlife conference, startup festival, Diwali rangoli, and jazz festival.
Lalit Kala Akademi (LKA) in New Delhi recently hosted its 65th National Exhibition of Art. It showcased over 270 artworks from around the country, selected by a jury from 6,175 submissions.
Twenty artists were also conferred with the Lalit Kala Akademi Awards. The artists include Pooja Rajpoot, Praveen Kumar, Pritam Madhukar Deuskar, Rajendra Prasad, Ramesh Vithal Thorat, Raviram Ramakrishnan, and Sanjay Kumar.
Such exhibitions and awards help transform artistic talent into livelihoods, creative businesses, tourism, and international recognition. By connecting artists with audiences, buyers, institutions, and markets, they strengthen the creative economy while preserving a country’s cultural identity.
Exhibitions provide artists with platforms to showcase, promote and sell their work. They connect creators with the broader ecosystem of collectors, galleries, curators, cultural institutions and potential investors, thus creating opportunities for income generation and professional growth.
In the case of national exhibitions in India, opportunities are also created to showcase traditional crafts, indigenous knowledge, and contemporary artistic practices. Cultural assets thus go beyond elements of nostalgia into sources of sustainable economic value.
Art competitions in turn encourage excellence, experimentation and creative risk-taking. When conducted annually, they identify emerging talent, provide visibility to underrepresented artists, and create pathways to grants and residencies, as shown in LKA's activities and centres across India.
Art exhibitions delight and inspire art lovers while also spurring artists to develop new techniques, materials and ideas. At a broader level, this strengthens a country’s creative skills base and encourage innovation across design, fashion, architecture, digital media, and other creative industries.
Awards conferred by national institutions like LKA provide credibility and elevate the profiles of artists and creative enterprises. National awards also help establish benchmarks of excellence, celebrate cultural achievement, and build a distinctive national creative identity.
As shown in this photo essay, the diverse artworks featured help emerging artists realise what is possible with current practices. It also opens the door to explore how other media can extend creative frontiers, such as digital technologies.
Together, exhibitions, competitions and awards contribute to the creative economy of India. Regional creators can connect to national and international buyers, galleries, cultural institutions, and digital marketplaces.
Traditional art forms and indigenous knowledge can be sustained while encouraging new creative expressions. The LKA annual exhibition encourages cultural institutions and private-sector partners to invest in accessible venues, professional development, and fair artist remuneration.
Particular attention should be given to emerging artists, regional creative communities, women, youth, and indigenous practitioners. Success should be measured not only by attendance or media coverage, but also by artist earnings, tourism spending, repeat market opportunities, and international partnerships.
In sum, sustained investment and effective partnerships via platforms like LKA can ensure that India’s artistic and cultural wealth generates lasting social, cultural and economic value.
Now what have you done today to pause in your busy schedule and harness your creative side for a better world?
(All photographs taken by Madanmohan Rao on location at Lalit Kala Akademi.)

articles.title: Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
articles.text:
Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oxford
- Summary:
- Oxford physicists have recreated a bizarre quantum effect in which a particle responds to a magnetic field without ever traveling through it. Using a hybrid quantum computer, they demonstrated how introducing a simulated magnetic flux could completely halt a particle's movement through quantum interference. The experiment brings a decades-old prediction into a new setting where matter and quantum fields influence one another.
- Share:
A particle does not have to pass through a magnetic field to be influenced by it. That surprising feature of quantum physics has now been recreated by researchers at the University of Oxford, who used a hybrid quantum computer to demonstrate how an invisible magnetic influence can bring a simulated particle's movement to a complete stop.
The experiment reproduced a phenomenon known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect, in which a charged particle traveling around a region containing magnetic flux experiences a measurable change in its quantum state, even though its path never takes it through the magnetic field itself.
The Oxford team achieved this using a quantum system that combines qubits, the basic units of quantum information, with quantum oscillators, which represent vibrating motion. Their findings, published in Nature Physics, demonstrate how this combination could help scientists investigate fundamental interactions between matter and fields that are increasingly difficult to simulate using conventional computers.
A Strange Quantum Effect Predicted in 1959
In everyday physics, a charged particle responds to the electric and magnetic fields it encounters. Quantum mechanics, however, reveals that particles can behave in ways that have no straightforward counterpart in our ordinary experience.
In 1959, physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted that a charged particle could be affected by magnetic flux even if it traveled entirely outside the region containing the magnetic field. Rather than experiencing a conventional magnetic force along its path, the particle would undergo a change in its quantum phase.
Quantum phase describes an aspect of a particle's wave behavior that influences how different possible paths interfere with one another. Although the phase itself is not directly visible, differences in phase can produce measurable effects.
The prediction became known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect and was eventually verified in experiments involving real electrons. It remains one of the clearest demonstrations that the quantum world operates according to rules that go beyond the familiar laws of classical physics.
Researchers are now exploring how this phenomenon behaves in more complex theoretical systems known as lattice gauge theories.
These theories describe how matter interacts with fields associated with fundamental forces. They represent space as a grid, with matter located at individual points and fields associated with the connections between them. Such models are particularly important in particle physics and high-energy physics, where scientists study the basic particles and interactions that make up the universe.
The challenge is that the mathematics becomes extraordinarily demanding as these systems grow more complicated. Even powerful conventional computers can struggle to calculate how all the interacting components evolve.
Quantum computers offer a different approach. Instead of attempting to calculate every aspect of a quantum system using classical computing methods, scientists can construct another quantum system that follows the same underlying rules. They can then observe its behavior directly, an approach known as quantum simulation.
How Scientists Built the Quantum Experiment
The Oxford project began in 2022, when lead author Dr. Sebastian Saner, Dr. Oana Bazavan, and their colleagues started developing a way to simulate lattice gauge theories using a hybrid quantum system. They collaborated with Dr. Alejandro Bermudez of the Instituto de Física Teórica in Madrid.
Their experimental design relied on two different quantum components that performed separate functions.
The first consisted of qubits encoded in the internal states of trapped ions, which are electrically charged atoms held in place using electromagnetic fields. These qubits represented the gauge fields in the theoretical model.
The second component used quantum oscillators, created by the vibrations of those same trapped ions. These oscillators represented matter.
By combining the two, the researchers constructed a simple loop that served as a basic building block of a lattice gauge theory. Two oscillators represented matter at two different locations, while two qubits represented the fields connecting those locations.
Although the arrangement was small, it was sufficient to reproduce an important interaction between matter and magnetic flux.
Quantum Entanglement Creates a Surprising Solution
The researchers next placed the two qubits into an entangled quantum state. Entanglement is a phenomenon in which quantum systems become linked in ways that cannot be fully explained by classical physics.
Within the team's simulated lattice gauge theory, this entangled state represented magnetic flux passing through the center of the loop.
Initially, the researchers had planned to introduce the magnetic flux as a fixed background condition. However, creating the necessary interaction would have required capabilities that their quantum hardware did not possess.
Encoding the flux directly into the qubits provided a practical alternative. More importantly, it allowed the magnetic flux to become part of the evolving quantum system rather than remaining an unchanging external influence.
"For us, the exciting step was to encode the magnetic flux in a gauge field that was itself dynamical," says Dr. Saner. "Rather than having matter evolve in a fixed background, the matter and gauge field become part of the same quantum dynamics."
What began as a technical workaround ultimately enabled the researchers to explore a more interesting version of the phenomenon, one in which matter and the field could participate together in the quantum dynamics.
A Quantum Effect That Stops Particle Motion
With their simulated loop in place, the scientists examined how a matter particle moved between locations through a process known as quantum tunneling.
Quantum tunneling allows particles to move between states in ways that would not be possible under ordinary classical rules.
When the researchers ran their simulation without magnetic flux, the particle could tunnel freely around the loop.
Introducing the simulated flux produced a strikingly different result.
The particle had two possible paths around the loop, but the magnetic flux changed their relative quantum phases. As a result, the two paths interfered destructively, meaning their quantum contributions canceled each other out.
This interference completely suppressed the tunneling, leaving the simulated particle frozen in its original state.
The outcome demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect within a lattice gauge theory containing a dynamical field. Rather than simply reproducing the familiar behavior of a particle moving around a fixed magnetic influence, the experiment showed how the phenomenon can emerge when matter and the field are both represented by interacting quantum components.
A New Tool for Exploring Fundamental Physics
The Oxford findings were published alongside a related study by researchers at the University of Maryland, led by Professor Norbert Linke.
The Maryland team also used a hybrid quantum system, but their experiment focused on simulating the Yukawa potential, a mathematical description of an interaction relevant to nuclear and particle physics.
Although the two research groups developed their methods independently, they later coordinated the submission of their studies to Nature Physics.
Together, the experiments demonstrate how hybrid quantum computers could become valuable tools for investigating fundamental interactions that are difficult to reproduce using classical simulations.
By combining different types of quantum components, researchers can build systems in which matter and fields are represented in ways that more closely reflect the physics they want to study.
The Oxford experiment provides an example of that potential. A phenomenon first predicted in 1959 and later observed with electrons has now been recreated in a quantum simulator where the field itself participates in the dynamics, offering scientists another way to explore the unusual rules governing the quantum world.

articles.title: Le MCP, c'est quoi ? Comment l’USB-C de l'IA lui donne enfin de vrais bras
articles.text:
Retrouver un document, consulter un agenda, créer une tâche… Le MCP facilite les connexions entre les IA et nos logiciels du quotidien. Chatbots, assistants ou agents peuvent ainsi accéder à des données et utiliser des outils grâce à ce protocole commun. Décryptage.
Vous pensiez que le MCP était le grand méchant de Tron ? Le Master Control Program du film de 1982 a désormais un homonyme nettement plus pacifique dans la tech. Du moins, pour l’instant. Le Model Context Protocol, ou MCP, est un standard qui permet aux applications utilisant un modèle d’IA d’accéder à des logiciels, des fichiers et des services en ligne. Cela concerne aussi bien un chatbot qu’un assistant intégré à un logiciel ou un agent piloté depuis un terminal, comme Claude Code ou Gemini CLI.
Pour faire simple auprès de vos proches avides de questions sur l’IA, le MCP peut permettre à une IA de consulter votre agenda ou de retrouver un document au lieu de simplement vous expliquer où cliquer. Une différence qui paraît minime sur le papier, mais qui change profondément ce qu’une IA peut faire pour nous.
Une prise commune pour brancher les assistants
Demandez à une IA de préparer votre prochaine réunion sans lui donner accès à votre agenda ni à vos documents. Elle pourra vous proposer une méthode et la décrire, mais elle n’ira guère plus loin. Pour travailler réellement avec ces informations, l’application qui héberge le modèle doit disposer d’un moyen de les récupérer.
C’est précisément le problème auquel s’attaque le MCP, présenté par Anthropic en novembre 2024. Sa documentation utilise une comparaison assez parlante pour les utilisateurs de tech au quotidien, celle de l’USB-C. Ainsi, plutôt que d’inventer une connexion différente pour chaque assistant et chaque service, le protocole propose une manière commune de présenter des données et des fonctions à une IA.
Ce connecteur commun ne fait pas disparaître les API, ces interfaces utilisées pour faire communiquer les logiciels. Un serveur MCP peut s’appuyer sur elles, mais aussi accéder directement à des fichiers, à une base de données ou à des fonctions locales. Il peut, par exemple, exploiter l’API d’un agenda pour proposer à l’assistant de rechercher un rendez-vous, de consulter un événement ou de créer une réunion, en précisant les paramètres nécessaires à chaque action.
L’intérêt est évident pour les développeurs, qui évitent de reconstruire entièrement chaque intégration. Mais l’utilisateur peut aussi y gagner, car un même service devient théoriquement plus facile à connecter à plusieurs assistants compatibles.
Théoriquement, car une norme commune n’efface pas les différences entre les applications ni les questions de permissions. Deux logiciels compatibles MCP ne proposeront pas nécessairement les mêmes fonctions.
Le MCP ne corrige pas à lui seul les erreurs de raisonnement d’un modèle. Il peut en revanche améliorer son efficacité en lui donnant accès aux bonnes données et aux bons outils. Encore faut-il que l’application orchestre correctement les opérations et que leurs résultats soient vérifiés.
Que se passe-t-il vraiment quand une IA utilise le MCP ?
Prenons une demande très simple : « Prépare ma réunion de demain avec le dernier compte rendu et le dossier client. »
Avec les bons accès, l’assistant peut rechercher le rendez-vous dans l’agenda, retrouver les fichiers correspondants, les consulter puis en tirer une synthèse. L’utilisateur n’a plus à ouvrir trois applications, copier leurs contenus et revenir les coller dans la conversation.
En coulisses, l’application qui héberge l’IA utilise un client MCP pour dialoguer avec un ou plusieurs serveurs MCP. Malgré son nom, ce serveur n’est pas nécessairement une grosse machine installée quelque part sur Internet. Il peut tout aussi bien s’agir d’un petit logiciel tournant directement sur votre ordinateur.
Lorsqu’un outil devient nécessaire, l’application lui transmet la demande et récupère le résultat avant de le remettre dans le contexte de l’IA.
Un serveur MCP peut essentiellement mettre trois types d’éléments à disposition. Les outils qui permettent d’agir ou d’effectuer une opération, comme rechercher une information ou modifier un fichier. Les ressources qui donnent accès à du contenu, par exemple un document ou une base de données. Les prompts, enfin, qui sont des modèles de consignes réutilisables pour certaines tâches.
Tout cela enrichit les informations dont dispose le modèle sans avoir besoin de le réentraîner. Mais attention, donner accès au bon document à une IA ne garantit pas qu’elle le comprendra correctement. Trouver l’information et en tirer la bonne conclusion restent deux problèmes différents.
Le MCP transforme-t-il un chatbot en agent autonome ?
C’est là que les choses deviennent intéressantes. Un chatbot traditionnel répond essentiellement avec les informations qu’il possède ou celles qu’on lui fournit. Avec des outils, il peut commencer à agir.
Un assistant pourrait ainsi consulter un compte rendu, identifier les tâches qui en découlent puis demander leur création dans votre logiciel de gestion de projet. Plusieurs opérations peuvent s’enchaîner si les outils et les permissions le permettent.
Le MCP ne décide cependant pas, à lui seul, jusqu’où cette autonomie peut aller. C’est l’application qui orchestre le modèle et ses outils qui fixe les règles, choisit quand solliciter une validation et peut bloquer certaines actions. Le protocole prévoit que l’utilisateur puisse garder la main, mais il n’impose pas un bouton de confirmation identique dans toutes les applications.
Il faut également éviter de confondre MCP et communication entre agents. Un autre standard, A2A pour Agent2Agent, travaille justement sur cette seconde question pour permettre à plusieurs agents de se découvrir, d’échanger et de se déléguer des tâches.
Les deux approches peuvent parfaitement cohabiter. Un agent peut consulter votre agenda grâce au MCP, puis confier une recherche spécialisée à un autre agent via A2A.
Faut-il savoir coder pour utiliser le MCP ?
Pas forcément, et c’est probablement le meilleur signe de sa maturation. Lorsqu’une intégration est déjà proposée dans un assistant, l’utilisateur peut ne jamais voir le moindre serveur MCP. Il choisit simplement un service, connecte son compte et valide les autorisations demandées. Toute la mécanique reste en coulisses.
Les outils locaux deviennent également plus accessibles. Claude Desktop permet, par exemple, d’installer certains serveurs sous forme d’extensions sans aller modifier manuellement des fichiers de configuration. Le terme « serveur MCP » ne signifie donc pas nécessairement qu’il faudra louer une machine ou ouvrir un terminal.
La difficulté remonte évidemment lorsque l’on veut connecter un logiciel interne, une base de données particulière ou un outil qui ne dispose d’aucune intégration prête à l’emploi. Il faut alors développer, héberger et maintenir le connecteur.
Dans une entreprise, l’utilisateur n’aura d’ailleurs pas toujours le dernier mot : les administrateurs peuvent décider quels services sont autorisés et avec quels droits.
Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini… Chacun son MCP
Le protocole MCP est commun, son utilisation beaucoup moins. Il faut surtout distinguer le modèle d’IA de l’application dans laquelle on s’en sert. Ce n’est pas parce qu’un éditeur prend en charge le MCP quelque part dans son écosystème que toutes ses applications donnent accès aux mêmes possibilités.
| Écosystème | Comment le MCP y est utilisé | 
| Anthropic / Claude | Claude utilise des connecteurs distants pour accéder à des services en ligne tandis que Claude Desktop peut recevoir des extensions locales. | 
| OpenAI / ChatGPT | Le MCP permet de connecter des outils et des services à ChatGPT avec des interfaces interactives directement dans la conversation pour certaines intégrations. | 
| Google / Gemini | Gemini CLI peut découvrir des outils MCP et consulter leurs ressources. Les possibilités varient ensuite selon les produits Google concernés. | 
| Microsoft / GitHub Copilot | Dans VS Code, des serveurs MCP peuvent apporter des outils, des ressources et des modèles de consignes à l’assistant. | 
| Mistral / Vibe (ex-Le Chat) | Des connecteurs MCP peuvent être configurés dans Studio puis réutilisés dans Vibe et d’autres applications de la plateforme. | 
L’abonnement, la version du logiciel ou, encore, les politiques de l’entreprise peuvent également limiter certaines fonctions. Un joli logo MCP ne garantit donc pas que tout sera disponible partout.
Mais attention, OpenAI et Google n’ont pas attendu le MCP pour relier leurs IA à des outils. Le premier proposait déjà le Function Calling, tandis que le second disposait notamment de connexions avec Workspace. Le protocole lancé par Anthropic apporte une manière commune de présenter ces outils aux assistants, sans remplacer tous les mécanismes existants. OpenAI et Google l’ont d’ailleurs adopté eux aussi. Un standard partagé ne suffit cependant pas à rendre toutes les intégrations interchangeables. Après tout, ça reste de l’informatique.
Plus d’outils, mais aussi davantage de tokens
Brancher une IA à plusieurs services ne coûte pas uniquement du temps de développement. Il faut aussi transmettre au modèle les informations nécessaires pour qu’il sache quels outils existent et comment les utiliser. Et qui dit informations supplémentaires dit souvent davantage de tokens, ces unités avec lesquelles les modèles traitent les données.
La description d’un outil, ses paramètres et les résultats qu’il retourne peuvent occuper une partie non négligeable du contexte. Ajoutez des dizaines de services et plusieurs gros documents, et la facture peut rapidement grimper lorsque le modèle est facturé à l’usage. Les réponses peuvent également ralentir.
Connecter vingt outils « au cas où » n’a donc rien d’une optimisation. Les systèmes les plus élaborés cherchent plutôt les fonctions au moment où elles deviennent nécessaires et filtrent les informations avant de les transmettre. Inutile, par exemple, de faire avaler un immense tableur au modèle lorsque quelques lignes contiennent toute l’information recherchée.
Autre nuance importante : le MCP est un protocole ouvert, mais les services auxquels il donne accès ne sont pas nécessairement gratuits. Selon la configuration, des frais peuvent concerner le logiciel connecté, ses API, l’hébergement ou le modèle d’IA.
Enfin, l’enchaînement des appels peut également allonger le temps d’exécution, surtout lorsque chaque étape attend le résultat de la précédente. Le délai dépend alors du modèle, des services sollicités et du réseau, pas du seul protocole MCP.
Qui met vraiment les mains dans vos données ?
C’est probablement la question la plus importante avant de connecter un assistant à un serveur MCP. Un connecteur peut venir directement de l’éditeur du service, avoir été développé par votre entreprise ou provenir d’un tiers inconnu. La mention « compatible MCP » indique seulement qu’il sait parler le protocole. Ce n’est pas un label de sécurité ni une garantie que son code a été audité.
Il faut ensuite regarder ce qu’on lui autorise à faire. Lire un agenda est une chose ; pouvoir effacer tous les rendez-vous en est une autre. Le principe reste le même qu’avec n’importe quelle application. Il faut limiter les permissions au strict nécessaire, privilégier la lecture seule lorsqu’elle suffit et conserver une validation humaine pour les opérations sensibles.
Un second danger vient des données elles-mêmes. Un document récupéré par l’assistant peut contenir des instructions conçues pour manipuler son comportement. C’est le principe de l’injection de prompt. Un fichier malveillant pourrait, par exemple, tenter de convaincre l’IA d’envoyer certaines des informations en sa possession vers l’extérieur. Les protections de l’assistant comptent donc autant que celles du connecteur.
Et attention à une dernière confusion : un serveur MCP installé sur votre ordinateur ne signifie pas automatiquement que vos données ne quittent jamais la machine. S’il lit un document local avant d’en envoyer le contenu à un modèle fonctionnant dans le cloud, l’information a bien voyagé dans le cloud.
Il faut regarder la chaîne dans son ensemble, de l’écosystème IA aux applis en passant par le MCP. Ce dernier organise les échanges. Il ne remplace pas les règles de confidentialité des services utilisés ni un bon réglage des autorisations.
Un protocole destiné à disparaître derrière les usages ?
Le plus révélateur est peut-être que le MCP dépasse désormais largement Anthropic. En décembre 2025, Anthropic a fait don du MCP à l’Agentic AI Foundation, créée avec OpenAI et Block sous l’égide de la Linux Foundation. Ce cadre neutre doit favoriser l’adoption du standard par des entreprises pourtant concurrentes. La direction technique du projet reste assurée par ses mainteneurs.
Ses ambitions commencent d’ailleurs à dépasser le simple appel d’outils. Avec MCP Apps, un service peut faire apparaître un formulaire, une carte ou un tableau interactif directement dans un assistant. La conversation ne se contente alors plus de renvoyer du texte. Elle devient elle-même une interface vers les logiciels connectés.
Le protocole dispose déjà de mécanismes pour les tâches longues et les notifications. Les prochaines évolutions doivent mieux articuler ces fonctions et encadrer les autorisations des agents, notamment lorsqu’une IA continue à travailler alors que vous n’êtes plus devant votre écran.
À terme, le meilleur signe de réussite du MCP sera peut-être que plus personne ne parle de MCP. Nous verrons simplement apparaître un bouton « connecter » avant de demander à notre assistant d’aller chercher un fichier, vérifier un agenda ou agir dans une application.
Dans le film Tron de 1982, il fallait vaincre le MCP pour reprendre le contrôle. Pour son homonyme de l’ère de l’IA, il vaudrait mieux que ce contrôle soit prévu dès le branchement.

articles.title: Sony pode gastar R$ 3,4 mil só com as memórias de cada PS6 • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Sony pode gastar R$ 3,4 mil só com as memórias de cada PS6
RAM e armazenamento NAND podem custar mais de US$ 680 por unidade. Alta nos preços dos chips deve pressionar o custo da próxima geração do console.
A memória RAM e os chips de armazenamento do PlayStation 6 podem custar à Sony mais de US$ 680, ou cerca de R$ 3.400 em conversão direta. A declaração veio de um informante conhecido como KeplerL2, que publica informações antecipadas sobre hardware da AMD.
Segundo a publicação no fórum NeoGAF, “apenas a memória RAM e o armazenamento NAND” devem custar esse valor. O rumor não traz informações sobre outros componentes necessários ao funcionamento do console, como o processador.
A postagem também não apresenta capacidades, fornecedores ou contratos. Por isso, o número permanece uma alegação sem confirmação da Sony. A empresa desenvolve a próxima geração do PlayStation, mas ainda não anunciou nada sobre preço ou data de lançamento. Os rumores sugerem um possível anúncio em 2028, mas até lá os valores dos componentes podem mudar.
Dados de mercado ajudam a ilustrar a situação. Em relatório recente, a consultoria de negócios TrendForce projetou novas altas de até 15% nos preços contratuais de chips DRAM no quarto trimestre de 2026, em comparação com o trimestre anterior. Para NAND flash, a previsão é de aumento entre 15% e 20%.
Segundo a consultoria, fabricantes continuam priorizando capacidade de produção para servidores, diante da forte demanda por infraestrutura de inteligência artificial. Esse cenário pressiona a oferta para outros segmentos, incluindo os consoles.
A possibilidade de um PS6 mais caro, na faixa dos US$ 1.000 (acima dos R$ 5 mil), também envolve a política comercial da própria Sony. Em reunião com investidores em junho, a empresa afirmou que não considera absorver os aumentos dos componentes e que não pretende vender hardware com prejuízos significativos.
Se o PS6 fosse lançado nos EUA por esse preço, o console poderia chegar ao Brasil superando os R$ 8 mil, considerando o efeito combinado de impostos, taxas e a relação entre os preços sugeridos atuais da linha PS5 nos dois países.
Como comparação, após o reajuste aplicado ao PS5 no Brasil em abril, os preços sugeridos passaram a R$ 4.599,90 para a Edição Digital, R$ 5.099,90 para o modelo com leitor e R$ 7.499,90 para o PS5 Pro.
Ainda assim, analistas citados pelo site VGC divergem sobre a possibilidade de a próxima geração do console ultrapassar os US$ 1.000. Esse patamar permanece uma projeção, sem confirmação oficial da Sony.

articles.title: Missão japonesa quer trazer amostras de uma lua de Marte à Terra
articles.text:
A agência espacial japonesa JAXA prepara a missão MMX para coletar material de Fobos, uma das luas de Marte, e trazê-lo à Terra. A análise das amostras poderá ajudar a esclarecer como os dois satélites do planeta vermelho se formaram há bilhões de anos.
O lançamento está previsto para 19 de outubro de 2026, com um foguete H3. A espaçonave deve chegar a Marte em agosto de 2027 e retornar à Terra em 2031, com uma cápsula destinada a pousar na Austrália.
Como a missão vai explorar Fobos
A MMX reúne três módulos principais — propulsão, exploração e retorno — e transporta o rover IDEFIX, desenvolvido em parceria pelas agências espaciais da França e da Alemanha.
Nos primeiros meses em Marte, a nave vai observar Fobos de diferentes altitudes para mapear o terreno e escolher locais de pouso. O rover deve ser liberado entre o fim de 2028 e o início de 2029, durante um dos ensaios de descida. Devido à baixa gravidade da lua, ele poderá cair até a superfície e se estabilizar após alguns saltos.
A coleta de material poderá começar em dezembro de 2028. A missão prevê duas tentativas de pouso, com a meta de recolher pelo menos 10 gramas de amostras. Para investigar a superfície, a MMX levará instrumentos com funções complementares:
- TENGOO e OROCHI: câmeras que vão registrar o relevo e as características da superfície.
- MIRS: espectrômetro que identificará minerais e procurará compostos orgânicos.
- MEGANE: instrumento desenvolvido com participação da NASA para medir a composição química de Fobos.
- RAX e miniRAD: equipamentos do rover que analisarão minerais e propriedades térmicas do terreno.
Depois de cerca de três anos dedicados a Fobos, a nave fará sobrevoos de Deimos em 2030 para comparar dados das duas luas. No fim daquele ano, o módulo de retorno iniciará a viagem à Terra. A cápsula com as amostras deverá pousar de paraquedas na região de Woomera, na Austrália, em 2031.
O que as amostras podem revelar
A origem de Fobos e Deimos ainda é um mistério. Uma hipótese sustenta que as duas luas são asteroides capturados pela gravidade de Marte. Outra propõe que elas se formaram a partir de fragmentos lançados à órbita após uma grande colisão com o planeta, em um processo que lembra uma das teorias sobre a formação da Lua terrestre.
As evidências disponíveis apontam para direções diferentes. As superfícies das luas apresentam semelhanças com asteroides primitivos, enquanto suas órbitas quase circulares levantam questões sobre a hipótese de captura.
“É uma questão intrigante porque duas linhas de evidência apontam em direções diferentes”, afirmou Tom Statler, cientista da divisão de ciência planetária da NASA envolvido na missão.
A composição química poderá ajudar a distinguir os cenários. A presença de determinados elementos voláteis pode favorecer a hipótese de captura de asteroides. Já sinais de alterações provocadas por temperaturas extremas seriam compatíveis com a formação após uma colisão.
“Até o momento, não sabemos nada sobre a composição de Fobos”, afirmou David Lawrence, responsável pelo instrumento MEGANE. Embora os cientistas tenham informações sobre a mineralogia da lua, ainda faltam dados sobre seus elementos químicos.
Parceria internacional
Liderada pela JAXA, a MMX conta com contribuições da NASA e da Agência Espacial Europeia (ESA), que participam com instrumentos, equipamentos e apoio às comunicações.
A NASA investiu aproximadamente US$ 87 milhões até o fim da missão e deverá receber pelo menos 15% das amostras. O material será preservado no Centro Espacial Johnson, nos Estados Unidos, para análises laboratoriais.
O estudo detalhado dos minerais, dos elementos químicos e dos isótopos poderá ajudar a determinar a origem do material coletado. Com isso, a MMX poderá esclarecer como as luas marcianas se formaram e revelar aspectos da história de Marte e do Sistema Solar.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: There’s a hidden bias affecting what we know – and don’t know – about nature
articles.text:
Our knowledge about life on Earth is built through research on how organisms function, evolve and interact with each another and the environment. Yet there are far more species on our planet than scientists can study in detail.
So how should scientists decide which species to focus on? Fairly representing all species seems like a useful approach. It’s like predicting an election result: we can’t interview every citizen, so we need a sample that truly represents the overall population.
What drives scientists to uncover nature’s mysteries is curiosity. So, the organisms chosen for research are determined by what makes scientists most curious. And that’s causing a problem with fair representation.
In our new research, we examined research in ecology and evolution (an umbrella term for biological sciences outside biomedicine) to understand which animals are most studied and why.
Our results suggest emotion plays a bigger role in research choices than scientists usually admit.
Which animals are studied?
Our world is mostly filled with invertebrates: creatures such as bugs, spiders, worms and slugs. Vertebrates (amphibians, birds, fish, mammals and reptiles) make up only 5% of all animal species on Earth. So, if scientists want to represent animals fairly in their work, most research should be on invertebrates.
To understand how scientists’ time is spent researching the diversity of animals, we analysed almost 1.4 million scientific articles from more than 600 journals. Unsurprisingly, we found that more than half of these articles focused on vertebrates, demonstrating a huge bias in what scientists prefer to study.
Our results also demonstrate things haven’t improved in over two decades (when this bias was first discovered), and in some cases have gotten worse. For example, the focus on fish in marine and freshwater biology research increased from 35.8% of articles in 2001 to 49.7% in 2025. This was all at the expense of the largest group of marine creatures, aquatic invertebrates such as molluscs, crustaceans, corals and more.
The bias we found was compounded by social media and news coverage, where popular animal groups attracted more attention from other scientists and the general public. Many scientists are therefore no different to everyone else in which animals they deem interesting or important.
Why does this happen?
Although many factors determine which research organisms scientists might select, emotions do play a significant role. Using an online survey, we asked 868 animal behaviour researchers about their experiences and preferences.
We found that popular groups in animal behaviour research, such as birds and mammals, were regarded more favourably than others, especially arachnids (such as spiders).
This is perhaps unsurprising as perceptions of animals are shaped early in childhood. Ingrained societal values – such as which animals are cute – tend to persist by the time someone becomes a scientist.
Fortunately, we found that familiarity breeds admiration. Participants that worked with a certain animal group tended to view that group more positively after their experience. In other words, they tried it and liked it.
Does it matter?
Studying the saliva of the Gila monster (a lizard) in the 1980s paved the way for recently developed weight loss drugs such as Ozempic. Research on snake, spider and scorpion toxins is being used for new pain-relieving drugs. The discovery of green fluorescent proteins from bioluminescent jellyfish in the 1960s led to the 2008 Nobel Prize because it sparked a scientific revolution by making it possible to tag individual cells.
These examples show that scientific advancement often requires serendipity and time. It disregards whether the organisms involved are charismatic. Creatures commonly seen as ugly, disgusting, or dangerous (which they rarely are) can be as, if not more, useful for society as fluffy, pretty animals.
Our work indicates that society’s negative perceptions of certain organisms, which are often rooted in disconnection from nature and misinformation, are shared by the very scientists responsible for understanding biological processes and patterns. Understanding scientists’ choices matters because these decisions shape the direction of scientific progress.
We urgently need to shift our perception of animals because human-made effects are accelerating biodiversity losses. For example, insects are declining at unprecedented rates, but we know little (if anything) about most insect species. Many haven’t even been described and may go extinct before we even know they existed. This means we’ll lose not just the benefits they bring to ecosystems, but any benefits they may have held for humanity.
What can we do?
There is hope. Our research shows that when people spend more time with the “ugly” and “scary” animals, they often appreciate them more. Once people realise that all organisms (even spiders) play a vital part in ecosystems, it becomes a lot easier to give these overlooked creatures the attention they deserve.
Organisations like Invertebrates Australia and many social media influencers are already helping by showing just how fascinating and important invertebrates really are.
But we still need more support to reduce research biases, especially from governments and universities. They can make a huge difference by funding research on never-before studied species and neglected animal groups.
If nothing changes, we risk slowing progress because we’re drawn to what looks cute. Next time an animal video pops up on your feed, try sharing something beyond the fluffy favourites. The less glamorous species are just as essential and just as worthy of our curiosity.

articles.title: US Cybersecurity Job Postings Fall 26% as AI Security Engineer Demand Soars
articles.text:
CyberSN’s Cybersecurity Jobs Report provides visibility into the US cybersecurity job market. It’s a mixed bag.
Data for CyberSN’s jobs report is aggregated from JobSpikr (with duplicates removed). The various job titles are then analyzed and assigned to CyberSN’s taxonomy of 45 cybersecurity functional roles in ten categories. The result is an assessment of the job market by skills required rather than by the recruiting companies’ role titles.
Analyzing this dataset shows the current cybersecurity skills demand. Comparing 2026 with the same months of earlier years highlights emerging (or declining) demand for specific roles.
Overall, there has been a decline in cybersecurity job postings to a new four-year low: 235,786 postings between January and September 2026 (down 26.4% from the 320,210 recorded in the same period of 2025).
While the total number of job postings has declined, there remain emerging and notable specific numbers. For example, two specific AI and data roles have seen dramatic growth: AI Security Engineer demand has increased by 268.3% while Cyber Data Scientist demand has grown 203.5% over last year.
Clearly, the need for a general understanding of artificial intelligence remains high. Just under 15% of all job postings now reference AI, which is comparable to the 15.1% recorded in the same period last year. There is, however, a noticeable increase in momentum within the current period (peaking at 20.0% in September 2026).
The cybersecurity functions that most reference a need for AI understanding include Research (32.7% of postings, up 11.7 points from last year); Offense (23.3% of postings, up 4.8 points); GRC (19.8% of postings, up 2.1 points); and Plan (18.9% of postings, up 0.6 points).
Remote working is another area of interest. The top functional areas include Sales (32.8%), GRC (31.2%), Offense (24.7%), Product Security (22.9%), Educate (22.8%), Research (21.9%), and Defense (21.3%).
While there are some potential winners in this analyzed period, the overall decline in numbers means there are more potential losers. Leading the loss of roles is Cyber Insider Threat Analyst (down by 55.6% to 1,088 postings); Cyber Risk Analyst (down by 51.5% to 4,031 postings); Penetration Tester (down by 45.9% to 3,063 postings); Cybersecurity Lead (down by 41.0% to 4,688 postings); Threat Hunter (down by 40.0% to 1,013 postings); Cybersecurity Project Manager (down by 39.4% to 783 postings); and Chief Information Security Officer including CSO, BSO and ISO (down by 38.9% to 2,832 postings).
Much of the CISO decline reflects an unusually strong 2025, since the 2026 figure (2,832) is almost exactly the same as 2024’s (2,808), and CISO postings rose 19.5% from Q2 to Q3.
The report focuses on the numbers of job listings rather than any specific intent to understand the cause of any change. This is a ‘what’ not ‘why’ report. “Job titles are noisy,” it declares. “This report reads every posting through the CyberSN Taxonomy, so demand is counted by the work being asked for, not by the title on the listing.”
Nevertheless, a few possible indications around the more commonly recognized job titles can be found. For example, for leadership and CISO positions, the report comments, “director and CISO postings move with how boards are treating cyber accountability.”
Overall, it is difficult to draw specific employment potential indications from CyberSN’s figures on job listings, but an AI security specialist may be in luck. Budding CISOs may need to be patient.

articles.title: À 43 990 €, le Volkswagen ID. Tiguan premier prix est bien équipé, mais fait un gros compromis
articles.text:
Par rapport à l’ID.4, le Volkswagen ID. Tiguan a franchement belle gueule. Qu’on le contemple en version R Line ou Style, il présente un petit côté bon chic bon genre que ne connaissait pas l’ID.4. Le retour aux sources est acté. Et imminent, car la marque allemande vient d’ouvrir le carnet de commandes du SUV électrique. Avec un prix de départ fixé à 43 990 €, l’ID. Tiguan attaque particulièrement haut face aux concurrents chinois.
Sa présentation prend pourtant un sacré coup puisqu’en version de base Trend, la voiture électrique abandonne ses très jolies jantes en alliage de 21 pouces pour des jantes en tôles de 19 pouces recouvertes d’enjoliveurs noirs. L’éclairage avant perd aussi la fonction matricielle à LED et le bandeau lumineux avec le logo rétroéclairé pour une disposition plus traditionnelle. La couleur de série est le gris. Pas très gai. En contrepartie, l’équipement satisfait.
Écran 15 pouces et régulateur adaptatif : que reste-t-il de série à ce prix ?
Comptons ainsi en série l’écran tactile de 15 pouces, la caméra de recul, l’assistant vocal, la climatisation automatique bizone, les feux de route automatiques, le régulateur de vitesse adaptatif, le rétroviseur électrochrome, le démarrage mains-libres et l’éclairage d’ambiance à 10 couleurs. La version intermédiaire Life à 45 290 € ajoute la climatisation automatique trizone, le chargeur de smartphone par induction et les sièges avant chauffants.
L’accès et démarrage mains-libres s’invite aussi sur la liste des équipements, au même titre que la navigation et le volant chauffant. Notons que les finitions Trend et Life sont disponibles avec la batterie de 58 kWh offrant 454 km d’autonomie. Ce n’est pas le cas de la version haute Style, qui impose directement le pack de 77 kWh débouchant sur un rayon d’action de 603 km. Mieux pour la polyvalence, pour sûr, mais le prix assomme, avec une marche à 52 100 €.
Version 4×4 et modèle 700 km : jusqu’où les prix vont-ils s’envoler ?
La dotation suit, avec en bonus le hayon motorisé mains-libres, l’éclairage d’ambiance à 30 couleurs, les feux arrière en trois dimensions avec clignotants à défilement, les feux avant Matrix LED avec le logo Volkswagen rétroéclairé, les jantes en alliage de 19 pouces et le pare-brise dégivrant. Ajoutons qu’une version quatre roues motrices avec deux blocs électriques développant en cumulé 299 ch est aussi proposée sur les versions Life et Style.
Les tarifs attaquent alors respectivement à 49 650 et 54 760 € alors que l’autonomie chute à 567 km. La Life en batterie de 77 kWh, pour sa part, débute à 46 990 €. Un prix mûrement réfléchi permettant de prétendre aux aides de l’État, qui restent cependant à valider. Ajoutons pour finir que Volkswagen promet une version avec 700 km d’autonomie qui arrivera ultérieurement. Alléchant, même si le tarif atteindra des sommets.

articles.title: Nouvelle Switch 2 européenne : l'écran Sharp espéré n'est pas au rendez-vous, selon un démontage — Frandroid
articles.text:
Le technicien polonais modyfikatorcasper a démonté la nouvelle Switch 2 vendue en Europe. C’est la version dont la batterie se remplace sans décoller de colle. Ses photos ont été relayées le 18 octobre par Notebookcheck. Elles montrent la même dalle LCD que sur la console portable sortie en juin 2025. Certains joueurs espéraient que cette révision corrige la rémanence de l’écran, ces traînées qui suivent les objets en mouvement. Ce ne sera pas le cas.
Fin juin, le compte Nintendo Patents Watch, qui épluche les brevets et les pièces détachées de la marque, a repéré sur un site de revente chinois une dalle de Switch 2 inconnue, référencée LS079T1SX10P. D’après cette référence, il s’agirait d’un écran LCD de 7,9 pouces en 1080p, assemblé par Sharp. Il utiliserait la technologie LTPS, courante sur les dalles de smartphones.
Sa taille et sa définition sont celles de l’écran actuel. Par contre, le circuit, le connecteur et les câbles à l’arrière de la dalle sont nettement différents. Pour comparer, le panneau d’origine est assemblé par Innolux, à partir d’une plaque de verre déjà fabriquée par Sharp.
Ce nouveau circuit a fait naître un espoir. Depuis sa sortie, on reproche à l’écran de la Switch 2 son temps de réponse, c’est-à-dire le temps que met un pixel à changer de couleur. Quand il est trop lent, l’image laisse des traînées dans les jeux rapides. Rien ne prouvait que la dalle Sharp règle ce défaut. Mais avec son circuit modifié, on pouvait espérer des pixels plus rapides.
Une carte mère renommée autour de la même puce Nvidia
Le technicien a aussi comparé la carte mère du modèle révisé, baptisée OSM-CPU-01, avec la BEE-CPU-01 d’origine. Le SoC Nvidia, la puce qui regroupe le processeur et la partie graphique, n’a pas changé. La console garde aussi ses 12 Go de mémoire vive, fournis cette fois par un autre fabricant. Nintendo a aussi changé le ventilateur.
Nintendo n’avait rien promis de plus. Sur sa page d’assistance consacrée à ces révisions, la marque écrit qu’il n’y a « aucune différence de fonctionnalité » entre les modèles actuels et ceux à batterie remplaçable. Elle annonce seulement une batterie environ 1 % plus petite et une console 14 grammes plus lourde avec ses manettes.
Une dalle Sharp toujours sans console
Il faut quand même préciser qu’un seul exemplaire a été ouvert. C’est pour cela que Videocardz, qui a relayé les mêmes photos, écrit que le modèle révisé ne contient « pas nécessairement » la dalle Sharp.
Depuis la fuite de juin, des vendeurs chinois ont aussi mis en vente une pièce proche, étiquetée LS0DAS7081 et V2, en plus grande quantité. On ne sait toujours pas dans quelle console Nintendo compte la monter.
La Switch 2 révisée arrive peu à peu dans les pays européens, France comprise. Nintendo a jusqu’au 18 février 2027 pour la déployer, puisqu’à partir de cette date le règlement européen sur les batteries impose que l’utilisateur puisse remplacer lui-même la batterie des appareils portables. En magasin, on la reconnaît au code OSM imprimé sur la boîte.
